videos.title: Giacomo Fogliano: L Amor donna chio te porto (c.1500) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Giacomo Fogliano: L Amor donna chio te porto (c.1500) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
L'amor donna chio te porto

   0:06 Instrumental arrangement: cornetto, 3 sackbuts, lute, percussion
   0:38 Verse 1: ATTB choir with lute, percussion
   1:10 Verse 2: Male alto with viols, percussion
   1:43 Verse 3: ATTB with recorder, lute, percussion
   2:15 Verse 4: Male alto with lute, percussion
   2:48 Reprise: ATTB with instruments
--------------------

This Italian frottola appears in at least two different sources and was likely a very popular song in early 16th century Europe:

El Cancionero Musical de Palacio, a huge collection of songs (both secular and sacred from various nations) was compiled for musicians at the court of the Catholic kings, Ferdinand and Isabel of Spain. 

Frottole Libro VII (1507), from Petrucci's neatly typeset anthology of Italian secular songs was published in the brand new printing presses of Venice.

As was typical of Italian and Spanish secular music at that time, this song is homophonic in structure and has a catchy melody line. The lyrics express the grief of a courtly lover who quietly suffers from unrequited love. The rhythm consists mainly of hemiolas alternating between 6/4 and 3/2 time. I added the tambourine line to highlight the irregular rhythm. The rhythm, theme and structure are very similar to another frottola copied in the Cancionero de Palacio, titled "Guarda, donna, el mio tormento." (see my video https://youtu.be/n42aqXhhWMo ).

In this latest rendering, I used the Synthesizer V program with only the Kevin voice bank singing the 4 lines of music -- each with distinctive voice qualities. The instrumental simulation was created with Music Studio 2 (an iPhone app). I added minor sound adjustments, reverb and echo using Audacity v.3.75. The text underlay is mostly my own with insights from the MIDI file compiled by  Fernando Gómez Jácome.

Original text:

L'amor, donna, ch'io te porto
Volentier voria scoprire,
El mio affanno voria dire
Che per te pena suporto.
L'amor, dona, ch'io te porto
Volentier voria scoprire.

Io non so come ti posa
Descoprir l'ardente foco
Che me bruza fino al ossa
E non vede tempo e loco;
E che, haime, bruzo in focho
Senza aver alcun conforto.

Non me fido a mandar meso,
Per che temo esser gabato;
S'io te passo per apreso
Tu te volti in altro lato;
Chiusi son piu giorni stato
E son anche a pegior porto.

Haime lasso chio son giunto
che non posso il mio amore dire
a chi mha ferito e punto
ma tacendo vo soffrire
me convien del mio servire
questo merto io ne porto

Translation

The love, my lady, that I have for you
I want to willfully reveal;
I want to tell of my sorrow
that for you I endure pain.
 
I know not how to
reveal to you the intense fire
that burns to the bones.
Not noticing the time and place,
the fire rages alas
without any reprieve.

I dare not send a message to you
on account of the fear to be mocked,
for if I come close,
you turn at once the other way.
[But] When I stay shut away for days,
I carry an even worse [burden].

Alas weary I have become
that I cannot say to my beloved
me whom she has hurt and stung.
But silently I want to suffer
It suits me to serve
this honor that I bear

--------------------

videos.title: Orlando di Lasso (Lassus): Omnes de Saba a 8 (c.1585)

localized.title: Orlando di Lasso (Lassus): Omnes de Saba a 8 (c.1585)
localized.description:
This work for 8 voice double choir brings to mind the polychoral motets of Giovanni Gabrieli in Venice and, later, Michael Praetorius in Thuringia. The back and forth between the evenly paired SATB choirs is typical of a genre popular among church composers of Lassus' generation. This particular work was published posthumously by his sons and dedicated to the Duke of Bavaria, Maximilian I. It was intended for use in the ceremony of the Epiphany (or the Visitation of the Magi) from the Christmas story of Luke's Gospel. 

I added the text using Synthesizer V with Solaria for the two soprano (cantus) lines and Kevin for the six ATB parts. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity v3.75. The original MIDI file was compiled by Pothárn Imre and can be found at cpdl.org.

Text:

Omnes de Saba venient,
aurum et thus deferentes,
et laudem Domino annuntiantes.
Alleluia. (Isaiah 60:6)

Reges Tharsis et insulae munera offerent,
reges Arabum et Saba dona adducent.
Alleluia. (Psalm 71:10)

Translation:

All from Sheba shall come,
bearing gold and frankincense,
and announcing praise to the Lord.
Alleluia.

The kings of Tharsis and the islands shall offer gifts ,
the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents.
Alleluia.

videos.title: Claude Janequin: Hellas mon Dieu (c.1545) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Claude Janequin: Hellas mon Dieu (c.1545) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Hellas mon Dieu ton ire

   0:06  Original chanson for 4 voices
   2:16  Lute setting by Antonio Rotta
   5:09  Instrumental setting (for flute, lute, harp, viol)

This delicate and somewhat existential chanson by Janequin comes from the "16ieme Livre des Chansons" (16th Book of Songs, 1545) of Pierre Attaingnant's multi-volume series of secular music. Although penitential in tone, this piece is likely a courtly love song. It is sequestered among other French Renaissance music about chivalric romance and unrequited love fashionable at the Valois court. 

I produced this soundtrack using the Synthesizer V program with the Solaria and Kevin voice banks. The original MIDI file for this piece was compiled by Brian Russell and uploaded to the website CPDL.org. I transposed Russell's transcription down by a minor third into the range of Attaingnant's 1545 publication. The lute setting was transcribed by Serge Gerbode and can be found on lutemusic.org. Reverb, echo and de-essing were achieved using Audacity 3.75. 

----------

Text and translation:

Hellas, mon Dieu, ton ire s’est tournée
Vers moi, ton serf, qui me poursuit sans cesse.
La peur que j’ay faict que l’âme estonnée
Donne à mon cueur une extrême destresse.
Le sens me fault et vertu me délaisse
Tousjours estant douleur devant mes yeulx.
Je te réclame et appelle en tous lieux
Pour mettre fin à l’ennuy qui me poingt.
Si tu ne veult, hellas, m’envoyer myeulx
Au moins, mon Dieu, ne m’abandonne point.

Alas, my God, your anger that is turned
against me, your servant, continues without end.
The fear that I have that astonished the soul
Gives my heart extreme distress.
My sense fails me and virtue forsakes me.
Always there is pain before my eyes.
I desire you and call for you everywhere.
To put an end to the annoyance which assaults me.
If you don't wish, alas to deliver me to a better [situation]
At least, my God, don't abandon me.

----------

videos.title: Andrea Gabrieli: Emendemus in melius (c.1585) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Andrea Gabrieli: Emendemus in melius (c.1585) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
The Venetian choir master Andrea Gabrieli was a protégé of his predecessor Adrian Willaert and uncle to one of the greatest of all Italian Renaissance composers, Giovanni Gabrieli. This motet for 6 voices is an a cappella work and a responsory for the Lent season. It memorializes the temptation of Christ in the desert and was intended for performance in St. Mark's Basilica in Venice.

Both Gabrielis made their mark on Western music with their increasingly more complex polyphonic works that included up to 16 independent parts for voices, double (and triple) choirs and instruments. This two-part motet is a relatively simple piece with mostly homophonic passages, frequently repeated passages and easily understood text - probably in response to the dictates of the Council of Trent.

This recording was created using the Synthesizer voice encoder with the Solaria (for boy soprano) and Kevin (for male altos, tenors and bass) voice banks. Reverb, echo and de-essing were added with Audacity. The original MIDI was created by Allen Garvin and uploaded to CPDL.org .

Text:

Emendemus in melius quae ignoranter peccavimus;
ne subito praeoccupati die mortis,
quaeramus spatium poenitentiae, et invenire non possimus.
Attende, Domine, et miserere; quia peccavimus tibi.

Translation:

Let us make amends for the better for we have sinned in ignorance;
not to be suddenly overtaken by the day of death,
We want a space for penitence, but we cannot go there [on our own].
Be present, Lord, and have mercy for we have sinned against you.

videos.title: Barbara Strozzi: Ferma il piede (1664)

localized.title: Barbara Strozzi: Ferma il piede (1664)
localized.description:
This song of forlorn love is the work of Barbara Strozzi (1619-1677), a singer and songwriter of the early Baroque period in Venice. Her Opus 8 collection, which includes this operatic tune, was dedicated to the Princess Sophia, Electress of Hannover. 

Text:

Ferma il piede, o traditore, non t'avvedi (Stay put, O traitor. You do not see)
ch'al miei danni tess'inganni (that you are plotting deceitfully to destroy me)
per traffiger il mio core, (and to pierce my heart?)
ferma'il piede, o traditore. (Stay put, O traitor)

negl'avori di quel seno (In the ivories [?} of that bosom)
sta la gioia del mio affetto, (lies the joy of my affection)
set'accosti in un baleno, (If you get close in a flash)
tu mi rubbi il cor dal petto, (you will steal my heart from my chest.)
dunque troppo m'offendi (Thus, you offend me so)
se qual Ape pretendi (if like a bee, you pretend)
per mio mal di succhiar il mio bel fiore. (to suck my flower, to my ruin)

Ferma'il piede, o traditore, (Stay put, O traitor)
ma se tenti la bocca (but if you try with your mouth)
cerch'insieme 'l tuo perire, (will find peril)
poi ch'il ciel fulmini scoccha, (the lightning from the sky will strike)
ferma il piede, o traditore, (Stay put, O traitor)
contr'ognun, ch'usa tradire (against anyone who uses betrayal)
e piu fieri gl'aventa contr'ogni cor, (avenges fiercest against every heart)
che tenta d'ingannar (that tries to deceive)
chi è legato in man d'Amore. (one who is bound in the hands of Love)

videos.title: Clément Janequin: Tresves damours (1536) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Clément Janequin: Tresves damours (1536) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Tresves d'amours

  0:06  four-part vocal with lute doubling
  1:36 instrumental setting (4 viols, harpsichord)
  
This short chanson is yet another little treasure from the archives of Pierre Attaingnant who expended great effort publishing throughout his printing career the large corpus of secular chansons by Clément Janequin. It is a somewhat existential love song without any concrete target of affection.

For this latest rendition, I used the Kevin voice bank and the Synthesizer V software. The instrumental sounds were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2. The original MIDI file without the words was compiled by André Vierendeels and can be found on CPDL.org. Reverb, echo and de-essing were added using Audacity v.3.75.

----------

Text:

Tresves damours,
cest une paix fourree,
sans fermete et sans foy asseuree.
Contre leffort de felone rigueur,
contre mercy plus forte
est la viguer de bien aymer,
c'est donc force forcee.

The truce of love
That is a loaded peace
without stability and guarantee.
Against the effort of the traitor
against very strong reward
there is the power to love well
that is therefore forced force

----------

1-3. "Tresves d'amour," cantus part, C. Janequin, Livre 1er, P. Attaingnant, 1536

videos.title: Francesca Caccini: Chi desia di saper (1618)

localized.title: Francesca Caccini: Chi desia di saper (1618)
localized.description:
Francesca Caccini is the earliest known female composer of Italian opera. Even for non-operatic repertoire, she wrote mostly monodies for solo voice and bass continuo. This particular canzonetta for soprano was written for a vocalist and Spanish guitar. The bass line was likely a figured bass part that was left as a single line of music in the printed edition of 1618.  

The soundtrack was created using Solaria with mostly Spanish phonemes in Synthesizer V. I used a chord progression written out by Daniel McGann. I generated the sound of a recorder, chitarrone and violone using Music Studio 2.0. 

Text:

Chi desia di saper, che cosa e’ Amore
io diro’, che non sia se non ardore
che non sia se non dolore,
che non sia se non timore,
che non sia sen non furore
Io diro’ che non sia se non ardore,
chi desia di saper che cosa e’ amore

Chi mi domanderà s'amor io sento,
Io dirò che'l mio foco è tutto spento.
Ch'io non prouo più tormento,*
Ch'io non tremo, nè pauento,
Ch'io ne vivo ogn'or contento,
Io dirò che'l mio foco è tutto spento
Chi mi domanderà s'amor’ io sento.

Chi mi consiglierà ch'io debb' amare
Io dirò che non vo' più sospirare,
Ne temere, nè sperare,
Ne auuampare, nè gelare, **
Ne languire, nè penare.
Io dirò che non vo' più sospirare
Chi mi consiglierà ch'io debb' amare.

Chi d'amor crederrà dolce il gioire
Io dirò che più dolce è amor fuggire
Ne piagarsi al suo desire,
Ne tentar suoi sdegni & ire
Ne provare il suo martire.
Io dirò che più dolce è amor fuggire
Chi d'amor crederrà dolce il gioire.

Translation:

To one who desires to know what love is
I will say that it is none other than burning,
that it is none other than pain,
non other than fear,
non other than fury!
I will say that it is none other than burning,
to whomsoever desires to know what love is.

To one who will ask if I feel love
I will say that my fire is burned out,
That I no longer experience torment,
I no longer tremble, no longer fear,
never live happily.
I will say that my fire is burned out,
to whomsoever asks if I feel love.

To one who counsels me that I should love
I will say I no longer want to sigh,
to tremble, to hope,
to burn up, to freeze,
to languish, nor to feel pain.
I will say I no longer want to sigh,
to whomsoever counsels me to love.

To one who will believe that love brings joy
I will say that the sweeter love is, flee,
do not give in to its desire,
nor tempt its disdain and anger,
nor attempt martyrdom.
I will say that the sweeter love is, flee,
To whomsoever will believe that love brings joy.

videos.title: Clemens non Papa: O Maria vernans rosa (1554)

localized.title: Clemens non Papa: O Maria vernans rosa (1554)
localized.description:
This motet for 5 voices in two parts is one of several devotional works by the Netherlander Jacobus Clemens non Papa. It was likely created during his tenure as singer and composer for the Illustrious Brotherhood of Our Blessed Lady in 's-Hertogenbosch at the Cathedral of Saint John’s (Sint Jans). The Cathedral's central icon is a medieval statue of the Virgin Mary and Baby Jesus which had been worshipped for centuries as an object bearing miraculous properties.

The motet contains many of the established polyphonic structures of early Renaissance music from the Franco-Flemish repertoire as developed decades earlier by Josquin des Prez and Jean Mouton. It also contains somewhat darker sonorities in the very long Amen section with minor shifts in mode through the insertion of musica ficta.

The vocal lines were generated using the Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V relying mostly on Spanish phonemes and a few English to simulate a Latin with Franco-Flemish undertones. The MIDI file and recommendations for text underlay were created by Adrian Wall and can be downloaded from the site CPDL.org.

Text (and translation):

O Maria, vernans rosa, (O Maria, rose of Spring)
Porta coeli speciosa, (beautiful gate into Heaven)
Clarior sideribus, (brighter than the stars)
Me guberna, me supporta, (direct and support me)
Me defende, me conforta (defend and comfort me)
Ne vincar ab hostibus. (so that I am not defeated by the hoards)

Tu lux pulchra, tu medela, (You fair light, you healing)
Tu pax vera, tu tutela, (you true peace, you protection)
Inimici frange tela (Destroy the enemies' weapons)
Succurre cadentibus. (Help those who have fallen)

Amen.

videos.title: Carlo Pallavicino: Dormite o pupille from "Il Nerone" (1678)

localized.title: Carlo Pallavicino: Dormite o pupille from "Il Nerone" (1678)
localized.description:
Dormite O pupille

  0:06  Instrumental setting (violin, chitarrone, bass violin, violone)
  1:25  Verse 1 (soprano, chitarrone, bass viol, violone)
  2:40  Verse 2 (soprano, chitarrone, bass viol, violone)

This short aria from a Baroque musical drama titled "Il Nerone" is loosely based on the historical character, the Emperor Nero. The composition by Carlo Pallavicino is an interlude at the beginning of Act III by a ephemeral, mythical creature, Endimione. One might appreciate the occasional use of passing dissonances to express the feeling of lamentation. The aria has been often misattributed to another Venetian opera composer, Pietro Andrea Ziani. 

The vocal line is "sung" by the Solaria voice bank in Synthesizer V using mostly Spanish language phonemes. The instrumental simulations (chitarrone, viola da gamba, violone and violin) were generated using the iPhone app, Music Studio 2.0. I reconstructed the figured bass line using both a facsimile of the original score and Felipe Dias’ modern edition (Early Music Scores). I adapted the MIDI from an arrangement by an anonymous editor at Musescore.com.

Text

Dormite o pupille (Sleep O pupils)
Fra taciti orrori (in the midst of quiet horrors)
Né deste v’aprite (Do not wake yourselves up)
Se voi non sentite (If you do not hear)
Che giung’a svegliarvi (who comes to wake you up)
Il nume de’ cori (the spirit of the chorus)
Dormite dormite (Sleep, sleep)
Dormite o pupille (Sleep O pupils)
Fra taciti orrori. (in the midst of quiet horrors)

Sognate o pensieri (Dream O thoughts)
Sognate sognate (Dream, dream)
Il ben per cui moro (The good for which I die)
Godrò pur felice ((I will enjoy happily)
Già ch’altro non lice (Since nothing else is permitted)
Tra l’ombre del sonno (Within the shadows of sleep)
Il sole che adoro (The sun, which I adore)
Sognate sognate (Dream, dream)
Sognate o pensieri (Dream, o thoughts)
Il ben per cui moro. (The good for which I die)

videos.title: Ludwig Senfl: Ach Elslein, liebes Elselein mein (c.1525), 2 settings with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Ludwig Senfl: Ach Elslein, liebes Elselein mein (c.1525), 2 settings with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Ach Elslein liebstes Elselein mein

  0:06  Verse 1 of the original Lied (SATB)
  0:53  Verse 2 (SATB, 4 viols, clavichord)
  1:39  Verse 3 (SATB, recorder, viols)
  2:27  Lied with quodlibet for 6 voices (ATT, cornetto, 2 sackbuts)

The love song "Ach Elslein" was a popular tune that appeared repeatedly in German Renaissance music with at least 10 different parody settings (3 by Senfl). The first setting is arranged for an a cappella quartet (ATTB) and the second for 6 performers (ATT voices + 3 instrumental lines). In verse 2 of the first setting, I superimposed Newsidler's lute parody with minimal changes in the ficta. The 6 part Elslein is a combinative lied with three independent melody lines containing three different texts based on two of Senfl’s best known songs, “Ach Elslein” and “Es taget vor dem Walde,” as well as a lesser known piece from an unknown source “Wenn ich des Morgens früh aufsteh.” These 3 tunes are woven together with 3 additional untexted lines in an intricate web of polyphonic counterpoint reminiscent of the Franco-Flemish masters of an earlier repertoire. The earliest sources for this popular folk melody include at least two German manuscripts from the late 15th century.

The vocal simulations were created with Synthesizer V using Spanish and English phoneme sets with the Solaria and Kevin voice banks  Reverb, echo and de-essing were added with Audacity. The instrumental parts (viol, keyboard and trombone parts) were created with Music Studio 2. The original MIDI for the 4 part piece comes from Brian Russell on CPDL.org and the 6 part quodlibet comes from Ulrich Alpers on IMSLP.org . The lute setting was transcribed by Serge Gerbode and can be found on his website lutemusic.com .

++++++++++

German text:

Ach Elslein, liebstes Elselein mein,
Wie gern wär ich bei dir!
So sein zwei tiefe Wasser
Wohl zwischen dir und mir,
So sein zwei tiefe Wasser
Wohl zwischen dir und mir

Das bringt mir grosse Schmerzen,
Herzallerliebster Gsell!
Und ich von ganzem Herzen
Halt's für gross Ungefäll,
Und ich von ganzem Herzen
Halt's für groß Ungefäll

Hoff, Zeit wird es wohl enden,
Hoff, Glück wird kommen drein,
Sich in all's Güts verwenden,
Herzliebstes Elselein,
Sich in all's Güts verwenden,
Herzliebstes Elselein.

how I wish I were beside you
but two deep (bodies of) water
stand between you and me

It brings me great pain

And I, in my heart,
See in it great misfortune

Dearest sweetheart, little Elsa

videos.title: Claudio Monteverdi: Pur ti miro (from "L'Incoronazione di Poppea," 1642) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Claudio Monteverdi: Pur ti miro (from "L'Incoronazione di Poppea," 1642) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Monteverdi's last opera "L'Incoronazione di Poppea" (The Coronation of Poppea) is highlighted by a love scene between the Emperor Nero and his courtesan Poppea Sabina. Despite the well-known cruelty of the historical Nero, Monteverdi took away his sting and emasculated the Emperor by pitching both characters in the soprano range. The melodies are plain and simple and arranged as an echo between two star crossed lovers. The cadences sometimes land on a dissonance with each singer sustaining a long passing note just one semitone apart and resolving on a major or minor third.

The score by Jorge Luis Gaete Calderon can be found in MIDI format on CPDL.org . I have generated the vocal tracks using Synthesizer V software and the Spanish language setting in Solaria; the instrumental sounds (violins, bass viol and chitarrone) using Music Studio 2 (iPhone).

Text:

Pur ti miro, (I also gaze on you)
Pur ti godo, (I delight in you)
Pur ti stringo, (I embrace you)
Pur t'annodo, (I capture you)
Più non peno, (no more grief)
Più non moro, (no more death)
O mia vita, o mi tesoro. (O my life, my treasure)
Io son tua… (I am yours)
Tuo son io… (Yours I am)
Speme mia, dillo, dì, (my hope, say it is so)
Tu sei pur, (You are also)
L'idol mio, dillo, dì, (my idol, say it is so)
Sì, mio ben, (Yes, my love)
Sì, mio cor, mia vita, sì. (yes, my sweetheart, my life, yes)

3. Poppea Sabina, a speculative Renaissance painting, Anon. French, School of Fontainbleau, c1550
4. Emperor playing a stringed instrument as Rome burns, workshop of Giulio Romano, c1539
5. Roman bust of Poppea Sabina, original from the 1st century
6. Colorized bust of Poppea Sabina (modern computer rendition simulating the probable original 1st century figure which was painted)
7. Temple of Venus in the sky, set for a Venetian opera stage around the time of Monteverdi's premiere of Poppea, Giacomo Torelli, 1642
8. Portrait of Monteverdi towards the end of his career, c1635

videos.title: Guido: Dieux gart (c.1380)

localized.title: Guido: Dieux gart (c.1380)
localized.description:
Very little is known about the composer "Guido" (likely French but possibly of Italian extraction) whose only historical reference describes him as a cantor in the Avignon Cathedral during the Great Schism of the Western Church. He was perhaps an occasional visitor at the court of the Papal Palace under the tenure of Pope Clement VII during a very turbulent time. Guido was born around the time of the Black Death and for all of his life, knew only a divided Catholic Church with a French Pope in Avignon and an Italian Pope in Rome. Although written in the spirit of the courtly love genre, this song has a somewhat lighthearted quality with elements of both the Ars Nova and the later Ars Subtilior period. It contains a mesh of complex (almost chaotic), endlessly melismatic polyphony for 3 vocal parts (or possibly for solo voice and two instruments). 

I used the Synthesizer V software with only the Kevin voice bank. I used Audacity 3.75 to add reverb as well as echo and subtract noise. The instrumental simulations (of medieval lute, psaltery and medieval harp) were generated using Music Studio 2.0 and double the vocals. The pronunciation of the words is a simulation of what was likely 14th century courtly French.

Text (and translation):

Dieux gart qui bien le chantera (May God look over he who sings well)
que c'est pour l'amour de ma dame. (that it is for the love my Lady)

Or boyve primier qui faudra. (Now let the one who fails to drink first)
Dieux gart ... (May God look over...)

Ma dame veut qui bien dira (My Lady wants one who is well spoken)
qui fait toute s'amour,  (who devotes himself entirely to love her,)
par m'arme. (upon my honor)

Dieux gart... (May God look over...)

videos.title: Adrian Willaert / Francesco Petrarca: L'aura mia sacra (c.1559) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Adrian Willaert / Francesco Petrarca: L'aura mia sacra (c.1559) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Adrian Willaert composed this mournful madrigal for five male voices based on a sonnet by the medieval Italian poet Francesco Petrarca. The madrigal in two parts is a dedication to his beloved and immortalized muse: the Lady Laura who was taken from this world by the Black Plague in 1348. The expression "L'aura" (the breeze) in the first line of the poem is a double entendre for the name of an aristocratic French woman "Laure de Noves." The poem is based on a dream in which he reconnects with the spirit of his beloved in a manner he could not express while she was alive.

This latest rendition was created using the Synthesizer V software with the Kevin voice bank. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity. I generated the MIDI file from Allen Garvin's pdf score (from CPDL.org) with a few adjustments in the text underlay.

Text: 

Prima parte

L’aura mia sacra al mio stanco riposo
spira sì spesso, ch’i’ prendo ardimento
di dirle il mal ch’i’ò sentito et sento,
che, vivendo ella, non sarei stat’oso.
I’ incomoncio da quel guardo amoroso,
che fu principio a sí lungo tormento,
poi seguo come misero et contento,
di dì in dì, d’ora in hora, Amor m’à roso.

My sacred breeze (or My sacred Laura) 
sighs upon my weary rest, so that I take courage
to tell her of the sadness I felt and feel, as,
when she lived, I would not have dared to do.
I begin with that loving glance,
which was the start of this long torment,
then followed with how love gnaws at me,
wretched or content, day by day, hour by hour.

(Adapted from a translation by A.S. Kline)

Seconda parte

Ella si tace, et di pietà depinta,
fiso mira pur me; parte sospira,
et di lagrime honeste il viso adorna:
onde l’anima mia dal dolor vinta,
mentre piangendo allor seco s’adira,
sciolta dal sonno a se stessa ritorna.

She is silent, and gazes at me intently,
pitying me and sighing at times,
her face adorned by virtuous tears:
so that my soul overcome with grief,
angered with itself, because of her weeping,
returns to itself, torn away from sleep.

(Adapted from a translation by A.S. Kline)

2. Possible portrait of the Laura de Noves who may have seen her in person or remembered a likeness of her in an earlier painting, detail from the mural "Church Militant and Triumphant," Andrea da Firenze, 1356

videos.title: Johann Schelle: Cantata "Machet die Tore weit" (c.1685) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Johann Schelle: Cantata "Machet die Tore weit" (c.1685) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Cantata "Machet die Tore weit"

  0:06  Machet die Tore weit (SATB choir, 2 trumpets, violins, violas, cello, organ, bassoon, tympani)
  2:21  Auf mein Herze schicke dich (soprano, basso continuo)
  3:39  Drum so wirf die Riegel ein (alto, basso continuo)
  4:57  Heil'ge dich mit Reu und Leid (tenor, basso continuo)
  6:16  Denn des Königs sanfter Mut (baritone, basso continuo)
  7:35  Laß ihn willig dann zu Dir (chorus soloists, basso continuo)

Johann Schelle, who was music director of the St. Thomas Church (Thomaskirche) in Leipzig between 1677 and 1701 bridged the most famous of Lutheran choir masters in Baroque Germany. As a boy, Schelle was a student under the maestro Heinrich Schütz, and as an adult, he was appointed Thomaskantor at the Thomas Church and thus became predecessor to Johann Sebastian Bach. This cantata was written for the Advent season and is a paraphrasing of Psalm 24. Despite its length, there is much hidden repetition in the work. The basso continuo part in each of the four solo segments and chorus finale are identical even though the solos each carry a unique tune. Also each of these 4 arias and chorus are followed by an identical ritornello. 

The vocal simulations were created using the Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V. I created the orchestral sounds using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.

Text and translation:

1. Machet die Tore weit (Open the gates wide)
  und die Tür in die Welt hoch (and door to the world high)
  daß der König der Ehren einziehe (that the honored King may enter)
2. Auf, mein Herze, schicke dich (Rise up my heart)
  Gott, mein Heiland der Gerechte, (God, my savior of the just)
  naht zu dir, und zeiget sich (approaches you and appears)
  Ja, so ehrt er, dein Geschlechte (Yes, he so honors your lineage)
  daß er, Gottes wahrer Sohn (that he, God's true son)
  er, der Herre, kömmt zum Knechte (He, the Lord comes to the oppressed)
  von des hohen Himmels thron (from throne of high Heaven)
3. Drum so wirf die Riegel ein (So throw away the bolts)
  die den Eingang ihm verhindern (that hinder him from entrance)
  und für ihm ein Abschau sein. (and be guard for him.)
  Gott wohnt nur bei frommen (God stay only with pious)
  Kindern die sich recht nach ihm gericht, (children who judge themselves righteous)
  bei Verkehrten und bei Sündern (with wrongdoers and with sinners)
  spürt man seine Zukunft nicht. (one does not feels his future)
4. Heil'ge dich mit Reu und Leid (Heal yourself with repentance and sorrow)
  wegen deiner Misetaten (because of your misdeeds)
  so sind Tür und Tore weit. (so the door and gate are wide.)
  Wenn die Vater übertraten  (When the fathers transgressed)
  wenn sie Gott zum Zorn erregt, (when God was brought to anger)
  und nur um Genade baten (and only asked for mercy)
  ward das Unheil begelegt (calamity was resolved.)
5. Denn die Königs sanfter Mut, (Because of the king's gentle courage)
  ist in Liebe ganz entzündet (is quite filled with love)
  gegen den, der Busse tut. (toward the one who repents)
  Ja, er ist's der Hülfe findet (Yes, it is he who finds help)
  wenn die Last der Sünden drückt, (when the burden of sins oppresses)
  wenn uns niemand nicht entbindet (if one does not deliver us)
  und wir kläglich geh'n gebückt.  (we go forth, miserably, bent over.)

videos.title: Juan Cornago: Gentil dama non se gana (c.1450) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Juan Cornago: Gentil dama non se gana (c.1450) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Gentil dama non se gana

Juan Cornago is one of the earliest named Spanish composers from the late Medieval period. Other Spaniards from his generation remain mostly anonymous. His villancico "Gentil dama" is included in both the Cancionero Musical de Palacio and the Cancionero de la Colombina, the two most important and voluminous song collections from the Aragon / Castille court. His long melismata and complex polyphony resemble the artistry of Franco-Flemish contemporaries like Busnois, Dufay and Enrique de Foix rather than later Spanish composers like dell Enzina and Escobar. As with most other Spanish courtly songs from that era, this work also has an ABBA sequence.

In this latest rendition, I used Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V to reconstruct the text underlay for all four voices parts. I am fairly certain that all parts were intended for singers since the first five words of the song is written beneath the first few notes of the each voice part. I also added reverb, echo and de-essing using Audacity v.3.75. I used a pronunciation schedule for 15th Century Spanish as recommended by Timothy McGee in "Singing Early Music."

Text:

Gentil dama non se gana
Otro bien de vos mirar
Si no ver y desear

El deleyte que se faze
Myrando vuestra belta
Se destruye desfaze
Notando vuestra bondad

Ansi que mi fin temprano
Non le tiene de causar
Si no ver y desear

Translation:

Noble lady, nothing is gained
From looking at you
Except to see and to desire.

The delight that is made
In gazing upon your beauty
Is undone and destroyed
When one observes your virtuousness.

Thus my early end
Will be caused by none other
Than seeing and desiring.

1. "Gentil dama" score, Juan Cornago, Cancionero de Palacio, assembled c1500
2. Garden of Love, c1470
3. Man and woman at the window, Filippo Lippi, c1444
4. "Gentil dama" score, diskant and tenor parts, Cancionero de la Colombina, c1480
5. Lady and the Unicorn, Desire, Anonymous French, c1490
6. Pleasure gardens of Alcazar, Seville which was a likely venue for posthumous performance of Cornago's music.

videos.title: Henry Purcell (?) / William Shakespeare: Full Fathom Five (c.1695) from The Tempest

localized.title: Henry Purcell (?) / William Shakespeare: Full Fathom Five (c.1695) from The Tempest
localized.description:
There is controversy about the authorship of Henry Purcell's Tempest; modern scholars have speculated that the actual composer was one of his pupils, perhaps John Weldon. The writer of the lyrics for this particular song was, indeed, William Shakespeare. The rest of the semi-opera is based on a markedly altered version of the original play by Thomas Shadwell (1674).

"Full fathom five" which is sung by the ethereal character Ariel in Shakespeare's Tempest, is instead performed by a new character Milcha (a later added girlfriend of Ariel) in Purcell's Tempest. Most likely, Purcell's version of the song was sung by an adult female singer whereas a completely different setting of the same poem was probably sung by a young boy in Shakespeare's play (c1610).

The vocal lines were generated using Solaria (sopranos and altos) and Kevin (tenors and basses) in Synthesizer V. The instrumental parts were simulated using Music Studio 2.0. Reverb, echo and noise filtering were added using Audacity 3.75.

Text:

Full fathom five thy father lies;
Of his bones are coral made;
Those are pearls that were his eyes:
Nothing of him that doth fade
But doth suffer a sea-change
Into something rich and strange.

Sea-nymphs hourly ring his knell
Hark! now I hear them, – Ding-dong, bell.

videos.title: André Campra: Quam dilecta tabernacula tua (c.1700) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: André Campra: Quam dilecta tabernacula tua (c.1700) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This petit motet for three voices (SAB) and basso continuo was probably written during Campra's tenure as church composer at the Notre Dame de Paris, although he may have also used it for festive occasions at the court of Louis XIV in Versailles. It is a paraphrasing of just the first two stanzas of Psalm 83 in the Vulgate Latin Bible (Psalm 84 in the modern edition) and was likely included as musical interludes during feasts for the Virgin Mary.

It starts with a simple homophonic duet for the soprano and alto with support from the bass / baritone. In the second section, the alto starts a solo, the bass repeats a similar passage in a lower range, they join together and finally conclude in full ensemble. Unlike the pomp and grandiosity of his contemporary Charpentier, this work is a soft, modest tune suited for a quiet setting rather than the ostentation of the court.

This rendition was created using the Solaria voice bank for the soprano and alto parts and the Kevin voice bank for the baritone. The accompaniment by cello, organ and theorbo was added using Music Studio 2.0. The reverb, echo and de-essing were applied using Audacity 3.75. I used a Latin pronunciation that is closer to that probably used in late 17th century Paris.

Text:

Quam dilecta tabernacula tua, Domine virtutum!
Concupiscit, et deficit anima mea in atria Domini

How delightful is your palace, Lord of hosts
My soul desires and languishes to enter the chamber of the Lord

videos.title: Thomas Tallis: Gaude gloriosa Dei mater (c.1540) (New rendition)

localized.title: Thomas Tallis: Gaude gloriosa Dei mater (c.1540) (New rendition)
localized.description:
Gaude gloriosa Dei mater

   0:06  Verse 1 (Su, D, B)
   1:56  Verse 2 (Ct, T, Sp, D)
   3:21  Verse 3 (tutti)
   3:54  Verse 4 (tutti)
   7:06  Verse 5 (Sp1, Sp2, Su1, Su2, B)
   9:05  Verse 6 (D, Ct, T)
 10:50  Verse 7 (tutti)
 12:01  Verse 8 (Su, Ct, B1, B2)
 13:44  Verse 9 (tutti)

[Abbreviations: Sp (sexta pars, high soprano), Su (superius, high alto), D (discantus, low alto or tenor 1), Ct (contratenor, tenor 2), T (tenor, bariton or tenor 3), B (bassus)]
  
Stylistically, Tallis' Gaude gloriosa, a Latin antiphon dedicated to the Virgin Mary, bears the features of earlier English composers such as William Cornysh, John Browne and Robert Fayrfax. It retains the traditional high soprano voice, the impossibly long melismata, the intricately interwoven polyphony and the ever-continuing false cadences. Director and researcher David Skinner has suggested that this magnum opus was probably composed at the end of King Henry VIII's reign. He cites a fragment containing the same melodic lines but with English lyrics ("Deliuer me from my deceytful ennemies") penned by the King's sixth and last queen, Catherine Parr during his French campaign. The dramatic effect of the piece comes with the repeated declaration of "Gaude Virgo" with the full chorus coming together in vertical alignment.

The English Reformation, which included the Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536-1541) weighed heavily on Tallis, a life long Catholic. His insistent devotion to the the Virgin Mary was his personal statement of belief in the midst of unprecedented, relentless persecution of his fellow faithful. 

This soundtrack was created using Charles Giffen’s MIDI (CPDL.org). In this rendition, I used the Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V, but I softened the tone and rebalanced the voices.  I approximated 16th century Anglo-Latin pronunciation according to recommendations by Timothy McGee. The original piece was written for 6 vocal ranges (sextus pars (SP), superius (Su), discantus (D), countratenor (CT), tenor (T) and bassus (B)) and at least 9 independent singers (because the SP, Su and B parts split into contrapunctal duets in the middle of the piece).  

Text:
Gaude gloriosa Dei Mater, Virgo Maria vere honorificanda,
quae a Domino in gloria super caelos exaltata adepta es thronum.
Gaude Virgo Maria, cui angelicae turmae dulces in caelis resonant laudes:
iam enim laetaris visione Regis cui omnia servirunt.
Gaude concivis in caelis sanctorum, quae Christum in utero illaesa portasti:
igitur Dei Mater digne appellaris.
Gaude flos florum speciosissima, virga iuris, form morum,
fessi cura, pes labentis, mundi lux, et peccatorum refugium.
Gaude Virgo Maria quam dignam laude celebrat ecclesia,
quae Christi doctrinis illustrata te Matrem glorificat.
Gaude Virgo Maria, quae corpore et anima ad summum provecta es palacium:
et, ut auxiliatrix et interventrix pro nobis miserimis peccatoribus, supplicamus.
Gaude Maria intercessorum adiutrix et damnandorum salvatrix celebranda.
Gaude sancta Virgo Maria cuius prole omnes salvamur
a perpetuis inferorum suppliciis et a potestate diabolica liberati.
Gaude Virgo Maria Christi benedicta Mater, vena misericordiae et gratiae:
cui supplicamus ut nobis pie clamantibus attendas,
itaque tuo in nomine mereamur adesse caelorum regnum. Amen.

videos.title: Ludwig Senfl: Ave rosa sine spinis (c.1535) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Ludwig Senfl: Ave rosa sine spinis (c.1535) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Although Ludwig Senfl became a follower of Martin Luther’s Reformist Movement in his later years, much of his musical inspiration came from the Catholic, Franco-Flemish composers of the late 15th and early 16th centuries. The imitative polyphony with its rising and falling modal scales, long melismata and richly textured polyphony, meters alternating between 2 and 3 were derived from the works of the likes of Jean Mouton and Josquin.

The initial word of each verse in "Ave rosa sine spinis" can be strung together to reconstitute the Marian prayer "AVE MARIA GRATIA PLENA." (see the full text below). As in many works of this period, the cantus firmus in "Ave rose" with its very long notes in the 2nd alto line constitutes a pedal point that seamlessly continues even as all the other voices briefly drop out.

This recording was created using the Solaria (boy soprano) and Kevin (all other male voices) in Synthesizer V. Reverb, echo and noise filters was added using Audacity. The original MIDI file was created by Allen Garvin and can be found at CPDL.org . I applied a slight Southern German accent to the Latin text as suggested in Timothy McGee's "Singing Early Music." (1996). For example, I changed the hard initial "v" to "f."

Text and translation

1  AVE rosa sine spinis, (Hail [you] rose without thorns)

videos.title: Anonymous Spanish: Si la noche es temerosa (c.1500)

localized.title: Anonymous Spanish: Si la noche es temerosa (c.1500)
localized.description:
This 3-part villancico comes to us from the Cancionero Musical de Palacio by way of a copyist at the Spanish royal court during the reign of the Catholic Kings, Isabella de Castilla and Fernando de Aragon. It is an allegorical piece comparing the sorrows of an unattainable love with a dark and lonely night. The darkness as metaphor was reiterated in a later 3-part work (also Spanish and anonymous) with a similar title "Si la noche haze escura" in the Cancionero de Uppsala. 

The MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and uploaded to Musescore.com. I adjusted the text underlay in the superius part slightly and added the words for the tenor and countertenor parts. The usual villancico sequence, abba, was slightly extended with a second set of lyrics to produce the sequence, abbabba.

I used the Synthesizer V program with the Kevin voice bank (for all 3 parts) and the Spanish language phoneme set. The simulated sounds of gambas, lutes and harp were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. 

Text:

Si la noche es temerosa, (If the night is full of dread)
¿quién la dormirá? (who will bring me sleep)

Que de verme lastimado (I see myself overcome)
con fatiga y con cuidado, (with weariness and anxiety)
si durmiere descansado, (Were I to [try] sleeping peacefully)
el sentido velará. (my senses would remain restless)

Con el dolor que me dais (With the pain you give me)
mi bevir mal lo tratáis. (you treat me so harshly)
Si vos, mi bien, me matáis, (If you, my love, slay me)
quién la vida me dará (who will give me my life?)

videos.title: Claudio Monteverdi: Dolcissimo uscignolo (1638) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Claudio Monteverdi: Dolcissimo uscignolo (1638) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This short madrigal by Claudio Monteverdi consists of a soprano soloist alternating with a chorus of 5 homophonic male voice parts plus basso continuo accompaniment.  It compares a gallant lover to a nightingale seeking his beloved. The cavalier gentleman expresses envy for a nightingale's simplicity and innocence in matters of love.

The original MIDI file was downloaded from CPDL.org and its author is Gerd Eichler.  I added the Italian lyrics using the Synthesizer V software with Solaria (for the soprano) and Kevin (for the males voices).  I also added the accompaniment of a chitarrone and bass viol in the obligatory 6th part using the iPhone app Music Studio 2. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity v.3.75

Text:

Dolcissimo uscignolo, (Sweetest nightingale)
tu chiami la tua cara compagnia (you call to your dear companion)
cantando: «Vieni, vieni, anima mia». (singing "come, come my soulmate")
A me canto non vale, (To me a song is no value)
e non ho come tu da volar ale. (and I have not wings like you to fly)
O felice augelletto, (O happy little bird)
come nel tuo diletto (how for your pleasure)
ti ricompensa ben l'alma natura: (kind nature compensates you well)
se ti negò saper, ti diè ventura. (-- though you know not -- with good fortune)

videos.title: Josquin des Prez (?): In te Domine, speravi (c.1500) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Josquin des Prez (?): In te Domine, speravi (c.1500) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
The three most famous Italian frottole by Josquin des Prez "Scaramella," "In te Domine, speravi," and "El grillo" were probably all composed during his tenure at the court of Cardinal Ascanio Sforza in Milan. "In te Domine," which expresses the most serious sentiment among these three works, may have been Josquin's homage to his spiritual idol Girolamo Savonarola, a Dominican priest who promulgated a puritanical view of Christianity in the midst of the hedonism of 15th century Florence. After Savonarola commandeered the reigns of power from the corrupt and weakened leadership, he imposed a fanatic, theocratic rule over the once powerful city-state and he organized a widespread plundering of the artistic and cultural treasures of Firenze. His young followers grabbed any paintings, books, musical instruments and decorations that could easily be carried off to be consigned to the Bonfire of the Vanities. Subsequently, Savonarola was excommunicated by the Pope; and then he was imprisoned, tortured, hanged and burned at the stake by the Florentine citizenry. While awaiting his death sentence in a prison cell, Savonarola wrote a commentary on Psalm 31 (Clementine Bible) titled "In te Domine, speravi" (In thee Lord, I hoped...).

Josquin's song is preserved in several 16th century sources but most completely in the Cancionero Musical de Palacio (an enormous Spanish collection associated with the court of Ferdinand and Isabella) and the Frottole Libro Primo (from the printing presses of the Venetian publisher Ottaviano Petrucci.) The version of the frottola that I used for this video is the one contained in the Cancionero de Palacio. The song is often described as macaronic - with its alternating Latin and Italian text.

The MIDI file was originally created by James Gibb and uploaded to CPDL.org.  I created this soundtrack using Synthesizer with the Solaria and Kevin voice banks. I added reverb and echo using Audacity. 

++++++++++

Text (in Italian and Latin)

IN TE DOMINE SPERAVI
Per trovar pietà in eterno.
Ma in un tristo e obscuro inferno
FUI IN FRUSTRA LABORAVI.
Rotto e al vento ogni speranza
Veggio il ciel voltarmi in pianto.
Suspir lacrime m'avanza
Del mio tristo sperar tanto.
Fui ferito, se non quanto
TRIBULANDO AD TE CLAMAVI.
IN TE DOMINE SPERAVI.

English Translation (adapted from CPDL.org)

In Thee O Lord, I hoped
To find pity for ever.
But in a sad and dark inferno
I was, and suffered in vain.
Broken and thrown to the wind is all hope.
I have seen heaven turn me to weeping.
Only sighs and tears remain
To me of my sad, strong hope.
I was wounded, but in my sorrow
I called upon Thee.
In Thee O Lord, I hoped.

Illustrations:

1. "In te Domine, speravi" all four voice parts, Josquin des Prez, Cancionero de Palacio, c1500
2. Castello Sforzesco (Sforza Castle), Josquin's likely stomping grounds in the late 1490s.
3. Courtyard of the Castello Sforzesco
4. Portrait of Girolamo Savonarola, the author of the treatise on the 31st Psalm "In te Domine speravi," c1500 
5. Palazzo della Signoria at night, Florence 
6. Woodcut of Savonarola's last testament in his cell,  reprinted in 1524.  This volume contains his commentary about Psalm 31 "In te Domine speravi."
7. Hanging and burning of Savonarola and his closest brothers, 17th century copy of an earlier painting by Francesco Rosselli (c1500)

videos.title: Anonymous Franco-Burgundian: Helas mon tetin (c.1460)

localized.title: Anonymous Franco-Burgundian: Helas mon tetin (c.1460)
localized.description:
This virelai from the mid-15th century has a complicated past. Both the composer and poet are unknown, but its intricate, imitative polyphony suggests a French or Burgundian origin. It was likely copied in Naples in the 1460s along with other works in French, Italian, Spanish and even English. The collection was kept at the court of Spanish aristocrats who ruled Naples throughout the 16th century. The theme is one of forlorn love that was stereotypical of courtly love songs in France and Burgundy.

The MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and uploaded to Musescore.com. I changed the sequence from abbc (where “a” is the refrain and “b” is the verse) to abba as was customary for 15th century virelai. I also extrapolated the text underlay for the tenor and bass parts as suggested in the original score.  The "a" segment is in a triple rhythm (3/4 or 6/8) and the "b" segment in a duple (2/4). The soprano part has an unusually high pitched sequence in the mid-portion. To avoid the shrillness of those few notes, I pitched the entire piece down by a major 3rd.

The vocal simulations were generated using Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Text:

Helas mon tetin je vous prie
que vous ares en souvenir
cheli qui tant vous veult servir,
que d'aultre riens il n'a envie.
Il vous servira a tous jours
si leaulment qu'onques fist homme,
sans jamais faire le rebours de nostre volente:
c'est la somme

Alas, my sweetheart, I beg you
to keep in remembrance
the one who so greatly wishes to serve you,
who desires nothing else.
He will serve you always,
so loyally as any man ever did,
never acting against our will:
that is how things are.

Description of the photos:

1. "Helas mon tetin," Anonymous French or Burgundian, El Escorial Ms. IV.a.24, copied c1460
2. Concert, Lorenzo Costa, c1495
3. "Desire" from the "Lady and the Unicorn" tapestries, Anon. French, c1490
4. Bust of Ippolita Maria Sforza, Francesco Laurana, c1470; Ippolita was Duchess of Calabria and posthumously titled Queen of Naples around the time of the creation of the El Escorial Ms.; as a highly educated and cultured lady raised in a palace visited by Josquin and other masters, she was likely familiar with this type of repertoire.
5. Poverty begging from Wealth; Harley Ms 4425, c1490; some of the yearning expressed by the court composers of the 15th century may have been inspired by their desire to curry the affections (albeit platonic) of their female patrons.
6. Cupid blindfolded, Pero della Francesca, c1460
7. A foolish girl, Anonymous German or French, 15th century
8. Castle of Fair Welcome, Roman de la Rose, Anon. French, Ms. Douce 195, Bodleian Lib., c1490

localized.title: Azzaiolo: Ti parti cor mio caro (1557) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Ti parti cor mio caro

  0:44  Verse 1 (ATTB + lute)
  1:22  Verse 2 (ATTB, lute, tambourine)
  2:01  Verse 3 (Tutti)

This very short love song comes to us from a collection of light, homophonic compositions by the Italian ethno-musicologist Filippo Azzaiolo. One can hear its direct descent from its immediate musical predecessor, the Italian frottola. Azzaiolo claims that these pieces were culled from Paduan and Neapolitan folk music repertoire.

This soundtrack was created using the Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V. I created a more crude, naturalistic rendition compared with my previous recording using Vocaloid which had a more refined style. As always, I used the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 for the instrumental simulations. Reverb and echo were added with Audacity.

mi lassi in piant‘amaro, (and you leave me bitterly weeping)
È senz‘alcun riparo (and without any reprieve)
L‘anima senza te (fa la li le la). (is my spirit without you)
Non ti partir da me, (Don't go away from me)
Deh, cor mio caro, per la tua fè. (alas, my sweetheart, for your faith)

E pur se vuoi andare, (And if you still want to leave)
Ricordati tornare, (remember to return)
mia vita non può stare (my life cannot be)
Un‘hora senza te. (an hour without you)

videos.title: Jacques Arcadelt: O sacrum convivium (c.1538) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Jacques Arcadelt: O sacrum convivium (c.1538) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
The antiphon "O sacrum convivium" in the Catholic liturgy is often dedicated to the Eucharist and to the Feast of Corpus Christi. This particular setting by the Flemish composer Jacques Arcadelt was written during his long tenure in Rome when he was a composer in residence and a member Sistine Chapel Choir. One can hear the elaborate polyphony that was standard fare prior to the rulings from the Council of Trent which discouraged complicated counterpoint, puzzle canons and inaudible text. Its steady sonority bears resemblance to later Roman works by the likes of Morales and Palestrina.

The original MIDI file was created by Allan Garvin and uploaded to the website cpdl.org. I used the Solaria (boy soprano) and Kevin (male alto, tenor 1, tenor 2 and bass) voices banks with mostly Spanish phoneme settings in Synthesizer V. I also pitched the score up by a half step (A = approx. 466) to better fit the range of boy sopranos. Reverb, echo and de-essing were added with Audacity.

Text (and translation):
 
O sacrum convivium. (A sacred banquet)
in quo Christus sumitur: (in which Christ is received)
recolitur memoria passionis eius: (recalled is the memory of his Passion)
mens impletur gratia: (The mind is filled with grace)
et futurae gloriae nobis pignus datur. (and the promise of future glory is given to us)
Alleluia.

1. Sistine Chapel interior
2. Concert of angels, detail from fresco, Gaudenzio Ferrari, c1535
3. Disputation of the Holy Sacrament, Rafael, c1510
4. The hand of Adam reaching out to God, detail from the ceiling  of the Sistine Chapel, Michelangelo, c1511
5. Detail of the sacrament from #3
6. The Mass at Bolsena, Apostolic Palace, Vatican, Raphael (Raffaello) Sanzio, c1514; the Catholic Church commemorates a miraculous event that occurred during a mass in 1263 as the start of the Feast of Corpus Christi.
7. Last supper, Juan de Juanes, c1562

videos.title: William Shakespeare & John Wilson: Take o take those lips away (c.1620) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: William Shakespeare & John Wilson: Take o take those lips away (c.1620) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Take o take those lips away

0:06  Instrumental setting (violin, theorbo, bass viol)
1:48  Boy soprano or alto with basso continuo 

This song was written by Shakespeare around 1603-4 and performed at the Whitehall Palace by a boy alto or soprano as an interlude between Acts 3 and 4 in the somewhat dark comedy "Measure for Measure." The meaning of the sonnet has been debated, but it is mostly a song of unrequited love. This version of the song with a slightly altered text in the first verse and an entirely new second verse was published by the Shakespearean actor, theater composer and lutenist John Wilson in 1652. It was re-introduced at least a decade after the Bard's passing, and was probably incorporated into performances of "Measure for Measure" after 1625.

This rendition was generated using the Natalie voice bank in Synthesizer V and the sound of theorbo, bass viol and violin. I used an Early Modern English pronunciation as suggested by Professor David Crystal.

Text:

1. Take, O take those lips away,
That so sweetly were forsworne;
And those eyes, the breake of day,
Lights that doe mislead the morne:
But my kisses bring againe;
Seals of love, but seal'd in vaine.

2. Hide, O hide those hils of snow,
Which thy frozen blossome beares;
On whose tops the pinks that grow
Are yet of those that April weares.
But first set my poor heart free,
Bound in those icy chaines by thee.

Description of the photos:

1. Gallery musicians with violin, cornetto and chitarrone, detail from a fresco, Colonna & Mitelli, Palazzo Ducale Sassulo, c1647
2. "Take o take those lips away," a song introducing Act 4, Scene 1 of “Measure for Measure,” First Folio of Shakespeare’s complete plays, 1623
3. An English gentleman playing a chitarrone or theorbo, Anthony van Dyck, c1630
4. "Take o take those lips away," a setting for solo alto and lute or bass viol, John Wilson, published by John Playford, Select Musicall Ayres and Dialogues, 1652
5. A view of the Globe Theatre on the Thames in London, c1600; the primary venue of Shakespeare's plays
6. Whitehall Palace interior as seen from the royal throne from which King James I viewed the first performance of Shakespeare's "Measure for Measure" around 1604.

videos.title: Heinrich Isaac: Ich stund an einem Morgen a 4 (c.1500) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Heinrich Isaac: Ich stund an einem Morgen a 4 (c.1500) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Ich stund an einem morgen

  0:06  Verse 1: SATB acapella
  1:31  Verse 2: SATB + lute
  2:55  Verse 3: SATB + recorder, lute, harp, viol
  4:20  Instrumental arrangement: cornetto, 3 trombones

Heinrich Isaac composed his own richly textured and moving setting of the song "Ich stund an einem morgen" just as his star pupil Ludwig Senfl had done around the same period. The original melody was likely a well known folk song in the late 15th century, perhaps in Austria, where Isaac and Senfl were employed as court musicians of Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor. The song is unusual for that era in that its protagonist is a forlorn young woman (rather than a male gallant), and that much tender empathy is expressed for a lady at the center of the drama. Most of the contemporary courtly love songs from that time were instead primarily focused on the self absorbed desires and needs of a forsaken male character. Although the only surviving printed copies of this Lied was published posthumously in and after 1544, Isaac likely wrote the piece many years earlier when he was alive and still a resident of Vienna.

The vocal simulations were created using a combination of English and Spanish phonemes in Synthesizer V with the Solaria (soprano) and Kevin (alto, tenor, bass) voice banks. Instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2. The original score and MIDI files were encoded by Ulrich Alpers and uploaded to CPDL.org. I adjusted some of the text underlay.

Text (and translation):

Ich stund an einem morgen (I stood one morning)
heimich an einem ort (secretly in a spot)
da het ich mich verborgen (therein hiding myself)
Ich hört klegliche wort (I heard sorrowful words)
von einem frewlein hübsch und fein (from a maiden pretty and fine)
sie sprach zu jrem buelen (she spoke to her love)
es muß geschieden sein. (as he was going away)

Hertz lieb ich hab vernumen (My love, I have heard)
du wölst von hinnen schier (you will depart from here)
wan wiltu wider kumen (When will you come back)
das soltu sagen mir (You should tell me that)
merk auf mein feins lieb ich sag (now pay attention love what I say)
mein zukunft thust mich fragen (I ask what my future holds)
was weder stund noch tag. (what is it: hours even days?)

Das frewlein weinet sere (The young lady wept much)
Sein hertz was unmuts wol (her heart was greatly displeased)
so gib mir weis und lere (so give me wisdom and teaching)
wie ich mich halten sol (how should I hold in me)
für dich so setz ich al mein hab (for in you I keep all I have)
und wiltu hie bebleiben (and will you remain here)
verzer dich iar und tag. (or leave year and a day)

videos.title: Josef Mons: O Heiland, reiß die Himmel auf (c.2007)

localized.title: Josef Mons: O Heiland, reiß die Himmel auf (c.2007)
localized.description:
This 2 voice setting of the 17th century German Advent hymn "O Heiland, reiß die Himmel auf" ("O Savior, tear open the heavens") was written for 2 recorders to be performed by a student and her teacher sometime between 2005-2010. I have lowered the pitch of Mons' original MIDI by a major 3rd and chose the simulated sounds of an alto recorder and a violin.

The earliest known version of the hymn tune was likely composed by the German Jesuit priest, Friedrich Spee von Langenfeld, around 1622. He is best remembered as a victims' advocate for the falsely accused in the witch trials of the early 17th century; he died during the Thirty Years' War from plague caring for injured soldiers returning from battle.

1. "O Heiland," the oldest surviving, printed score of the melody, Rheinfelsisches Gesangbuch, 1666
2. Annunciation, Tilman Riemenschneider, c1485
3. Candles during mass, video by padrinan (Pixabay)
4. Vanitas (still life with violin, recorder and musical score), Edwaert Collier, c1670

videos.title: Nicholas Lanier: Mark how the blushful morn (c.1635) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Nicholas Lanier: Mark how the blushful morn (c.1635) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Mark how the blushful morn

  0:06  Instrumental arrangement (flute, theorbo, bass viol)
  1:08  Verse 1 (soprano, theorbo, bass viol)
  2:10  Verse 2 (soprano, theorbo, bass viol)

Nicholas Lanier was an English composer who hailed from a lineage of musicians in France. He presented himself in the public realm writing music for the London stage, and he also worked as Master of Music for the royal court of Kings Charles I and Charles II. This song, penned by court poet Thomas Carew, was likely incidental music for the London playhouses in the mid 1630s before the onslaught of Civil War and regicide. It was published in 1669 by the prolific publisher John Playford. Its operatic flair was likely inspired by the great maestro Claudio Monteverdi whom Lanier met on his grand tour of Italy.

Text:

Mark how the blushful morn in vain
Courts the amorous marigold
With sighing blush and weeping rain,
Yet she refuses to unfold.
But when the planet of the day
Approacheth with his pow'rful ray,
Then she spreads, then she receives
His warmer beams into her virgin leaves.

So may'st thou thrive in love, fond boy,
If silent tears and sighs discover
Thy grief, thou never shalt enjoy
The just reward of a bold lover.
But when with moving accent thou
Shalt constant faith and service vow,
Thy Celia shall receive those charms
With open ear, and with unfolded arms.

1. Portrait of Nicholas Lanier, Anonymous English, c1613
2. A broken consort with details of flute, bandora, lute, spinet
3. The lutenist, Caravaggio, c1596

5. A London stage actor in costume, Inigo Jones, c1613
6. Portrait of Margaret Lemon with viol, Anthony van Dyck, c1638

This latest rendition was created using the Synthesizer V software with the Solaria voice bank. The sounds of the theorbo, bass viol and transverse flute were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. Reverb, echo and noise filtering were added using Audacity 3.75.

videos.title: Henry VIII: Pastyme with good companye (c.1510) with Synthesizer V (Original Pronunciation)

localized.title: Henry VIII: Pastyme with good companye (c.1510) with Synthesizer V (Original Pronunciation)
localized.description:
Henry VIII: Pastyme with good companye (Pastime with good company)

  0:06  Verse 1: ATB (a cappella)
  0:38  Verse 2: tenor + recorder, lute, bass viol, tambourine
  1:09  Verse 3: alto + lute, tambourine
  1:42  Instrumental interlude: shawm, 2 sackbuts, tambourine
  2:13  Refrain: ATB + recorder, shawm, 2 sackbuts, tambourine, drum
----------

The song "Pastyme with good companye" was the signature anthem composed by a still young and vivacious Henry VIII.  He wrote this song for three vocalists during his earliest years as a newly crowned monarch in a period of relative peace, stability and joy at the English royal court - more than a decade before a dark cloud would descend over Queen Catherine of Aragon, his inner aristocratic circle and the entire Catholic Church in England.

"Pastyme" has a very catchy melody (unlike other more intricate works by Henry like his instrumental "Taundernaken"), an unwavering 6/8 rhythm, simple text underlay and 3 part homophony. In the so-called "Henry VIII Songbook" (Brit. Libr. Add. 31922), the full lyrics of "Pastyme" were written very legibly on one page for all three vocal parts (cantus, tenore and bassus). It is thus likely that this manuscript copy was a performance edition for the royal musicians at court. I generated 4 separate settings of the theme using both soft and loud Renaissance instruments based on a posthumously discovered list of the king's private collection of instruments. 

--------------------

Original text & modern transcription

Pastyme wt good (com)panye (Pastime with good company)
I loue & schall vntyll I dye (I love and shall until I die)
gruche who lust but none denye (grudge who lust but none deny)
so god be plesyd thus leve wyll I (so god be pleased thus live will I)
for my pastence (for my pastance [i.e. recreation])
hunt syng & daunce (hunt, sing and dance)
my hart is sett (my heart is set)
all goodly sport (all goodly sport)
for my comfort (for my comfort)
who schall me let (who shall me let)
 
youthe must haue som daliance (Youth must have some dalliance)
off good or yll som pastance. (of good or ill some pastance)
Company me thynkes then best (Company me thinks then best)
all thoughts & fansys to deiest. (all thoughts and fancies to digest)
ffor Idillnes (for idleness)
is cheff mastres (is chief mistress)
of vices all (of vices all)
then who can say. (then who can say)
but myrth and play (but mirth and play)
is best of all. (is best of all)
 
Company wt honeste (Company with honesty)
is vertu vices to ffle. (is virtue vices to flee)
Company is good & ill (Company is good and ill)
but ev’ry man hath hys fre wyll. (But every man has his free will)
the best ensew (The best ensue)
the worst eschew (the worst eschew)
my mynde schal be. (my mind shall be)
vertu to vse (virtue to use)
vice to refuce (vice to refuse)
thus schall I vse me. (that shall I use me.)

--------------------

Description of the photos:

1-4. "Pastyme with good companye" cantus part, Henry VIII, Brit. Libr. Add. 31922 (a.k.a. Henry VIII Songbook), assembled around c1513
5. Musicians in a garden, Chigi Codex VIII.234
6. Detail of an early 16th century lute from the double portrait "Ambassadors" (most likely painted at the court of Henry VIII), Hans Holbein the Younger, c1533
7. Gallery musicians possibly at Henry's court (with detail of sackbut, shawm and cornetto or recorder), Hans Holbein the Younger, c1526. 
8. Portrait of a young Henry VIII around the time of his coronation and the composition this song.

--------------------

NOTES ON THE RECORDING:

This soundtrack was created using Synthesizer V software with 3 different ranges of the Kevin voice bank.  The pronunciation of the words is not standard modern English but rather a simulated pre-Early Modern English based on a number of different sources including ChatGPT. The reverb, echo, noise-reduction were all added afterwards using Audacity version 3.75. The instrumental simulations were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 (Steinberg)

videos.title: Michael Praetorius: Wie schön leuchtet der Morgenstern (1619) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Michael Praetorius: Wie schön leuchtet der Morgenstern (1619) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This motet for 9 parts by Michael Praetorius was written for double choir, instruments (likely doubling the 8 singers) plus basso continuo. The left choir and right choir each contain four voices (SATB+SATB). He indubitably adapted this compositional style from the Venetians (the Gabrielis and Monteverdi) but also Hans Leo Hassler who had introduced the multiple choir concept to German speaking choruses. The non-liturgical text and melody line of this tune were composed by Philipp Nicolai. Nicolai in turn adapted the words from the 45th Psalm.

The MIDI files was compiled by Adrian Wall and uploaded to CPDL.org. I added the text using Synthesizer V loaded with the Solaria (soprano and alto for both choirs) and Kevin (tenor and bass for both choirs) voices banks. Reverb, echo, de-essing and low pass filters were applied using Audacity v3.75. Instrumental simulations were created using an iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. For Choir I, I used violin, 3 viols, sackbut and pipe organ; for Choir II, I used violin, 3 viols, sackbut, chitarrone. These were the the typical orchestral pieces in German cathedrals of that period as can be seen in the cover pages of Praetorius' printed editions.

Text (and translation)

Wie schön leuchtet der Morgenstern (How beautiful the morning star shines)
Voll Gnad und Wahrheit von dem Herrn, (full of grace & truth of the Lord)
Die süße Wurzel Jesse! (the sweet root of Jesse)
Du Sohn Davids aus Jakobs Stamm, (You son of David from Jacobs line)
Mein König und mein Bräutigam, (my King and Bridegroom)
Hast mir mein Herz besessen, (You have captured my heart)
Lieblich, freundlich, (lovely, friendly)
Schön und herrlich, groß und ehrlich, (Beautiful, glorious, great and honored)
Reich von Gaben, (rich in gifts)
Hoch und sehr prächtig erhaben! (Lofty and magnificently sublime!)

Description of the photos:

1. "Wie schön leuchtet der Morgenstern," Cantus part, Michael Praetorius, Polyhymnia caduceatrix et panegyrica (Wolfenbüttel), 1619
2. Marienkirche Hauptkirche (Wolfenbüttel) organ; the pipes are new, but the organ casing was constructed for Praetorius (probably with his suggestions) as he was the resident composer for the church.
3. Cover page of Polyhymnia caduceatrix et panegyrica (Wolfenbüttel), 1619
4. Early Baroque orchestra, details from "KIng David brings the ark into Jerusalem and makes music to the people's rejoicing," Pieter Lastman, 1618
5. Marienkirche (Wolfenbüttel) altar
6. Angel statue on the frame of the Haberstadt Organ (Gröningen), David Beck, 1596; a detailed sketch of this instrument appears in the Syntagma Musicum (1615-1620) by Michael Praetorius.

videos.title: Guillaume Dufay: Sanctus from Missa Ecce ancilla Domini (c.1460)

localized.title: Guillaume Dufay: Sanctus from Missa Ecce ancilla Domini (c.1460)
localized.description:
The Missa Ecce ancilla Domini (behold the handmaiden of God) was likely composed in the later years of Guillaume Dufay's long and illustrious musical career -- perhaps during his second and final tenure at Cambrai Cathedral. It was intended to commemorate the Annunciation, or the prophesy by the angel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary of the coming of baby Jesus. Note the complex interweaving, imitative polyphony between the alto and tenor 1 voices which alternates with the luminous harmony of the complete four part ATTB choir. The unfolding drama of the Advent story is expressed in the richness of the full chorus intoning "Hosanna in excelsis."

I used a MIDI file uploaded to the Josquin Project website, and I added text with the Synthesizer V software (Solaria and Kevin voice banks). The Latin I applied simulated late Medieval French pronunciation. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity v.3.75.

Text (and translation):

Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, (Holy, holy, holy)
Dominus Deus Sabaoth. (is the Lord our God of the Sabbath)
Pleni sunt caeli et terra gloria tua.
    (Filled are heaven and earth by your glory)
Hosanna in excelsis. (Hosanna in the highest)
Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini.
    (Blessed is he who goes in the name of the Lord)
Hosanna in excelsis (Hosanna in the highest)

2. Singing angels, detail from the Ghent Altarpiece, Jan van Eyck, c1439
3. Annunciazione di cestello, Sandro Boticelli, 1490
4. Porte de Paris, Cambrai; a vestige of the once great walled rampart that would have been a familiar site to Dufay who spent much of his youth and later years behind its confines.
5. Annunciation, Andrea della Robbia, Firenze, c1463
6. City wall of Cambrai, detail from Charles IV entering Cambrai in 1378, Jean Fouquet, c1460 
7. Annunciation, Leonardo da Vinci, c1475
8. Cambrai Cathedral before its destruction in the French Revolution, Adam van Meulen, c1660
9. Virgin Mary, detail from the Annunciation, Carlo Crivelli, 1482
10. Annunciation in 3D, Francesco di Valdambrino, c1411
11. Annunciazione di volterra , Luca Signorelli, 1491
12. Frontal view of the Virgin Mary in Fig. 10

15. Detail from Fig. 14
16. White lilies, a frequent motif in Annunciation paintings during the Renaissance symbolizing the purity of the Virgin Mary, photo by PgmJanssen (Pixabay)

videos.title: De tous biens plaine and variations (c.1460-1490) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: De tous biens plaine and variations (c.1460-1490) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
"De tous biens plaine" (3 variations on a theme by Hayne van Ghizeghem)

  0:06  Original rondeau for 3 by van Ghizeghem (verses 1 & 3)
  3:19  Instrumental parody for 3 by Agricola (vielle, medieval harp, viol)
  4:49  Instrumental parody for 4 by Josquin des Prez (2 trombones, 2 viols)

The rondeau "De tous biens plaine" by the 15th Century Franco-Flemish composer Hayne van Ghizeghem was perhaps the most widely parodied chanson of the late French Medieval period with no fewer than 28 different variations conceived over 4 decades.  The repertoire included secular songs, mass movements and virtuosic instrumental duos and trios. Although it was likely conceived around 1460, it has a surprisingly modern sound that contained linear, lyrical lines in all 3 voices without any imitative canons or rhythmic surprises (such as hemiolas.) The most ingenious setting is perhaps Josquin’s four part version which pits the top two melody lines from Ghizeghem’s original tune against a fast moving canon in the lower two parts. Agricola’s setting is also quite surprising with its seamless transition from a 4 (or 2) rhythm to a 6 (or 3) rhythm.

In this latest rendition, I rendered the vocal tracks using Synthesizer V with Solaria (female alto) and Kevin (tenor and bass). I downloaded the untexted MIDI file from the Aeolian Consort's Japanese website and transposed the piece down one octave. I chose the text from the Copenhagen Chansonnier rather than the better known Leuven, Nivelle or Dijon Mss. The reverb and echo were added using Audacity. 

Text:

De tous biens plaine est ma maistresse
Chascun lui doibt tribut d'honneur;
Car assouvye est en valeur
Autant que jamais fut deesse.

Translation:

My lady is full of all good things.
Everybody pays her honorable tribute,
for she is full of nobility
as much as any goddess ever was.

-------------------------------
