videos.title: Salamone Rossi: Al naharot Bavel (1623) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Salamone Rossi: Al naharot Bavel (1623) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Despite the long history of Jewish communities in Italy tracing as far back as Greco-Roman times, it was only in 1623 that the first collection of polyphonic music with Hebrew text for liturgical use was printed in Venice by the Mantuan composer Salamone Rossi (aka il Ebreo, or the Jew). Due in part to its slightly less intolerant anti-Semitic policies, Mantua was one of the last city-states in Italy to build a walled ghetto for its Jewish population. Rossi, however, being a composer of significant importance, regularly commissioned by Vincenzo, the Gonzaga Duke of Mantua, traversed easily past the ghetto walls to mingle with the outside world -- the likes of Claudio Monteverdi, Giovanni Gastoldi and others. Rossi created a large body of works both secular and sacred, instrumental as well as choral. This four part setting is a lamentation based on the Hebrew Psalm 137, which refers to the Babylonian Captivity in the 6th Century BCE. It was likely intended for use in the Norsa Synagogue of Mantua during the 9 days of mourning leading up to Tisha B’av. It is difficult to imagine that Rossi would have ignored the plight of European Jews in his own time when composing this mournful song.

The original MIDI for this soundtrack minus the singing was created by John Hetland and uploaded to cpdl.org. I inserted the Hebrew text using Synthesizer V software with the Solaria and Kevin voice banks. The pronunciation of Hebrew is a simulation of Venetian Sephardic phonemes in the early 17th century. The harsh overtones in the finished soundtrack was reduced using Audacity v.3.75.

Text:

Psalms 137

עַ֥ל נַהֲר֨וֹת ׀ בָּבֶ֗ל (Al naharot bavel)
שָׁ֣ם יָ֭שַׁבְנוּ גַּם־בָּכִ֑ינוּ (sham yashavnu gam bachinu)
בְּ֝זׇכְרֵ֗נוּ (bezochrenu)
אֶת־צִיּֽוֹן׃ (et tsiyyon)
עַֽל־עֲרָבִ֥ים בְּתוֹכָ֑הּ (al aravim betochah)
תָּ֝לִ֗ינוּ כִּנֹּרוֹתֵֽינוּ׃ (talinu kinnoroteinu)
כִּ֤י שָׁ֨ם שְֽׁאֵל֢וּנוּ שׁוֹבֵ֡ינוּ דִּבְרֵי־שִׁ֭יר (ki sham sh'elunu shoveinu divrei shir)
וְתוֹלָלֵ֣ינוּ שִׂמְחָ֑ה (vetolaleinu simha)
שִׁ֥ירוּ לָ֗֝נוּ (shiru lanu)
מִשִּׁ֥יר צִיּֽוֹן׃ (mishir tsiyyon)
אֵ֗יךְ נָשִׁ֥יר אֶת־שִׁיר־יְהֹוָ֑ה (ech nashir et shir adonai)
עַ֗֝ל אַדְמַ֥ת נֵכָֽר׃ (al admat nechar)
זְכֹ֤ר אֲדֹנָי לִבְנֵ֬י אֱד֗וֹם (Zechor adonai livnei edom)
אֵת֮ י֤וֹם יְֽרוּשָׁ֫לָ֥‍ִם (et yom yerushalaim)
הָ֭אֹ֣מְרִים עָ֤רוּ ׀ עָ֑רוּ (ha omerim aru, aru)
עַ֗֝ד הַיְס֥וֹד בָּֽהּ׃ (ad hayesod bah)
בַּת־בָּבֶ֗ל הַשְּׁד֫וּדָ֥ה (bat bavel hasheduda)
אַשְׁרֵ֥י שֶׁיְשַׁלֶּם־לָ֑ךְ (ashrei sheyshallem lach)
אֶת־גְּ֝מוּלֵ֗ךְ (et gemulech)
שֶׁגָּמַ֥לְתְּ לָֽנוּ׃ (shegamalt lanu)
אַשְׁרֵ֤י ׀ שֶׁיֹּאחֵ֓ז (ashrei sheyochez)
וְנִפֵּ֬ץ אֶֽת־עֹ֝לָלַ֗יִךְ (venipets et olalayich)
אֶל־הַסָּֽלַע׃ (el hassala)

Translation:

By the rivers of Babylon
we sat and wept
remembering Zion.

Upon the willows
we hung up our lyres.

For there our captors asked us for songs,
our tormentors told us to rejoice,
“Sing for us,
a song from Zion!”

How can we sing a sacred song of the Lord
on foreign soil?

If I forget you, Jerusalem,
let my right hand lose its strength.

Let my tongue stick to my palate
if I do not remember you,
if I do not place Jerusalem
above all my greatest joy.

Remember, o Lord, the Edomites,
that day in Jerusalem! —
they said, “Strip her, strip her,
to her foundations!”

O daughter of Babylon, you despoiler,
happy is the one who pays you back,
for what you did to us!

Happy be the one who grabs
and smashes your babies
against the rocks!

Description of the photos:

1. “Al naharot bavel” cantus part, S. Rossi, Hashirim asher Lishlomo, Venice, 1623
2. Destruction of Jerusalem, from the Nuremberg Chrinicles, 1493
3. Cover page of the collection Hashirim asher Lishlomo, Song of Solomon, 1623
4. The Norsa synagogue interior first built in 1513 in the Jewish Ghetto of Mantua and rebuilt according to the original plans using original materials in the early 20th century
5. View of the Jewish Ghetto of Mantua near where Rossi composed his Psalm settings
6. The Great Psalm Scrolls 11Q5 (Dead Sea Scrolls) which includes one of the oldest surviving copies (albeit damaged) of Psalm 137 “Al naharot Bavel.” copied around CE 30-50
7. Fall of Giants, Hall of Giants, Palazzo Te, Mantova; perhaps a mural familiar to Rossi
8. Close up of Figure 6 with the “Al naharot” appearing at the right lower margin which has been mostly destroyed.

videos.title: Anonymous German: Ich sachs eyns mols (c.1460)

localized.title: Anonymous German: Ich sachs eyns mols (c.1460)
localized.description:
This courtly love song in the German vernacular for 3 voices appears twice in the Glogauer Liederbuch, a large manuscript of mostly German and Latin texted religious and secular music. The full text of the song is provided only in the second appearance of the score. The tenor and countertenor parts, being without text underlay, may have been written for instrumentalists.

The vocal simulations were created using Synthesizer V with Solaria (pitched down to the range of a male alto) and Kevin for the two interweaving tenor voices. Slight sound adjustments such as reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Text:

Ich sachs eyns mals, 
den lichten morgensterne
bey meynem bulen
zo wer ich alzeit gerne
und mag doch leyder nicht geseyn

Translation:

I once said,
to the bright morningstar
besides my beloved
there is where I will always be gladly
but, sadly, I may not be seen.

videos.title: Clément Janequin: Va Rossignol (c.1535) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Clément Janequin: Va Rossignol (c.1535) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Va Rossignol

  0:06  Original 4 part chanson (ATTB) with lute doubling
  2:45  Arrangement for 4 viols and lute

------------------------------

The chanson "Va rossignol" by Janequin revolves around a certain nightingale, an often used motif in Medieval and Renaissance French music. This particular avian species symbolized at once love and death which were Medieval preoccupations, frequently expressed exquisitely in the world of music and literature. In this song, a nightingale is the deliverer of an amorous poem to an unattainable beauty who lives far away.  

In this latest rendition, used Synthesizer V with the Solaria and Kevin voice banks. The lute doubling and the instrumental arrangement were created using MusicStudio2.  The original MIDI without the text was compiled and uploaded to IMSLP.org by Daniel van Gilst. 

Original French text:

Va rossignol, amoureux messaigier
Va faire ouyr a ma seule maistresse
Ton chant joyeulx pour elle soulager
Meslé d'amour et d'ung peu de tristesse.
Qu'est-ce Magdaleyne m'amye
Qu'est-ce que de tant aymer
Qu'en dictes vous Magdaleyne jolye ?
Venez, venez vostre amy conforter
Accourez tost, plus ne fault séjourner,
Il vous attend, prenez vers luy l'adresse.
O grant beaulté de toutes le mirouer
Gardez vous bien que par vous l'amour cesse.

Translation:

Go nightingale, my amorous messenger
Go let my my only lady hear
Your joyous song and comfort her
Mixing love and of a little bit of melancholy.
What is it? Magdeleine my love?
What did you say, pretty Magdaleine?
Come, come to comfort your love
Run quickly, and do not delay
He awaits you, go in his direction.
O greatest beauty among all, 
Look at yourself well in the mirror, my love ends with you.

-------------------------

2. Façade, Château de Fontainebleau, the palace where works by the greatest masters of the French High Renaissance were frequently performed.
3. A pair of lovers, Paris Bordone, c1550
4. Mary Magdalene with lute, Anonymous Franco-Flemish, c1540

videos.title: Dieterich Buxtehude: Ihr lieben Christen, BuxWV 51 (c.1690) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Dieterich Buxtehude: Ihr lieben Christen, BuxWV 51 (c.1690) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This Advent cantata by Dietrich Buxtehude calls for an unusually large array of accompanying instruments: 2 clarino trumpets, violins, violas (or viole da gamba), cello, violone, church organ, bassoon, cornetti (doubling violins), trombones (i.e. sackbuts) and, most importantly, a 5 part choir to match the massive orchestral sound. It was most certainly intended for the professional musicians and choir of St. Mary’s church in Lübeck where Buxtehude had been music director for decades. This late work by the maestro appends the first verse of a mystical / religious poem by Erasmus Alber to later non-liturgical text. Alber's original words were published in 1542 during the first generation of Lutheran lyricists. The instrumental parts, with its full compliment of brass and strings is similar in spirit to the grandiose and dramatic motets and masses of Heinirch Ignaz Franz Biber in Salzburg (Austria) as well as the much earlier polychoral masterpieces of Giovanni Gabrieli in Venice and Michael Praetorius in Thuringia. 

In this latest rendition, I used the Synthesizer V software with Solaria (for soprano and alto parts) and Kevin (for the tenors and bass).  The instrumental accompaniment was created using Music Studio 2. Reverb was added using Audacity.

++++++++++

German Text:

Ihr lieben Christen, freut euch nun,
bald wird erscheine Gottes Sohn,
der unser Bruder worden ist,
das ist der lieber Jesus Christ.

Siehe, siehe, der Herr kommt 
mit viel tausend Heiligen,
Gerichte zu halten über alle.
Siehe, siehe, ich komme bald 
und mein Lohn mit mir.
So komm doch, Jesu, komme bald, 
und gänzlich zu befreien
komm unser Seelen Aufenthalt, 
komm uns ewig zu erfreuen.
Komm, Jesu, komm und säume nicht,
lass uns in deines Himmels Licht
dein ewiges Lob ausschreien.
Amen.

Ei, lieber Herr, eil zum Gericht,
Lass sehn dein herrlich Angesicht,
das Wesen der Dreifaltigkeit.
Das hilf uns, Gott, in Ewigkeit.
Amen.

Translation:

Dear Christians, rejoice now,
Soon the Son of God will appear,
He who became our brother,
that is the beloved Jesus Christ.
Behold, the Lord is coming
with many thousand Saints
The Righteous stands over all
Behold, I come soon
and my reward with me.
So come, Jesus, come soon
and to completely free our souls.
Let us shout your eternal praise
In thy Heaven's light.
Come to bring us joy forever
Let us see your beautiful face
The essence of the Trinity
God, who saves us, for all eternity.

videos.title: Adrian Willaert: Quando nascesti Amor (1559) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Adrian Willaert: Quando nascesti Amor (1559) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Adrian Willaert (c.1490-1562) was a Flemish composer who was a seminal figure in the development of the Renaissance madrigal in Italy. He was also a pioneer of the polychoral motet which influenced an entire generation of Venetian masters that included Andrea and Giovanni Gabrieli, and later Claudio Monteverdi.  Willaert's long tenure as music director of San Marco in Venice was the beginning of the era of dominance by an Italian School which became the model for High Renaissance music throughout Europe during the middle to late 16th century. This short masterpiece "Quando nascesti Amor" for 7 voices has some of the hallmarks of Venetian polychoral music with two distinct choirs separated into an upper range (SAA) and a lower range (TTBB) singing in playful dialogue with one another. The lower voices pose a question and the higher voices give the corresponding answer. The lyrics were written by the Italian humanist poet Panfilo Sasso (1455-1527) at the tail end of long history of courtly love songs.

In this latest rendition, I used the Solaria (soprano) and Kevin (the other 6 voices) in Synthesizer V. The reverb and echo were added using Audacity v3.75. 

----------

Italian text

Quando nascesti Amor?
  Quando la terra si riveste di verd' et bel colore.
Alhor di che nascesti?
  D'un ardore che otio et lascivia in se richiud' et sera.
Con ti costringe a farne tanta guerra?
  Calda speranza et gelido timore.
In cui fai la tua stanza?
  In gentil core che sotto el mio valor' tosto s'atterra.
Chi fai la tua nutrice?
  Giovinezza.
E le serve furno a lei d'intorno?
  Vanità, gelosia, pompa e bellezza.
Di che ti pasci?
  D'un parlar adorno.
Offendeti la morte o la vecchiezza?
  No, che io rinasco mille volte il giorno.

Translation

When were you born, Love?
  When the earth wraps itself in green and beautiful color.
Why did you come into existence?
  From an ardor that dispenses with laziness and lasciviousness
Who forces you to fight such a war?
  Fiery hope and frigid fear.
Where is your place?
  In a gentle heart which I with my valor can conquer.
Who give you sustenance?
  Youth.
And those who serve you?
  Vanity, jealousy, pomp and beauty.
How did you rise up?
  From florid speech
Do death or old age offend you?
  No, because I am reborn a thousand times a day.

----------

videos.title: Johann Sebastian Bach: First Chorus from "Herz und Mund und Tat und Leben" (BWV 147) (1723)

localized.title: Johann Sebastian Bach: First Chorus from "Herz und Mund und Tat und Leben" (BWV 147) (1723)
localized.description:
Cantata #147 composed in 1723 was one of JS Bach's earliest contracted works at the Thomaskirche in Leipzig. It was an expanded version of an even earlier six movement Cantata from his youth in Weimar at the court chapel of Duke Wilhelm Ernst in 1716. The first movement features a 4 part chorus accompanied by trumpet, 2 oboes, 2 violins, viola, cello and organ. It was based on a non-liturgical text commemorating the Visitation to the Virgin Mary by Elizabeth, mother John the Baptist.

The vocal simulation was created with Synthesizer V using the Solaria voice bank for the boy soprano and alto and the Kevin voice bank for the tenor and bass. The instrumental sounds were generated on an iPhone using Music Studio 2.0.

videos.title: Hans Leo Hassler: Ein feste burg ist unser Gott (1607)

localized.title: Hans Leo Hassler: Ein feste burg ist unser Gott (1607)
localized.description:
The German composer and organist Hans Leo Hassler published this Lutheran hymn setting after his homecoming to his birthplace of Nuremberg. Although he was an unabashed Protestant during a period of intense religious turmoil in Central Europe, Hassler had spent many years studying Italian polyphony in Venice and was employed for a time in the Catholic state of Augsburg. 

Nuremberg, a southern city-state in a mostly Catholic Bavaria, was an open city which tolerated Protestants of all sorts and followers of the Lutheran Movement. "Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott," a sometimes battle hymn of the Lutheran revolution, was a defiant song emblematic of the robust faith in the rapidly growing German Reformation. The original melody of Luther's song is well preserved throughout this piece with its canonic entrances by the four SATB voices.

The voice parts were generated using the Solaria and Kevin voice banks (with both English and Spanish phonemes) on the Synthesizer V platform. Reverb was added later using Audacity. 

Text:

Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott
ein gute Wehr und Waffen.
Er hilfft uns frey auß aller Noth,
die uns jetzt hat betroffen.
Der alte böse Feind,
mit Ernst ers jetzt meint.
Groß Macht und vil List,
sein grausam Rüstung ist.
Auf Erd ist nicht seins Gleichen.

Translation:

A mighty fortress is our God,
a fine shield and weapon;
He helps to free us from every need
that has now overtaken us.
The ancient and evil Fiend
He goes forth with
Great might and deception
Donning his cruel armor,
on Earth there is not his equal.

videos.title: Alessandro Coppini: La citta bella (Canto dei Giudei) (c.1490)

localized.title: Alessandro Coppini: La citta bella (Canto dei Giudei) (c.1490)
localized.description:
According to the editor Joseph Gallucci Jr., this late 15th Century, Florentine carnival song expresses the thoughts of a Jewish sojourner from outside the city walls visiting town to see friends and to do business. As a Jew, he is allowed to remain in Florence for only 3 days -- a span of time that varied from one Italian city-state to another. The song may have been performed by musicians masquerading as Jewish merchants during carnival season in the streets of Florence.

In this soundtrack, I have included only the first verse. In the remaining four verses, the poet expounds expansively on the virtues of honest money lending (a business that a few European Jews practiced on a small scale but which Gentile bankers in Florence took over and grew into a massive industry spanning all sectors of Europe's economy.) 

Text:

La città bella et conforme natura 
ch'oggi è fra voi et noi ,
ci ha mossi a star con voi 
tre dì come la legge ci sicura, 
portato abbian de’ nostri caliconi 
che v’insegniamo fare, 
et son de’ vostri anche più begli et buoni; 
et vedrete al gustare, 
ma più per vicitare, 
gli amici già perduti siano oggi qui venuti, 
benché non stian sospetto et paura. 

Translation:

The beautiful city, in harmony with nature,
that today is shared by us all
We were moved to stay with you,
for (only) three days, as the law allows us.
We have brought our caliconi (pastries ?),
to show you how to make them,
for ours are even finer and better than yours,
and you’ll see when you taste them,
but more so we visit you,
friends once lost are back together today,
so let there be no suspicion or fear.

videos.title: Guillaume de Machaut: Fons totius superbie / O livoris / fera pessima (c.1355)

localized.title: Guillaume de Machaut: Fons totius superbie / O livoris / fera pessima (c.1355)
localized.description:
This isorhythmic motet by Guillaume de Machaut consists of three lines of non-liturgical Latin poetry with a somewhat bitter edge. Each of the three voices speaks out against an unseen evil in a world that was left in chaos in the aftermath of the Black Plague (1346-1353.) The Pestilence of the Fourteenth Century resulted in an apocalyptic collapse of Western civilization during which a quarter of the population of Europe was decimated. Leadership had all but disappeared, crime was rampant and corruption became the norm.

And yet, this sourly spirited piece has an almost jaunty quality infused with sarcasm and even a bit of optimism. As is often the structure of Machaut motets, the upper two voices present an elaborately hocketed passage that gives the piece an almost light and carefree air. The tenor meanwhile intones a slow, repeating cantus firmus that imparts a supportive role for the virtuosic upper parts.

I used the MIDI file of Wilinori and the text underlay of Jacques Boogaart. The text was entered using Synthesizer V with the Kevin voice bank in a Spanish language mode. The late Middle French pronunciation of Latin was based on recommendations by Chatgpt and Timothy McGee (Singing Early Music). Reverb and echo were added using Audacity v3.75

Triplum:

Fons totius superbie, (Fountain of all Pride)
Lucifer, et nequitie (Lucifer and iniquity)
Qui, mirabili specie decoratus, (who adorned with marvelous beauty)
Eras in summis locatus, (was placed on the highest place)
Super thronos sublimatus, (above the thrones)
Draco ferus antiquatus qui dicere (the fierce and ancient dragon who spoke)

Ausus es sedem ponere (You would sit)
Aquilone et gerere (in the North and)
Te similem in opere Altissimo. (work to be like Lord).
Tuo sed est in proximo (But soon thereafter)
Fastui ferocissimo (your fierce arrogance)
A judice justissimo obviatum. (met with the answer of the just Judge)
Tuum nam auffert primatum; (He takes away your primacy)
Ad abyssos cito stratum (Into the abyss from the heights)
Te vidisti per peccatum de supernis. (you were cast down for your sin)

Ymis nunc regnas infernis; (Now you reign in Hell)
In speluncis et cavernis (in caves and holes)
Penis jaces et eternis agonibus. (you lie in pain and eternal agony) 
Dolus et fraus in actibus (Deceit and fraud are your deeds)
Tuis et bonis omnibus (and to all goodness)
Obviare missilibus tu niteris; (you damage with your missiles)
Auges que nephas sceleris (You increase the crime of sin)
Adam penis in asperis (that kept Adam in bitterness)
Te fuit Stigos carceris. (ithat was the prison of Styx).
Sed Maria Virgo, que, plena gratia, (But the Virgin Mary, full of grace)
Sua per puerperia (through her childbearing)
Illum ab hac miseria liberavit, (liberated him from this misery)
Precor et anguis tedia (I pray that torment)
Augeat et supplicia ([for Lucifer] increase)
Et nos ducat ad gaudia (while he leads us to joy)
Quos creavit. (us, whom he created).

Motectus:

O livoris feritas, (O fierce Envy)
que superna rogitas (who strive for the heights)
Et jaces inferius! (and lie in the depths)
Cur inter nos habitas? (why do you dwell among us)
Tua cum garrulitas (Your flattery)
Nos affatur dulcuis, (sweetly softens us)
Retro pungit sevius, (from behind it stings)
Ut veneno scorpius: (as the venom of the scorpion).
Scariotis falsitas (Judas Iscariot's falseness)
Latitat interius. (remains inside)
Det mercedes Filius (May the mercy of the Son)
Dei tibi debitas! (of God give you what is owed!)

Tenor:

Fera pessima. (The worst beast.)

videos.title: A. Brumel or J. Agricola & J. Ockeghem: Du tout plongiet (c.1490) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: A. Brumel or J. Agricola & J. Ockeghem: Du tout plongiet (c.1490) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Du tout plongiet / Fors seulement

This richly textured masterpiece by Antoine Brumel (or possibly Johannes Agricola based on different sources) contains some unusual features for that period. It excludes any soprano or alto parts, and the lowest of the voices dips down to an incredible 2 Cs below middle C.  Hence the music would most aptly fit a TTBB quartet. Additionally, it interweaves two different French tunes into one: the "Du tout plongiet" (presumably by Antoine Brumel) supplies the outer voices (tenor, baritone and low bass) while the superius from "For seulement,  l'actente que je meure" by Johannes Ockeghem is transposed down an octave plus a whole tone into the second tenor range. Although printed in the early decades of the 16th century, this combinative chanson was likely a product of the late 15th century - perhaps slightly before or around the time of Ockeghem's death in 1497. Nevertheless, the structure of the tune was somewhat "old school" by around 1500 with its irregular and unpredictable melody lines — reminiscent of an older 15th century French style.
 
"Du tout plongiet" comes to us from multiple sources: principally, the exquisite Chansonnier of Margaret of Austria (a.k.a. Bibliothèque royale de Belgique ms 228) and the Basevi Firenze ms 2439. As was common for books gifted to aristocratic patrons, the Brussels ms 228 is one of the most elaborately illuminated manuscripts of the High Renaissance. 

The French text for this piece was entered using the Synthesizer V voice encoding program and the Kevin voice bank. Pronunciation of 15h century French was adapted from Chatgpt and Timothy McGee’s textbook “Singing Early Music.”

Text 1:

Du tout plongiet au lac de desespoir,
Trouve me suis sans attente n'espoir
D'avoir jamais des biens de Fortune;
Mais, se trouver puis scayson oportune,
Je me assairay d'en quelque chose avoir.

Translation:

Plunged completely into a lake of despair,
I can neither expect nor hope
to ever enjoy Fortune's graces.
But should I find the opportunity,
I shall try to have it.

Text 2:

Fors seulement latente que je meure,
En mon las cueur, nul espoir ne demeure,
Car mon malheur si fort me tourmente
Qui n'est douleur que par vous je ne sente,
Pourceque suis de vous perdre bien seure.

Translation:

Except waiting for death
there remains no hope in my heart,
because my sorrow fiercely torments me
that I feel nothing but sorrow for you,
for I am very certain of losing you.

Descriptions of the photos:

1. The superius (Tenor 1) line from "Du tout plongiet", Brumel / Ockeghem, Brussels ms 228
2. You or Death, detail from ornamental shield, c1480
3. The cantus firmus line with the words "For seulement", Brumel / Ockeghem, Brussels ms 228
4. Orfeo playing and singing to the beasts of the forest, Luca della Robbia, c1439
5. Amour and the forlorn Lover, from Roman de la Rose, British Library Harley 4425,

videos.title: Robert Whyte (White): Tota pulchra es (c.1558) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Robert Whyte (White): Tota pulchra es (c.1558) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Robert Whyte (c.1538-1574) was born during the lifetime of King Henry VIII but achieved musical success during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I. There has been some debate regarding the purpose of his Marian antiphon "Tota pulchra es." Some scholars have speculated that it was dedicated to Mary I on the occasion of her coronation in 1553. The retro feel of this work with its high pitched boy soprano lines with richly textured, imitative 6 part polyphony (SATTBB), certainly suggests a pre-Elizabethan provenance. However, Whyte would have been only 15 years old and probably too young to have been granted a commission of such auspicious and grandiose import. Instead, this piece, with its thrice repeated finale "shall be crowned" ("coronaberis") may have been intended for the coronation of Elizabeth in 1558. There is no mention of the Virgin Mary which would have more directly targeted the yet unmarried Queen Mary in this setting of "Tota pulchra es." Whyte used a more secular (somewhat erotically themed) Old Testament text "Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te" instead of the more frequently used 4th Century Catholic prayer "Tota pulchra es, Maria. Et macula originalis non est in te" (which would have been more appropriate for the previous queen, Mary I.) The more "retro" compositional style may have been Whyte's assertion of his Catholic roots just like Tallis' use of similar musical elements in the antiphons "Gaude gloriosa" and "Videte miraculum." The original Medieval chant is tucked away in the first bass line.

In this rendition, I used the Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V to simulate boy sopranos and 4 adult male voices. The antiphon is pitched a half step up to be closer in range to A4=466. The original, non-texted MIDI was created by Gervais Frykman and can be found at cpdl.org. The Latin pronunciation here has been adjusted to approximate late Medieval Anglo-Latin. "Recessit" is therefore rendered as "resessit" instead of the more Italianate "ret͡ʃessit" familiar to modern choruses; and "macula" is "makyula" instead of "macula."

Text and translation:

Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te;
 favus distillans labia tua; mel et lac sub lingua tua;
 odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata:
 jam enim hiems transiit, imber abiit et recessit.
 Flores apparuerunt;
 vineae florentes odorem dederunt,
 et vox turturis audita est in terra nostra:
 surge, propera, amica mea:
 veni de Libano, veni, coronaberis

You are all fairness, my lady, and spotless.
 Your lips distill nectar. Honey and milk are under your tongue
 The scent of your perfumes surpass all aromas.
 For now the winter is past and the rain is receded and gone.
 The flowers have appeared.
 The flowering vines yield up their fragrance
 And the voice of the turtle dove is heard in our land.
 Rise up my love,
 Come from Lebanon, come, and you shall be crowned.

4. Octagon dome and ceiling of Ely Cathedral

8. South Nave aisle, Ely Cathedral

videos.title: Heinrich Isaac: Isbruck (Innsbruck) ich muß, dich lassen (c.1495) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Heinrich Isaac: Isbruck (Innsbruck) ich muß, dich lassen (c.1495) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Isbruck ich muss, dich lassen

  0:06  Isbruck I. Original lieder for 4 voices with verse 1
  1:13  Isbruck II with verse 2
  2:07  Isbruck I. Original lieder for 4 voices with verse 3

"Isbruck ich muß" (or "Innsbruck ich muss, dich lassen" in modern German) is a sentimental song of lost love in the quiet Alpine foothills of a nascent Austrian Empire.  It was composed by the Flemish master Heinrich Isaac who spent some time in the city during the reign of the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I. The explicit mention of Innsbruck in the text of the poem suggests that Isaac perhaps dedicated the song to the Emperor who had a close association with the Austrian town. The structure of the original lieder (Isbruck I) is somewhat more Italian and reminiscent of Josquin's "In te Domine, speravi" - homophonic and lyrical. Isbruck II is a very different musical setting although it uses the same text and vocal range. The latter is more elaborate with its crossing, imitative lines and elaborate counterpoint.

I entered the text using the Kevin voice bank in Synthesizer V applying both English and Spanish phonemes to approximate Early New High German pronunciation. The original MIDI file of Isbruck I was created by Gerd Eichler while Isbruck II was compiled by Virginia Kaycoff. Both can be found on cpdl.org . 

Modern German text:

Innsbruck, ich muß dich lassen,
ich fahr dahin mein Strassen 
im fremde Land da hin.
Mein Freud ist mir genommen,
die ich nicht weiß bekommen,
wo ich im Elend bin.

Groß Leid muss ich jetzt tragen,
das ich allein tu klagen 
dem liebsten Buhlen mein
Ach Lieb, nun lass mich Armen
im Herzen dein Erbarmen
daß ich muss von dannen sein.

Mein Trost ob allen Weiben,
Dein tu ich ewig bleiben 
stets treu, der Ehren fromm.
nun muss dich Gott bewahren,
in aller Tugend sparen,
bis daß ich wieder komm!

Translation:

Innsbruck, I must leave you
I travel the road
to a foreign land.
My joy has left me
and I know not how to find it,
Here I will be in misery.

I must carry a great sadness
That I can only share
With my dearest love
O Love, now let me 
bear in my heart your pity 
That I must part from you.

My comfort above all women,
I stay yours forever,
always faithful, in true honor.
Now, may God protect you,
In all virtue,
Until I return.

videos.title: Guillaume Dufay: O sancte Sebastiane (c.1423)

localized.title: Guillaume Dufay: O sancte Sebastiane (c.1423)
localized.description:
This isometric motet for four voices by Guillaume Dufay was dedicated to the victims of the bubonic plagues that began in the middle of the 14th Century and sporadically recurred throughout the 15th century. He was a prolific composer in great demand who travelled widely across Western Europe, and, therefore, it is unclear if this musical work was referencing the outbreak of plague in Bologna, Florence or his hometown of Cambrai. Nevertheless, the style is suggestive of his early period of music making circa 1420-1430.

Saint Sebastian, from whom the composer seeks divine intervention, was a Roman martyr (and incidentally the patron saint of Cambrai), and a mystical figure who was broadly regarded as the intercessor who could rescue humanity from the ravages of the Black Plague.

The musical structure is derived from the French Ars Nova and Ars Subtilior ballades, virelais and motets of the previous century. Certain elements such as differing texts in each vocal part, the hocketed passages, the long melismatic lines on single vowels harken back to Machaut's generation in the mid-14th Century.

I used a MIDI file compiled by N. Nakamura on his website Atrium Maucamedi. I used the Kevin voice bank with Spanish language settings in the Synthesizer V program. Since the fourth vocal part (designated "Tenor" in the original score) has no text, I applied the words from the Countertenor part just above it since there are many rhythmic similarities between the two voices.

++++++++++

TEXT:

Triplum / Cantus I

O sancte Sebastiane,  
Semper, vespere et mane,  
Horis cunctis et momentis  
Dum adhuc sum sanae mentis,  
Me protege et conserva  
Et a me, martyr, enerva  
Infirmitatem noxiam  
Vocatam epidemiam.  
Tu de peste hujusmodi  
Me defende et custodi  
Et omnes amicos meos,  
Qui nos confitemur reos  
Deo et sanctae Mariae  
Et tibi, o martyr pie.  
Tu Mediolanus civis  
Hanc pestilentiam, si vis,  
Potes facere cessare  
Et ad Deum impetrare,  
Quia a multis est scitum,  
Quod de hoc habes meritum.  
Zoe mutam tu sanasti  
Et sanatam restaurasti  
Nicostrato ejus viro,  
Hoc faciens modo miro.  
In agone consolabas  
Martyres et promittebas  
Eis sempiternam vitam  
Et martyribus debitam.  
Amen  

Motetus / Cantus II

O martyr Sebastiane,  
Tu semper nobiscum mane  
Atque per tua merita  
Nos, qui sumus in hac vita,  
Custodi, sana et rege  
Et a peste nos protege  
Praesentans nos trinitati  
Et virgini sanctae matri.  
Et sic vitam finiamus,  
Quod mercedem habeamus  
Et martyrum consortium  
Et Deum videre pium.  

Contratenor

O quam mira refulsit gratia  
Sebastianus, martyr inclytus,  
Qui militis portans insignia,  
Sed de fratum palma sollicitus  
Confortavit corda pallentia  
Verba sibi collato caelitus.  

TRANSLATION:

Triplum / Cantus I

O Saint Sebastian,  
always, in the morning and at night,  
at all hours and moments  
while I am still of sound mind,  
protect me and preserve me,  
and remove from me, O martyr,
The harmful sickness
that is the epidemic.  
From a plague of this sort  
defend me and guard me  
and all my friends,  
who confess ourselves as sinners  
before God and holy Virgin Mary  
and you, O faithful martyr.  
You, a citizen of Milan,  
if you will it,  
can make this pestilence cease  
and beseech God,  
because it is known to many
that you have merit in this matter.  
You healed Zoe the mute  
And restored her
to her husband Nicostratus,  
doing so in a miraculous manner.  
In their agony you comforted  
the martyrs and promised them  
eternal life  
and all that is due to martyrs.  

Amen  

Motetus / Cantus II

O martyr Sebastian,  
you always remain with us  
and by your merits  
guard, heal, and rule over us  
who live this life,  
and from plague protect us  
Present us to the Trinity  
and to the virgin mother Mary.  
so may we finish our life,  
and be rewarded with 
the companionship of martyrs  
And witness our holy God.  

Contratenor (and perhaps Tenor)

O how wondrously illuminates his grace.
St. Sebastian, illustrious martyr,  
who bearing a soldier’s insignia,  
but caring for the victory of his brothers,  
strengthened the faint hearted  
with words from heaven.

localized.description:
Woods, Rocks and Mountains

  0:06  Instrumental setting (flute, theorbo, bass gamba)
  1:51  Original lute songs (soprano, theorbo, bass gamba)

This lute song is a sole remnant of "Cardenio," a lost play by William Shakespeare and co-author John Fletcher. Most likely it was performed as a musical interlude at Blackfriars Theatre (or the Globe) in London during a performance of the dramatic work by the King's Men.

This vocal simulation was generated using the Solaria voice bank in Synthesizer V.  The theorbo and viola da gamba simulations were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2. The pronunciation was adjusted from the original Synthesizer V settings to simulate Early Modern English vowels and diphthongs according to Professor David Crystal's recommendations. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity v3.75

Text:

Woods, rocks and mountains and ye desert places
Where nought but bitter cold and hunger dwells,
Hear a poor maid's last words, killed with disgraces.
Slide softly whilst I sing, you silver fountains.
And let your hollow waters like sad bells
Ring, ring to my woes, whilst miserable I, 
Cursing my fortunes, drop a tear and die.

Griefs, woes, and groanings, hopes and all such lies
I give to broken hearts that daily weep; 
To all poor maids in love, my lost desiring. 
Sleep sweetly while I sing my bitter moaning,
And last, my hollow lovers that ne'er keep
Truth, truth in their hearts; while miserable I, 
Cursing my fortunes, drop a tear and die.

videos.title: Mille regretz and its instrumental parodies (c.1520-1540) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Mille regretz and its instrumental parodies (c.1520-1540) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Mille regretz

  0:06  Mille regretz a 4 (Josquin des Prez's original chanson, c.1520)
  1:58  Mille regres for lute or vihuela (Luis de Narváez, 1538)
  4:05  Pavane "Mille regretz" a 4 (Tielman Susato, 1551)
            a. chamber instruments (recorders, lutes, harp, viol)
            b. loud instruments (cornetto, sackbuts, tympani)

"Mille regretz" was likely a late work by the Franco-Flemish master Josquin des Prez (although some have disputed his authorship).  He probably composed this piece late in life after his return to his French-speaking homeland following a very long and illustrious musical career in Italy.  The earliest known copy of the song that has survived is the facsimile shown in this video (printed by the German-Flemish publisher Tielman Susato in 1549).

The Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, a Netherlander by birth, first heard this work probably as a teenager. The tune is melodious and lyrical, and it probably stayed with him for the rest of his adult life. Luis de Narváez, the Spanish lutenist, in 1538 describes "Mille regretz" as the Emperor's favorite. Vocal parodies on Mille Regretz include an entire mass by the Spaniard Cristóbal de Morales and a complex 6 part chanson by Nicholas Gombert (Please see my Spanish playlist for these two pieces). The 4 part Pavane "Milles regrets" by Tielman Susato has a more straightforward homophonic structure and is suited for a dignified slow dance.

Text:

Mille regretz de vous abandonner
Et d'eslonger vostre fache amoureuse,
Jay si grand dueil et paine douloureuse,
Quon me verra brief mes jours definer.

Translation:

A thousand regrets for leaving you
and parting from your loving face,
I feel so much sadness and such painful distress,
that it seems to me my days will soon fade away.

videos.title: Giuseppino Cenci (del Biado): Fuggi fuggi fuggi (c.1600) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Giuseppino Cenci (del Biado): Fuggi fuggi fuggi (c.1600) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Fuggi, fuggi, fuggi da questo cielo

  0:01  Original dance melody (violins, viols, recorders, dulcian, lute, tambourine)
  1:12  Verse 1 (male alto & instruments)
  2:18  Verse 2 (male alto & instruments)

------------

On the surface, "Fuggi, fuggi, fuggi" is a short and free-spiriated song about the delights of the Spring season based on a popular Renaissance dance tune. But its metamorphosis through the centuries has been quite remarkable. Originally, the melody was titled Il Ballo di Mantua (The Dance from Mantua) or Il Mantovano (the Mantuan). Then around the year 1600, Giuseppino Cenci (del Biado), a well known tenor of that era, assembled a songbook that was likely his own performance edition (since it is roughly scribbled out in his own handwriting).  That once catchy tune mutated into a huge range of different song genres: a ballroom dance tune by Gasparo Zannetti (1645), an early Baroque violin sonata by Biagio Marini (1655), an English country dance by John Playford, a 19th Century symphonic fantasy by the Czech composer Bedřich Smetana in the Moldau (from Má vlast) and last, but not least, the Israeli national anthem "Hatikva." There has even been a 1970s folk rock arrangement with the same melody by the 20th century Italian singer-songwriter Angelo Branduardi.

I created the MIDI file from a pdf file of the full score by Steven Hendricks. The instrumental parts were rendered using the iPhone app MusicStudio2 and the falsetto voice was encoded in Synthesizer V using the KEVIN voice bank with a Spanish language phoneme set. 

----------

Text:

Fuggi fuggi fuggi da questo cielo
Aspro e duro spietato gelo
Tu che tutto imprigioni e leghi
Né per pianto ti frangi o pieghi
fier tiranno, gel de l'anno
fuggi fuggi fuggi là dove il Verno
su le brine ha seggio eterno.

Vieni vieni candida vien vermiglia
tu del mondo sei maraviglia
Tu nemica d'amare noie
Dà all'anima delle gioie
messaggera per Primavera
tu sei dell'anno la giovinezza
tu del mondo sei la vaghezza.

Translation:

Fly fly fly from this sky,
harsh and difficult, relentlessly cold.
You, who shackle all in prison
neither bending nor weeping.
You, the year's cruel, frozen tyrant,
fly fly fly to wherever winter
has its eternal throne in frost.

Come, come white, come vermilion,
you are the marvel of the world.
You, nemesis of all things dreary,
give joy to the soul
by your message of spring.
You are the youth of the year
and the beauty of the world.

-----------

videos.title: Michael Praetorius: Gott der Vater wohn uns bei (1605) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Michael Praetorius: Gott der Vater wohn uns bei (1605) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This Lutheran hymn is based on the essential Catholic tenet of the Holy Trinity: the Father, Son and Holy Ghost. This opus for 8 voices was Michael Praetorius' Protestant German re-imagining of the Northern Italian polychoral motet developed by Giovanni Gabrieli, cultivated by Claudio Monteverdi, and finally imported by Hans Leo Hassler to Germany. It is not clear whether or not instruments were used in the performance of such pieces, but the iconography on the cover of Musae Sioniae (whence this particular motet comes) illustrates a large (albeit fanciful) ensemble consisting of church organ, brass band, string band, harp and a grand host of singing angels. The two choruses join together in tight vertical formation on the words "mit allen rechten Christen" (with all true Christians) and again at the end on "Amen. Das sei wahr" (Amen. Let this be done). 

This recording divides the eight voices into a SATB Chorus with boy soprano (in the right gallery) and lower pitched AATB Chorus II (in the left gallery), string band (doubling the SATB group) and brass band (doubling the AATB group). The singing voices in this video were rendered using the Solaria (two boy sopranos) and Kevin (for all the other voices) in Synthesizer V. The instrumental sounds were created with Music Studio 2 on an iPhone. The string ensemble consists of 2 violins, 2 viols (with harpsichord and violone). The brass ensemble consists of cornetto, 3 sackbuts (with pipe organ doubling the bass) and chitarrone. The reverb, echo and de-essing steps were applied with Audacity v 3.75. This recording is best heard on a good set of headphones that can effectively separate the left and right stereo fields.  

++++++++++

German text

Gott der Vater wohn' uns bei
Und laß uns nicht verderben.
Jesus Christus wohn' uns bei
Und laß uns nicht verderben.
Heiliger Geist der wohn uns bei,
Und laß uns nicht verderben,
Mach' uns von allen Sünden frei
Und hilf' uns selig sterben.
Vor dem Teufel uns bewahr,
Halt' uns bei festem Glauben,
Und auf dich laß uns bauen,
Aus Herzens Grund vertrauen,
Dir uns lassen ganz und gar;
Mit allen rechten Christen
Entfliehen des Teufels Listen,
Mit Waffen Gottes uns rüsten.
Amen! Amen! das sei wahr,
So singen wir, Alleluja!

Translation

God, our Father, stay with us,
Let us never be corrupted.
Jesus Christ, stay with us,
Let us never be corrupted.
Holy Ghost stay with us,
Let us never be corrupted
Free us from all sins
And give us a blessed death.
Save us from the Devil
Keep us firm in faith.
And let us trust in you
With humble hearts.
Let us flee completely,
with all true Christians 
The devil's trickery
With God's armor and shield.
Amen, amen! Let this be done.
So sing we, Halleluia!

++++++++++

videos.title: Thomas Tallis: Gaude gloriosa Dei mater (c.1545) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Thomas Tallis: Gaude gloriosa Dei mater (c.1545) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Gaude gloriosa Dei mater

   0:06  Verse 1 (Su, D, B)
   1:56  Verse 2 (Ct, T, Sp, D)
   3:21  Verse 3 (tutti)
   3:54  Verse 4 (tutti)
   7:06  Verse 5 (Sp1, Sp2, Su1, Su2, B)
   9:05  Verse 6 (D, Ct, T)
 10:50  Verse 7 (tutti)
 12:01  Verse 8 (Su, Ct, B1, B2)
 13:44  Verse 9 (tutti)

[Abbreviations: Sp (sexta pars, high soprano), Su (superius, high alto), D (discantus, low alto or tenor 1), Ct (contratenor, tenor 2), T (tenor, bariton or tenor 3), B (bassus)]
  
Stylistically, Tallis' Gaude gloriosa, a Latin antiphon dedicated to the Virgin Mary, bears the features of earlier English composers such as William Cornysh, John Browne and Robert Fayrfax. It retains the traditional high soprano voice, the impossibly long melismata, the intricately interwoven polyphony and the ever-expansive false cadences. Director and researcher David Skinner has suggested that this magnum opus was probably composed at the end of King Henry VIII's reign. He cites a fragment containing the same melodic lines but with English text ("Deliuer me from my deceytful ennemies") penned by the King's sixth and last queen, Catherine Parr during the French campaign. The dramatic effect of the piece comes with the repeated declaration of "Gaude Virgo" with the full chorus coming together in vertical alignment.

The troubled period of the English Reformation, which included the Dissolution of the Monasteries, lasted 5 years (1536-1541), and it weighed heavily on Tallis, a life long Catholic. His effusive, insistent devotion to the memory of the Virgin Mary was a statement of personal faith in the midst of unprecedented, relentless turmoil and persecution. 

This soundtrack was created using Charles Giffen’s MIDI (CPDL.org). In this rendition, I used the Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V.  I adjusted the phonemes to approximate 16th century Anglo-Latin pronunciation according to recommendations by Timothy McGee. The original piece was written for 6 vocal ranges (sextus pars (SP), superius (Su), discantus (D), countratenor (CT), tenor (T) and bassus (B)) and at least 9 independent singers (because the SP, Su and B parts split into contrapunctal duets in the middle of the piece).

fessi cura, pes labentis, mundi lux, et peccatorum refugium.

localized.description:
Antonilla es desposada

  0:06  Villancico for 3 voices (ATB)
  1:56  Instrumental arrangement (shawm, 2 trombones)

Juan del Encina (or Enzina) is considered by some to be the father of modern Spanish drama. Indeed, even this very short villancico has a self-contained storyline, albeit somewhat lighthearted. The simple, monophonic piece can be found in the huge collection of late Spanish Medieval and early Renaissance music "El Cancionero Musical de Palacio."

I used the Synthesizer V program with the Natalie and Kevin voice banks to reproduce the original Spanish text. The instrumental sounds were created using Music Studio 2.0 (iPhone app). Reverb and echo were added with Audacity. The Spanish phonemes were slightly altered to simulate late 15th century pronunciation.

Text:

Antonilla es desposada; (Antonilla is married)
hagotelo, Juan, saber. (Let him know, Juan)
¡Jur'á diez, no puede ser! (Swear to God, it can't be!)

No seas tan rebellado, (Don't get so rebellious)
que yo la vi desposar; (that I saw her marry)
y mucho de su cantar (and much of his singing)
vi el lugar regocijado; (I saw the place rejoicing)
y a Toribio el desposado (and Toribio, the groom)
vi atestado de placer. (I saw [him] full of joy)
¡Jur'á diez, no puede ser! (Swear to God, it can't be!)

videos.title: Johann Walter: Vias tuas, Domine (c.1535) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Johann Walter: Vias tuas, Domine (c.1535) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This motet by Johann Walter was one of many pieces that he wrote in Latin for use in the early Lutheran Church. Although one might associate the Walter, who was a close adherent to Martin Luther, with homophonic hymns written in the Germanic vernacular, he was also a transitional figure who found inspiration in both the old Franco-Flemish and new German musical styles. This song for 5 voices derives its text from two lines tucked away in the 24th Psalm of King David declaring God to be the ultimate path to salvation. It, along with many other pieces by the same composer, were copied in Torgau under Walter's supervision into a little known manuscript 83795 (olim M 369m) catalogued at the Bibliothek des Germanischen Nationalmuseums. Only the tenor voice has survived in this earliest known transcription. A later, more professionally copied score for all 5 voices appears in the so-called Gothaer Chorbuch from 1545.

The Latin text for this MIDI rendition was inputted using the Synthesizer V software with the Solaria (boy soprano) and Kevin (alto 1, alto 2, tenor and bass) voice banks with the Spanish phoneme setting. I adjusted the Latin to reflect 16th century German pronunciation according to recommendations in "Singing Early Music" (ed. Timothy McGee). Thus “vias” is “fias” and “edoce” is “edotse” (instead of the Italian “edotʃe.”) . Reverb and echo were added with Audacity.

Text: 
Vias tuas, Domine, demonstra mihi, (Show me your ways, O Lord)
et semitas tuas edoce me. (and teach me your narrow path)

Description of the photos:

1. Score for the soprano and bass for "Vias tuas," Johann Walter, Gothaer Chorbuch, 1545
2. Concert of sacred music, Hans Burgkmair, c1530. 
3. Interior of All Saints' Church, commonly referred to as Schlosskirche (Castle Church, Wittenberg) where Luther preached his sermons and Walter directed the church choir in hymns and motets.
4. King David with psaltery singing the Psalms, illustration from MS Harley 2953, Anon. Southern German, c1530
5. Christ risen, Matthias Grünewald, c1515

videos.title: Guillaume de Machaut: Trop plus est bele / Biauté paree / Je ne sui (c.1355) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Guillaume de Machaut: Trop plus est bele / Biauté paree / Je ne sui (c.1355) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Trop plus est bele / Biaute paree / Je ne sui mie certeins

  0:06  Je ne sui (cantus firmus line transposed one octave up)
  0:31  Original 3 part motet for voices alone (AAT)
  2:17  Arrangement for chamber instruments
             (portative organ, citole, harp)
  3:51  Arrangement for outdoor instruments
             (shawm, vielle, medieval trumpet, psaltery)

In a style typical of late French Ars Nova, Guillaume de Machaut's secular motet "Trop plus est bele" is complex and, at times, nearly chaotic. It consists of 3 vocal parts, each with different lyrics. He most likely began writing the piece with a simple tenor line and then added the other two parts as ornamentation which included bold flourishes, oddly syncopated notes and hemiolas.  "Trop plus est bele" is thought to have been dedicated to his patron the Lady Bonne of Luxembourg, who succumbed at an early age during the Black Plague of 1349. All three parts are filled with yearning in the spirit of courtly love. It concludes on a final note in which the upper two voices intones "Amen" as if in prayer to Cupid (or God) while the tenor sings "Amis" (i.e. friend or lover). This and other motets can be found in a large, richly illuminated collection that Machaut commissioned towards the end of his life.

In this latest rendition, I used Synthesizer V and the Kevin voice bank to simulate 14th century French. For the pronunciation, I used the suggestions in "Singing Early Music" edited by Timothy McGee. The instrumental settings were created using Music Studio 2 on an iPhone.

Text (and translation):

Tenor:

  Je ne sui mie certeins d'avoir amie, (I am not certain to have my love)
  Mais je suis loiaus amis. (but I am a faithful lover)

Triplum:

 Trop plus est bele que Biauté (More beautiful than Beauty)
 Et millour que ne soit Bonté. (and better than Goodness she is)
 Pleinne de tout ce, a dire voir, (full of all this, speaking true)
 Que bonne et bele doit avoir, (That good and beauty she should have)
 Ce m'est vis. celle que desir (This I see. That which I desire)
 Et aim sans nul villain desir; (and I love with no wicked desire.)
 Dont se je l'aim, et je, qu'en puis. (Thus I love her, and I can do only that)
 Quant en sa fine biauté truis (When I find in her fine beauty)
 De tous mes maus la garison, (the sanctuary to all my woes)
 Leesse, confort, guerredon (Freedom, comfort, reward)
 Et secours de tous les meschiés (and safety from all the maladies)
 Dont par Desir sui entichiés, (Therefore, through desire I am in love)
 Comment qu'elle n'en sache rien; (How does she not know?)
 Car toute la joie et le bien (For all the joy and the good)
 Que j'ay, de sa grace me vient (which I have, comes from her grace)
 Sans plus, quant de li me souvient, (No more, when I remember her)
 N'autre bonte’ de li n'en port; (No other good do I take away)
 Si pri Amours qu'en tel acort (Thus I pray Love)
 Soit, pour ce que miex l'aim que my, (because I love her more than I love myself)
 Qu'elle me teingne pour amy. Amen. (That she take me for her lover. Amen)

Motetus:

  Biaute’ paree de valour, (Beauty adorned with valor)
  Desirs qui onques n'a sejour (Desires which never stops)
  D'acroistre, eins croist de jour en jour (Growing, grow one day to the next)
  En plaisance et en douce ardour; (In pleasure and in sweet ardor)
  Dous Regars, pris par grant savour, (Sweet looks taken with great joy)
  Tous pleins de promesse d'amour, (All filled with promise of love)
  D'espoir de joie, de tenrour  (of hope, joy and tenderness)
  Et de pointure de doucour, (And from the dart of sweetness)
  Font que j'aim des dames la flour. (make me love the flower of all ladies)
  Or me doint Diex grace et vigour (Thus God grant me grace and vigor)
  Que au gre’ d'Amours et a s'onnour  (by the will of Cupid and to his honor)
  La puisse servir sans folour. Amen. (I can serve without folly)

videos.title: Johann Walter: Nun bitten wir den heiligen geist a 6 (c.1535) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Johann Walter: Nun bitten wir den heiligen geist a 6 (c.1535) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Nun bitten wir den heiligen Geist / Kom heiliger Geist Herre Gott

  0:06  Original Walter setting for 6 voices
  2:10  Instrumental setting for outdoor band (2 cornetti, 2 sackbuts, 2 shawms) 

Johann Walter wrote two beautifully crafted versions of "Nun bitten wir" (one for 5, and this one for 6 voices) based on a popular Lutheran hymn, which in turn was loosely based on a 13th Century Leise "Veni sancte spiritus" from the Catholic liturgy. The Lutheran service has historically used this hymn for the Feast of the Pentecost, or the service for the Holy Ghost. Luther added 3 additional sets of lyrics although they were not included in the 1537 edition by Walter. Unlike the Lutheran hymns with homophonic alignment of the voices, this piece is more akin to the elaborate polyphonic motets of his Catholic contemporaries in the Netherlands such as Gombert and Clemens non Papa. In this 6 voice composition, the second descant line is the cantus firmus from another popular Lutheran hymn tune "Komm heiliger Geist." After repeating "Komm heiliger" 3 times, the singer switches into Latin with the pre-Lutheran text "Veni sancte spiritus." 

The text for the hymn was entered using the Synthesizer V software with the Solaria voice bank for the two boy sopranos and Kevin for the alto, tenors and bass.  I created the instrumental sounds using MusicStudio2. 

Text and translation:

Nun bitten wir den heiligen Geist (We now plead to the Holy Ghost)
umb den rechten Glauben aller meist (for the true faith above all else)
das er uns behüte an unserm Ende (that He protects us at our end)
wen wir heim fahrn aus diesem elende (when we leave this wretchedness to go home)
Kyrie eleison. (Lord have mercy)

Cantus:

Kom heyliger Geyst, herre Gott (Come, Holy Ghost, Lord God)
Veni sancte spiritus (Come Holy Spirit)

videos.title: Paul Hofhaimer: Zucht eer und lob ir wonet bey with Synthesizer V (1500)

localized.title: Paul Hofhaimer: Zucht eer und lob ir wonet bey with Synthesizer V (1500)
localized.description:
Zucht eer und lob ir wonet bey (Zucht, Ehr und Lob ihr wohnet bei)

  0:06  Original Lieder for AATB
  2:20  Arrangement for Stadtpfeifer band (2 shawms, 2 trombones)

Paul Hofhaimer, a native Austrian composer of the Renaissance, was a colleague of Heinrich Isaac and organist-composer at the Viennese court of Emperor Maximilian I. Much of his vocal output consisted of German Lieder with lyrical melodies and relatively simple harmonies. This song however, with its more complex interplay between the upper voices, is more akin to the works of his Franco-Flemish contemporaries. The theme is one of courtly love and the worship by a lonely young gallant for a noble lady.

The original MIDI file was compiled by Allen Garvin and uploaded to CPDL.org.  I used the Kevin voice bank in Synthesizer V to generate the vocal simulation. The instrumental sounds were generated with an iPhone app Music Studio 2. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Zucht eer und lob ir wonet bey, (Nobility, honor and praise are with you)
gantz frey on alle reuw (completely free of all remorse)
bin ich verpflicht zu dienen ir; (I am obliged to serve you)
Sy hat fürwar das feinst gepert (You indeed have the finest bearing)
beschwert und höchlich mert (But burdened and great increased)
sich herzlich klag und sehnlich gir. (heartfelt sorrow and longing desire)

Seid ich nun weiß. zukünfftig not (Since I now know future trouble)
kein rhat auff erdt mich helffen mag (No advice on earth may help me)
es leit am tag erhör mein klag (I comes out in the day hear my shout)
die ich stets trag (that I always carry.)
sendt gnad mein glück ce ich verzag. (Send grace, O Fortune, as I despair)

videos.title: Henry Purcell: Countertenor arias from "Come Ye Sons of Art" (1694) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Henry Purcell: Countertenor arias from "Come Ye Sons of Art" (1694) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Come, Ye Sons of Art

   0:06  Duet: Sound the trumpet (2 male altos, harpsichord, cello, theorbo, double bass)
   2:51  Aria: Strike the viol (male alto solo, 2 violins, 2 recorders, cello, double bass, theorbo, harpsichord)

++++++++++

"Come Ye Sons of Arts" also known as the Ode for Queen Mary's Birthday was an entirely secular composition by Henry Purcell dedicated to Mary II Stuart of the co-regents William and Mary. There is occasional word painting interspersed throughout the ode such as in the song "Sound the trumpet" written for 2 countertenors whose long vowels imitate the penetrating and hollow sonority of competing trumpets. In contrast to the first aria, "Strike the viol" is a celebration of small chamber instruments listing violins, viol, lute, harp and flutes (or, more likely, recorders). Most likely, only male voices were used in courtly circles of Restoration England (in contrast to early English opera which was often presented with mixed gender casts).

The countertenor simulation was generated using the Kevin English language voice bank and the Synthesizer V software. The instrumental sounds were generated on the iPhone using Music Studio 2. The raw MIDI files were downloaded from the website classicalarchives.com; they were uploaded by John Cowles and Sirot Thongkam. I corrected a few errors in the viola line. I adjusted the pronunciation to reflect something closer to Original Pronunciation in late 17th century London based on Wikipedia's "Great Vowel Shift" chart.  

++++++++++

Lyrics:

1. Sound the trumpet

Sound the trumpet, till around
You make the list'ning shores rebound.
On the sprightly hautboy play;
All the instruments of joy,
That skilful numbers can employ,
To celebrate the glories of this day.

2. Strike the viol

Strike the viol, touch the lute,
Wake the harp, inspire the flute.
Sing your patroness's praise,
In cheerful and harmonious lays.

++++++++++

videos.title: Francisco Guerrero: Maria Magdalena (c.1565)

localized.title: Francisco Guerrero: Maria Magdalena (c.1565)
localized.description:
Despite the existence of an enormous number of Renaissance paintings and sculptures re-imagining the face and figure of Mary Magdalen (or Mary of Magdala, known to many as "the Apostle among apostles") there are very few musical works from any historical era that commemorate this central figure in the Christian faith.  The narrative events in Guerrero's magnum opus were based on the text of Mark 16:1-6 which begins with Mary's visitation to Jesus' tomb and ends with the announcement of Jesus' resurrection. One can hear intricate canonic passages, homophonic lines for emphasis and long suspensions reminiscent of his contemporary Giovanni Palestrina. The 6 voice motet is divided into two equal length parts, each ending with an extended and elaborate "alleluia." There are a pair of sopranos, a pair of tenors and a pair of basses each imitating the other and sometimes joining together in dense harmony. The elaborate polyphony is somewhat of a throwback to an earlier Franco-Flemish style that by the 1560s was no longer sanctioned by the Papal Curia which encouraged a more simple homophonic structure. The publication of Guerrero’s works in Venice while he resided in Seville attests to his international fame.

This soundtrack was created using the Solaria (soprano 1 and 2) and Kevin (tenor 1, tenor2, bass 1 and bass 2) voice bank in Synthesizer V. Reverb and echo was added using Audacity. The original MIDI file and pdf score were created by John David Eaton and uploaded to CPDL.org. I shifted the notes up a whole step to attain the pitch range of the original score. I adjusted the Spanish language phonemes in both the Solaria and Kevin to accommodate the likely pronunciation of Iberian Latin in the 16th Century.   

Latin Text:

[Prima pars]
Maria Magdalene et altera Maria emerunt aromata
ut venientes ungerent Iesum.
Et valde mane una Sabbatorum
veniunt ad monumentum
orto iam sole, alleluia.

[Secunda pars]
Et introeuntes in monumentum
viderunt iuvenem sedentem in dextris
coopertum stola candida
et obstupuerunt.
Qui dicit illis:
'Iesum quem queritis Nazarenum cruxifixum:
surrexit, non est hic.
Ecce locus ubi posuerunt eum.' Alleluia.

Translation:

[Prima pars]
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary brought spices
so that they might anoint Jesus.
And early on the Sabbath,
they came to the tomb,
just after sunrise. Alleluia.

[Secunda pars]
And entering the tomb,
they saw a young man sitting on the right
dressed in a pure white robe,
and they were astounded.
He said to them:
"You are looking for the crucified Nazarene:
he has risen, he is not here.
Look, there is the place they put him." Alleluia.

videos.title: Philippe Verdelot: Italia mia (1538) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Philippe Verdelot: Italia mia (1538) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
"Italia mia" is a madrigal for 5 voices by the Franco-Flemish expatriate Philippe Verdelot who spent most of his adult life in Italy.  This hymn-like tune is based on a Petrarchan sonnet written two centuries earlier. Although the title might suggest a nationalistic fervor extolling the beauty of Italy and Italian Renaissance culture, the actual theme is one of mourning and despair.  It is a lamentation of sorts similar in spirit to the biblical lamentations of Jeremiah and Isaiah for the fallen Israelites. The song references the many devastating wars that ravaged the Italian peninsula during Petrarch's lifetime (especially his beloved city of Florence). The Rivers Tiber and Arno are the wellsprings of the two greatest cities devastated by conflict and plague, Florence and Rome -- which incidentally were the same two Italian city states in which Verdelot spent time during the late 1520s to witness a different kind of catastrophe. During Verdelot's own lifetime, Rome was sacked by the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V in 1527 and Florence was attacked in 1530 by the same Emperor and a new Pope. Musically this madrigal is a blend of Franco-Flemish counterpoint with imitative passages punctuated by homophonic choruses in the Italian frottola tradition.

Allen Garvey created the original MIDI file and uploaded it to CPDL.org. In this most recent rendition, I used Synthesizer V with the Natalie voice bank in the alto part and the Kevin voice bank in the four male vocal parts. Reverb and echo were added with Audacity.

++++++++++

Text:

Italia mia, ben ch’el parlar 
Sia indarno a le piaghe mortali
Che nel’ bel corpo tuo spesse veggio
Piacem’ almen’ ch’ e’ mia sospir’ sien quali
Sper’ il Tever’ et l’Arno
E’l Pove doglioso et grave hor seggio.
Rector’ del ciel’, io cheggio
Che la pieta che ti conduce in terra
Ti volgha al tuo dilect’ almo paese:
Vedi, Signor’ cortese,
Di che levi cagion che crudel guerra
I cor’, ch’ indur’ et serra
Marte superb’ et fero
Apri tu, padr’ e’ntenerisci et snoda;
Ivi fa ch’el tuo vero
Qual’ io mi sia per la mia lingua s’oda.

Translation (adapted from Anthony S. Kline):

My Italy, though words cannot heal
the mortal wounds
so dense, I see on your lovely body,
at least I pray that my sighs might bring
some hope to the Tiber and the Arno,
and the Po, that sees me now sad and gloomy.
Ruler of Heaven, I hope
that the pity that brought You to earth,
will turn you towards your soul-delighting land.
Lord of courtesy, see
such cruel wars for such slight causes:
and hearts, hardened and closed
by proud, fierce Mars,
and open them, Father, soften them, set them free:
and, whatever I may be, let your Truth
be heard in my speech.

++++++++++

videos.title: William Billings: "Africa" or Now shall my inward joys arise (c.1770) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: William Billings: "Africa" or Now shall my inward joys arise (c.1770) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This short hymn with the fanciful title "Africa" was one of William Billings' earliest compositions and also one of the earliest examples of harmonized music published in Colonial America. It was likely one of Billings' favorite tunes since he revised and reprinted the song twice more during the ensuing decade. The words in Verse 1 were taken from the hymn "Now shall my inward joys arise"  by the English Congregationalist minister Isaac Watts. Billings' first published version of this song dropped all references to God in Verse 1, perhaps to project a slightly more secular tone in accordance with the sentiments of the Enlightenment thinkers who tried to curb the religious sectarianism of the Old World. He may have added the final verse in his last edition (printed towards the end of the War in Independence) to capture the spirit of renewal in an America that needed much rebuilding after a long and bruising war against England. Not unlike compatriots like Ben Franklin and Thomas Jefferson, Billings was emblematic of the self-educated man. He was a tradesman who learned, composed, performed and published music on his own.

The original MIDI file was compiled by Stewart Lauters and uploaded to CPDL.org. For this "performance," I used the NATALIE voice bank for the soprano and alto parts and KEVIN for the tenor and bass parts.  In every other iteration of the hymn tune, I swapped the octave range of the soprano and tenor -- a common practice in Billings' time. I left out any doubling by organ or harpsichord since it was the composer's wish that amateurs be allowed to perform without being lorded over by professionals. The rough and ready quality of the singing in this soundtrack reflects a style of performance that has been kept alive by subsequent American choirs over the next centuries, especially in the rural South.

++++++++++

Text:

Now shall my inward joys arise,
And burst into a song;
Almighty love inspires my heart,
And pleasure tunes my tongue.

God on his thirsty Sion hill
Some mercy-drops has thrown,
And solemn oaths have bound his love
To show'r salvation down.

Why do we then indulge our fears,
Suspicions, and complaints?
Is he a God, and shall his grace
Grow weary of his saints?

Can a kind woman e'er forget
The infant of her womb,
And 'mongst a thousand tender thoughts
Her suckling have no room?

"Yet," saith the Lord, "should nature change,
And mothers monsters prove,
Sion still dwells upon the heart
Of everlasting love."

"Deep on the palms of both my hands
I have engrav'd her name;
My hands shall raise her ruin'd walls,
And build her broken frame."

++++++++++

1. Cover page from the 1st edition of William Billings' works (which contained the original, short version of "Africa,") printed by Paul Revere, 1770
2. Faneuil Hall (Boston) in 1775 (Billings' old stomping grounds), Charles Bryan, 1840
3. A printed version of "Africa" from the 1781 edition which contains the all six verses by Isaac Watts, published during the American Revolutionary War.
4. New South Church, Boston (where Billings may have learned to read and write music), Anonymous photo from c1860
5. Southeast view of Boston city proper, c1730
6. Map of the world with Africa at the center (perhaps similar to a map Billings might have arbitrarily glanced in order to give this piece its title), Jacques Nicolas Bellin, 1778 (reprinted from a 1748 original)

videos.title: Guillaume Dufay (?): Je vous pri / Tant que mon argent / Ma tres doulx amie (c.1450)

localized.title: Guillaume Dufay (?): Je vous pri / Tant que mon argent / Ma tres doulx amie (c.1450)
localized.description:
Je vous pri etc.

0:06  Original chanson for 4 voices
1:44  Instrumental arrangement (lute, bass lute, dulcimer, harp)

This combinative chanson for 4 lower voices (ATTT) appears in no fewer than six French and Italian manuscripts. The bottom two lines are cantus firmus from two different folk melodies whereas the upper two lines may have been added by Dufay to create four part polyphony. It is divided into a slow ponderous portion and a second part with faster tempo in a 3 rhythm. In the triple time segment, all four voices sing the same set of lyrics. Scholars have debated whether or the not the attribution of Dufay is correct since his name appears only in one very late, non-texted Florentine source. The untexted variants may have been intended for instrumental ensemble.

The vocal simulations were created with the Kevin voice bank in Synthesizer V. Reverb and echo were added with Audacity. Instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. The MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and uploaded to Musescore.com. The pronunciation of French that I used approximates what was likely heard in the mid-15th century.

videos.title: Pierre de Manchicourt: Ego sum panis vivus (c.1535)

localized.title: Pierre de Manchicourt: Ego sum panis vivus (c.1535)
localized.description:
This motet for the ceremony of the Eucharist for Ember Wednesday services was composed by the French composer Pierre de Manchicourt and printed by the Paris publisher Pierre Attaingnant in a collection dedicated solely to the works of this often ignored master of Renaissance polyphony. The piece consists of two parts of the which the second half concludes in a 3 rhythm. The imitative passages begin with a sequence introduced by a middle tenor and in quick succession, the other 4 voices (SATB) interweave a restless counterpoint throughout. The text is a passage recalling the imagery and mystery of the Last Supper and is paraphrased from John 6:48-52. Manchicourt spent much of his professional career in the service of the Spanish monarchy under Phillip II as director of the Flemish Chapel (capilla flamenca), but this specific work comes to us from his earlier years as a resident composer in the French city of Tours. One can hear the back and forth interchange of scalar passages among the 5 voices in a manner similar to the motets of Jean Mouton of the previous generation.

I compiled the MIDI file using a pdf score by Richard Mix which can be found at cpdl.org. I used the Solaria voice bank in Synthesizer V for the soprano (cantus) part and the Kevin voice bank for the male alto, tenor 1, tenor 2 and bass parts. I added reverb and echo using Audacity.

Text (and translation):

Ego sum panis vivus (I am the living bread)
qui de coelo descendi (who descended from heaven)
Si quis manducaverit ex hoc pane, (If anyone eats from this bread)
vivet in æternum: (he will live for eternity)
et panis quem ego dabo, (and the bread which I shall give)
caro mea est pro mundi vita.(is my flesh for the life of the world).
Alleluia.

Caro enim mea vere est cibus (for my flesh is truly food)
et sanguis meus vere est potus. (and my blood is truly drink)
Qui manducat meam carnem (He who eats my flesh)
et bibit meum sanguinem (and drinks my blood)
in me manet et ego in illo. (with remain in me and I in him)
Alleluia.

videos.title: Jacopo da Bologna: O cieco mondo (c.1350)

localized.title: Jacopo da Bologna: O cieco mondo (c.1350)
localized.description:
This mysterious 14th century madrigal for two voices by Jacopo da Bologna appears in at least 7 separate manuscript editions from the same period as the composer. Perhaps the poet was railing again the "The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune" relating to one of the many horrors of the mid-14th Century: the Black Death, the Great Schism, ecclesiastical corruption, devastating wars, etc. Or, perhaps the song was an oblique reference to Luchino Visconti of Milan (Jacopo's patron) who may have been murdered with poison by his third wife who feared his wrath after a marital indiscretion on her part.

The vocal simulations were generated using the Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V. Doubling of the voices with the sound of dulcimer and organetto was achieved with Music Studio 2.0. The MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and can be found on Musescore.com.

Text:

O cieco mondo di lusinghe pieno 
mortal veleno in ciascun tuo dilecto
fallac' e pien d' inganni e con sospetto
 
Foll'e coluy ch'a tte driçça' l freno 
quando a per men che nulla 'l ben che perde
Che sopr' ogn' altro amor luce er sta verde
 
Pero gia may de ti coluy non churi
Che frutto vuol gustar di dolci fiori

Translation:

O blind world, so full of flattery,
every pleasure you offer hides a deadly poison—
you're full of lies, tricks, and constant suspicion.

It's foolish to follow your lead,
when what you give is worth less than nothing
compared to the greater love that truly shines and lasts.

So let no one who seeks real sweetness
ever waste their time on you again.

videos.title: Claudin de Sermisy (or Jacotin?): Au pres de vous (c.1525) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Claudin de Sermisy (or Jacotin?): Au pres de vous (c.1525) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Au pres de vous

 0:06  Original chanson for 4 voices (ATTB) doubled by lute
 2:04  Instrumental arrangement for flute, lute, harp and bass viol

Although the actual authorship of this work is uncertain (Jacotin or Claudin de Sermisy), its popularity during the first half of the 16th century is not in question whatsoever.  There were multiple versions of this piece (for 2, 3 and 4 parts) printed in several editions by the best known music publishers in Paris including Pierre Attaingnant, Adrian Le Roy and Nicolas du Chemin. In Attaingnant's 1528 collection of 34 chansons, "Au pres de vous" is printed on the first page of his tome.  Moreover, an anonymous Franco-Flemish painting titled "Prodigal son" depicts a flautist playing from a manuscript of this same chanson and a lutenist playing from its corresponding tablature (see notes below in the Description of the photos)

This rendition of the chanson was created using the Synthesizer V software with the Solaria and Kevin voice banks. Both English and Spanish phonemic elements were used to generate an approximation of a 16th century northern French dialect. The instrumental arrangements were created using Music Studio 2. The original MIDI file was compiled by Laura Conrad using a reed organ setting and uploaded to the website serpentpublications.org . 

Text:

Au pres de vous secretement demeure
mon povre cueur, sans que nulle conforte,
et si languit pour la douleur qu'il porte
Puisque voulez, qu'en ce tourment il meure.

Translation

My poor heart secretly stays by you,
Without any comfort, it languishes for the pain it carries
Because you wish it dies of this torment.

-----------

videos.title: Michel Lambert: Ombre de mon amant (c.1660)

localized.title: Michel Lambert: Ombre de mon amant (c.1660)
localized.description:
Lambert was a prominent member of the musical hierarchy at the court of Louis XIV but was overshadowed by his more flamboyant and grandiose son-in-law, Jean-Baptiste Lully. This short air de cours was likely an earlier work written for voice and basso continuo. It starts with an instrumental ritornello in the manner of Italian opera from the generation of Claudio Monteverdi and Michelangelo Rossi. As with earlier airs, the monody is simple and probably gave latitude to the performer to improvise ornaments and flourishes.

The original MIDI file was compiled by Théau Lizon and uploaded to Musescore.com. I used the Natalie voice bank in Synthesizer V. Instrumental simulations were created using Music Studio 2.0. This instrument "ensemble" includes two violins, cello, double bass, theorbo and harpsichord.

Text (and translation):

Ombre de mon amant, (Shadow of my lover,) 
ombre toujours plaintive, (ever plaintive shadow,)
Hélas! que voulez-vous! je meurs. (Alas! What do you want? I die.)
Soyez un moment attentive (Be attentive for a moment)
Au funeste récit de mes vives douleurs. (To the grim tale of my sorrows.)
C'est sur cette fatale rive (It was on this fatal shore)
Que j'ay veu vostre sang couler avec mes pleurs.
    (That I saw your blood flow with my tears.)
Rien ne peut arrester mon ame fugitive (Nothing can restrain my fleeing soul)
Je cède à mes cruels malheurs. (I yield to my cruel misfortunes.)

Ombre de mon amant,... etc.

videos.title: Paul Hofhaimer: Mein einigs A (c.1500) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Paul Hofhaimer: Mein einigs A (c.1500) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Mein einigs A

  0:06  Instrumental arrangement (recorder, 3 viols, 2 lutes, harp) 
  2:26  Verse 1, or the original Lied (ATTB, 2 lutes, harp)
  4:47  Verse 2 (soprano, 2 lutes, harp, bass viol)
  7:07  Verse 3 (ATTB, 3 viols, 2 lutes, harp)

This mostly homophonic tune is a gentle love song in the German vernacular by the Austrian court composer Paul Hofhaimer. The singer refers to a love interest as  ‘A.’ and does not use a full name. Thus the target of affections will remain forever gender neutral. After all, "A" could just as well have been "Anna" or "Albrecht." The piece begins with a staggered, imitative entrance by the four singers, but they all neatly line up harmonically to finish each short segment in a unified cadence.

This soundtrack was generated using the Synthesizer V software with Solaria and Kevin voice banks. The instrumental sounds were produced using the iPhone app MusicStudio 2.0. Reverb and echo were added with Audacity. The original MIDI file was compiled by Allen Garvin and uploaded to CPDL.org.

2. Ob ich mit wesen von dir bin (Though I am physically far from you)
doch pleibt mein sin (still my thoughts [of you] remains
in lieb on falsch alweg bey dir; (in true love for you without deceit)
Und halt mich dein gehe wie es wöll (And hold myself as yours as is)
nit von mir stel (do not take from me)
mein hort bedenck der lieb an mir. (my treasure, remember my love for you)
Was frucht die selb uns bringen mag (whatever fruit this love may bring us)
auch wirt altag (still each day)
durch mich dein lob mit fleiß gemert (my praise of you is fast increased)
und pleib ... usw.

3. Ob ich fchon nit bin dein geleych (Though I am not your your equal)
ich ye nit weych (I will not stray)
in keynen weg von deinr zir; (in any way from your grace)
Was mir dein zucht vertrawen mag (What virtue you may entrust in me)

alweg in heimlich bey mir. (always, secretly in me)
Meinr lieb ich dir für andren gan (My love, I give myself to you above all)
biß zweifels an (without doubt)
du bist die recht (You are the true one)
