videos.title: Anonymous Spanish: Vi los barcos madre (c.1550) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Anonymous Spanish: Vi los barcos madre (c.1550) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Vi los barcos madre

  0:06  Tenor duet & instruments (recorder, vielle, lute, harp)
  2:06  Original villancico (SATT) with lute doubling

This somewhat melancholic song for four voices was likely written for mixed ensemble (1 woman and at least 2-3 men) given the high notes in the cantus part. It is a villancico from the mid-16th century collection of Spanish tunes known as the Cancionero de Upsala. It has a melody line in both the cantus and tenor parts that are counterpoint to one another. The two tenor parts also have a separate imitative passage. The format is the typical ABBA sequence, which gives it a somewhat repetitive and insistent quality. Despite the paucity of lyrical material, a deeper story may be embedded in these lines. In an age when Spain ruled the seas, men seeking gold and adventure travelled the Atlantic Ocean on grand galleons. A peasant girl may have seen such ships from the Iberian shores but knew that those imagined men were of a different world.

I compiled the MIDI file for this soundtrack from a score facsimile and entered the words using the Solaria and Kevin voice banks in the Spanish language in Synthesizer V. The instrumental simulations were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2. I adjusted the reverb and echo using Audacity.

Text:

Vi los barcos, madre, (I saw the ships, mother)
Vi los y no me valen. (I saw them and they are not for me)

Madre, tres moçuelas (Mother, three young girls)
No de aquesta villa, (not from this town)
En aguas corriente (in the running stream)
Lavan sus camisas. (wash their blouses)

Sus camisas, madre, (Those dresses, mother)
Vi los y no me valen. (I saw them and they are not for me)

videos.title: William Byrd: Praise our Lord, all ye Gentiles (1611) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: William Byrd: Praise our Lord, all ye Gentiles (1611) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
William Byrd: Praise our Lord, all ye Gentiles (1611), Original Pronunciation

This English verse anthem was printed in a curious collection of works titled "Psalmes, Songs and Sonnets" which contains a panoply of religious and secular vocal music as well as instrumental pieces by the greatest master of the English Renaissance, William Byrd. (He had assembled another earlier album of works with the same title in 1588.) It was to be the last publication who printing he personally supervised, and Byrd knew as much with his comment in the Dedication stating his weariness in old age.

Although Byrd is primarily remembered as an Elizabethan composer, this particular work was likely created during the reign of James I. It is an interesting hybrid of Anglican and Catholic elements. The text was taken from a 1599 translation of Psalm 117 by the Catholic intellectual Richard Verstegan.  Yet its richly textured canonic passages and English text suggest more kinship with the later Anglican services of Orlando Gibbons. The piece concludes with a long and winding "Amen" that almost forms an entire movement of its own.

The vocal simulations were created using the Solaria and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V. The original MIDI file without the words was compiled by David Fraser and uploaded to the website cpdl.org . The English phoneme presets in Synthesizer V were altered to mimic "Original pronunciation" from the Jacobean period. For example, mercy was likely pronounced "marsəi" and praise "prɛ:z."

Text:

Praise our Lord all ye Gentiles, praise him all ye people,
Because his mercy is confirmed upon us, and his truth remaineth for ever.
Amen.

videos.title: Juan del Enzina: Pues que jamás (c.1495) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Juan del Enzina: Pues que jamás (c.1495) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Pues que jamas olvidaros

  0:06  Original villancico for solo tenor (with viols and harp)
  2:22  Original villancico for 4 voices (ATTB)
  4:38  instrumental arrangement (cornetto, viols, sackbut, harp)

++++++++++

Juan dell Enzina (a.k.a. del Encina or de Fermoselle) is one of the best-represented composers in the largest collection of late Medieval / early Renaissance Spanish music known as "El Cancionero Musical de Palacio" (or "the Palace Songbook").  He was a prolific and masterful composer of the new style of Villancicos and other genres of Spanish courtly music. This little treasure "Pues que jamas olvidaros" was typical of a late 15th century villancico: a courtly love theme, a melody line in the cantus (with a convincingly standalone counterpoint line in the tenor), an ABBA sequence and an overall homophonic structure - similar to the frottole in Italy from the same period. Del Enzina served the royal court for most of his career and was intimately associated with King Ferdinand of Aragon and Queen Isabella of Castile.

This soundtrack was created using the Synthesizer V voice encoder program with only the KEVIN voice bank and the Spanish language setting. The default phoneme set was slightly altered to simulate early 16th century Spanish pronunciation. The original MIDI file without text was created by James Gibb and can be found on CPDL.org. 

--------------------

Text (with modern spelling)

Pues que jamás olvidaros
No puede mi coraçon
si me falta galardón
¡Ay, que mal hize en miraros!

Sera tal vista cobrar,
Gran dolor y gran tristura

Sera tal vista penar
Si me falleçe ventura.

Mas si vos, por bien amaros
Queréis darme galardon
No dira mi coraçon
Ay, que mal hize en miraros.
-----------------

Translation:

Since my heart can never forget you,
if I don't receive the reward,
how wrong I was to look upon you.

Seeing you will cause me
great pain and great sadness
This vision will pain me
if fortune fails to [grant my wish]

But if, for my true love
you want to give me reward,
my heart will not be sorrowful
Oh what a mistake I made to look upon you

-------------------

videos.title: Jean-Baptiste Lully: Incidental Music from "Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme" (1670)

localized.title: Jean-Baptiste Lully: Incidental Music from "Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme" (1670)
localized.description:
Instrumental music from the comedy-ballet “Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme”

  0:06 Ouverture
  2:35 Deuxieme Air
  3:24 Chaconne des Scaramouches Trivelins et Arlequin
  5:52 March pour la Ceremonie des Turcs
  
King Louis XIV of France and Navarre, often referred to as the Sun-King by his circle of royal sycophants, was also compared to the Greek god Apollo by the master artists of his generation.  Louis was a connoisseur of fine paintings, architectural marvels, colossal musical events, grand ballet spectacles and flamboyant ladies at court.  He was an extravagant extrovert, a dancer and a dandy who enjoyed dressing up in opulent finery and tall-heeled shoes.  He was also an absolute dictator and a formidable warrior who defeated the Dutch in pitched battle and established France as an undisputed European powerhouse both culturally and militarily.

Jean-Baptiste Lully (born Giovanni Lulli) was the King's court conductor and master of the instrumentalists. He was a naturalized French citizen, recognized for his mastery of the decadent and pompous style of Louis XIV's court musicians. He was born in Florence to modest means and frequently incorporated Italian characters and themes into his grand operatic productions.

The comedy-ballet "Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme," whose script was written by the great French playwright Molière and whose musical interludes were composed by maestro Lully, is a tale of a certain Monsieur Jourdain, a wealthy man who desperately sought membership in the French aristocracy. The story is one that describes a class tension that was ubiquitous throughout the 17th Century. A stereotypical buffoon, sometimes labelled nouvelle riche, born of humble origins, aspiring to reach a higher social standing through learning of art and music, fails to assimilate with the upper echelon due to his crude ways and fundamental ignorance. Humiliation of the bourgeoisie was a topic that may have entertained King Louis XIV and his entourage, but a century later would become the linchpin for the French Revolution and the downfall of the French monarchy under Louis XVI.

A full score of this semi-opera / ballet can be viewed at this link:

https://clara.imslp.org/work/5360?imslpIndex=30656

Although the original instrumentation is not specified throughout this magnum opus, I used the sounds of violins and oboes for the melody lines - as was customary in Lully’s court orchestra. Basso continuo instruments in the simulated ensemble include cellos, double bass, bassoon, harpsichord and theorbo. Percussion instruments include tympani and sleighbells. I used a MIDI editor app on the iPhone Music Studio 2.0.

localized.description:
This aria appears near the beginning of the Comedy-Ballet "Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme" (LWV 43) a multimedia music and dance production for the royal theater in Chambord for King Louis XIV's court. The satirical play and overall concept were the work of Molière. The music was written by Jean-Baptiste Lully, a French composer of Italian origin.

De puis qu'a ont rigueurs nos beaux yeux m'ont soumis
Si vous traitez ainsi, belle Iris qui vous aime,
Hélas, que pouriez vous faire a vos ennemis

Translation:

I languish night and day, my suffering is extreme.
Since to your control your lovely eyes subjected me;
If you thus treat, fair Iris, those you love [in this way],

videos.title: Harchadel (Arcadelt?): Deux vrays amantz (publ.1543)

localized.title: Harchadel (Arcadelt?): Deux vrays amantz (publ.1543)
localized.description:
Deux vrays amantz

  0:06  Original chanson for SATB
  1:42  Instrumental arrangement (four viols and harpsichord)

This chanson is given the attribution of "Harchadel" (without a first name) by the Parisian printer and publisher Pierre Attaingnant. Perhaps this is a misspelling of Jacques Arcadelt, a prolific Franco-Flemish composer from the first half of the 16th Century who was mostly active in Italy. It is a well-formed polyphonic piece with predictable repeats, and it presents an existential perspective on courtly love.

The original MIDI file was compiled by John Smith and uploaded to Musescore.com. I generated a vocal rendition using Synthesizer V with the Solaria (for soprano) and Kevin (for alto, tenor and bass) voice banks. Instrumental sounds were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. The reverb and echo and noise filter were applied with Audacity. As far as I can tell, this may be the first recording of this piece. 

Text: 

Deux vrays amantz
n'ont qu'ung vouloir ensemble
et par raison de raison se contentent
disant ainsy pour bien finir nos jours
honneur vault mieulx qui tristesse a tousjours
qui en la fin pert l'ame et corps ensemble

Translation:

Two true lovers
have but one will together,
and by the reason of reason, they are content,
saying thus, to end our days well:
honor is worth more than sorrow everlasting,
for in the end, both soul and body are lost together.

videos.title: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina: Credo from Missa Papae Marcelli (c.1562) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina: Credo from Missa Papae Marcelli (c.1562) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (1525-1594) is regarded, by many early music enthusiasts and musicologists, as the greatest composer of church polyphony in the Catholic tradition. He created an enormous corpus of liturgical masterpieces for the Papal Choir during his long and productive tenure in and around the Vatican. But the Missa Papae Marcelli (Mass for Pope Marcellus II, published in 1567) stood out as his most original and enduring single work. The Credo is based on the Nicene Creed which is a summary statement of the core belief of the Roman Catholic faithful, but it has been the cornerstone of all Christian institutions since at least the late 4th Century.

I have chosen the Credo movement from the Marcellus Mass as an example of Palestrina's "new" style.  Many church composers in his lifetime were influenced by the inventive spirit of the Franco-Flemish masters in the late 15th and early 16th centuries. They often obscured an already convoluted Latin text with an ever more elaborate web of imitation, counterpoint and embellishment.  Instead, Palestrina, In accordance with the new recommendations put forth by the Council of Trent (1562), introduced a new type of polyphony that emphasized simplicity and clarity similar to Luther's Reformation hymns.

In this latest rendition, I used the Synthesizer V software with the Solaria voice bank for the boy soprano part and Kevin voice bank for the other 5 voices (presumably comprising an all male choir).  Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Text:

Patrem omnipotentem,
factorem caeli et terrae,
visibilium omnium et invisibilium,
Et in unum Dominum Iesum Christum,
Filium Dei unigenitum,
et ex Patre natum, ante omnia saecula,
Deum de Deo, lumen de Lumine,
Deum verum de Deo vero,
genitum, non factum, consubstantialem Patri:
per quem omnia facta sunt.
Qui propter nos homines et propter nostram salutem descendit de caelis. Et incarnatus est de Spiritu Sancto ex Maria Virgine, et homo factus est.

Crucifixus etiam pro nobis sub Pontio Pilato;
passus et sepultus est,
et resurrexit tertia die, secundum Scripturas,
et ascendit in caelum, sedet ad dexteram Patris.
Et iterum venturus est cum gloria,
iudicare vivos et mortuos,
cuius regni non erit finis.

Et in Spiritum Sanctum, Dominum et vivificantem:
qui ex Patre Filioque procedit.
Qui cum Patre et Filio simul adoratur et conglorificatur:
qui locutus est per prophetas.
Et unam, sanctam, catholicam et apostolicam Ecclesiam.
Confiteor unum baptisma in remissionem peccatorum.
Et exspecto resurrectionem mortuorum,
et vitam venturi saeculi. Amen.

Translation:

We believe in one God, the Father, the Almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all that is, seen and unseen. We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, eternally begotten of the Father, God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one Being with the Father. Through him all things were made. For us men and for our salvation, he came down from heaven: by the power of the Holy Spirit he was born of the Virgin Mary, and became man.

For our sake he was crucified under Pontius Pilate; he suffered died and was buried. On the third day he rose again in fulfillment of the Scriptures; he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father. He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

We believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son. With the Father and the Son he is worshipped and glorified. He has spoken through the Prophets. We believe in one holy catholic and apostolic Church. We acknowledge one baptism for the forgiveness of sins. We look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come. Amen.

Dolce mia cara e singular signora

  0:06 Instrumental arrangement (flute, lute, harp, viola da gamba)

  1:36 Verse 2 (alto, lute, harp, gamba)

This is yet another frottola based on the theme of courtly love by an unnamed Italian author. It appears in an obscure source listed in diamm.ac.uk as Biblioteca Estense (Modena) Ms. F.9.9 (collected and assembled around 1495-96). The MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and the score can be found on musescore.com. I used a digital facsimile* of the original manuscript to enter the text. For the vocal simulations, I used Synthesizer V from Dreamtonics equipped with the Natalie and Kevin voice banks. Reverb and echo were added with Audacity. The translation from 15th Century Northern Italian is mine with some assistance from ChatGPT.

* http://bibliotecaestense.beniculturali.it/info/img/mus/i-mo-beu-alfa.f.9.9.pdf

Text:
Dolce mia cara e singular signora
ben che non possi dire dolce mia cara.
Dolce non posso dir sio piango ognhora
si fo la vita mia trista et amara.
Ma si ben cara che lo sangue fora
le forze mancha perche tua voglia avara.
Soccorime ti prego anzi chio mora
per che ormai la fossa si prepara

Translation:
My sweet darling and lady without equal,
though I can no longer call you sweet, my dear.
Sweet I will not say because I weep constantly,
and my life has become sorrowful and bitter.
Yet so dear are you that my blood runs dry,
exhausted by your covetous desire.
Help me, I beg you, before I die,
for already the grave is prepared [for me].

This Christmas cantata (TWV 1:1066) was written by Telemann during his tenure in Frankfurt-am-Main for the Advent season of 1714. The text is non-liturgical and was a religious poem by Erdmann Neumeister. Most likely it was composed for the congregation of St. Katherine Cathedral in Frankfurt.

videos.title: Jean Mouton: Nesciens mater (c.1500) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Jean Mouton: Nesciens mater (c.1500) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Jean Mouton was one of the greatest composers in a vast pantheon of Renaissance masters from the Franco-Flemish School. The complexity and beauty of his compositions stand en par with the works of his predecessors Josquin des Prez (perhaps his mentor) and Johannes Ockeghem as well as Mouton's star pupil Adrian Willaert in the decades after.

This 8-part Marian motet, written expressly for the Christmas season, overlaps historically with another glorious "Nesciens mater" by a contemporary, the Englishman Walter Lambe. The popularity of Mouton's rendition cannot be in doubt, for there were many copies made throughout Europe in both manuscript and printed form over the next half century.  Mouton's setting was written for two choirs (SSAT, SSTB) in which pairs of voices from each choir sing in near perfect canon a fifth apart. It is possible that this piece was performed as a polychoral echo between two choruses in a manner similar to later works of the Venetian School such as the double choir works of Giovanni Gabrieli. Together, the voices coalesce into a seamless mesh of suspended harmonic chords and passing dissonances until the very last dramatic cadential sequence.

This electronic rendition was created using the Synthesizer V with Solaria simulating the boy sopranos and altos in the two choirs as well as Kevin in the tenor and bass sections.  Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.  The pronunciation of the Latin is Gallicized in honor of its composer according to the recommendations of Tim McGee unlike in many modern recordings in which an Italianate Latin is used. There are several textless versions of this MIDI which can be found on the website CPDL.org. Here is the link: 

https://www.cpdl.org/wiki/index.php/Nesciens_mater_virgo_virum_(Jean_Mouton)

++++++++++

Latin text

Nesciens mater virgo virum
peperit sine dolore
Salvatorem saeculorum
Ipsum regem angelorum
sola virgo
ubera de caelo plena*

* in some transcriptions of this motet the last line is written out as "uberre de caelo pleno"

Translation:

The virgin mother not knowing man,
delivered without pain
the savior of the world.
He who is king of the angels
only the Virgin suckled
with breast filled by heaven.

++++++++++

2. The Virgin Mary and Child Jesus of the San Sisto, Raffaello (Raphael) Sanzio, c1513
3. Amiens Cathedral, close up of the nave

videos.title: Guillaume Dufay: Lamentatio Sanctae Matris Ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae (1454) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Guillaume Dufay: Lamentatio Sanctae Matris Ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae (1454) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Lamentatio Sanctae Matris Ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae

Guillaume Dufay's "Lamentation of the Mother Church of Constantinople" is one of the rare musical works that commemorated the Fall of the Byzantine capital to the Ottoman Army in 1453. Although the Catholic See in Rome had for centuries upheld a deeply contentious relationship with the Eastern Roman Church, the fall of the Byzantine Empire nevertheless came as a great shock to Western European leaders as they learned of the event.  They saw Constantinople as the last bastion of a much mythologized Roman Empire that had all but faded from Western memory by the late Middle Ages.

This brief, but richly textured, masterpiece by Dufay is a secular motet in the late French Medieval style interlaced with a Latin plainchant extracted from the Requiem mass.  It is, nevertheless, melodically, harmonically and rhythmically much closer to the early Renaissance Franco-Flemish repertoire. There has been considerable debate regarding the original venue for this work.  Some have speculated that it was used for the grandiose "Banquet of the Pheasant" ordered by Phillip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, one year after the conquest of Byzantium. According to his legend, a lady in white mounted on a large beast (an elephant according to one account) personifying the Mother Church (or perhaps a man dressed as a woman) sang the cantus line before a courtly audience presided over by the Duke. In this elaborate polyphonic exchange among four voices, the listener is induced to mourn for Constantinople in the same spirit as the lamentations recalling the fall of ancient Jerusalem (as expressed in the words of Isaiah and Jeremiah). One is also reminded of the theme of courtly love in which a female protagonist suffers abandonment by her ever-fickle lover. Another story has it that the piece was gifted to Pope Calixtus III in Rome by the composer himself as an appeal for a new crusade to free the fallen city.

This latest rendition was created using Synthesizer V instead of Vocaloid. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

++++++++++

French & Latin text:

O très piteulx de tout espoir, fontaine,
Père du fils dont suis mère éplorée,
Plaindre me viens à ta cour souveraine
De ta puissance et de nature humaine
Qui ont souffert, telle dure vilaine,
Faire à mon fils qui tant m’a honorée,
Dont suis de bien et de joie séparée,
Sans qui vivant veuille entendre mes plaintes.
À toi, seul dieu, du forfait me complains
Du gref tourment et douloureux outrage
Que voit souffrir plus bel des humains
Sans nul confort de tout humain lignage.

Tenor: Omnes amici ejus spreverunt eam
            Non est qui consoletur eam
            Ex omnibus caris ejus.

English translation (from cpdl.org):

Most merciful source of all hope,
Father of the son whose weeping mother I am,
I come to complain at your sovereign court
Of your authority and of human nature,
Which have allowed such harsh cruelty
To be inflicted on my son, who has so honored me;
Whereby I have been parted from happiness and joy,
Without any living being who will hear my complaints.
To you, only God, I appeal from the sentence,
From the grievous torment and painful injury
That I watch the fairest of men suffer,
With no consolation from your human speech.

Tenor: All her friends have betrayed her:
            Among all her lovers there is none to comfort her.

++++++++++

localized.description:
De tout le mal

  0:06 Original chanson for 4 voices (ATTB)

This chanson by Pierre Certon is one of his earlier works published by the Imperial Printer of Music, Pierre Attaingnant. The theme of Certon's song is a common motif for the period: the unrequited love for a lady who will not return the protagonist's affections.  Not much is known about Certon except that he was employed for a time by King Francis I of France in the 1530s and later by church choirs across Paris. He was also likely patronized by the powerful Lady Diane de Poitiers, courtesan and adviser to a later King of France, Henry II. Certon is known for both sacred and secular works, but unlike his contemporary and mentor, Claudin de Sermisy, Certon made use of a broader vocal range and more intricate counterpoint.

The text for the chanson was entered into the Synthesizer V vocal simulator using the KEVIN voice bank. The simulated 16th Century French pronunciation was generated using both the Spanish and English phoneme sets. The instrumental sounds were created using MusicStudio2.

De tout le mal (Of all the pain)
que d'ung vouloir constant (that a constant will)
Me faict souffrir sa grande honnesteté. (makes me suffer, her great honesty)
Me rend si bien satisfaict et content (makes me very satisfied and happy)
Que je ne puis hair sa chasteté. (that I cannot hate her chastity)
Ayant trop myeulx estre plus mal traicté (Having been treated so badly)
Et le sçavoir par vertu estimée (and know it by esteemed virtue)
Que d'avoir tout ce que j'ay merité, (that to have all that I deserve)
La congnoissant moins digne d'estre aymée. (to know her less worthy of being loved)

videos.title: Josquin des Prez: Stabat mater dolorosa (c.1495) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Josquin des Prez: Stabat mater dolorosa (c.1495) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
The motet "Stabat mater dolorosa" is likely a work from Josquin's middle period in Italy. It captures the suffering of Mary, Mother of Jesus Christ, full of sorrow, kneeling beneath her crucified son on the mound of Golgotha. The earliest printed copy of Josquin's masterpiece is preserved in the luxuriously illuminated Chigi Codex, assembled in the Netherlands, now housed in the Vatican Library. The exquisite tome is one of the most important compilations of Franco-Flemish masters and includes nearly all the known masses of Josquin's mentor, Johannes Ockeghem.

The cantus firmus is placed in the tenor voice and is based on a secular piece "Comme femme descomfortee" by an earlier Franco-Flemish master, Gilles Binchois. The chanson describes an inconsolable woman abandoned by the love of her life. (Josquin likely intended that the listener conflate the scene of the two Marys mourning at the cross with the image of a distraught woman who lost her earthly lover.) The tempo in the motet accelerates to a fast 6 rhythm from a steady 4 in the last sentence as the singers plead for Mary's intercession on the Day of Judgment. 

In this latest rendition, I used Synthesizer V with Solaria (to simulate the boy soprano) and Kevin (to simulate the adult male voices). The original MIDI file was created by John Hetland and uploaded to CPDL.org. I applied reverb and echo with Audacity.

Latin text:

Stabat Mater dolorosa (The sorrowful mother stood)
 Juxta crucem lacrymosa, (tearful beside the cross)
  Dum pendebat Filius,  (while her son was hanging)
Cujus animam gementem, (whose sighing soul)
 Contristantem et dolentem (sorrowed and pained)
  Per transivit gladius. (pierced by a sword)
O quam tristis et afflicta (Oh, how sad and afflicted)
 Fuit illa benedicta  (was that blessing)
  Mater Unigeniti. (mother of her first-born)
Quae maerebat et dolebat, (who mourned and grieved)
 Et tremebat, dum videbat (and trembled when she saw)
  Nati poenas inclyti. (the suffering of her offspring)
Quis est homo qui non fleret, (Who does not weep)
 Christi Matrem si videret (if he saw the mother of Christ)
  In tanto supplicio? (in such torment?)

 Me sentire vim doloris (make me feel your pain)

localized.description:
L'Orfeo, excerpts from Act I.

   0:00  Toccata (trumpets) and ritornello (strings)
   1:24  Prologo "Dal mio permesso amato" (La Musica) (soprano & bass continuo)
   6:40  Aria "In questo lieto e fortunato" (Il Pastore) (tenor & basso continuo)

--------------------
Monteverdi's magnum opus Orfeo, based on the Greek tale of unfulfilled love, human frailty and tragic death, sets a theme for later Italian operas both in structure and in content. This full scale opera, which was dedicated to Francesco Gonzaga of Mantua, was first presented in a public performance in 1607 for the annual city-wide festival.  It became one of the earliest and most celebrated grand operas in Europe.

The tale of Orpheus and Euridice permeated all areas of late Renaissance and early Baroque art across Italy - particularly in the realms of music and painting. The operas Orfeo (1647) of Luigi Rossi and Euridice (1600) by Jacopo Peri were just two of several such works in the early 17th century.

I created this electronic rendition using the first 6 movements of the original 1607 version "L'Orfeo" using MusicStudio 2 (iPhone app) for the instrumental parts (trumpets, cornetto, sackbuts, violins, viola, viole da gamba, violone, recorder, chitarrone, clavicembalo and tympani) and Synthesizer V for the computer generated voices. The voice banks that I used included Solaria, Natalie and Kevin while the default language setting was Spanish with a few English phonemes. The original MIDI file (with oboe in place of human voices) was uploaded to the website CPDL.org by Peter Rottländer.

videos.title: Adrian Willaert: Passa la nave (1559) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Adrian Willaert: Passa la nave (1559) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Passa la nave

  0:06  Pars primo "Passa la nave" (SATTBB)
  3:01  Pars secondo "Pioggio di lagrimar" (SATTBB)

This song in two parts by Adrian Willaert is a free style fantasy based on a sonnet by the medieval Italian poet and humanist Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch).  It comes to us from Adrian Willaert's 1559 collection "Musica Nova" (New Music) which contains both sacred and secular compositions from Willaert's most productive years in Venice. One can hear Willaert's Franco-Flemish roots with the richly ornamented suspensions, flowing scalar passages and intricate counterpoint that recalls the musical texture of his master Jean Mouton. The theme of this song is more serious and elevated than most other contemporary works from the Venetian school of that time. It is existential at its core and expresses a feeling of imagined lost -- similar to that famous prologue from Dante's Inferno "Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita mi ritrovai per una selva oscura" (in the middle of the road of our life, I found myself in a dark forest.")  Petrarca compares the ups and down of life to a lethal tempest at sea. There is a fleeting reference to Greek mythology and Homer's Odyssey - symbols frequently utilized in secular songs of mid-16th Century Italian madrigals.

In this latest rendition, I used the Natalie and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V.  Reverb and echo were added with Audacity. The original, MIDI file prior to my adding text was compiled by Steven Langley Guy and uploaded to the website IMSLP.org.

----------

Italian text:

1. Passa la nave mia colma d’oblio
 per aspro mare, a mezza notte il verno,
 enfra Scilla et Caribdi; et al governo
 siede ’l signore, anzi ’l nimico mio.
 Ciascun remo un pensier pronto et rio
 che la tempesta e ’l fin par c’abbi a scherno;
 la vela rompe un vento humido eterno
 di sospir’, di speranze, et di desio.

2. Pioggia di lagrimar, nebbia di sdegni
 bagna et rallenta le già stanche sarte,
 che son d’error con ignorantia attorto.
 Celansi i duo miei dolci usati segni;
 morta fra l’onde è la ragion et l’arte,
 tal ch’incomincio a desperar del porto.

Translation from poetryintranslation.com

My ship, full of oblivion, sails
on a bitter sea, at winter’s midnight,
between Scylla and Charybdis: at the helm
sits the captain, or rather my enemy.
At each oar there’s a cruel eager thought,
that scorns the tempest and its end:
the sail’s torn by an eternal moist wind
of sighs, of hopes, and of desire.

A rain of tears, a mist of disdain
drench and slacken the already tired shrouds,
woven from error and ignorance.
My two usual guiding lights are so hidden:
reason and art so drowned by the waves,
that I begin to despair of finding harbor.

----------

localized.description:
Come away sweet love

  0:06  Original madrigal for 5 voices (SSATB)
  2:16  Instrumental arrangement for 2 recorders and 3 viols

Greaves' collection "Songes of Sundrie Kindes" contained a variety of music from different English genres popular at the end of the Elizabethan era: lute songs as well as 5 part madrigals. This particular madrigal is a lighthearted song reminiscent of Giovanni Gastoldi and Thomas Morley with the very prominent "fa la la" passages. It's bawdy lyrics were typical of that period of English music.

I used the Synthesizer V program and two English language voices (Natalie and Kevin) for the singing portion while I used the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 for the instrumental simulations. The MIDI file was compiled by James Gibb and can be found at CPDL.org. The pronunciation here is late Elizabethan Early Modern English as prescribed by Prof. David Crystal.

Text:

Come away, sweet love, and play thee,
lest grief and care betray thee,
Fa la la.

Leave off this sad lamenting
and take thy heart's contenting.
The nymphs to sport invite thee,
and running in and out delights thee.
Fa la la

videos.title: Ludwig Senfl: Was wird es doch a 7 (c.1530)

localized.title: Ludwig Senfl: Was wird es doch a 7 (c.1530)
localized.description:
Was wird es doch des Wunders noch

  0:06  Original Lied for 7 (by Ludwig Senfl) & lute accompaniment (by Hans Neusidler)
  1:58  Instrumental only (7 Renaissance trombones)

This potent and meaningful Lied for 7 voices is one of at least 2 different settings. He wrote another for 4 voices and Hans Neusidler published a lute song based on Senfl's Tenor line. The theme of this work is one of discontent and anger likely directed at the corruption of the Papacy in which Senfl was a clergyman. Although Senfl never formally declared himself a Lutheran, his sentiments were often in synchrony with the Reformist movement to an extent that he himself was investigated by the Inquisition. The date of this composition is probably early 1530s since a lute song setting of Senfl’s tune by Hans Neusidler was already available in 1536. The musical style is that of the Franco-Flemish School of Jean Mouton with the undulating scales and interweaving counterpoint.

The vocals were generated using the Kevin voice bank and Synthesizer V. The instrumental simulations were created with Music Studio 2.0, an iPhone app. The original MIDI file was compiled by Allen Garvin and can be found at the following link: 

https://www.cpdl.org/wiki/index.php/Was_wird_es_doch_des_Wunders_noch_a_7_(Ludwig_Senfl)

The lute accompaniment was compiled by Sarge Gerbode and can be found at the following link: 

https://browse.lutemusic.org/sources/NewsidlerH/ein_newgeordent_kunstlich_lautenbuch/v.2_1536/48_was_wirt_es_doch_senfl/midi/

Text:

Was wird es doch
des Wunders noch
sogar ein seltsams Leben
als jetzund ist
all Welt voll List
mit Untreu übergeben!
Gut Wort, arg Tück,
viel Grüß, bös Blick,
das ist der Sitt auf Erden;
günnt keiner mehr
dem andern Ehr.
Was will noch daraus werden?

Translation:

What will it yet become,
this wonder some
strange life we’re living now?
The world is full
of cunning, cruel,
betrayal’s at the prow!
Fair words, false guile,
sweet greetings, vile
looks — that’s the earthly way;
no one grants
the other honor.
What’s to come of it?

videos.title: Gregorio Allegri / arr. David Willocks: Miserere mei (c.1638 / c. 1964) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Gregorio Allegri / arr. David Willocks: Miserere mei (c.1638 / c. 1964) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
The earliest version of this piece -- absent the high C (C6) -- was a rather austere composition consisting mostly of monotonous recitations of psalm text. It was composed by Gregorio Allegri eight decades after the Council of Trent delivered the edict that plainchant would be the standard to which all church music should aspire. Liturgical music, going forward, had to contain clear and audible text for the untrained ear to hear and assimilate. Allegri's Miserere was such a work: straightforward chant augmented with mostly chordal harmony. The first manuscript edition appeared in the late 18th century, and an apocryphal legend suggested that Mozart was its first transcriptionist. My “performance” used a modern score by David Willcocks who based his late 20th century arrangement on a late 19th century much-altered, re-imagining of Allegri’s original.

In this rendition, I used the Synthesizer V software and both Solaria and Kevin voice banks (with Spanish language phonemes). I spatially separated the ensemble into a 5 part Chorus 1 on the left (which includes the tenor cantor) and a 4 part Chorus 2 on the right (which includes the cantus who carries the high C). 

Text:

Miserere mei, Deus: secundum magnam misericordiam tuam. Et secundum multitudinem miserationem tuarum, dele iniquitatem meam. Amplius lava me ab iniquitate mea: et a peccato meo munda me. Quoniam iniquitatem meam ego cognosco: et peccatum meum contra me est semper. Tibi soli peccavi, et malum coram te feci: ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis, et vincas cum judicaris. Ecce enim in iniquitatibus conceptus sum: et in peccatis concepit me mater mea. Ecce enim veritatem dilexisti: incerta et occulta sapientiae tuae manifestasti mihi. Asperges me hysopo, et mundabor: lavabis me, et super nivem dealbabor. Auditui meo dabis gaudium et laetitiam: et exsultabunt ossa humiliata. Averte faciem tuam a peccatis meis: et omnes iniquitates meas dele.
Cor mundum crea in me, Deus: et spiritum rectum innova in visceribus meis. Ne projicias me a facie tua: et spiritum sanctum tuum ne auferas a me. Redde mihi laetitiam salutaris tui: et spiritu principali confirma me. Docebo iniquos vias tuas: et impii ad te convertentur. Libera me de sanguinibus, Deus, Deus salutis meae: et exsultabit lingua mea justitiam tuam. Domine, labia mea aperies: et os meum annuntiabit laudem tuam. Quoniam si voluisses sacrificium, dedissem utique: holocaustis non delectaberis. Sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus: cor contritum, et humiliatum, Deus, non despicies. Benigne fac, Domine, in bona voluntate tua Sion: ut aedificentur muri Ierusalem. Tunc acceptabis sacrificium justitiae, oblationes, et holocausta: tunc imponent super altare tuum vitulos.

Translation

Have mercy, God, with Your goodness. By the multitude of Your mercies erase my offences. Wash away my wickedness, cleanse me of sin, for I know my faults and sins are before me. Only against You I sinned, and done this evil in Your sight that You might be justified in saying so.
Lo, I was shaped in wickedness: and in sin my mother conceived me. But, You require truth inside me and shall make me understand wisdom quietly. You shall purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: You shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. You shall make me hear of joy and gladness: that the bones which You have broken may rejoice. Turn Your face away from my sins and cover my misdeeds. Make me a clean heart, God and renew a proper spirit in me. Cast me not away from You and take not the Holy Spirit from me. Give me the comfort of Your help and remake me with Your free Spirit. Then shall I teach Your ways to the wicked and sinners shall turn to You. Deliver me from guilty, God who is the God of my health and my tongue shall sing Your righteousness. You shalt open my lips, O Lord and my mouth shall praise. You desire no sacrifice, otherwise would I give it for You delight not in burnt offerings. The sacrifice of God is a troubled spirit: a broken and contrite heart. Be favorable and gracious to Zion: build You the walls of Jerusalem. Then You shall be pleased with the sacrifice of righteousness, with the burnt-offerings and oblations: then shall they offer young bulls on Your altar.

videos.title: Giulio Caccini: Amarilli mia bella (1601) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Giulio Caccini: Amarilli mia bella (1601) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Amarilli mia bella

  0:06  Original monody (male alto, bass viol, chitarrone)
  2:45  Instrumental setting (cornetto, chamber organ, chitarrone, trombone)

Giulio Caccini, though born in Rome, spent a significant part of his musical career in Florence, the city of the famed Medici family and center of the newly evolving genre of grand opera. It is in the spirit of this revolutionary dramatic development that this song was conceived.  The melody and accompaniment are simple and repetitive, but the expressive power of the work lies in its buildup to the climactic cadence.

I added a cornetto performance as a reminder that many songs from this period were re-interpreted and re-dedicated as instrumental arrangements.  Caccini's "Amarilli" was parodied several times during the following decades: two variations by Jakob van Eyck for recorder and one by Johann Nauwach for violin.

This rendition was created using the Kevin voice bank and the Synthesizer V program.  The instrumental parts were simulated using the iPhone app MusicStudio2. Reverb and echo were added with Audacity. 

Text:

Amarilli, mia bella,
Non credi, o del mio cor dolce desio,
D'esser tu l'amor mio?
Credilo pur: e se timor m'assale,
Prendi questo mio strale,
Aprimi il petto e vedrai scritto in core:
Amarilli, Amarilli, Amarilli è il mio amore.

Translation:

Amaryllis, my beautiful one,
Don't you believe, O sweet desire of my heart
That you are the one whom I love?
Believe this also, and if fear assails me,
Take this arrow
Open up my breast, and you shall see written on my heart
Amaryllis, Amaryllis, Amaryllis is my love.

videos.title: Heinrich Schütz: Habe deine Lust an dem Herren (1639) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Heinrich Schütz: Habe deine Lust an dem Herren (1639) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This small scale work for two voices and basso continuo is a German language adaptation of Psalm 37 and is one of many virtuosic treasures in Schütz's compilation "Kleiner geistlichen Concerten" ("Little Spiritual Concerts").  One can hear the Italian influences from the likes of Giovanni Gabrieli and Claudio Monteverdi with the imitative echoes of a polychoral motet and the mellifluous, playful coloratura of an operatic duet. One might also anticipate the weightier dramatics from the arias of J.S. Bach and G.P. Telemann in the late Baroque period nearly a century thenceforth.

It was perhaps because of the scarcity of resources and personnel in the midst of the Thirty Years' War that Schütz created works on a smaller scale compared to the opulent polychoral opuses of the Venetian masters from whom the Kapellmeister had his earliest musical instruction. This "concerto," like others, contains a simple line for one low pitched instrumental part intended for organist and other basso continuo players. The entire last third of the concerto is based on the word "Alleluia" traded back and forth between the cantus and the altus. The Alleluia also transitions into a 3 rhythm perhaps to generate some energy and excitement.

++++++++++

Text:

Habe deine Lust an dem Herren, 
der wird dir geben was dein Herz wünschet.
Befiel dem Herren deine Wege, 
und hoffe auf ihn, 
er wirds wohl machen. 
Erzürne dich nicht über die Bösen, 
sei nicht neidisch über die Übeltäter, 
denn wie das Gras werden sie bald abgehauen, 
und wie das grüne Kraut werden sie verwelken. 
Hoffe auf den Herren, und tue Guts; 
bleib im Lande und nähre dich redlich.
Alleluia!

Translation:

Let your joy be in the Lord; 
he will give you what your heart desires.
Dedicate your ways to the Lord,
and trust in Him; 
he will make things well. 
Trouble not yourself over the wicked; 
do not be envious of the evildoers, 
since like the grass they will soon be mowed down, 
and like the green weed they will wither. 
Hope in the Lord, and do good; 
so shall you dwell in the Kingdom, 
and be well nourished. 
Hallelujah!

++++++++++

The score of this piece was originally created and uploaded to IMSLP.org by Vincent Carpentier.  I added an accompaniment section with a chamber organ, a bass viola da gamba as well as a chitarrone (to add a slightly percussive effect to an otherwise bland background). I also inserted a likely figured bass sequence to the final cadenza.

This most recent rendition was created using the Solaria and Kevin voice banks with both English and Spanish phonemes in Synthesizer V.  The reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

The facsimile clips of the original score comes from the cantus part of Schütz's collection of works for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 voices published in Dresden in 1639.

localized.title: Thomas Morley: What ayles my darling (1593) by Synthesizer V
localized.description:
What ayles my darling

   0:06   Original canzonet for 3 voice (SSA)
   3:01   Arrangement for broken consort (flute, lute, viol)

The canzonet "What ayles my darling" is one trio in a collection of songs for 3 voices. Unlike John Dowland's arrangements of similar madrigals, this piece does not include a lute or viol accompaniment.  It begins with a salutation from a man who finds his female love interest sad and lonely and thereof invites her to dance and frolic with him.  Despite the somewhat imitative nature of the 3 voice parts, the lyrics and scales are slightly different between the parts.

I entered the song text using the Synthesizer V voice encoder equipped with the Natalie (2 soporanos) and Kevin (baritone) voice banks.  Using Professor David Crystal's recommendations, I adjusted the vowels to emulate Early Modern English from Shakespeare's time. For example, "what" is likely pronounced "hwat", "mine" is "məin," "pretty" is "pritəi," and "lie" is "ləi." The lute, flute and viol sounds were generated using MusicStudio2.

++++++++++

Lyrics (for the cantus part):

What ayles my pretty darling,
say what ayles my darling?
What ails my sweet prettie darling,
what ayles mine own sweet darling
what ayles my darling deere
thus sitting all alone so weary?
Say, why is my dear now not merry?
O cease thus to grieve thee,
cease alas to grieve, thus to grieve thee
And a kisse with all heere take to releeve thee.
Up now, arise thee;
O how can my love alas lye sleeping,
and see you lusty, lusty leaping?

++++++++++

videos.title: Johannes Regis: Puisque ma dame (c. 1465)

localized.title: Johannes Regis: Puisque ma dame (c. 1465)
localized.description:
Puisque ma dame

  0:06  Original chanson for SAAT
  1:50  Instrumental arrangement (2 lutes, psaltery, harp)

Johannes Regis was a Franco-Burgundian composer of some repute and also a secretary to the 15th century musical master par excellence, Guillaume Dufay, during the latter's last decade of life. The complete score of this work can only be found in the lushly illuminated Mellon Chansonnier (Yale-Beinecke MS 91).

It is a combinative chanson in which the cantus, contratenor 2 and bassus present one set of lyrics while the contratenor 1 sings a totally different set of words, simultaneously. It appears that the last few notes of the contratenor 1 may be missing in this setting since the music abruptly ends several notes earlier than in the other voices. The sentence also seems to be lacking the word "pleure" (to rhyme with the word demeure in the 1st line of the stanza). Also, it is unclear if the lower two parts, for which a text underlay is absent, were intended for singers or players. The music is non-imitative throughout and is comprised a complex web of counterpoint. I reconstructed the text underlay for the contratenor 2 and bassus lines.

The MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and his complete score can be found at Musescore.com. I used the Natalie and Kevin voice banks, both English and Spanish phoneme sets and the Synthesizer V software to simulate the one female and 3 male voices. The instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app MusicStudio 2.0. Reverb and echo were added with Audacity.

Text:

Puisque ma dame ne puis voir.
Ne delle ouir quelque nouvelle
et se ne puis aultre amer
quelle annoy
et deuil me fault avoir.

Je men vois et mon demeure.
Je chante et fay larmes de leuil.
Je mesbas et si nay que deuil.
Je ris et mon euil [pleure].

Translation:

Since my lady cannot see me,
Nor hear anything new [about me],
And [because] I cannot love another,
I must bear only sorrow and grief.

(Countertenor)
I see myself and my [sorry] state.
I sing while I shed tears of grief.
I abase myself, for all I know is sorrow.
I smile, and yet my eye [weeps].

Description of the photos:

1. Page 1 of the "Puisque ma dame," Cantus & Contretenor II parts, Johannes Regis, Mellon Chansonnier, copied c1475
2. Le Livre de la Cité des dames, Christine de Pisan, copied by Jean de Barry, Bibl.Natl.de France, c1405
3. Page 2 of the "Puisque ma dame," Contretenor I and Bassus parts, J. Regis, Mellon Chansonnier
4. The belfry of the Church of St. Martin, Cambrai, a familiar site to Regis who spent many years in the town as an assistant to the internationally renown maestro Dufay.
5. Courtly ladies with musical instruments, Book of Hours of Louis de Savoye, Bibl.Natl.de France Latin 9473, Anon. Italian, c1460
6. Charles IV entering the city of Cambrai, c1450

videos.title: Claudin de Sermisy: Amour me poingt (publ.1529) by Synthesizer V

localized.title: Claudin de Sermisy: Amour me poingt (publ.1529) by Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Amour me poingt

  0:06  Original chanson for 4 voices (ATTB + lute)
  1:46  Instrumental arrangement (flute, lute, harp, bass viol)

This chanson by Claudin de Sermisy, the great song-master of the French High Renaissance, bears many of the typical elements of courtly music from the first half of the 16th century. Its length is very short and contains just one verse that is repeated multiple times. The overall structure is similar to late Italian frottole and early madrigals with their vertically stacked chords. In the middle voices, there are often passages in which interweaving scales add some stimulating counterpoint to an otherwise simple metrical framework.

The original MIDI file and pdf score were created and uploaded to IMSLP.org by Eric Haas. I added the text using the Kevin voice bank combining Spanish and English phonemes in Synthesizer V. The instrumental simulations were generated using Music Studio 2, an iPhone app. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Text:

Amour me poingt et si ne me veult plaindre
ma peine double et sans espoir demeure
par quoi vault mieulx quen me taisant ie meure
doulce est la mort qui peult douleur estaindre

Translation:

Love pierces me, and yet if I don't want to complain,
my pain will double and remain without hope.
Why would it be better that I remain silent
sweet is the death which can extinguish the pain.

videos.title: Walter Lambe: Nesciens mater (c.1490) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Walter Lambe: Nesciens mater (c.1490) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
The Eton Choirbook (a.k.a. Eton College MS 178) is one of the last collections of English Catholic church music that survived the Anglican Reformation and the Dissolution of the Monasteries.  Nearly half of the original folios were lost, but the portion that remains within the current binding gives us a glimpse into the wonderous polyphonic repertoire prior to the reign of Henry VIII. Each folio is exquisitely illuminated with flourishes and ornamental initials. Nearly all the works, like this one, is based around Latin liturgical text and carries an ever expansive, celestial quality. Using a minimum of text material, Lambe managed to create a full length motet through repetition and melismata. Lambe also alternates pairs or trio of voices (soprano & bass, soprano & alto, tenors 1/2 & bass) with the full chorus to create a dramatic buildup followed by a triumphant climax.

The soundtrack for this video was creating using a MIDI file that was compiled by John Hetland and uploaded to CPDL.org. This latest rendition was created using Synthesizer V (not Vocaloid) equipped with the Solaria (soprano) and  Kevin (alto, tenors and bass). The notes in this "performance" were shifted up a whole tone into a slightly higher range to highlight the boy sopranos' range and better emulate music from this period. I used an Anglicized Latin, which is nearer to French, rather than Italian, pronunciation.

++++++++++

Latin text:

Nesciens mater virgo virum
peperit sine dolore
Salvatorem saeculorum
Ipsum regem angelorum
sola virgo lactabat
ubera de caelo plena

Translation

The virgin mother not knowing man
delivered without pain
the savior of the world.
He who is king of the angels
only the Virgin suckled 
breasts filled from heaven.

6. Initial "O" and handwritten composer name "Lambe", EC MS 178
7. King Henry VI, founder of Eton College and the Seal of Eton
8. Eton College Chapel, ceiling

videos.title: Anonymous Italian / ? Leonardo Giustiniani: Piangete done (c.1445)

localized.title: Anonymous Italian / ? Leonardo Giustiniani: Piangete done (c.1445)
localized.description:
This song is written only for two voices, possibly by the great Venetian poet and intellectual Leonardo Giustiniani. It has many of the same vocabulary and allegorical elements commonly seen in his other strambotti. It is mostly written in an early frottola style with the lower voice providing a mostly supportive role rather than an independent, canonic line. The theme is an oblique reference to courtly love, but shrouded somewhat in a more colorful poetry.

I added the voice parts using the Natalie and Kevin voice banks in Synthesizer V. The instrumental doubling by lute, citole, vielle and viol were generated with MusicStudio 2.0 and the echo / reverb effects were added using Audacity. The original MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and can be found on Musescore.com .

Text:

Piangete done et vuy fedele amanti
Co' meco insieme poyche a torto privo
Me vedo de quel divo
Lume celeste, et angelici sembianti.

Ogni solazo e festa et joya et canti
Rivolti sono in tanta amara doglia
Che par che'l cor se voglia
Da me fugir e l'alma per desdegno

Translation:

Weep, ladies, and you faithful lovers,
for I, like you, am wrongfully deprived
I see that divine light
Light of heaven, and angelic visions

All solace, celebration, joy and songs
are turned into bitter sorrow.
So that my heart desires
to flee from me as the soul on account of disdain

videos.title: Orlando Gibbons: Blessed are all they (1613), Original Pronunciation

localized.title: Orlando Gibbons: Blessed are all they (1613), Original Pronunciation
localized.description:
This verse anthem based on Psalm 128 (followed by the Doxology "Glory be to the Father, etc."), was composed by the grand master of Anglican church services in the Jacobean era, Orlando Gibbons. The occasion was the wedding of Sir Robert Carr and Lady Frances Howard. Carr (or Kerr) had been groomed to become Earl of Somerset by King James I of England and Scotland; and the auspicious ceremony took place on St. Stephen's Day (December 26), 1613 at the Chapel of Whitehall. The scandal that would lead to the downfall of the Earl and the Countess was still several years in the future. As was the preoccupation of aristocrats everywhere, marriage was the means to guarantee future heirs to family titles and estates. Note the lines: "Thy children like the olive-branches: round about thy table" and "Yea, that thou shalt see thy children's children."

The original MIDI file was created by Michael Gibson and uploaded to CPDL.org. I transposed Gibson's arrangement down by a minor 3rd to restore the original pitch indicated by Gibbons. This latest rendition was created using Synthesizer V with  the Solaria and Kevin voice banks. The sound of the viol consort was generated using the iPhone app MusicStudio 2.0.

++++++++++

Text:

Blessed are all they that fear the Lord: and walk in his ways.
For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: O well is thee, and happy shalt thou be.
Thy wife shall be as the fruitful vine: upon the walls of thine house.
Thy children like the olive-branches: round about thy table.
Lo, thus shall the man be blessed: that feareth the Lord.
The Lord from out of Sion shall so bless thee: that thou shalt see Jerusalem in prosperity
all thy life long.
Yea, that thou shalt see thy children's children: and peace upon Israel.

Glory be to the Father and to the Son
and to the Holy Ghost.
As it was in the beginning, and ever shall be
world without end.
Amen.

++++++++++

videos.title: Josquin des Prez: Inviolata integra et casta es Maria (c.1490)

localized.title: Josquin des Prez: Inviolata integra et casta es Maria (c.1490)
localized.description:
The international reach of Josquin could be attested to by the earliest surviving editions of "Inviolata" -- first, in a 1520 Augsburg collection and then in a Venetian printing the following year. And although its actual date of composition is unclear, some of the cadential formulas and surprise hemiolas suggest a late 15th century provenance. The motet's popularity among the elite maestri of the early 16th century is reflected in the large number of parody pieces written after Josquin's death. There were at least two motets attributable to the Franco-Flemish maestro Nicholas Gombert and one lute German intabulation by Hans Gerle.

In this short motet, there are several hidden musical puzzles. The first is the cantus firmus sung in canon between the alto and tenor 2 parts separated by a melodic 5th. Meanwhile, the cantus, tenor 1 and bassus weave an astoundingly longwinded passage in counterpoint around the alto / tenor 2 duet. The second interesting gimmick is the relentless repetition of the word "inviolata" by the superius at the very beginning. Each time, Josquin introduce a new voice on the last syllable of IN-VI-O-LA-TA: first the bassus, then tenor 2, tenor 1 and finally the altus. Then, there is a nearly homophonic segment in which all the voices come together to sing "O Benigna, O Regina, O Maria" on a repeated rising scale as if to implore the Virgin Mary's intercession at the end of times. There is a brief sequence near the end of the piece when the middle voices break into a 3 rhythm to create a hemiola effect and an almost giddy mood.

Latin text

Inviolata, integra et casta es Maria:
Quae es effecta fulgida caeli porta.
O Mater alma Christi carissima:
Suscipe pia laudum praeconia.
Te nunc flagitant devota corda et ora:
Nostra ut pura pectora sint et corpora.
Tua per precata dulci sona:
Nobis concedas veniam per saecula.
O benigna! O Regina! O Maria!
Quae sola inviolata permansisti.

English translation

Inviolate, whole and chaste are you, Mary:
you are the the luminous gate of heaven.
O kind mother, dearest to Christ,
accept our faithful hymn of praise.
To you our hearts and mouth cry out:
may our breast and bodies be pure.
Through your prayers' sweet sounds
grant us forgiveness for ever.
O kindly one! O Queen! O Mary!
you alone remain inviolate.

videos.title: Johannes Martini: Fortuna d'un gran tempo (c.1480)

localized.title: Johannes Martini: Fortuna d'un gran tempo (c.1480)
localized.description:
Fortuna d'un gran tempo

0:06  Tenor only with instrumental accompaniment (tenor, lutes, psaltery, harp)
3:00  Four part vocal arrangement for ATTB

This Italian language song was copied uniquely into an extravagantly illuminated Florentine source, the MS Banco Rari 229. It is not the typical barzelletta or frottola from the same period. Unlike countless homophonic canzonette written as progressions of modal chords, this piece has all the attributes of the Franco-Flemish chanson with its imitative passages and complex counterpoint wrapped around a tenor melody line. Martini was likely a Netherlander who transplanted himself to Northern Italy and spent most of his adult life at the courts of Ferrara and Milan. During those years, he successfully adapted the northern European style of composition to a still evolving Italian Renaissance repertoire. 

I reconstructed the text underlay for the tenor 1 and bassus parts since the manuscript score contains words only for the cantus (alto) and contratenor (tenor 2). It is possible that the tenor 1 part was intended for an instrumentalist since it is less melodic and more improvisatory like many "si placet" line to vocal music of that era. Nevertheless, with the repetition of some key phrases, it was not difficult to fill out the lyrics for all four voice parts.

I created my own MIDI file from a modern score that can found on IMSLP.org. I added the Italian text using the Synthesizer V software and the Kevin voice bank (with a mix of Spanish and English phonemes). Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Text and translation:

Fortuna d’un gran tempo mi se stata.
Tanto leggiadra, gratiosa et bella.
solo una gratia taggio 'a dimandata
et a quella mi se stata ribella
et chi lo vuol sapere si lo sappia
in questa terra voglio bene ad una
Un degli sua 'manti mi minaccia
credendo chio la lasci per paura

Fortune, for a long time, has stood by me.
So graceful, gracious, and fair [she is].
Yet one favor I asked,
And to that [plea], she turned [against me].
And whoever wishes to know, it shall be known:
In this land, I love so much the one.
One of the lovers threatens me,
believing that I leave her for fear.

videos.title: Anonymous Franco-Burgundian: Enferme suys en la tour (1460)

localized.title: Anonymous Franco-Burgundian: Enferme suys en la tour (1460)
localized.description:
This short chanson captures a particular spirit of courtly love that was familiar among the French aristocratic circle. The "bel accueil" (Castle of Fair Welcome) was the symbol of love's embrace that was both formidable and ensnaring at the same time. The Castle was amply represented in the richly illuminated 15th century rendition of the "Roman de la Rose"  (Douce 195) in the Oxford Bodleian Library.

The counterpoint and back-and-forth banter of this musical work is quite extraordinary despite its being limited to only three voices. I included only the first set of lyrics in this initial offering of this work.

The MIDI file was created by bojopigeon and uploaded to musescore.com. I added the words using Synthesizer V with the Kevin voice bank for all 3 parts. The instrumental simulations (lute, citole and harp) were generated using the iPhone app MusicStudio 2.0.

Text (and translation):

Enferme suys (I am imprisoned)
en la tour de bel accueil (in the castle of fair welcome)
par bien amer. (for truly loving)
Dame blanche comme la flour. (My lady white as the lily)
Je sers le et de penser. (I serve her and think about her)
Au bon command de mon signour. (as my Lord kindly allows)

Description of the photos:

1. Score of "Enferme suys," Mellon Chansonnier MS 91. The richly illuminated manuscript was copied in Naples and dedicated to Beatrice of Aragon on the occasion of her wedding to King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary in 1476.
2. Ceremonial dish with the seals of house of Naples and Buda likely gifted to Beatrice of Aragon.
3. Garden of courtly love, painting on a cassone based on Petrarch's Filocolo's Parable, Giovanni Toscani, c1425
4. Bust of Beatrice d'Aragon, Francesco Laurana
5. A muse showing the Lover the way to the Castle of Fair Welcome, Roman de la Rose" (Oxford Bodleian Library, Douce 195), c1480

videos.title: Cristóbal de Morales: Agnus Dei from "Missa Mille Regretz" (1544)

localized.title: Cristóbal de Morales: Agnus Dei from "Missa Mille Regretz" (1544)
localized.description:
Agnus Dei from Missa Mille Regretz

  0:06  Agnus Dei I (SSAATB)
  2:13  Agnus Dei II (SAT)
  3:52  Agnus Dei III (SSAATB)

Cristóbal de Morales was one of the last great Renaissance composers to regularly compose complex polyphony for the Papal Choir at the Vatican.  Shortly after his death in 1553, the Council of Trent discouraged the use of intricate counterpoint and embellishment in all Catholic services. It probably also would have disapproved of his use of secular themes in religious services. (The most widely accepted musical form was the plainchant.) There were two versions of the Mass "Mille regretz" created by Morales of which this version is the later and more developed in its complexity.

The Missa "Mille regretz" was an homage to the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V of Spain and the Netherlands, whose favorite song was Josquin des Prez's 4-voice chanson "Mille regretz."  Morales' mass was written for 6 vocal parts: two cantus (likely boy sopranos), two altus (likely male voices) and two tenor (or baritone) parts. Agnus Dei II is pared down to only the middle 3 voices. 

The original MIDI file for this soundtrack was downloaded from the Aeolian Consort's website at geocities.co.jp with a few corrections based on the online facsimile score of the 1544 edition and tuned an octave lower. I used the Synthesizer V software with the Solaria (Cantus 1 & 2) and Kevin (4 male voices) voice banks.  I added reverb and echo using Audacity. 

++++++++++

videos.title: Diego Pisador: Guardamos las vacas (1552)

localized.title: Diego Pisador: Guardamos las vacas (1552)
localized.description:
The relentlessly repeating bass line of "Guardamos las vacas" is sometimes called a Romanesca and is an ancient melody that predates this particular set of variations by more than half a century. The inspiration for Pisador's series of diferencias (variations) is likely Luys de Narváez's "Guardame las vacas" published in 1538. Pisador probably held this piece in high esteem since out of the 186 separate works he wrote or arranged for vihuela (with and without a vocalist), "Guardamos" is #2. As can be observed in the photo descriptions, the vihuela is the Spanish precursor of the modern guitar.

The MIDI file was compiled by Sarge Gerbode and uploaded to his website lutemusic.org. The vihuela simulation was created using the iPhone app MusicStudio 2.0. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

1. "Guardamos las vacas," 1st page of the principal theme and the 1st variation, Libro de Musica de Vihuela, Diego Pisador, 1552

3. Torre del Gallo of the Old Cathedral, a familiar site for Pisador who spent much of his life in Salamanca.

videos.title: Pierre de la Rue: Myn hert altyt heeft verlanghen (c.1500)

localized.title: Pierre de la Rue: Myn hert altyt heeft verlanghen (c.1500)
localized.description:
Although abundantly printed in Italy by the Venetian publisher Ottaviano Petrucci in 1503 and meticulously copied into a Florentine manuscript (Basevi 2439), this Dutch / Flemish song of courtly love is likely an earlier work from the Low Countries perhaps from the court of Margaret of Austria where the composer was employed in the 1490s.  Pierre de la Rue (a.k.a. Pierchon or Peteren van Straeten), a contemporary of Josquin des Prez and Heinrich Isaac, has mostly been overshadowed by the great masters of his generation. However, during his lifetime, de la Rue was held in the highest esteem among the pantheon of early Renaissance titans of Franco-Flemish origin. This specific liedt appears in no fewer than 11 sources.

Text:

Myn hert altyt heeft verlanghen
Naer u die alderliefste myn
U liefde heeft my ontfanghen
U eighen vry wil ick zyn
Voor al de weerelt gemeene

Hebdy myn herte alleene
Daarom lief en begheeft my niet

My heart has always longed
for you, my most beloved.

only yours, I want to be.

videos.title: Walter Frye: De Sancto Nicolao (c.1460)

localized.title: Walter Frye: De Sancto Nicolao (c.1460)
localized.description:
Preserved only in an early 16th Century manuscript copied in the hinterlands of eastern Germany, this hymn dedicated to Saint Nicholas (i.e. Santa Claus) was likely the creation of an English composer from a half century earlier. It starts with a solemn chordal progression and then evolves into a playful, imitative polyphony. In this spliced version of an earlier hymn, Frye tries to capture the main highlights of a little known (but much celebrated) Third Century Greco-Roman bishop from Myra.

It should be noted in Frye's overzealous effort to abbreviate the text (presumably to appeal to a simple audience), he critically altered the spirit of the original legend of the "Cheated Jew." In the story, as it was told in the late Middle Ages, a Jewish man lends gold to a gentile who does not want to return the money and indefinitely delays payment. The Jew takes the man to court whereupon the cheating fellow brings a hollow staff filled with gold coins before a magistrate, hands the staff to the Jew and swears by the staff that he has returned the money to the lender. The magistrate releases the con artist from the loan, the latter takes back the staff and quickly walks away from the courtroom. In his haste leaving the building, the con artist is hit by a speeding wagon and instantly killed. The staff breaks apart and the Jewish man sees gold coins spilled out onto the street. Seeing the dead man and the treasures laid side-by-side on the ground, he beseeches St. Nicholas (who appears miraculously) to bring the man back to life. The man is resurrected and thenceforth the Jewish man submits to baptism. The tale can be seen both as an ancient, anti-Semitic trope of a Jewish usurer who is converted (as was the invariable conclusion of medieval Christian lore) or an empathetic view of a victimized Jewish man who chose the life of a person who cheated him over the monetary treasures owed to him.

The MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon. The song simulation was created using the Solaria (soprano) and Keven (alto, tenor, bass) voice banks in the Synthesizer V program. The instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app MusicStudio 2.0. Reverb and echo were added with Audacity.

baptizatur auri viso Iudeus indicio (He baptized the Jew with the sight of gold, in a sign [of Him])
o quam probat sanctum dei farris augmentatio (Oh, the increase of wheat proves him a saint of God)
ergo laudes Nicolao concinat hec concio (Therefore, let this assembly sing praise to Nicholas)

videos.title: Giacomo Fogliano: Segui cuor' e non restare (c.1505) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Giacomo Fogliano: Segui cuor' e non restare (c.1505) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Segui cuor e non restare

  0:06  Original frottola for 4 (ATTB)
  2:32  Instrumental arrangement (recorder, crumhorn, two viols)

Although the frottola "L'amor donna chio te porto" is one of the most frequently performed songs among modern early music ensembles all over the world, its composer Giacomo Fogliano has been all but forgotten, overshadowed by other more prolific Italian and Franco-Flemish contemporaries. His lesser known work "Segue cuor" (sp. Segui cuore) is typical of the frottola genre with its overall chordal, homophonic structure with a few surprising rhythmic twists at the end. It must have been a well regarded song in its time since one ceramicist even painted it on a decorative plate given as a gift to a wealthy patron. One can hear the three alto/tenor voices crossing lines -- perhaps competing for pre-eminence.

This recording was generated using the Kevin voice bank with English and Spanish phonemes in the Synthesizer V program (instead of Vocaloid). The reverb and echo were added with Audacity. Since the frottola is pitched comfortably in the alto to bass range, I used an all "male" vocal ensemble for this recording. I only included the first two verses (of five) in the interest of avoiding excessive repetition.

Text (and translation):

Segue cuor e non restare (Follow your heart and do not stop)
De servir chi te non cura (from serving one who does not care for you)
Chio gia inteso chi la dura (for it is said that the one who endures)
Vitorioso sole andare (goes forth like the victorious sun)

Segue cuor e non restare (Follow your heart and do not stop)
De servir chi te non cura (from serving one who does not care for you)

Non ti muova ira o disdegno (Do not be moved towards anger or disdain)
Dal servir o no tormento (and away from service or torment)
Che arivar non si po al segno (because one cannot reach the goal)
Defiato senza stento (without struggle)
Nel gran mar contrario al vento (in the great sea against the wind)
El nochier si vede stare (the sailor is seen standing firm)

2. Four singers in a garden, Chigi MS VIII.234
3. "Seguj cuore e non stare" alto line painted on a ceremic plate, c1530
4. A pensive poet, Giacomo Palma il Vecchio, c1516
5. Musical angels, detail of recorder and vielle, Francesco Botticini, c1490

videos.title: Richard I "Lionheart": Ja nus hons pris (1194)

localized.title: Richard I "Lionheart": Ja nus hons pris (1194)
localized.description:
Ja nus hons pris

Richard I King of England, known as the Lionheart for his brash exploits in the Third Crusade (and other battles before and after), composed this lamentation while imprisoned in Dürnstein Castle (lower Austria) by Duke Leopold V of Austria -- proxy of his nemesis Philippe Auguste. The chanson could have been just another one of the countless monophonic trouvère songs by a travelling European minstrel in the 12th Century had it not been for his royal identity and unusual circumstances. The song may have been addressed to his half sister the Countess Marie de Champagne, but perhaps it was also indirectly directed to his mother Queen Eleanor of Aquitaine who could have ordered his release from prison using her considerable power and influence.

The date of the composition can be narrowed to late 1193 or early 1194 since the author declares it is the second winter since his capture in December of 1192. Clearly, it resonated with the public of that time since at least nine copies in different dialects and orthographies of Old French have survived. The text was likely written originally in the Norman French of Richard Lionheart's lineage, which was considerably different from Modern Parisian French. Final consonants were enunciated. Many words were closer to Latin in both spelling and pronunciation than to any current French vocabulary.

I only included the first three verses of a much longer poem to avoid repetition. I improvised the instrumental accompaniment using fourths, fifths and octaves - the so called “perfect” intervals - as was customary in early French polyphony. Although not recorded in any surviving manuscripts, it is highly unlikely that any songs from this period were completely monophonic. 

In this latest rendition, I used the Kevin voice bank (with the English and Spanish phoneme sets) and Synthesizer V instead of Vocaloid.  I used the text from the 13th century  Chansonnier de Saint-Germain-des-Prés (Bibliothèque Nationale de France, MS 20050) to generate the pronunciation of First Period Old French (1100-1250). I applied Robert Taylor's diachronic sound chart contained in Timothy McGee's "Singing Early Music." The psaltery and harp sounds were inserted using the iPhone app MusicStudio2. The reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Text:

I  Ja nus homs pris ne dirat sa raison
  Adroitament s'ansi con dolans hons;
  Mais per confort puet il faire chanson.
  Molt ai d’amins mais povre sont li don;
  Honte en auront se por ma raençon
  Suis ces deus yvers pris.

II  Ceu sevent bien mi home e mi baron,
  Englais, Normant, Poitevin et Gascon,
  Que je n’avoie si povre conpaignon
  Que je laissaisse por avoir an prison.
  Je no di pas par nulle retraison,
  Mais ancor suis je pris.

III  Or sai je bien de voir certainement
  Que mors ne priset n’a amins ne parant,
  Cant on me lait por or ne por argent.
  Molt m’est de moi, mais plus m’est de ma gent,
  C’apres ma mort auront reprochier grant,
  Se longement suis pris.

Translation:

No man imprisoned will speak his mind adroitly unless as a man in sorrow; but he can, for comfort, make a song. I have many friends but few gifts; they will be ashamed if merely on account of a ransom I am imprisoned for two winters.

This my men and my barons know well – [whether} English, Norman, Poitevin and Gascon: I never had a companion so poor that I would leave him in prison. I do not say this betrayal, but I am still a prisoner.

Now I know well certainly that the dead or prisoner has no friend or relations, since I am left here because of silver coins. I fear much for myself, but even more for my people, for after my death they will be greatly reproached, if I am held prisoner for long.

---------

Description of the photos:

1. Richard I coronation scene, Chetham MS 6712 A.6.89, c1195
2. Quarrel between Richard Lionheart and Philippe Auguste that lead to the former's eventual arrest by the proxies of the latter, Bibliotheque Nationale de France MS, c1300 
3. Richard I apprehended by the soldiers of Duke Leopold V, Anonymous sketch from c1196
4. The rocky foothills around Dürnstein Castle (now in ruins) where Richard was imprisoned and ransomed by Duke Leopold V in December 1192 and held for 4 months (beyond which point Richard was handed over to Emperor Henry VI, again for ransom)
5. The ruins of Burg Dürnstein where Richard was held prisoner for a hefty ransom.

videos.title: Enrique de Foix: Mi querer tanto vos quiere (c.1465) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Enrique de Foix: Mi querer tanto vos quiere (c.1465) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This passionate villancico in the Spanish language by a lesser known Franco-Flemish composer Enrique de Foixer is one of many courtly love songs contained in the Cancionero Musical de Palacio, a large collection of mostly secular music at the court of Ferdinand and Isabella.  It is one of the earlier works in the tome and likely dates to before 1470 since its creator was known to have been employed by the Catalan kings in the 1460s. It is a lamentation of a man yearning for a lady whom he cannot have.

The 4 singing parts were created using the Synthesizer V software with the Solaria (soprano) and Kevin (alto, tenor, bass) voice banks.  Reverb and echo were added later using Audacity.

Text (translation)

Mi querer tanto vos quiere, (My desire yearns after you so much)
muy graciosa doncella, (my very gracious young lady)
que por vos mi vida muere (that for you my life dies)
que por vos mi vida muere (though for you my life may end)
y de vos no tien querella (of you there is no complaint)
con amor y lealtad. (with love and loyalty)
que de vos no se que diga (I don't know what he says about you) 
viendo vuestra honestad (seeing your honesty)
Si mi querer tanto vos quiere, (If my desire yearns so much)
sois tan bella (you are so beautiful)
que por vos mi vida muere (though for you my life may end)
y de vos no tien querella (of you there is no complaint)

De long travail

  2:02  Instrumental arrangement (recorder, lute, harp and viol)
