videos.title: Anonymous Italian: Amor tu non me gabaste (c.1470)

localized.title: Anonymous Italian: Amor tu non me gabaste (c.1470)
localized.description:
Amor tu non me gabasti

0:06  Original canzone (ATTB) with instruments
2:53  Instrumental (2 lutes, citole, harp)

This barzelletta in two parts for 4 voices (ATTB) appears in two late Medieval / early Renaissance sources: the Montecassino MS 871 and the Pixérécourt MS. The well-formed, imitative polyphony suggests inspiration from or composition by a Franco-Burgundian author since much of the native Italian music from the mid- to late 15th century is mostly homophonic in structure. The copyist of Montecassino 871 sketched the musical notes minus the lyrics of only the Pars 2 ("Io havea voluntate") on the first page of the manuscript at the bottom of the page almost hidden beneath another piece.

The vocal simulations were generated using Synthesizer V with only the Kevin voice bank. The instrumental sounds were created using the Music Studio 2.0 app in the iPhone. The addition of reverb and echo were performed with Audacity.

Text (and translation):

Pars 1 (Part 1)
Amor tu non me gabasti (Cupid, you did not fool me)
ch'io gia te conoscia (because I already knew you)
m'a forczao la voglia mia (for she has forced my wishes)
la segnora che dasti (the lady you gave me)

Pars 2 (Part 2)
Io havea voluntate (I had willed myself)
non servirte piu de grato (not to serve you any more)
per le toe falze passate (for your past falsehoods)
che con mico tu ay usato (that you have used with me)

(Refrain)
Pero fin che su' incapato (But at last by my obstinacy)
non fu per credere actia (I shall not believe)
m'a forczao la voglia mia (for she has forced my wishes)
la segnora che dasti (the lady you gave me)

videos.title: Anonymous Spanish: Si la noche haze escura (c.1550) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Anonymous Spanish: Si la noche haze escura (c.1550) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This moving villancico is yet another one of thousands of songs about courtly love from the High Renaissance. In the Cancionero de Uppsala, no attribution is given, but scholars have proposed that it might be the work of the Spanish master of Renaissance polyphony Francisco Guerrero.

Despite the small size of the ensemble (only 3 parts), it is rich in harmony and counterpoint. It is unusual in that time for all 3 singers to start on the same note and end on the same note (G4 in the original notation).  Much of the rest of the villancico consists of an imperfect canon between the two upper voices. The words in this song express the sorrows of a jilted woman waiting for the return of her lover.

This rendition was created using only the Kevin voice bank in Synthesizer V with the Spanish phoneme setting. I adjusted the default phoneme settings to simulate an early 16th century southern Spanish dialect.

----------

Text:

Si la noche haze escura
y tan corto es el camino,
¿Como no venis, amigo?

La media noche es pasada
Y el que me pena no viene;

Mi desdicha lo detiene,
¡Que nasçi tan desdichada!

Hazeme bivir penada
Y muestra se me enemigo.
¿Como no venis, amigo?

Translation:

If the night is dark
and the road so short,
How come you do not come, my love?

Midnight has passed
and he who pains me does not come

My sadness delays him
[Woe] that I was born so unfortunate

He makes me live in pain
and reveals himself to be my enemy
How come you do not come, my love?

----------

videos.title: Johann Sebastian Bach: Terzetto "Ach! wann wird die Zeit erscheinen?" (1734), with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Johann Sebastian Bach: Terzetto "Ach! wann wird die Zeit erscheinen?" (1734), with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Besides the St. Matthew Passion, the Christmas Oratorio is probably J.S. Bach's most massive and elaborate creation. A complete performance of all the movements would have likely run at least 3 hours, and the virtuosic passages throughout his magnum opus would have tested the limits of even the most skilled musicians and singers of his time. It was likely composed for the Lutheran congregation of St. Thomas Church in Leipzig for the Advent season of 1734. It is, at least in part, a compilation of earlier snippets from his cantatas and other smaller works. It was divided into 6 cantatas of which this Terzetto Aria was embedded in the 5th.

The aria was written for four parts: solo violin, 3 vocalists (soprano, alto, bass) and continuo (which could have been any combination of cello, contrabass, harpsichord or organ). The alto part is added as a response to the other two agitated voices who are impatiently anticipating the coming of the Messiah, but his interjections are abrupt and brief. The listener might find particularly jarring, the shouts of "Ach, wann?" ("O, when") and the response "Schweigt" ("Silence"). Otherwise the movement is mostly a mellifluous trio of violin, cantus (probably a boy soprano) and bassus. 

This latest rendition was created using the Synthesizer V software with the Solaria and Kevin voice banks. The German phonemes were generated from a mix of English and Spanish elements. The instrumental parts (violin, cello, double bass and harpsichord) were simulated using Music Studio 2.0. The reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Text:

Sopran:
Ach! wann wird die Zeit erscheinen? Wann? (O, when will the Time appear? When?)
Jesu, ach! so komm zu mir! (Jesus, Oh, come to me!)
Ach! Wann kommt der Trost der Seinen, wann? (When will his comfort come?)

Alt:
Schweigt, er ist schon wirklich hier (Silence, he is really, already here)

Bass:
Ach! Wann kommt der Trost der Seinen (When will his comfort come?)
Jesu, ach! so komm zu mir! (Jesus, Oh, come to me!)
Ach! Wann wird die Zeit erscheinen, wann? (O, when will the Time appear? When?)

videos.title: Josquin des Prez: Illibata Dei virgo nutrix (c.1490)

localized.title: Josquin des Prez: Illibata Dei virgo nutrix (c.1490)
localized.description:
This unusual motet by Josquin des Prez appears near the end of a manuscript (Cappella Sistina MS 15) that is filled with religious music by the greatest composers of the late 15th century -- most of whom served the Vatican. The text is entirely original, unique and non-liturgical. The initial letters of each line form an acrostic that spells the composer's full name: IOSQVIN DES PREZ. The tenor part is a relentless repetition of the musical notes LA-MI-LA, which corresponds to the vowels in MA-RI-A to whom the piece is dedicated. The two part work was probably composed in the final decades of the 15th century when Josquin was a member of the Sistine Chapel choir. As is typical of Josquin's music from the Roman period, the choir forms pairs of voices that sing in close support of one another and two pairs sing in imitation of the other. Embedded in the text are references to Greek mythology such as Olympus and Muses which is surprising for a Marian motet.

Text (and translation)

Illibata Dei virgo nutrix (Undefiled virgin, nurse of God)
Olympi tu regis o genitrix (you the mother of the king of Olympus)
Sola parens verbi puerpera  (only parent of the word, child bearing woman)
Quae fuisti Evae reparatrix (who was Eve's repairer)
Viri nephas tuta mediatrix (intercessor of wicked men)
Illud clara luce dat scriptura (That clear light, the scripture grants)
Nata nati alma genitura (The birth of birth, soul forming)
Des ut laeta musarum factura (Give that joyous work of the Muses)
Prevaleat hymnus et sit ave (the hymn prevails and yields all hail)
Roborando sonos ut guttura (potentiating the sounds like a voice)
Efflagitent laude teque pura (that cries out in pure praise of you)
Zelotica arte clament Ave. (zealously they cry All hail.)

Ave virginum decus hominum (Hail glory of virgins)
Coelique porta (and gate of heaven)
Ave lilium, flos humilium (Hail the lily of the field, flower of humility)
Virgo decora. (beautiful virgin)
Vale ergo tota pulchra ut luna (thus so beautiful as the moon)
Electa ut sol, clarissima gaude. (chosen like the sun, brightly rejoice)
Salve tu sola cum sola amica, (Hail, you alone with your only friend)
Consola "la mi la" canentes in tua laude. (consoling "la mi la" singing your 
  praise)
Ave Maria, mater virtutum, (Hail Mary, mother of virtues)
Veniae vena, ave Maria, (river of forgiving, hail Mary)
Gratia plena, Dominus tecum, (full of grace, Lord be with you)
Ave Maria, mater virtutum. (Hail Mary, mother of virtues)
Amen.

localized.title: Heinrich Isaac: Puer natus est nobis (c.1507)
localized.description:
This Christmas introit was one of 375 works contained in the magnum opus "Choralis Constantinus" compiled by maestro Heinrich Isaac and his student Ludwig Senfl. The tome includes tunes based on Gregorian chant and conforms to the church calendar. It was commissioned by the Diocese of Konstanz in Southern Germany in 1507 perhaps on the occasion of Emperor Maximilian’s call to assemble the Reichstag in that city.

I have included the sounds of a cornetto and trombones to double the “singers” because Maximilian’s choirs are often depicted with instrumental accompaniment in woodblock prints. The motet is alternates familiar Latin plainchant and 4 part Franco-Flemish style Renaissance polyphony.

The MIDI file was compiled by Willem Verkaik and uploaded to cpdl.org. I used the Synthesizer V vocal simulator with the Solaria (soprano) and Kevin (alto, tenor, bass) voice banks. Spanish phonemes were used to approximate the Latin text. The instrumental simulations were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Text:

Puer natus est nobis. (To us a child is born.)

et filius datus est nobis: (and to us a son is given)
cuius imperium super humerium eius: (Empire is on his shoulder)
et vocabitur nomen eius (and his name will be called)
magni consilii Angelus. (Angel of great counsel)

Cantate Domino canticum novum (Sing to the Lord a new song)
quia mirabilia fecit. (on account of his doing marvels)
    
Gloria patri, et filio, et spiritui sancto, (Glory to the father, son & holy ghost)
Sicut erat in principio, (As it was in the beginning)
et nunc, et semper, (and now and always)
et in saecula saeculorum. (and in age of ages)
Amen

videos.title: Ludwig Senfl: Ich stund an einem morgen a 4 (c.1530) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Ludwig Senfl: Ich stund an einem morgen a 4 (c.1530) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Ich stund' an einem Morgen

  0:06  Verse 1 of the original 4 part Lied (a cappella)
  1:52  Verse 2 (soprano, tenor and lute)
  3:37  Verse 3 (tenor and lute)
  5:22  Verse 4 (SATB, harp, bass viol)

The Swiss composer Ludwig Senfl wrote at least 5 different settings of this popular German melody. "Ich stund an einem Morgen" was a favorite tune to parody among German-speaking composers of the early 16th century including his mentor Heinrich Isaac.  The musical score from the 1534 Hans Ott edition may have been intended for tenor and 3 instrumentalists, since only the tenor part contains the full set of lyrics.  The tenor part contains the original folk melody and constitutes the cantus firmus. The other three "voices" contain an intricate counterpoint more typical of lute music from the same period and does not match very well with the text underlay.

The main character of this ballad is a woman being left behind by her lover who is likely a mercenary soldier (a Landsknecht). Since most songs of this period were about men being rejected or abandoned by women, this piece was somewhat unusual for its gender reversal.

In this rendition, I used the Syntheizer V software loaded with the Solaria (soprano) and Kevin (alto, tenor, bass) voice banks  The instrumental sounds were generated using MusicStudio2. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

Text (and translation):

Ich stund an einem morgen (I stood one morning)
heimich an einem ort (secretly in a spot)
da het ich mich verborgen (therein hiding myself)
Ich hört klegliche wort (I heard sorrowful words)
von einem frewlen hübsch und fein (from a maiden pretty and fine)
sie sprach zu jrem buelen (she spoke to her love)
es muß gescheiden sein. (as he was going away)

Hertz lieb ich hab vernumen (My love, I have heard)
du wölst von hinnen schier (you will depart from here)
wen wiltu wider kumen (When will you return)
das soltu sagen mir (You should tell me that)
nun merk mein feins lieb was ich sag (now, love, listen to what I say)
mein zukunft thust mich fragen (I ask what my future holds)
was weder stund noch tag. (how long: hours even days?)

Das frewlein weinet sere (The young lady wept much)
Sein hertz was unmuts wol (her heart was greatly displeased)
so gib mir weis und lere (so give me wisdom and teaching)
was ich mich halten sol (what should I hold in me)
für dich so setz ich al mein hab (for in you I keep all I have)
und wiltu hie bebleiben (and will you remain here)
verzer dich iar und tag. (or leave year and a day)

Das knab sprach aus seinem muete (The knave spoke from his mouth)
dein wil ich wol soüer (I want you so sweetheart)
verzer ich dir dein guete (but I will consume your good name)
ein iar wer bald hinfür (a year will go by soon)
darnach mus es gescheyden sein (therefore, must we separate)
ich wil dich freundlich bitten (I will bid you politely)
setz deinen willen darein. (settle your mind thus)

videos.title: Mikołaj Zieleński: Viderunt omnes fines terrae (1611)

localized.title: Mikołaj Zieleński: Viderunt omnes fines terrae (1611)
localized.description:
This rare treasure of Polish Renaissance music comes to us from the printing presses of early Baroque Venice. As the choir director and organist of the main cathedral of Gniezno (Poland), Zieleński held a highly esteemed position of a vitally important Catholic stronghold in the north of Europe.

The mellifluous harmonies of his music can be traced back to Palestrina, the master of choral music in Rome, where Zieleński learned his art. However, unlike the plainchant and chordal homophony of Gregorio Allegri -- the official preference of the Council of Trent -- this particular work, with its imitative polyphony, harkens back to an earlier Roman repertoire of the likes of Cristóbal de Morales.

The original MIDI file for this soundtrack (minus the words) was created by John Smith and can be found at musescore.com .  I used the Synthesizer V software with Solaria (soprano) and Kevin (alto, tenor, bass) voice banks. Reverb, echo and upper range noise cancellation were performed with Audacity.

Text:

Viderunt omnes fines terrae (Everyone from world's have seen)
salutare Dei nostri. (the salvation of our God)
Alleluia.

Description of the photos:

1. Cover page of Zieleński's complete score for "Viderunt omnes," from Communiones toti anni, Venice, 1611.
2. Gniezno Cathedral (Church of the Assumption) where Zieleński' was employed as organist and choir director.
3. Saint Adalbert (patron saint of Gniezno) in prayer, detail from the door of Gniezno Cathedral, c1175
4. Interior of Gniezno Cathedral
5. Stained glass windows of the Gothic interior of Gniezno Cathedral

videos.title: Thomas Tallis: Blessed are those that be undefyled (c.1550) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Thomas Tallis: Blessed are those that be undefyled (c.1550) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
The period in which Tallis' composed this English language realization of Psalm 118 remains a mystery. The only surviving copy of the full score was found in the Ludlow Parish Church Partbook which has been dated to around 1565-1570 (the early years of Queen Elizabeth I's reign). It is an early hybrid of older Anglo-Catholic tradition and newer English Protestant innovation. It is in some ways emblematic of Tallis himself who was an ardent Catholic adjusting to and thriving in the newly Anglican nation.

The words of the anthem were lifted from Myles Coverdale's English translation (1535) of the Latin Bible: a product of Henry VIII's theological revolution. The structure of Tallis' music, however, is more reminiscent of pre-Reformation repertoire -- similar to the works of John Taverner, John Shepphard and Christopher Tye. One can hear a rich, imitative polyphonic exchange between boy chorister and adult male voices interspersed with occasional high notes that pierce the ether. It finally concludes with the Trinitarian doxology familiar to all Christian traditions, but written in the straightforward, homophonic style of the new English order. The melismatic and dramatic "amen" at the final cadence adds the unique touch of Tallis' mastery in the art of high choral writing.

Having been written in the English vernacular, this music was certainly intended for use in the Chapel Royal under King Edward VI or Queen Elizabeth I. The text of this piece can also be found in the first English language Book of Common Prayers (1549) for use by Anglican priests for the First Service after Trinity Sunday.

I used a MIDI file created by James Gibb and uploaded to CPDL.org . Instead of the Vocaloid voice encoder, I employed Synthesizer V with the Solaria (soprano) and Kevin (alto, tenor I, tenor II and bass) voice banks.  Reverb and echo were added using Audacity. I adjusted the default phoneme set to approximate Elizabethan pronunciation as outlined by Professor David Crystal. For example, I dropped the "h" sounds from the beginnings of words like "heart" "hast" "him" and "holy" but not from "whole."

Text in Modern English:

Blessed are those that be undefiled in the Way
and walk in the law of the Lord.
Blessed are those that keep his testimonies
and seek him with their whole heart
For they that do no wickedness
walk in his ways
Thou hast charged us O Lord
that we shall diligently keep thy commandments
O that our ways were made so direct
that we might keep thy statutes
So shall we not be confounded
while we have respect unto all thy commandments.

Glory be to the Father and to the Son
and to the Holy Ghost.
As it was in the beginning and ever shall be
world without end.
Amen.

Description of Photos:

1. "Blessed are those" Psalm 118 (Psalm 119 in later translations), Myles Coverdale translation of the Bible, 1535; this is the original text that Tallis used in this anthem.
2. Choir of Canterbury Cathedral where Thomas Tallis had his first directorship.
3. Cover page of the first Book of Common Prayer in the English language, 1549, mostly assembled by Thomas Cranmer. Another version of the text for Psalm 118 appears in this psalter as well.
4. King Edward VI of England, son of Henry VIII and Jane Seymour, and patron to the young Thomas Tallis. Edward issued the official approval for membership to Tallis as Gentleman of the Chapel Royal.
5. Waltham Abbey gateway and bridge, the last two remaining structures from the original Abbey which was destroyed during Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries. Tallis was employed at Waltham just before its demise.
6. Interior of the Chapel Royal, Hampton Court, London where Tallis was a member under King Edward VI, Queen Mary I and Queen Elizabeth I.
7. An early portrait of Queen Elizabeth I, c1560
8. Chapel Royal choir, Hampton Court, the venue for many musical performances by England's greatest masters including Thomas Tallis.

videos.title: Anonymous Aztec / Hernando Franco (?): Dios itlaçonantzine (c.1580)

localized.title: Anonymous Aztec / Hernando Franco (?): Dios itlaçonantzine (c.1580)
localized.description:
This song is the earliest known example of music with lyrics in Classical Nahuatl, the language of the Aztec peoples at the time of the Spanish Conquest. The sequence of plainchant followed by four part polyphony is clearly based on earlier Spanish models of Renaissance church music. It is quickly apparent that the rhythmic patterns were atypical for contemporary Spanish music and were custom fitted to the meter of the native language. It is unclear if this lively piece was intended for a religious festivals or for liturgical services. Much is known about the Nahuatl language (including its orthography and pronunciation) since several modern dialects have survived throughout Mexico. The attribution (Hernando Franco or Francisco) is uncertain but was likely a Native Aztec composer.

The MIDI file was created by Vicente Chavarría and uploaded to cpdl.org. I added the Nahuatl words using a combination of Spanish and English phonemes in the Synthesizer V program. I used the Natalie voice bank for the soprano line and the Kevin voice bank for the alto, tenor and bass lines.

Text:

Dios itlaçonantzine
cemicac ichpochtle
cenca timitztotlauhtiliya
ma topan ximotlatolti
yn ilhuicac ixpantzinco
in motlaçoconetzin Jesu Christo.
Ca onpa timoyeztica yn inahuactzinco
Yn motlaçoconetzin Jesu Christo.

Translation (from cpdl.org):

Dearest Mother of God,
Eternal Virgin,
we earnestly implore you:
intercede for us
in heaven in the presence
of your beloved Son, Jesus Christ.
For you are there, near
to your beloved Son, Jesus Christ.

Description of the photos:

1. Complete score of "Dios itlaçonantzine," Anonymous, Codex Valdés, copied around c1620
2. Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán (c. 1490 – 1558), governor of New Spain (Mexico), depicted on his rampage through Aztec territories in 1529, Codex Telleriano Remensis, c1550
3. Chichen-itza pyramid, Yucatan, Mexico; located in a region controlled by remnants of the once mighty Mayan Empire but occupied first by Aztec settlers and later by the Spanish conquistadores in the 1530s; photo by darwinsantos (Pixabay)
4. Aztec warriors, Codex Mendoza, probably compiled after 1521

videos.title: William Byrd: Come pretty babe (c.1585) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: William Byrd: Come pretty babe (c.1585) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This Elizabethan lullaby is a consort song for solo voice (either soprano or male alto) and 4 viols. It was likely produced during the middle period of William Byrd's long and illustrious composing career. Although it appears to be a secular work capturing the sorrows and complaints of a desolate, single mother consoling her baby boy, it may also be a veiled reference to the Virgin Mary and the baby Jesus. Byrd had written other consort songs in the same period (such as "From Virgin's womb" and "Lulla lullaby) which more directly mentions the holy mother and child. It is one of many standalone pieces not included in any anthologies or printed editions sanctioned by Byrd. The earliest surviving version is contained in the Drexel manuscript 4180-4185 (New York Public Library) hand-copied by John Merro between 1615-25.

++++++++++

The MIDI file was compiled by Peter Krivda and uploaded to the website IMSLP.org. In this latest rendition, I used the Solaria voice bank and the Synthesizer V software. The viol simulations were created using Music Studio 2.0, an iPhone app. Sound editing was performed with Audacity. The default phoneme settings were manually modified to simulate Early Modern English.

Lyrics

Come, pretty babe
thy father's shame, thy mother's grief;
born, as I doubt,
to all our dole,
and to thyself unhappy chief;
Come lullaby
and wrap thee warm
poor soul, thou think'st no creature harm.

Come, little wretch;
ah, silly heart
mine only joy, what can I more?
if there be any wrong thy smart
that may the destinies implore,
'twas I say against my will
I wail the time, but be thou still.

Come little boy
and rock asleep,
Sing lullaby and be thou still.
I that can do naught else but weep
Will sit by thee and wail my feel.
God bless my babe and lullaby
from this thy father's quality.

++++++++++

videos.title: George F. Handel: Sinfony, "Comfort ye," & "Ev'ry valley" from Messiah with Synthesizer V (1741)

localized.title: George F. Handel: Sinfony, "Comfort ye," & "Ev'ry valley" from Messiah with Synthesizer V (1741)
localized.description:
Messiah, Part I

  0:06  Sinfony (Grave) (violins, viola, cello, double bass, organ, theorbo)
  1:33  Sinfony (Allegro moderato) (violins, viola, cello, double bass, organ, theorbo)
  3:36  Recitative: Comfort ye, my people (tenor, violins, viola, cello, double bass, harpsichord)
  6:45  Aria: Ev'ry valley shall be exalted (tenor, violins, viola, cello, double bass, harpsichord)

George Frideric Handel (1685-1759) composed the oratorio Messiah, his magnum opus, in a furious frenzy of inspiration while sequestered in his London apartment for 24 days. His audience at the 1742 Dublin premiere was enthralled despite inadequate rehearsal time, primitive stage sets, no special effects, amateur musicians and lackluster costumes.  Handel had demonstrated his knack for musical drama with his many blockbuster Italian operas of earlier times and was quite the international celebrity through the English-speaking world. After Dublin, he brought his magnificent creation back home to England to raise money for the Foundling Hospital (the central orphanage) in London. And there, until his passing in 1759, he continued his philanthropy for the poorest of the poor children with annual concerts featuring ever more elaborate (and robust) instrumentation and ever-increasing choir size.

The lyrics for Handel's oratorio were extracted from the pages of the King James Bible by his deeply religious friend and patron Charles Jennens. The texts for the recitative  "Comfort ye, my people" and the aria "Every valley shall be exalted" were paraphrases from Isaiah 40. Their words expressed the hope for a brighter future for the Israelite nation which had been conquered in the 6th century B.C.E. by Nebuchadnezzar and held captive for generations by subsequent Babylonian kings.  

The soundtrack for this latest rendition was generated using the Synthesizer V software and the KEVIN English language voice bank; the instrumental parts were simulated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.  My electronic orchestra consists of violins, violas, cellos, double bass, theorbo, chamber organ and harpsichord - as was typical of early 18th century chamber groups.  We know that Handel had, at his disposal, violins, trumpets, harpsichord and organ. Other doubling instruments, like oboes, bassoons and flutes, were described only in later performances. The modern score that I used was created by J. Wagner in MuseScore format. The pronunciation is adjusted to emulate early 18th Century London English.

Illustrations:

1. Early manuscript copy (not in Handel's hand) from around 1743 
2. The study room of the Handel House Museum in London; Handel composed Messiah in this apartment room which he occupied from 1723 until his death in 1759.
3. Fishamble Street Music Hall (aka Neale's Theatre), Dublin, Ireland, the location of Handel's premiere of Messiah in 1742
4. The interior of the Fishamble Music Hall in Dublin
5. View of London and St. Paul's Cathedral around the time of Handel's composing the Messiah Oratorio, Antonio Joli, c1744
6. Foundling Hospital exterior. This was the site of Handel's first fundraising campaign for the orphans of London that continued until his death in 1759.
7. Foundling Hospital Chapel. Handel directed countless performances of the Messiah in this still unfinished main hall.
8. The Prophet Isaiah, Antonio Balestra, c1725
9. King James Bible from 1762, a source of scriptural text similar to what Charles Jennens used to cobbled together the libretto for "Messiah."
10-27. Pages from "Comfort ye" and "Ev'ry valley," autographed copy by Handel, 1741
28. Prophet Isaiah, Benedetto Gennari, c1690

videos.title: George Frideric Handel: Aria "The trumpet shall sound" from Messiah (1741) by Synthesizer V

localized.title: George Frideric Handel: Aria "The trumpet shall sound" from Messiah (1741) by Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Messiah excerpt: Part 3, Scene 2

++++++++++

The dramatic tenor aria "Trumpet shall sound" from Part III, Scene 2 of Handel's Messiah takes its text from First Corinthians Chapter 15 in the King James Bible.  In this epistle, Paul writes about his vision of a Day of Judgement when God raises up the dead from their graves to restore their original living forms. The "last trumpet" announces the end times when true believers of the Christian faith will be summoned to paradise alongside the righteous dead. Handel developed this musical interpretation using a libretto by his friend, occasional patron and frequent critic, Charles Jennens.

The soundtrack for this video was electronically generated using a modified baritone voice KEVIN and the Synthesizer V software. I then added an electronic simulation of a Baroque chamber orchestra using the iPhone app MusicStudio 2.0. The instruments include solo trumpet, 3 first violins, 3 second violins, 2 violas, 2 cellos, 1 double bass, harpsichord, chamber organ and bassoon.  The raw MIDI file was created by D.Viens on the website kunstderfuge.com. In this latest rendition, I corrected some of my earlier pronunciation scheme to emulate an 18th Century London dialect. The reverb and echo were added using Audacity.

++++++++++

Text:

Aria: The trumpet shall sound,
and the dead shall be raised incorruptible,
and we shall be changed.

For this corruptible must put on incorruption
and this mortal must put on immortality

[Refrain] The trumpet shall sound ...

++++++++++

videos.title: Anonymous French: Degentis vita / Cum vix artidici / Vera pudicitia (c.1360)

localized.title: Anonymous French: Degentis vita / Cum vix artidici / Vera pudicitia (c.1360)
localized.description:
This philosophical Latin motet is most peculiar in its theme: namely a bitter lamentation on the loss of morals, honor, social norms, aesthetics and other daily concerns. Since the earliest 3 part version of this complex polyphonic piece appears in a mid-14th Century manuscript, it was likely composed during, or shortly after, the Black Death which had decimated Europe's population and caused unprecedented disruption (and often complete collapse) to nearly every institution. Perhaps the author was despairing over the chaos that ensued in the years after the acute horrors of the Pestilence.

I have given an approximate translation of the text with the assistance of Wiktionary, Google translate and ChatGPT. I welcome any corrections or refinements to my crude interpretation. There are two contratenor lines, but the second one is untexted. Because the two parts seem to be in counterpoint to one another, I speculated that the second part might use the same text. Otherwise, it may have been an instrumental line. The cantus firmus tenor is clearly a repeating line on the same words.

The soundtrack was created using the Synthesizer V software and the Kevin voice bank (with Spanish and English phonemes). My pronunciation simulates French Latin from that period. Reverb and echo were added with Audacity. The MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and posted to Musescore.com.

Original text:

Cantus:
Degentis vita quid prodest arte polita nil sed invita precio manus et redimita et pro dulcore prebenda vel artis amore non fertur flore stirpis sed sanguinis ore.
Atque precatore doni fit et eris honore divitis horore terrore que laudis honore.
Vera regens et falsa tegens cunctis adamatur sed degens et iura legens non deliciatur.
O sors quam vilis vite degentis inepta ullius incepta.
Destructus undesibilis des miserere vitis mundi dignos tibi vitis feris quesitis et opes non sunt nisi.
Litis dare pauperies nunc sibi grata
Dies est nunc maneries nec valet ulla quies.
Virtus decrescit sed symonis
Ypocrisia clero vigessit perit hinc cum flore sophia hoc apte mentis non complicet arte intentis
In spiritus lentis ideo dant dicere ventis infortunatum quidquid me deserit iste mundus me gratum tibi do.
Sit gloria Christe.

Contratenor 1 & 2:
Cum vix artidici promote sint ad habere astrologi logici quid agam.
Petrus miserere nominis et modici quod scientifici miserere nescio blandici Dicantur eo miserere.
Leno scurra malus et adulans qui ioculatur
Herens et talis quails cito deliciatur
Expars istorum cum sim sed non miserorum
Te rogo flos florum michi parti regna polorum cordis tu scelera mea
Purgans virgo
Decora celi dans dulcora vera salutifera.

Tenor:
Vera pudicitia.

Translation:

Cantus:
Of what use is the life of one who lives with refined skills but unwilling hands, bound by money, richly adorned, but creating nothing (of value)? And not for the sake of offering sweetness or for the love of art, not borne as a flower on the stem, but as blood from the mouth.
And with the prayer of the gift, you will be honored with the richness of awe, fear, and the honor of praise.
The true leader, who hides his falsehoods, is loved by all; but the one who lives in poverty and follows the law is unpopular.
O fate, how worthless is the life of one living foolishly, without any purpose.
Unrelenting destruction, have mercy on the life of the world; grant life worthy of you, sought amid hardships, and wealth is nothing without it.
Now poverty, pleased with itself, gives rise to disputes
This is now the world in which we live, and no rest is of any value
Virtue diminishes while simony increases
Clerical hypocrisy abounds. They perish with the flower of wisdom and do not engage the mind with useful intentions.
Like the gentle wind, they say, such misfortune will leave me; this world, I will give it away gratefully.
Glory be to Christ.

Contratenors:
Are they those who promote the arts astrologers?
Peter, have mercy on the name and modesty of the scientific, whom I do not know but speak of with grace.
A pimp, a buffoon, and a flatterer make jokes,
for those who are easily delighted.
One who is apart from these, though not one of the miserable,
I ask you, flower of flowers, to grant me the kingdom of heaven and cleanse the crimes of the heart.
O Virgin who purges [our sins],
Beauteous one in heaven, giving sweet and truly salutary things.

Tenor:
True chastity.

Description of the photos:

1. Full score of "Degentis vita," Chantilly Codex
2. Charivari from Roman de Fauvel, a satirical romance, Anonymous French, c1315
3. A nude priest lecturing a farting monk, Gorleston Psalter, c1310-1320

videos.title: Giulio Caccini: Alme luci beate (1614) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Giulio Caccini: Alme luci beate (1614) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Giulio Caccini, one of the greatest masters of the art song in the early Italian Baroque era, has been often overshadowed by his more famous contemporaries, Claudio Monteverdi and Giovanni Gabrieli. This particularly elaborate aria by Caccini contains a virtuosic flare and dramatic effect repeatedly expressed in the opera movements and madrigals of Monteverdi from the same decade. As was customary in that period, Caccini wrote out, in detail, every note of every ornament and division.

This latest soundtrack was created using Synthesizer V and the Solaria voice bank. The instrumental track consisting of violin, chittarone and bass viol were generated with Music Studio 2 on the iPhone. The original MIDI file without the sung text was created by Sarge Gerbode and can be found at lutemusic.org.

Text (with translations)

Alme luci beate (Souls, blessed lights)
Che dolcemente ardeste (that sweetly burned)
E dolce distruggeste (and gently destroyed)
L'incenerito core, (the incinerated heart)
Chi di bei lampi or farà lieto Amore? (who with beautiful light now makes happy love?)
Io vi lasso mie scorte, (I leave you, my escorts)
Io mi parto bei numi, (I am leaving beautiful gods)
Io vò lungi miei numi, (I go far, my gods)
E non ho spem' ohimè che mi conforte. (and I have no hope alas that comforts me)

Alme luci beate, (Souls, blessed lights)
Se per si lunga etate (If for a long time)
Amando e rimirando (loving and gazing)
Voi foste il mio gioire, (you were my joy)
Or per si lunga etate (Now for such a long time)
Amando e rimembrando (loving and remembering)
Sarete il mio martire. (You will be my martyr)

videos.title: Thomas Mawdyke & Robert Croo: Lully lulla, thou little tiny child (1591) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Thomas Mawdyke & Robert Croo: Lully lulla, thou little tiny child (1591) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This English Christmas carol has had a long and convoluted history. It was one of several songs included in a medieval mystery play about the Nativity and presented by the Coventry guild for Shearmen and Taylors. Its earliest text was transcribed by a Robert Croo in 1534 and the current tune with harmonization was added by Thomas Mawdyke in 1591. The original 1591 manuscript was lost in a library fire in 1879, but a detailed copy meticulously created by a Coventry historian Thomas Sharp in 1817 has survived. The song is a lullaby to the baby Jesus and a song of mourning for the Massacre of  Innocents which had taken place in the Holy Land while the holy family sought refuge in Egypt. In this soundtrack, I used the 1591 arrangement for 3 voices using so called late 16tth Century Early Modern English Pronunciation as prescribed by David Crystal.

This latest rendition was created using the Natalie (alto) and Kevin (tenor & bass) voice banks in Synthesizer V instead of the earlier version that used Vocaloid. The Vocaloid rendition can be seen with this link: https://youtu.be/hE-_GFrF8cY

Original text

1. Lully, lulla, thow littell tine child,
By by, lully, lullay
thow littell tyne child,
By by, lully, lullay!

2. O sisters too, how may we do
For to preserve this day
This pore yongling for whom we do singe
By by, lully, lullay?

3. Herod, the king, in his raging,
Chargid he hath this day
His men of might in his owne sight
All yonge children to slay,

4. That wo is me, pore child, for thee,
And ever morne and may
For thi parting nether say nor singe,
By by, lully, lullay.

3. Holy Family, Annibale Carracci, c1589
4. Massacre of the Innocents, Cornelisz van Haarlem, c1591
5. Mystical Marriage of St. Catherine, Annibale Carracci, c1585

videos.title: Josquin Des Prez: Comment peult avoir joye (c.1490) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Josquin Des Prez: Comment peult avoir joye (c.1490) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Comment peult avoir joye

  0:06  Original chanson (SATB)
  2:13  Instrumental arrangement (cornetti and trombones)

This Josquin chanson for 4 parts may have been written for 2 voices and 2 instruments since the alto and bass parts of surviving manuscripts have no text underlay. Moreover, the alto and bass lines have more intricate divisions that perhaps were better suited for instrumentalists than singers.  The cantus and tenor parts are sung mostly in canon, and each carries a beautifully soaring melody. The song text, like most other secular French pieces of this era, centers on a courtly love theme and compares the gallant lover to a solitary bird searching far and wide for his desired mate. Since all the earliest copies of this piece appear in Northern Italian sources (both handwritten and printed editions), it is assumed that Josquin compose this chanson during his tenure in Rome, Ferrara and Milan.

The vocal simulations for the this soundtrack were created using the Solaria (soprano) and Kevin (alto, tenor, bass) voice banks with the Synthesizer V encoder. The previous edition was developed using the Vocaloid software and can be found here: 

  https://youtu.be/eLBn30V2xmE

I have added the two missing text lines (alto and baritone) based on the imitative patterns of the other two voices. The instrumental simulations were generated with the iPhone app MusicStudio2. 

Text:

Comment peult avoir joye,
Qui Fortune contraint?
L’oyseau qui pert sa proye
De riens ne lui souvient :
Au boys sur la verdure
N’a point tout son desir :
De chanter il n’a cure
Qui vit en desplaisir.

Translation:

How can he have joy,
whom Fortune constrains?
The bird which loses its prey
thinks nothing of it:
in the woods on the green
it has not a desire.
He does not care to sing
He, who lives in sorrow.

videos.title: Claude Janequin: Le chant des oyseaulx (c.1528) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Claude Janequin: Le chant des oyseaulx (c.1528) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
"Le chant des oyseaulx" (The song of the birds) is one of 2 thematic chansons by Janequin based on light-hearted poetry and onomatopoeia (The other is "La Guerre" or "The War"). Throughout this rather complex song, the listener can hear the mimicking of bird calls - an often repeated motif in Medieval and Renaissance composition. The happy sound of twittering birds in spring is used as a wake up call to lovers who have endured a long "winter" of silence, solitude and melancholy.

The facsimile reproduced at the periphery of each frame is the Superius line from a printed publication "Chansons de maistre Clement Janequin nouvellement et correctement imprimeez a Paris par Pierre Attaingnant. 1528" (Bibliothèque nationale de France, département musique, RES VM7-181). The English translation is: "Songs of Master Clément Janequin newly and correctly printed in Paris by Pierre Attaingnant." It is one of Attaingnant's earliest printed chanson part books in his long and illustrious career as music publisher for the greatest composers of the French High Renaissance. Janequin was resourceful in spelling out his desired sound effects. For example, he used the French word for the number "eight" -- "huit, huit, huit, huit" (a rapid of succession of "weet, weet, weet, weet") to create the sound "tweet, tweet, tweet." For the trills, he wrote "trrr" "krrr" "vrrr" or "frrr." After the introductory verse, each of the 3 remaining sections was divided into a song of a different bird containing its specific birdcall.

In this latest rendition, used the Synthesizer V encoding software with three voice banks: Solaria (soprano), Natalie (alto) and Kevin (tenor and bass). Although imperfect, I attempted to simulate Early Modern French pronunciation by combining English and Spanish phonemes. I used two different MIDI files compiled by Brian Russell and Claudio Macchi both posted on CPDL.org, but I made several corrections to the text underlay (including one complete line of poetry) using Attaingnant's original 1528 facsimile. 

++++++++++

French text (from CPDL.org)

Reveillez vous, coeurs endormis
Le dieu d’amour vous sonne.
A ce premier jour de may,
Oyseaulx feront merveillez,
Pour vous mettre hors d’esmay
Destoupez vos oreilles.
Et farirariron (etc…)
Vous serez tous en ioye mis,
Car la saison est bonne.

Vous orrez, à mon advis,
Une dulce musique
Que fera le roy mauvis (le merle aussi)
D’une voix autentique.
Ty, ty, pyty. (etc…)
Rire et gaudir c’es mon devis,
Chacun s’i habandonne.

Rossignol du boys ioly,
A qui le voix resonne,
Pour vous mettre hors d’ennuy
Vostre gorge iargonne:
Frian, frian, frian (etc…)
Fuiez, regrez, pleurs et souci,
Car la saison l’ordonne.

Ariere maistre coucou,
Sortez de no chapitre.
Chacun vous donne au bibou,
Car vous n’estes q’un traistre.
Coucou, coucou (etc…)
Par traison en chacun nid,
Pondez sans qu’on vous sonne.

Reveillez vous, coeurs endormis,
Le dieu d’amours vous sonne.

++++++++++

English translation (from CPDL.org)

Awake, sleepy hearts,
The god of love calls you.
On this first day of May,
The birds will make you marvel.
To lift yourself from dismay,
Unclog your ears.
And fa la la la la (etc…)
You will be moved to joy,
For the season is good.

You will hear, I advise you,
A sweet music
That the royal song thrush will sing (the blackbird, too)
In a pure voice.
Ti, ti, pi-ti (etc…)
To laugh and rejoice is my device,
Each with abandon.

Nightingale of the pretty woods,
Whose voice resounds,
So you don’t become bored,
Your throat jabbers away:
Frian, frian (etc…)
Flee, regrets, tears and worries,
For the season commands it.

Turn around, master cuckoo
Get out of our company.
Each of us gives you a ‘bye-bye’
For you are nothing but a traitor.
Cuckoo, cuckoo (etc…)
Treacherously in others' nests,
You lay without being called.

Awake, sleepy hearts,
The god of love is calling you.

----------

LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS

1. Entrance to the Château de Fontainebleau, residence of François I (King of France in Janequin's time) & center of musical activity in France's aristocratic circles for most of the 16th century.
2. Rustic concert, Anon.Italian, 16th cent. Note the sole male singer with 3 other singers who likely were performing 4 part harmony.
3. Songbirds in a tree, generated by ChatGPT
4. Pleasures at the Valois Court, Anon. French, c1560?
5. Galerie de François I, Château de Fontainebleau: a likely venue for many of Janequin's music.
6. Lady and Unicorn (detail with parakeet), c1510
7. Goldfinch, Sherborne Missal, c1400
8. Allegory of Music, a muse playing before an audience of birds, Franco-Flemish, 16th cent.
9. Nightingale? Sherborne Missal, c1400
10. Birds singing to one another, Douai BM 0108, c1544
11. Bird with wings outstretched, Book of Hours of Joanna I, c1506
12. Concert of singers, School of Fontainbleau
13. Château de Chenonceau, another center of musical culture in the 16th century.

videos.title: Orlando Gibbons: See see the Word is incarnate with Synthesizer V (c.1620), Original Pronunciation

localized.title: Orlando Gibbons: See see the Word is incarnate with Synthesizer V (c.1620), Original Pronunciation
localized.description:
Similar in theme of Handel's Messiah, this English verse anthem by Orlando Gibbons (composed more than a century earlier) begins with Luke's birth narrative of Jesus and ends with the resurrection of a messiah. It is comprised of 7 vocal parts and an obligatory instrumental accompaniment (likely organ or viols). As with other verse anthems in the Gibbons repertoire, the declamations alternate between an alto soloist and various combinations of singers.

In this latest rendition, I used the Synthesizer V vocal simulation software with the Kevin and Solaria voice banks. As in the previous versions, the original MIDI file was created by James Gibb and can be found at the website CPDL.org. I transposed the pitch down a minor third to its original notation as indicated in the earliest surviving manuscript.  I adjusted the default phoneme settings to imitate a version of early Modern English based Professor David Crystal's suggestions. The "r" sound is rhotic as in Modern American English and the final "y" has a "əɪ" sound rather than "i:". For example, the "glory" becomes "glo:rəɪ" and "victory" was likely "vɪktorɪ." The initial "h" in "high" "he" "hell" and "Hosanna" were silent. "Heaven" maybe particularly difficult to pick up for the modern ear since it was likely pronounced "evn." Words ending with "-tion" such as salvation, motion and ascension were pronounced "-sɪən."

Text: 

See, see the Word is incarnate; God is made man in the womb of a Virgin.
Shepherds rejoice, wise men adore and angels sing
"Glory be to God on high: peace on earth, good will towards men."
The law is cancelled,
Jews and Gentiles are converted by the preaching of glad tidings of salvation.
The blind have sight and cripples have their motion;
diseases cured, the dead are raised, and miracles are wrought.
Let us welcome such a guest with Hosanna.

The Paschal Lamb is offered, Christ Jesus made a sacrifice for sin.
The earth quakes, the sun is darkened, the powers of hell are shaken;
and lo, he is risen up in victory.
Sing Alleluia.

See, O see the fresh wounds, the gored blood,
the prick of thorns, the print of nails.
And in the sight of multitudes a glorious ascension.

When now he sits on God's right hand
where all the choir of heaven all jointly sing:
Glory be to the Lamb that sitteth on the throne.
Let us continue our wonted note with Hosanna:
Blessed be He that cometh in the Name of the Lord;
with Alleluia, we triumph in victory,
the serpent's head is bruised, Christ's kingdom exalted,
and heaven laid open to sinners.
Amen.

Description of photos:

videos.title: Adrian Willaert (& Domenico Bianchini): Le dur traveil (1544) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Adrian Willaert (& Domenico Bianchini): Le dur traveil (1544) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Le dur traveil (travail)

  0:00. Original chanson for 4 voices (accompanied by lute reduction by Domenico Bianchini)
  1:57  Instrumental arrangement (flute, 2 lutes, harp, bass viol)

Although Willaert spent most of his adult life in Venice as music director of the Basilica San Marco, he published a small number of madrigal-like chansons in the French language in a densely stacked 4 voice polyphony reminiscent of his Parisian contemporaries Sermisy and Sandrin.  

Willaert’s birthplace was situated near the western edge of the Flemish heartland, so he likely grew up in a bilingual milieu that included French, Dutch and various dialects of both. He studied, in his younger years, with the master Jean Mouton (a contemporary of Josquin's) in Paris. There is an anecdote that his composition was even mistaken by a professional choir as Josquin's at some point early in his career.

As with other secular works of Willaert that included adaptations of the Petrarchan sonnets, this piece has a certain melancholic and serious mood.  It is a meditation on sorrow without a clearly named object. It seems that he intentionally kept the song’s meaning ambiguous so that we are left wondering if its theme is romantic or spiritual or both. Bianchini's lute reduction preserves most of the chanson but gently includes passing ornaments and quick scales (connecting large leaps in the notes) that were typical of early 16th century Italian lute solos. 

This latest rendition was created entirely using the Synthesizer V software (and the Kevin voicebank - combining both English and Spanish phonemes) instead of Vocaloid 4.0 which was my previous go-to program. Here is my link to my earlier rendition using Vocaloid 4 and the Maika Spanish language voice bank:

https://youtu.be/Sz7TGRFYrsY

Let me know which one you prefer.

I obtained the MIDI for the lute reduction from Sarge Gerbode’s excellently indexed website, lutemusic.org .  I made a single ficta change to one of the original flourishes in Gerbode's transcription in order for the lute solo to blend in with the vocal parts. The MIDI for the original chanson and the text underlay were compiled by André Vierendeels and uploaded to cpdl.org. The instrumental simulations (renaissance flute, lutes, harp and bass viol) were added using MusicStudio2. 

Text:

Le dur traveil ou mon cueur est confit
contraint l'esprit d'avoir des maulx assez
Mais le povoir du tres puissant
souffit d'y pourveoir et les rendre cassez

The harsh pain that freezes my heart
forces the soul to be filled with distress,
but the power of the Almighty
is enough to see through them and make them go away.

----------

videos.title: Pierre Guedron: Belle qui m’avez blessé (1609) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Pierre Guedron: Belle qui m’avez blessé (1609) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Belle, qui m'avez blessé

  0:06  Arrangement for soprano recorder, chitarrone
  1:00  Verse 1: alto with chitarrone, bass viol, violone
  1:54 Verse 2: alto with harpsichord
  2:49  Verse 3: alto with chitarrone, bass viol, violone

The French repertoire known as "Airs de cour" (airs for the court) were the rage in Paris in the early decades of the 17th century, and their soaring tunes resonated through the spacious dance halls of the Château de Fontainebleau and other pleasure palaces of King Henry IV of France and his family.

In this latest rendition, I experimented with the Natalie voicebank and the Synthesizer V program instead of the usual Vocaloid software. The earlier rendition using Vocaloid is here: 

https://youtu.be/iBF2r92Kozs

I think the pronunciation of 17th Century French sounds better with the earlier Vocaloid recording but the vocal quality with Synthesizer V seems warmer and closer to human.

The original MIDI file and pdf score were compiled by Serge Gerbode and can be found on his website lutemusic.org . The instrumental simulations were created using an iPhone app, MusicStudio2. Originally, Guedron composed 6 verses of which I chose only the first 3 to avoid excessive repetition. 

Text:

Belle, qui m'avez blessé (Lady, who has injured me)
d'un trait si doux (with a gentle stroke)
Hélas! pourquoy me laissez vous?  (Alas, why do you leave me?)
Moy, qui languis d'un cruel désespoir (I, who languish in cruel despair)
Quand je suis sans vous voir (when I am unable to see you...)

Las! vous emportés en ce triste départ (Alas, you go away in this sad departure)
De mon coeur meilleure part (from my heart, its best part)
Et vous laissez l'autre en proye (and you leave the rest as prey)
aux douleurs, aux soupirs et pleurs (to pains, sighs and tears)

Ou me rendés l'une, ou belle par pitié (Either made me the one, or beauty in compassion)
Ne laissés pas l'autre moyttié, (don't leave behind the other) 
Ou bien donnés d'un pitoyable effort (Or in a pitying way)
A toutes deux la mort (both bring death)

videos.title: Francisco de Millán: Que puedo perder (c.1500) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Francisco de Millán: Que puedo perder (c.1500) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
This rare gem of a villancico by Francisco de Millán is one of the hundreds of Spanish secular songs in the Cancionero Musical de Palacio. As was quite familiar to the period, this work too is a song of courtly love.

The original MIDI was created and uploaded to Musescore.com by Bojopigeon. I used the KEVIN voicebank (with the Spanish language setting) in Synthesizer V to generate the three vocal lines. The instrumental sounds (lute, vihuela, citole and harp) were simulated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0.

Text:

Qué puedo perder que pierda,
aunque ya la vida sea,
pues por vos tan bien s'enplea? 

El perder será ganar;
vencimiento, ser vençido.
Verme yo por vos perdido
m'es vitoria singular.
Pues asý a mi desear
su penar tan bien se enplea,
no ay penar que pena sea.

Quiero sofrir los tormentos,
las cuitas en que me veo,
pues voluntad y deseo
rrazón los haze contentos;
é por bien los perdimientos
que la ventura acarrea,
porque más ganado sea.

Translation:

What can I lose,
although life already is lost,
since it is so much spent for you?

Losing will be winning;
defeat, being defeated.
Seeing myself lost for you
is a singular victory for me.
since to desire your grief
very much pleases [me]
there is no grief that is painful.

I want to suffer the torments,
the troubles in which I see myself,
since will and desire
reason makes them happy;
and for good the losses 
that fortune brings,
so that I may gain more.

videos.title: Johann Walter: Nun komm der heiden Heiland (1524) with Synthesizer V

localized.title: Johann Walter: Nun komm der heiden Heiland (1524) with Synthesizer V
localized.description:
Nu kom der heyden heyland (Nun komm der heiden Heiland)

This iconic Christmas motet by Johann Walter, printed in 1524, has been adapted and reshaped into countless Lutheran chorales until modern times. The most famous are the two cantatas (#61 and #62) by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Walter and Luther's original cantus firmus is loosely based on the plainchant "Veni Redemptor gentium" by the Church Father Pope Ambrosius (c. 340 – 397 CE), and the most frequently used lyrics are Luther's German translation of the Latin. Unlike the Lutheran hymns designed for congregational singings, this elaborately arranged imitative polyphony for 5 voices can be traced to the Franco-Flemish tradition.

In the interest of limiting repetitiveness, I rendered only the 1st and 8th verses for this soundtrack. The chorus in this recording uses the Solaria and Kevin voice banks (with the Spanish and English language phoneme sets) in the latest version of Synthesizer V. 

Text from Luther's original German translation:

1. Nu kom, der heyden heyland,
der yungfrawen kynd erkannd,
dass sych wunnder alle welt,
Gott solch gepurt yhm bestelt.

8. Lob sei Gott dem Vater getan;
Lob sei Gott seim eingen Sohn,
Lob sei Gott dem Heilgen Geist
immer und in Ewigkeit.

English translation:

1. Now come, Savior of the peoples
Known as son of the Virgin
that the whole world marvels
That God chose such a birth.

8. Praise be to God the Father,

videos.title: John Dowland: All people that on earth do dwell (Psalm 100) with Synthesizer V (1621)

localized.title: John Dowland: All people that on earth do dwell (Psalm 100) with Synthesizer V (1621)
localized.description:
All people that on earth do dwell (Psalm 100), Original Pronunciation

This is a new soundtrack using Synthesizer V instead of Vocaloid 4.

Along with "Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott" ("A mighty fortress is our God"), Psalm 100 (the "Old One Hundredth") has become one of the most iconic hymns of the Protestant Reformation both in Anglican England and in Lutheran Germany. The so called "100th" has been adopted by the likes of J.S. Bach in the 18th Century all the way to Ralph Vaugh Williams in the 20th Century. It was also one of the first published hymns in the Massachusetts Bay Colony's "Bay Psalm Book" (1640) and a song tune that was carried across the Atlantic in the "Ainsworth Psalter" by Pilgrim Father, William Bradford.

This 4 part arrangement by Dowland is based around a monophonic tune likely composed by the French Calvinist Loys (Louis) Bourgeois in the middle of the 16th century. The melody is taken from Psalm 134 in the Genevan Psalter (1551) while the text come from William Kethe's Scots-English translation of Psalm 100.

This particular 4 part hymn setting comes to us from Thomas Ravenscroft's 1621 Psalter. In this latest soundtrack, I experimented with the Natalie and Kevin voicebanks in the Synthesizer V voice encoding software. I tried to capture the raw, uncultivated and unrestrained quality of congregational singers who were the new cantors in some Protestant circles. I adjusted the default phoneme settings to capture the sound of the English language during Shakespeare's time. Unlike with Received Pronunciation, the "r" sound was rhotic as in modern day American or Scots English. Final "y" or "ie" at the end of a syllable was "əi" rather than "i." So that joy was "jəi" and mercy (or mercie) was "mersəi."

Description of photos:

1. "All people that on earth do dwell," John Dowland's 4 part arrangement of Loys (Louis) Bourgeois' monophonic melody, from Whole Booke of Psalmes, ed. Thomas Ravenscroft, London, 1621
2. King David singing the Psalms (accompanied by harp), Sir Peter Paul Rubens & Jan Boeckhorst, c1616
3. The Mayflower ship riding out stormy seas, a ChatGPT creation
4. Puritans singing psalms, a ChatGPT creation

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous French & Jean-Baptiste Besard: La voila la nacelle damour (1603)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous French & Jean-Baptiste Besard: La voila la nacelle damour (1603)
localized.description:
This charming, playful monody chanson by an anonymous author was reimagined as a lute song by the Franco-Burgundian physician - lawyer - lutenist Jean-Baptiste Besard. An earlier version of this song with an additional verse was realized for chamber chorus by his contemporary Pierre Guédron.

The original MIDI was compiled by Sarge Gerbode. I added the words using the Maika Spanish language Vocaloid. In this latest rendition, I created a more expansive sound using the combination of cello, violone, chitarrone (alternating with harpsichord), enhancing the male alto voice and augmenting the echo / reverb effects. I also added natural dynamics, generated a more legato effect and added a light vibrato at the cadences.

Text:

1. La voila la nacelle d'amour ou ma maistresse arrive,
La voicy la voila de retour de sa prison captive.

[Refrain]

Qu'un chascun luy fasse omage
Et d'un courage que l'on chante tousiours la la la
La voicy la voila que l'on chante tousiours la la la
La voicy la voila la la voila.

2. Le voila le voici ce bel oeil sur le crystal de l'onde.
Le voicy ce soleil non pareil, le seul astre du monde.

3. Les voila les voicy ses cheveux de ma belle maistresse,
Approchés regardés curieux, admirés ceste tresse.

Translation:

1. There it is, the boat of Cupid on which my Lady arrives
Here it is, there it is, returning from its captive prison

[Refrain]

That each one gives it homage
and courage
And they all sing always
La, la, la it's here, it's there

2. It is there, it is there this pretty eye over the crystal wave
Here, this sun without equal, the only star of the world.

3. It is here, it is there, the hair of my beautiful mistress
Approach, look, curious ones, admire these tresses

videos.title: [New Rendition] John Dowland: Time stands still (1603)

localized.title: [New Rendition] John Dowland: Time stands still (1603)
localized.description:
Time stands still (Original Pronunciation

  0:06 Ver)se 1  (soprano, lute, viol)
  2:09 Instrumental arrangement (flute, lute, bass viol)

Although this lute song by John Dowland was written while he was employed by King Christian IV of Denmark, it was published in London like nearly all his other major works. The year of its publication coincided with the year of Queen Elizabeth's passing. As such, the song may have some relevance to the Queen's declining health and her vain attempts to hide her departed youth. Portrait painters from the same period also depicted Elizabeth as a young and vivacious woman up until her final years.  This particular song may also obliquely express Dowland's continued loyalty to the English crown despite his expatriate status.

This soundtrack was created using the Prima Vocaloid as the "soprano."  The instrumental sounds were created using Music Studio 2 for the iPhone and integrated with the voice using Audacity.  In this latest rendition, I have created a more legato effect, added natural dynamics, rebalanced the voices, enhanced the echo / reverb effects and softened the "singer's" timbre.

Text:

Verse 1:

Time stands still with gazing on her face,
stand still and gaze for minutes, houres and yeares, to her give place:
All other things shall change, but shee remaines the same,
till heavens changed have their course & time hath lost his name.
Cupid doth hover up and downe blinded with her faire eyes,
and fortune captive at her feete contem’d and conquerd lies.

Verse 2 [not included in this recording] 

When fortune, love, and time attend on
Her with my fortunes, love, and time, I honour will alone,
If bloudlesse envie say, dutie hath no desert.
Dutie replies that envie knowes her selfe his faithfull heart,
My setled vowes and spotlesse faith no fortune can remove,
Courage shall shew my inward faith, and faith shall trie my love.

videos.title: Leonardo Giustiniani & Anonymous: Dov'e, dov'e ordonne (c.1450)

localized.title: Leonardo Giustiniani & Anonymous: Dov'e, dov'e ordonne (c.1450)
localized.description:
Leonardo Giustiniani (1388-1446) was a Humanist intellectual and a top tier politician from one of the most powerful patrician families in mid-15th Century Venice. For private recreation, he translated the works of Plutarch, transcribed Petrarca's Canzoniere and dabbled in poetry. A few of the poems he composed were transformed into songs during his lifetime (perhaps by him, perhaps by others), but they gained such a following that the songs themselves were often called “gli giustiniani.” This particular piece is a somewhat bastardized version of his lyrics written in the Venetian dialect of his era. Its theme is one of courtly love, which was the principal literary motif of the time.

I generated the simulated singing voices using the Maika Vocaloid and added the instrumental doubling using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. The original MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon.

Text:

Dov'è, Dov'è or donne le mio signore
qui piu non a pieta del mio tormento
de non me neghe el tuo bel viso amore

Occhi mi lassi
or ma coment fare te
poi che lizadro viso a mi s'asconde
Per consumare la vita fra la fronde

Spesso diro Cupido traditore
che n'a da l'amor l'alma se non pianto
ne per questo fia spento el foco al core

Dov'è, Dov'è or donne... .

Translation:

Where is she, where are my ladies now my lord
no longer pitying my torment here.
Don't deny me your beautiful face, my love
Lay your eyes on me
but now ... do you
then that graceful face hides from me
To consume life between the trees.

I often say, the traitor Cupid
what can the soul have from love if it has not cried
nor will the fire in the heart be extinguished for this reason.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Antoine Boësset: Divine Amarillis (1632)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Antoine Boësset: Divine Amarillis (1632)
localized.description:
Divine Amarillis

  0:06  Instrumental arrrangement (flute, chitarrone, viol)
  0:49  Original madrigal (tenor, chitarrone, viol)

Antoine Boësset, master of music at the French court of King Louis XIII, expanded the newly formed genre of courtly lute songs following in the footsteps of his father-in-law and prior master of the king's music, Pierre Guedron, as well as well as John Dowland and Giulio Caccini of earlier decades. This song takes after the Amaryllis character of Greek mythology frequently invoked by the late Renaissance masters (e.g. "Though Amaryllis dance in green" by William Byrd and "Amarilli mia bella" by Giulio Caccini). In this latest rendition, I have rebalanced the voices with the chitarrone, added natural dynamics, enhanced the reverb & echo and created a more legato effect.

I used a MIDI file compiled by Sarge Gerbode. It can be found on his fantastic website lutemusic.org .

----------

Text:

Divine Amarillis (Divine Amaryllis)
Ton teint brun comme il est fait honte a tous les lys (Your looks bring shame to all the lilies)
Ta grace est admirable: (Your grace is admirable)
Mais ta vertu qui passe ta beauté. (But your virtue goes beyond your beauty)
Dessous le ciel n'a rien de comparable (There is nothing to compare under heaven)
Que ma fidelité. (that is my loyalty)

Tes attraits sont pareils, (Your attractions are the same)
Tes yeux que justement on nomme des soleils, (Your eyes which justly we call suns)
Ont un ésclat semblable (have a similar shine)
Mais ta vertu qui passe ta beauté, (But your virtue which surpasses your beauty)
Dessous le ciel n'a rien de comparable (Under the heavens, has no comparison)
Que ma fidelité. (that is my loyalty)

Bel astre des mortelz! (Beautiful star of the mortals)
Le ciel n'est point jaloux de te voir des autelz: (Heaven is not jealous to see you from the altar)
N'est tu pas adorable? (Are you not adorable?)
Et ta vertu qui passe ta beauté, (And the virtue that surpasses your beauty)
Void elle rien qui luy soit comparable (Nothing to her is comparable)
Que ma fidelité. (that is my loyalty)
----------

videos.title: Diego Ortiz: Tres Recercadas (1553)

localized.title: Diego Ortiz: Tres Recercadas (1553)
localized.description:
Tres recercadas

0:06 Recercada Tercera sopra “la Spagna” (viol, harp, organ)
2:16  Recercada Ottava sopra “la Folia” (viol, harpsichord)
4:19  Recercada Settima sopra “la Romanesca” (viol, organ)

Diego Ortiz, a well travelled Spanish composer from Toledo, published his collection of Recercadas, titled "Tratado de Glosas" in Rome in 1553. One edition was printed in Italian, the other in Spanish. Although his arrangements are based on tunes that were widely familiar to early 16th Century audiences, Tratado was a first-of-its-kind compilation of original music specifically targeting bowed instruments (vihuelas de arco or bowed violas). It explored the expressive range and virtuosic potential of the viola da gamba for both high and low pitch instruments. It was also an instructional manual on how to play improvisations using ornaments and divisions on stringed instruments. Because of its meticulous notation of the ornamentation, we are able to glimpse into the world of performance practices during the High Renaissance.

4. Close up view of #2 above.
5. "Recercada Ottava" score for the solo instrument, Diego Ortiz, Tratado de Glosas, Rome, 1553

videos.title: [New Rendition] Juan Vásquez: De los álamos vengo madre (1551)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Juan Vásquez: De los álamos vengo madre (1551)
localized.description:
Juan Vásquez: De los álamos vengo madre

   0:06  Original 4 villancico for four voices (SATB) accompanied by lute (lute reduction from Miguel de Fuenllana)
   2:23  Instrumental arrangement for cornetto, 3 viols and lute. 

The villancico was the most popular form of Spanish song in late 15th century and early 16th century Spain.  Juan Vásquez's "De los álamos" ("From the aspen trees") is a very short villancico with only a few words repeated again and again. It is a song consisting mostly of mood and texture rather than complicated poetry with hidden meaning. A man goes to Seville and sees a beautiful high-born woman and later obsesses about her to his mother. The lady is likely out of reach from his station in life - a common situation in a world rigidly segregated by class structure.

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, slowed the tempo a bit, toned down the harshness of the soprano voice, rebalanced the voices, added natural dynamics and enhanced the reverb / echo. In this soundtrack, I inserted the lute reduction of Miguel de Fuenllana in both the vocal and instrumental arrangements. The MIDI file for the singing parts was created by Mr. Nimura on the Japanese website http://aeolianconsort.chakin.com . I transposed the notes down an octave because the original MIDI was intended for a 4' recorder quartet. The lute reduction was created by Sarge Gerbode and can be found on his website lutemusic.org. I added an instrumental arrangement for cornetto, 3 viols and lute using the iPhone app MusicStudio2.

++++++++++

Text:

De los álamos vengo, madre,
de ver cómo los menea el ayre.

De los álamos de Sevilla,
de ver a mi linda amiga.

De los álamos vengo, madre,
de ver cómo los menea el ayre.

Translation:

I come from the aspen trees, Mother,
I saw how they shake in the breeze.

From the aspen trees of Seville,
where I saw my beautiful girl.

I come from the aspen trees, Mother,
I saw how they shake in the breeze.

++++++++++

2. Courtyard of Alcázar, Sevilla, the royal palace in which Charles V (Holy Roman Emperor) and Isabella of Portugal were married. Emperor Charles was an avid patron of music in Spain, and nearly all scores published between 1535-1550 acknowledge his name.
3. Portrait of Beatrix Pacheco (a Spanish noblewoman married to a French aristocrat around the time this composition was written), Jean Clouet, 1550
4. La Giralda, bell-tower of the Catedral de Sevilla (a landmark that Vasquez likely saw everyday going to and from his home)

6. Ivory cornetto, Southern German, c1575

videos.title: John Sheppard: In pace in idipsum (c.1550)

localized.title: John Sheppard: In pace in idipsum (c.1550)
localized.description:
This staid antiphon by John Sheppard was likely composed around the same period as three other settings of the same title by his esteemed contemporaries Thomas Tallis, John Blitheman and John Taverner. All four works were consecutively copied into a single large collection known as the "Gyffard Partbooks" around 1570. It was likely used for Compline services at the end of a day and perhaps also for the celebration of Holy Saturday when Christ's body was resting in the tomb.

The MIDI file was created and uploaded to cpdl.org by Jason Smart. Text was entered using the Maika Spanish language Vocaloid. It is pitched around A466. The videos can be accessed at the website Pixabay.com . I used an anglicized Latin pronunciation as recommended by Timothy McGee in “Singing Early Music.”

Text:

In pace, in idipsum dormiam et requiescam.
Si dedero somnum oculis meis,
et palpebris meis dormitationem,
dormiam et requiescam.
Gloria Patri, et Filio, et Spiritui Sancto.

Translation:

In peace and into the same I shall sleep and rest.
If I give slumber to my eyes
and to my eyelids drowsiness,
I shall sleep and rest.
Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Adrian Willaert: Ave virgo, sponsa Dei (1542)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Adrian Willaert: Ave virgo, sponsa Dei (1542)
localized.description:
This Marian motet comes from a collection of Venetian church music for 6 voices by Adrian Willaert, master of music at Basilica San Marco. It is written in the tradition of High Renaissance Franco-Flemish polyphonists just before guidelines by the Tridentine Council discouraged intricate counterpoint in church services. Some of the richly textured polyphony is prescient of later works by Palestrina and Victoria. In this motet, there are 5 voices that sing in imitation of one another while a sole tenor, tucked away in the middle, repeatedly intones an entirely different liturgical text, the plainchant "Inviolata, integra et casta, es tu Maria." (Undefiled, pure and chaste are you, Mary). The motet is divided into 3 parts (outlined below).

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, added natural dynamics, rebalanced the voices and enhanced the reverb / echo. The original MIDI was created and uploaded to cpdl.org by John Hetland.

Text and translation:

1. Ave Vírgo, sponsa Dei, (Hail, virgin, spouse of God)
sancti spíritus sacrarium, (santuary of the holy spirit)
in quo praeter ordinem (in which beyond this order)
mirabili mysterio (a miraculous mystery)
verbum caro factum est, (The word is made flesh)
et tu Chrísti redemptoris (and you, are Christ redeemer's)
immaculata genitrix. (immaculate birth mother)

2. O María, benedícta in mulieribus, (O Mary, blessed among women)
tu sola fons pietatis (you alone are the font of piety)
et foelix coeli porta; (and auspicious way to heaven)
tu sola es mater gratiae;  (you alone are the mother of grace)
tu spes sola pauperum (you alone are the hope of the poor)
et advocata nostra (and our advocate)
ante conspectum Domini. (before God's sight)

3. Igitur nos merito (Therefore, we deservedly)
errata nostra flentes (grieving our errors)
in hac lacrimarum valle (in this valley of tears)
ad te confugimus! (flee to you)
Ora pro nobis Dominum, (Pray for us to the Lord)
quia paenitet peccasse, (as we repent our sins)
ora eum jugiter, (Pray to him always)
ut nobis indulgeat (so that he may indulge us)
sola ejus clementia. (with his forgiveness)
Amen.

videos.title: Tarquinio Merula: Folle è ben che si crede (1638)

localized.title: Tarquinio Merula: Folle è ben che si crede (1638)
localized.description:
This extravagant monody captures the wildly romantic passions of the Early Italian Baroque opera developed by the likes of Claudio Monteverdi and Michelangelo Rossi.  Merula, a lesser known figure in the first half of the 17th Century, is mostly remembered for his instrumental works, but also a handful of religious works and a few arias for soprano or tenor voice. The original score of this piece consists only of a solo voice part and a basso continuo.

The figured bass line was beautifully written out with ornamentation by eagri1967 in an arrangement for oboe and guitar. It can be found on the site Musescore (link: https://musescore.com/user/8752261/scores/4443656 ). I created the voice simulation using the Maika Spanish language Vocaloid and I generated the instrumental sounds (violin, bass viol, chitarrone, harpsicord) using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0.

Text (and translation)

Folle è ben che si crede (Folly it is to believe)
che per dolci lusinghe amorose (that for sweet, amorous flattery)
o per fiere minaccie sdegnose (or by arrogant threats)
dal bel idolo mio rittraga il piede (turns me away from my beautiful idol)
Cangi per suo pensiero (Change your mind)
ch'el mio cor prigioniero (my imprisoned heart)
spera che goda la libertà (that hopes to enjoy freedom)
dica chi vuol dica chi sa. (Speak, he who wishes, speak he who knows)

Altri per gelosa (Others through jealousy)
Spiri pur empie fiamme dal seno (breath foul flames from the breast)
Versi pure Megera il veneno (may Megera [the Fury] pour her venom) 
Perchè rompi al mio ben la fede mia (to break the faith in my beloved)
Morte il viver mi toglia (Death may take away life from me)
Mai fia ver che si scioglia ([but] will never dissolve)
Quel caro laccio che preso m'ha (this sweet bond that holds me)
Dica chi vuole dica chi sa. (Speak, he who wishes, speak he who knows)

Ben havrò tempo, e loco (I will have both time and place)
Da sfogar l'amoroser mie pene (to vent my amorous pain)
Da temprar de l'amato mio bene (to temper the hidden flame)
E de l'arso mio cor, l'occulto foco (from my love and from my burnt heart)
E trà l'ombre, e gli orrori (and between the shadow and horrors)
De nuturni splendori (of the nightly splendor)
Il mio ben furto s'asconderà (my love will be hiding quietly)
Dica chi vuole dica chi sa. (Speak, he who wishes, speak he who knows)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous: Madame damours all tymes or ours (c.1510) (Original Pronunciation)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous: Madame damours all tymes or ours (c.1510) (Original Pronunciation)
localized.description:
Madame damours

  0:06  Verse 1: a cappella chorus (SATB)
  1:31  Verse 1 repeated: soprano, 3 viols, harp
  2:56  Verse 2: chorus + harp

--------------------

This tender song of courtly love comes from the Henry VIII Songbook (a.k.a. British Libary Ms. Add. 31922) which contains a large collection of works by King Henry himself.  The author of the lyrics to this piece, although unattributed, may indeed have been Henry himself since it stylistically shares similarities with his other works of poetry.

It should not come as a surprise that French words and Franco-Flemish musical style were interjected into English songs such as this one. French was the language of courtly love at the Tudor court and throughout Western Europe in the late Middle Ages.  And much of the English repertoire of the late 15th Century was heavily influenced by the polyphony of the Burgundian courts.

Madame damours (Lady, my love)
all tymes or ours (all the time is ours)
[from] dole dolours (from deepest despair)
or lorde you gy (our Lord will deliver)
in all socours (all help)
vnto my pours (to empower me)
to be as yours (to be yours)
vnytll I dye (until I die)
vntyll I dye
vntyll I dye. 

And make you sure (And make you certain)
no creatur (no creature)
shall me so lur. (will lure me)
Nor yet reayne. (nor rule me)
but to endure (but to endure)                                   15
ye may be sure. (you may be certain)
Whyls lyf endur (whilst life continues)
loyall and playne. (loyal and plain).

--------------------

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, corrected some of the pronunciation as well as the text underlay, rebalanced the voices, added some natural dynamics and enhanced the reverb & echo effects. The vocal simulations were created using Prima V2 Vocaloid in the soprano and Cyber Songman Vocaloid in the 3 lower voices. The viol and harp sounds were created using Music Studio 2.0 for the iPhone. I used the vowel sounds of very Early Modern English that predates the Elizabethan / Shakespearean era.

--------------------
