videos.title: [New Rendition] Johannes Vincenet de Bruecquet: La pena sin ser sabida (c.1470)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Johannes Vincenet de Bruecquet: La pena sin ser sabida (c.1470)
localized.description:
La pena sin ser sabida

  0:06  Original villancico for 4 vocal parts (ATTB)
  3:04  Arrangement for instruments (4 viols)

----------

Johannes Vincenet was a Flemish contemporary of Guillaume Dufay who was a singer in the Papal chorus alongside the older master.  It is known that he resided both in Naples (which was under Aragonese Spanish rule at the time) and in Rome.  This composition is Franco-Flemish in style with its imitative polyphony, but Spanish both in its text and its villancico structure (i.e. ABBA). It is interesting to note the two locations in the piece when the rhythm shifts from a free style to a sudden strict triplet group reminiscent of some late 14th century Ars Subtilior compositions (but also a commonly used device in Franco-Flemish music of the late 15th Century). The so-called Mellon Chansonnier (Yale University, Beinecke Library) in which this song survives, was dedicated to the Princess Beatrice (or Beatrix) of Naples and Aragon, later Queen of Hungary. 

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, added natural dynamics, corrected the text underlay, rebalanced the voices and enhanced the reverb / echo effects. I also changed the instrumental arrangement to all viols.  The "vocal" simulations were generated using the Spanish language Maika Vocaloid (Yamaha), and the viol simulation was created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 (Sternberg).

----------

Text:

La pena sin ser sabida
Es incurable dolor; 
Mas quien es de mi servida 
Ben sabe que por su amor 
Soy triste to[d]a mi vida.
Et finge de non saber 
La causa de mi tristura 
Por que mas a su plazer 
Me pene su fermosura.

La gente non entendida 
None sabe mi disfavor, 
Mas quien es de mi servida 
Ben sabe que por su amor 
Soy triste toda mi vida.

Translation:

Hidden suffering
is my incurable pain
But the one I serve
Knows well that for her love
I am sad all the days of my life.
But she pretends not to know
the cause of my sorrow
and she is pleased [knowing]
that her beauty pains me.

Uninformed people
do not know my displeasure
But the one I serve
knows well that for her love
I am sad all my life.

----------

videos.title: Anonymous Franco-Flemish: Tambur, tambur (c.1490)

localized.title: Anonymous Franco-Flemish: Tambur, tambur (c.1490)
localized.description:
Tambur, tambur, tamburelaridon

  0:06  Original chanson for 4 voices (ATTB)
  3:09  Instrumental arrangement (shawm, 3 sackbuts)

This anonymously composed chanson for 4 voices can only be found in isolated part books scattered across several Florentine sources. Only one manuscript (once the property of Giuliano de' Medici in Florence now in the collection of the Bibliothèque Nationale de France) contains the full original text, but only the tenor part. The song was likely written by a foreigner (or an Italian pretending to be a Frenchman) for the raucous Florentine festivals, and it may have been performed both with singers and instruments. The “tambur” and “tamburelaridon” likely refers to the sound of a percussive instrument, like a drum (or tabor). The text is difficult to translate and may either be nonsensical or a mixture of more than one language (including, perhaps, Flemish on the word “soet.”)

The textless MIDI was compiled by the Josquin Project at Stanford University. The text underlay is entirely my own. Since the parts are imitative, I used the one surviving, fully texted tenor line to extrapolate the other 3 voice parts. I believe this is the first recording that includes all 4 voice parts. I used the Maika Vocaloid to simulate a somewhat bastardized Renaissance French.

Text:

Tambur, tambur, tamburelaridon, tamburelaridene, tamburelaridon.

Le roy a fet crier (The king made them scream)
Par villes et fabors (in towns and farms)
Que le joyeulx mestier (that the joyous profession)
Soet mantenu tousjors.  (always kept sweet (?))

Tambur, tambur, tamburelaridon, tamburelaridene, tamburelaridon.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Elisabethe Cruciger & Johann Walter: Herr Christ der einig Gotts Sohn (1524)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Elisabethe Cruciger & Johann Walter: Herr Christ der einig Gotts Sohn (1524)
localized.description:
"Herr Christ der einig Gotts Sohn" (also known by its alternate title "Eyn Lobsanck von Christo" [A Song in Praise of Christ]) is one of the oldest surviving Lutheran hymns. The original cantus firmus melody (tucked away in the tenor voice) was composed by the former nun and early Lutheran convert, Elisabethe (or Elisabet) Cruciger (or Kreutziger, née von Meseritz). Her name has all but disappeared from history books and even replaced by that of a male contemporary in one German source. The source of the melody line remains unknown and may have been a secular love song from the early 15th Century.

This mystical, spiritual song by Cruciger is included in the two oldest printed editions of Reformation hymns: the "Erfurt Enchiridion" (1524) as well as in the "Eyn geystlich Gesangk Buchleyn" (The Little Spiritual Songbook, 1524). Unlike many of Walter's other hymn arrangements which were inspired by the polyphonic complexities of Ludwig Senfl and Heinrich Isaac, this piece has a strict homophonic structure that foreshadows later Lutheran congregational songs. The piece is usually performed during the season leading up to Christmas.

The words for this song were entered using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid. Reverb and echo were added using Audacity.  The lute accompaniment was created using MusicStudio2. In this latest rendition, I added some natural dynamics, corrected some pronunciation, added two additional verses by the lyricist, rebalanced the 4 voices (SATB) and created a more legato effect.

Original text (from Enchiridion):

1. Herr Christ, der eynig Gotts son
Vaters yn ewigkeit,
Aus seym hertzen entsprossen,
Gleich wie geschryben steht,
Er is der morgensterne,
Seyn glentze streckt er ferne
Fur andern sternen klar;

2. Fur uns ein mensch geboren
Ym letzten teil der zeit,
Der mutter unverloren
Yhr jungfrewlich keuscheyt
Den tod fur uns zu brochen,
Den Hymel aussgeschlossen,
Das Leben wider bracht:

3. Lass uns yn deiner liebe
Und kentnis nemen zu,
Das wir am glauben bleiben,
und dienen ym geist so,
Dass wir hie mugen schmecken
deyn sussigkeyt ym Herzen
und dursten stet nach dir.

4. Du Schepffer aller dinge
du vetterliche krafft.
Regirst von end zu ende
krefftig aus eigen macht.
Das hertz uns zu dir wende
und ker ab unser synne
das sie nicht yrrm von dir.

5. Ertöt uns durch deyn gute
erweck uns durch deyn gnadt.
Den alten menschen krencke
das der neu leben mag.
Wol hie auff dyser erden
den synn und all begerden
und danken han zu dir..

++++++++++

English translation

1. Lord Christ, the only Son of God
the Father for all eternity,
from his heart coming forth,
as it is written:
He is the morning star,
who makes his radiance shine far
beyond all other stars;

2. Unto us a man is born
in the last span of time
The mother untouched
her virginity restored
he has defeated death for us,
opened up heaven,
and brought back life.

3. Let us into your love
and knowledge gain,
that we may stay with the faith,
serve you in spirit
so that we may here taste
your sweetness in our hearts
and always thirst for you.

4. The maker of all things
you fatherly power.
You rule for ever and ever
Powerful from your own might.
The heart turns to you
and turn away from our senses
that we do not stray from you.

5. Erase us with your goodness
wake us through your grace.
Subdue the old man
so that the new man lives
and here on this earth
[our] sense and desire
and gratitude we give to you.

++++++++++

videos.title: Edmund Turges: Alas, it is I that wote nott (c.1490)

localized.title: Edmund Turges: Alas, it is I that wote nott (c.1490)
localized.description:
Edmund Turges was a composer mostly of church music during the reign of King Henry VIIth, at the height of pre-Reformation polyphony. This rare secular song appears in a collection known as the Fayrfax Manuscript and it preserves the courtly love themes long standardized in aristocratic circles across the Channel in Burgundy and France. It is a complex piece of music with very long melismata, imitative polyphony and polyrhythmic passages.

The original MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and can be found at Musescore.com . I used the Cyber Songman Vocaloid and adjusted the pronunciation to suit late 15th Century late Middle English. I also added the sound of lute, citole and harp to double the voices.

Text:

Alas, it is I that wote (1) nott what to say
for why I stond (2) as he that is abusyd
ther as I trusted, I was late cast away
and no cause gevyn (3) to be so refusyd
Butt pite (4) it is that trust shulde (5) be mysusyd
other by color or by fals semblaunce (6)
where that is usyd can be no suraunce (7)

Glossary: (1) wote: know, (2) stond: stand, (3) gevyn: given, (4) pite: pity, (5) shulde: should, (6) semblaunce: appearance, (7) suraunce: promise

Description of the photos:

videos.title: [New Rendition] Adrian Willaert: Se’l veder voi m'ancide (1549)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Adrian Willaert: Se’l veder voi m'ancide (1549)
localized.description:
Se'l veder voi m'ancide

This madrigal for 3 voices can be found in multiple sources all published in Willaert's adopted hometown of Venice between 1549 and 1561.  In the earliest of these editions, the editor mentions that all the compositions in the collection can be performed by voices alone or instruments or both. In the ascending and descending scales traded between the two upper voices, one can hear similarity to other Franco-Flemish works from an earlier time such as the grand "Nesciens mater" of Jean Mouton and the chansons of Claudin de Sermisy. 

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, corrected some pronunciation, added a harp sound to double the voices, added natural dynamics and adjusted the echo and reverb.

Text:

Se'l veder voi m'ancide.
Et evi'a grat' il mio morir
dicete, perche si spesso
mi vi ritogliete
Se per rimover fiamma
un maggior foco
Raccender vi pensate
A vana speme vi trapporta errore
Ma se della mia vita il fin bramate
Et cosi a poco a poco
Cresce alla doglia mia maggior dolore
Lontana dal mio core
La fiamma che l'accende non tenete
Chi'io morro donna
ed voi lieta vivrete

Translate:

It kills me to see you
and my death is to be thanked.
Tell me, why so often
you take me down
To remove the flame
you stoke a greater fire
To a vain hope ...
but if from my life you desire the end
Little by little
My hurt grows into a greater pain
Far from my heart
the flame that raises me up does not stay
So that I will die lady
and you will live happy.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Robert Morton: Le souvenir de vous me tue (c.1450)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Robert Morton: Le souvenir de vous me tue (c.1450)
localized.description:
Robert Morton was one of several English composers associated with the Burgundian court (along with John Bedyngham and Walter Frye) who wrote courtly love songs with flowing melodies and rich harmonies. While this version is written for a 4-part vocal ensemble; there is another attributed to Morton with the same title for 3 parts. The popularity of this rondeau can be attested to by the more than 14 copies of this tune that have survived the centuries through French and Italian sources. Unlike the works of his French counterparts, Morton's song is more homophonic and less imitative. There is also an intricately ornamented parody of this piece for virtuoso organist contained in the Buxheimer Book. 

I used a MIDI file created by Kitty Hawke and uploaded to CPDL.org.  I arranged the repeats according to Hawke's scheme: A-B-A-A-A-B-A. In this latest rendition, I slowed the tempo, created a more legato effect, corrected a few text underlays and some pronunciation, rebalanced the voices and enhanced the reverb / echo effects.

++++++++++

Text:

Le souvenir de vous me tue,
mon seul bien, quant je ne vous voy
car je vous jure sur ma foy:
Sans vous ma liesse est perdue.

Quant vous estes hors de ma veue,
je me plains et dis a par moy.

Le souvenir de vous...

Seule demeure despourveue,
d'ame nul confort ne reçoi, 
et si seuffre sans faire effroy
jusques a vostre revenue.

Le souvenir de vous...

--------------------

Translation

The memory of you kills me,
my only joy, when I do not see you,
for I swear to you upon my faith,
without you my happiness is lost.

When you are out of my sight,
I grieve and say to myself:

The memory of you...

I remain alone and desolate,
I receive no comfort from anyone,
and thus suffer quietly,
until your return.

The memory of you...

--------------------

videos.title: Gabriel Mena: Aquella mora garrida (c.1510)

localized.title: Gabriel Mena: Aquella mora garrida (c.1510)
localized.description:
This tender song was the creation of a man named Gabriel Mena or Gabriel de Texerana (probably the same person), who served at the pleasure of King Ferdinand of Aragon. Its sole source is the greatest collection of late Medieval and early Renaissance music in Spain, El Cancionero Musical de Palacio. At least 18 of Gabriel's works were fully preserved between its covers.

The song is a poignantly worded villancico based on a young man's yearning for a Moorish lass who appears to be beyond the reach of his undying love. We don't know if the girl left the protagonist for another man or if she was exiled to North Africa after the defeat of the Muslim rulers on the Iberian Peninsula in 1492. Even as he is being captured by Moorish pirates and taken across the sea, he continues to pine away for the girl of his dreams -- so much so that a kidnapper is brought to tears.

The original MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and uploaded to Musescore.com. I used some of Bojopigeon’s text underlay for the cantus part and then added the full text underlay for the three lower voices as well as for the 2nd and 3rd verses. As always, I generated the sound of two male altos, tenor and bass using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid. I used a pronunciation scheme for late 15th Century Spanish as described by Tim McGee in his textbook "Singing Early Music." The instrumental sounds of two lutes, citole and harp were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0.

Text (and translation)

Aquella mora garrida, (That pretty Moorish girl)
sus amores dan pena a mi vida. (her loves give my life such pain)
 
Mi madre, por me dar placer, (My mother, to give me pleasure)
a coger rosas me envía; (sent me to gather roses)
moros andan a saltear ([Meanwhile] the Moors come to attack)
y a mí llévanme cautiva; (and take me captive)
sus amores dan pena a mi vida. (her loves give my life such pain)
 
El moro que me prendiera (The Moor that has taken me)
allende la mar me envía; (sends me beyond the sea)
lloraba cuando lo supo (he cried, like a friend, when he knew)
un amigo que yo había; (what I had)
sus amores dan pena a mi vida. (her loves give my life such pain)
 
Con el gran dolor que siente (With great pain that he feels)
estas palabras decía: (these words were said)
Aquella mora garrida, (That pretty Moorish girl)
sus amores dan pena (her loves give my life such pain)

videos.title: Simone Molinaro: Three lute pieces (1599)

localized.title: Simone Molinaro: Three lute pieces (1599)
localized.description:
Suite of 3 luite pieces

  0:06  Ballo detto il Conte Orlando
  2:15  Saltarello 6
  3:12  Saltarello 7

The sole surviving printed edition of Molinaro's lute solos comes to us from a 1599 collection of dance music titled "Intavolatura di Liuto." Molinaro seems to have spent his entire professional career as maestro di cappella at the main cathedral in Genoa. Unfortunately, compositions for church services have not been preserved in their entirety. Only a small number of partbooks have been found.

The first of the three pieces on this soundtrack, "Ballo detto il Conte Orlando," was adapted by the 20th Century Italian composer Ottorino Respighi for a modern chamber orchestra in Suite 1 of the "Ancient Airs and Dances." 

The MIDI file for this soundtrack can be found on Serge Gerbode's website lutemusic.org . I adjusted the sound using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 (Sternberg) to resemble the timbre and reverb of a late Renaissance lute.

4. Woman playing lute, Parrasio Micheli, Venice, c1570
5. Score of "Saltarello 6"

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous French: Quant la doulce jouvencelle (c.1430)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous French: Quant la doulce jouvencelle (c.1430)
localized.description:
Quant la doulce jouvencelle

  0:06  Original chanson with harp accompaniment
  2:44  Instrumental arrangement (medieval harp, citole)

-----------

Contemporary with Gilles de Binchois and Guillaume Dufay, this Anonymous free-style song of courtly love has slightly more optimism and tenderness compared to other similar works with darker themes of bitterness and death.  It is full of longing melismata as was common for French chansons of the early 15th century. Only the alto (or mezzosoprano) line has the underlying text in the original manuscript, and even that includes long gaps without any words. As was probably intended by the anonymous composer, I have inserted instrumental interludes where there is a complete absence of text.

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, adjusted the timbre of the soprano voice, added some natural dynamics, corrected a few vowel sounds and deepened the reverb. The original MIDI file without the words was adapted from an upload by Serge Gerbode on his lute website gerbode.net.

Text and translation (adapted from lyricstranslate.com):

Quant la doulce jouvencelle, (When the sweet young lady)
La tres gracieuse et belle, (the very gracious and beautiful one)
Celle dont suy amoureux (with whom I am in love)
Veult que me tiengne joyeux, (wants to make me happy)
Ne doy je obeir a elle? (Should I not obey her?)

Certes ouy, car cest celle,  (Sure, yes, because that is)
Qui son doulx amy mapelle; (who calls me her sweet friend)
Estre ne puis plus joyeux. (I could not be more joyous)

Plaisir en moy renouvelle, (Pleasure in me renews)
Nautre amer je ne quier quelle, (bitterness I do not seek)
Servir la vueil en tous lieux, (to serve desire in all places)
A mon pouvoir, (in my power)
De bien en mieux, (from good to better)
Ma volonte si est telle. (my wish it is)

Description of photos:

1. "Quant la doulce jouvencelle," Anonymous Franco-Burgundian, Escorial B Chansonnier, c1460
2. "Vous ou Mort," detail from a ceremonial shield depicting a scene of courtly love, Anonymous French, c.1460
3. A castle from the late French Medieval period, leaf from "September," Les Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry, c1410.
4. Euryalus Sends His First Letter to Lucretia, Historia de Duobus Amantibus, Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, 1467
5. Orpheus and Eurydice, second half of 15th century
6. Musical angels including a harp player, Hans Memling, 1490
7. Lancelot and Guinevere, Anon. French, c1480

videos.title: [New Rendition] Orlando Gibbons / David Wulstan: Praise the Lord, O my soul (c.1620)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Orlando Gibbons / David Wulstan: Praise the Lord, O my soul (c.1620)
localized.description:
The sole surviving source for this verse anthem is the Batten Organ Book (a.k.a. Tenbury MS 791) compiled around 1630. Its 6 vocal parts were reconstructed by David Wulstan in the second half of the 20th Century from a keyboard manuscript containing hundreds of organ reductions from the late Elizabethan and early Jacobean periods. The text was adapted from the 103rd Psalm of King David in the English translation of the Geneva Bible. Many modern groups have arranged performance for a 5 viol ensemble and 6 part choir (as was commonly done in the Jacobean court), but I chose organ as the accompanying instrument and a brass ensemble (2 cornetti and 4 trombones) to double the choir.  

I attempted to simulate Original Pronunciation throughout the piece especially in spots where the text matching would otherwise fail. For example the word "generations" is repeated multiple times by all the voices in tandem. As was customary for the time, I broke up the syllables into "d͡ʒɛ-nɛ-rɛ-sɪ-ənz." The words "our" and "pow'r" were likely pronounced "ower" "powr" with an emphatic rhotic "r" as in modern American English.

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, corrected some vowel pronunciation, rebalanced the voices, swapped out brass instruments for viols (to double the choir) and added natural dynamics in all the Vocaloid parts. The Prima V2 Vocaloid simulates the boy soprano pair while the Cyber Songman Vocaloid covers the other four male voice parts.

I dedicate this anthem to our dearest, beloved Oreo (2006-2024). You were born a cat, but you became a person in our eyes. You have made us better versions of ourselves. Requiescat in pace. May you prance in the eternal ether as you did in our earthly forest. You are in our hearts forever and ever.

Text:

Praise the Lord o my soul
and all that is within me praise his holy name
and forget not all his benefits 
Praise the Lord all ye his works
in all places of his dominion
Great is our lord
and great is his pow'r
Marvellous, worthy to be prais'd
Yea, and his wisdom is infinite
O Lord thy God of Zion
shall be king forever more
and throughout all generations.
O sing praises
sing ye praises unto God.

Description of the photos:

1. Psalm 102 and 103 from the first edition of the King James Bible (1611). Although the newly released King James was the more popular and widely distributed bible in Gibbons' time, it appears that Gibbons (and other contemporary composers) used the English translation of the Geneva Bible for song text.
2. Choir of the Hampton Palace Chapel where Gibbons likely performed his music as a Gentleman of the Chapel Royal.
3. Cover page of the first edition of the King James Bible, 1611. During Gibbons lifetime, there was a renewed interest in creating a more perfect translation of the bible into the English language, and this was its final product after a 7 year long project.
4. Pipes from the organ at St Nicholas in Stanford on Avon
5. Ceiling of the Hampton Palace Chapel
6. Pipe organ from the St Nicholas in Stanford on Avon (Northhamptonshire). The original base for this instrument was created by Thomas and Robert Dallam for Magdalen College (Oxford) around 1631 and was a design familiar to Gibbons.
7. King David singing the psalms and playing his harp, Peter Paul Rubens
8. Memorial bust for Orlando Gibbons, Nicholas Stone, 1626

videos.title: Hugh Ashton (attrib.): Masque on a Ground (c.1530)

localized.title: Hugh Ashton (attrib.): Masque on a Ground (c.1530)
localized.description:
Hugh Ashton was one of the rare composers of the early Tudor period who, despite high acclaim among the elites of English courtly circles, chose to remain outside the political realm and preferred the peaceful air of Leicestershire. Despite his avoidance of religious or political leanings, however, during the Dissolution of the Monasteries, he likely did witness the destruction of Leicester's main Abbey which had stood in the center of town since the 12th Century.

This rather long, meandering and meditative masque for 4 parts does not (like most pieces of that era) stipulate any specific instrumentation. Modern performers, for some reason, seem to prefer recorders, but I instead selected a plucked string ensemble with lute, cittern and harp. The composition often has contemplative passages of three closely imitative lines (mostly modal scales) written above a ground (i.e. repeated bass notes) consisting of a series of 8 whole notes (AEFEGCEA) each repeated twice.

Description of the photos:

1. Ashton's Masque, Hugh Ashton (?), Baldwin Partbook, copied c1575
2. Detail of lute and flutes, detail from the Ambassados, Hans Holbein the Younger, c1533
3. A street section of Historic Leicester mostly unchanged since Ashton's lifetime
4. Warwickshire lute (c.1550) by Hans Frei, a rare surviving instrument from the period AND the Sheldon tapestry
5. St. Mary de Castro, a church in Leicester appearing much the same as in the 16th Century with recent repairs to the tower.
6. Cittern, Ashmolean Museum, c1560
7. St. Mary de Castro Seilia, a fine example of authentic Normal Architecture from the 13th Century.
8. Warwickshire lute close up

11. Lutenist, Francesco Salviati, c1529

videos.title: [New Rendition] Claudin de Sermisy: Le content est riche (c.1525)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Claudin de Sermisy: Le content est riche (c.1525)
localized.description:
Le content est riche

  0:06  Original chanson (ATTB)
  2:25  Pavane "Le content" (cornetto, 3 trombones, tympani)

The Parisian composer, Claudin de Sermisy, was one of the most prolific composers of the High Renaissance -- contributing a large corpus of secular music to the vast polyphonic repertoire of 16th century France.  This tune, "Le content" was particularly popular across the whole of the Continent for most of the 16th Century thanks in part to the many publishing houses in France and the Netherlands. There were multiple copies of the chanson in printed form and various different lute reductions published even long after his death. Because the original tune was written in 4/4 time, one can easily imagine its setting as a Pavane such as the one I included in this soundtrack.

----------

French text:

Le content est riche en ce monde
Et bien heureux en ce temps ci.
À cœur joyeux, liberté, monde,
vivre toujours hors de souci.
Être amoureux non point transi.
Et à tous deuil clore les yeux.
Toujours, gaillards, faites ainsi
Et vous vivrez cent ans et mieux.

English translation:

The content individual is rich in this world
and happy in this moment.
To a joyous heart, free and pure,
he lives always without suffering.
To be amorous but not to excess.
And to all sorrow close the eyes.
Always, gallants, do like so
and you will live a hundred years and more.

-----------

The original MIDI file was created by André Vierendeels and uploaded to CPDL.org. The French text to the chanson was entered using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid. The instrumental parts were added using Music Studio 2. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, completely revised the soprano voice with a more mature-sound female voice, corrected some pronunciation, slowed the tempo a bit, removed the lute doubling and removed the Phalese reduction.

----------

Illustrations:

1. Singers and lutenist playing in the Garden of Pleasure, Harley 4425, Anon. Flemish, c1500
2. Galerie de François I, Château de Fontainebleau, the scene of countless musical performances in Sermisy's time
3. Rustic Concert, Anon. Italian, c1550
4. Henry II ballroom, Château de Fontainebleau
5.Angels playing wind instruments, fresco detail depicting cornetti and trombone, Domenico Brusasorzi, Chiesa di Santo Stepheno, Verona, c1552
6. Musicians' gallery, Château de Fontainebleau, a balcony from which loud instruments could play pavanes and galliardes for the ballroom dancers below
7. Wind band in the musicians' gallery, Hans Holbein the Younger, c1520
8. Silhouette painting of François I, King of France, Tiziano (Titian), 1539; most composers and publishers in the first half of the 16th Century dedicated their works to Francis I, a well regarded patron of music and the arts.

videos.title: Johann Pachelbel: Aria Sexta “La Sebaldina” for theorbo (1699)

localized.title: Johann Pachelbel: Aria Sexta “La Sebaldina” for theorbo (1699)
localized.description:
This rendition of Aria Sexta is my second upload of a keyboard aria by Johann Pachelbel. Here is the link to my rendition of Aria Prima:

https://youtu.be/DunuF9ZtKNo 

The six arias formed a collection known as Hexachordum Apollinis (or Six Strings of Apollo) which Pachelbel dedicated to the famed composer Dieterich Buxtehude (and one other organist). Although he probably envisioned a performance by a keyboardist for all these pieces, he might have also considered a lutenist given the frequent arpeggiated passages. For this soundtrack, I used the sound of a theorbo (a.k.a. a chitarrone) to span the range of all the notes. The lute was an often heard instrument in chamber music circles throughout the late 17th Century as is attested by the countless French composers at the court of Louis XIV and the German maestro Silvius Leopold Weiss in J.S. Bach’s generation.

The secular tune from which Aria Sexta is derived remains a mystery. It is the only one of the six arias which is written in 3/4 time instead of 4/4. It is the longest of the six arias and is the only subtitled piece "La Sebaldina" -- named after the church St. Sebaldus where Pachelbel was employed for 9 years.

The MIDI file for this piece was compiled by Bojopigeon and the complete score can be found at Musescore.com. I sped up the tempo, emphasized the bass notes (as would be natural for a theorbo) and fashioned a rapid decrescendo on the trills (as might be expected on any plucked instrument).

Description of the photos:

videos.title: [New Rendition] Thomas Morley: Sing wee and chaunt it (1595), Original Pronunciation

localized.title: [New Rendition] Thomas Morley: Sing wee and chaunt it (1595), Original Pronunciation
localized.description:
Sing wee and chaunt it (Sing we and chant it)

  0:06  Dance arrangement for 2 recorders, 3 viols and bandora
  0:59  Verse 1: SATTB + 2 violins, 3 viols and bandora
  1:50 Verse 2: tutti

* * * *

Many of Morley's Ballets (1595) were lifted nearly note for note from Giovanni Gastoldi's Balletti (1591), an Italian collection of dance music figured for voices  or instruments (and hence the titles). "Sing wee and chaunt it" is the English language rendering of Gastoldi's "A lieta vita." It conveys a light and frivolous spirit similar to King Henry VIII's "Pastyme with good companye" written more than 80 years earlier. Despite the joyous character of the tune and its jaunty rhythm, there is embedded in the lyrics a melancholic resignation to the steady march of time and the inevitability of death for all mortals. This piece is written in a fast 3 rhythm and could easily have been adapted into a lively volta for the Queen's pleasure.

In this most recent rendition, I created a more legato effect, added natural dynamics, added more reverb & echo, rebalanced the voices and changed the instrumental doubling. The words in the soundtrack were inserted into a MIDI file using Vocaloid 4 and two English language voice banks: Prima (for the soprano and alto parts) and Cyber Songman (for the tenor and bass).  I simulated Original Pronunciation from Shakespeare's era using Professor David Crystal's recommendations. Words such as "pleasure" "leisure" "treasure" sounded more like "plezər" "lezər" and "trezər." Initial "h"s were usually silent so that "hasten" would become "ast'n." There were many MIDI files of this piece from which to choose, but I used the one created by James Gibbs who generously uploaded both the notes and the lyrics to CPDL.org.

* * * *

Text:

Sing wee and chaunt it
while love doth graunt it,
fa la la, etc.
Not long youth lasteth,
and old age hasteth;
now is best leysure
to take our pleasure,
fa la la, etc.
All things invite us
now to delight us,
fa la la, etc.
Hence, care, be packing!
no mirth be lacking!
Let spare no treasure
to live in pleasure,
fa la la, etc.

* * * *

Description of photos:

1. "A lieta vita," Giovanni Gastoldi (Balletti, 1591), the original tune from which "Sing wee and chaunt it" was parodied.
2. Ball at the Valois court of France in Elizabethan times, c1580; France and Italy were often points of cultural reference for English courtiers during that period.
3. "Sing wee and chaunt it," printed score from Morley's First Book of Ballets, 1595
4. Music-making company in a pastoral setting, David Vinckboons, c1610
5. Dancers and a viol ensemble, print from Bodleian Lib., 16th Century
6. Queen Elizabeth (?) dancing the volta probably with Robert Dudley, French School, late 16th Cent

videos.title: [New Rendition] Francisco Guerrero; Oyd, oyd una cosa (1589)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Francisco Guerrero; Oyd, oyd una cosa (1589)
localized.description:
Oyd, oyd una cosa

  0:06  Original cancion for 5 voices (SSATB)
  2:28  Instrumental arrangement for 2 cornetti and 3 sackbuts

The cancion "Oyd, oyd" was a Christmas song that was perhaps written around the time of Guerrero's travels in Italy. It was published in Venice in 1589 along with many other songs dedicated to the Spanish cardinal Rodrigo de Castro. Most of Guerrero's career was spent in Seville like his contemporary Juan Vasquez, but unlike Cristobal Morales and Tomas Luis de Victoria who were employed by the See in Rome.

This soundtrack is based on a MIDI file created by Paco Marmol and Manolo Casaus that can be found at CPDL.org .  In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, corrected some pronunciations to a 16th Century sound, rebalanced the voices and adjusted the reverb & echo effects.

++++++++++

Text (and translation):

Oyd, oyd una cosa divina (Hear, hear this divine news:)
gracioza y bella: (gracious and beautiful,)
El que crió la donzella generosa (One created by the generous maiden)
esta noche nasció della. (tonight was born from her. )

Sentid, sentid con cuydado (Feel, feel with care)
aquesta hazaña bella: (this beautiful deed)
El que crió la donzella generosa (One created by the generous maiden)
esta noche nasció della. (tonight was born from her. )

Oyd que dichosa nueva (Hear what a delightful new thing)
qué hecho regozijado: (what a joyful thing)
oy parió la Eva nueva (Oh, the new Eve gave birth)
al Hijo de Dios amado. (to the beloved son of God)

+++++++++++

videos.title: Johann Pachelbel: Aria Prima (1699)

localized.title: Johann Pachelbel: Aria Prima (1699)
localized.description:
Johann Pachelbel's six keyboard arias were part of a single volume collection, Hexachordum Apollinis (Six strings of Apollo) that he dedicated to the great Danish-German maestro, Dieterich Buxtehude and another lesser known organist in Austria, Ferdinand Tobias Richter. These works from Pachelbel's late period were intended for performance by either an organist or a harpsichordist. The frequent trills, simple lyrical melodies, lightness and style brisé ("broken" or arpeggiated) in Aria Prima are evocative of the French music at the court of Louis XIV. Therefore either a clavichord or harpsichord may have been the most appropriate choice of instrument. Hidden in this series of variations are familiar themes from "La Folia" which were wildly popular across all Western Europe during that period such as by Marin Marais and Jean Baptiste Lully (who were both Pachelbel's contemporaries). However, Pachelbel was most famous as an organist and therefore, he may have accepted both keyboard instruments as viable options.

The MIDI file for this piece was compiled by Bojopigeon and can be found at Musescore.com. I slowed the tempo a bit, changed the instrument to a harpsichord (from pipe organ) and sped up the trills.

7. Traxdorf organ, the instrument played by Pachelbel during his tenure at St. Sebaldus Church  (1695-1706); it was originally designed by Heinirch Traxdorf in 1440 and rebuilt in 1691 just prior to Pachelbel's appointment. This photo was made in 1937 prior to its destruction in WW2.

videos.title: Anonymous English: 2 Consort pieces at the court of Henry VIII (c.1510)

localized.title: Anonymous English: 2 Consort pieces at the court of Henry VIII (c.1510)
localized.description:
Two Consort pieces

0:06  Consort #13 (recorder, harp, bass viol)
0:59  Consort #2 (cornetto, 3 trombones)

These two instrumental pieces were included along with 30+ short works by King Henry VIII in a collection of late 15th century and early 16th century music from the early Tudor court. Instrumentation is not specified nor the composers explicitly (except for Henry VIII who features prominently). The longer of the two works has a mysterious phrase at the end, "Flude in armonia graduat," (flood rises in harmony) and scholars have speculated that it is an attribution to John Lloyd (or Floyd) who was a court musician in Henry VIII's time.  Consort XIII is a puzzle canon with three lines of imitative polyphony supported by an unidentified cantus firmus line in the tenor. Although Henry VIII had several royal palace across Southern England which he frequented, Windsor Castle, the largest, was a place where he himself supposedly performed music.

videos.title: Anonymous Franco-Burgundian: Rolet ara la tricoton / Maistre Piere / La tricotée (c.1450)

localized.title: Anonymous Franco-Burgundian: Rolet ara la tricoton / Maistre Piere / La tricotée (c.1450)
localized.description:
This so called "combinative" chanson has a surprisingly complex structure with its 3 vocal parts polyphonically interweaving three different sets of lyrics (see below). The music was copied in such a way that there are gaps in the text underlay that may have indicated instrumental passages. It is also possible that the copyist who was possibly Italian did his (or her) best to approximate phrases to fit the notes wherever it was obvious, but left out the text underlay in other areas. I proceeded with the latter hypothesis and filled in all the gaps. 

Like a few other secular pieces in the Escorial B manuscript, this chanson, despite it soft sonority, has a rather rambunctious storyline with overlapping images of a lovers' tryst, a pretty nymph and a drinking scene. The Alto 2 part has a melodic line that is nearly identical to a Spanish villancico “La Tricotea” from a slightly later period in the collection Cancionero de Palacio. The two alto parts are tied together with the double entendres “tricotée” which can mean either knitted item (shirt or blouse) or a term of endearment.

Alto 1:
Rolet ara la tricoton (Rolet will have his shirt)
Et Gillaine la tricotée (and Gillian her knitted blouse)
Pour ceu quel est tousiours croutée  (which is always creased)
Quant elle mest son sourconton (when she puts her overskirt)
Je vous suplie, or tricotons (I beg of you, let's make love)
E vous ores la bone usée (and you will have a good experience)
Alons y tost et nous hastons (Let's go quick and we hasten)
Si servirons de la porée (if we serve the porridge)
La feste en era mieulx parée (The feast will be better trimmed)
Qu'en dictes-vous, n'est-il pas bon? (what do you say to this, is it not good?)

Alto 2:
La tricotée (The sweet girl)
fu par matin levée (woke up in the morning)
Quonque de bien baler (to dance well)
Ne fu lasée (She has not tired)
La tri, la tri, la joli tri (the girl, the pretty girl)
La belle tricotée (the beautiful girl)

Tenor:
Maistre Piere du Cugnet (Master Pierre of Cugnet)
Donne boire a mon varlet (give drink to my servant)
De celle bonne vendange formentee (from this fine vintage)
Qui sera en ceste annee en Avignon (which shall be this year's in Avignon)
Vous estes un grant trompere, frere Piere, (You are a big liar, brother Pierre)

Description of photos:

1. "Rolet ara la tricoton / Maistre Piere / La tricotée," Escorial B Chansonnier, Anonymous, c1460
2. Sempronia, from De Mulieribus Claris, Giovanni Boccaccio, copied c1430
3. Lovers, details from Garden of Earthly Delights, Hieronymous Bosch, c1490
4. Wine being poured for a feast, Les Vendanges, Anonymous French, Cluny, c1490
5. The lovers Lancelot and Guinevere, Anonymous French, c1410
6. Lovers harvesting grapes, Les Vendanges, Anonymous French, Cluny, c1490

videos.title: Antoine Busnoys (Busnois): Je ne puis vivre ainsi (c.1460)

localized.title: Antoine Busnoys (Busnois): Je ne puis vivre ainsi (c.1460)
localized.description:
This chanson by Antoine Busnois was perhaps a dedication to an aristocratic lady who was at least his love interest (and perhaps even his lover) during his tenure in Paris. The initial letters of each line form an acrostic which spells the name of a woman, "Jaqueline d'Aqvevile," The structure of the song is ABbaA (where A and a indicate differing lyrics underlying the same notes) and is described as a bergerette or virelai. Two upper voices alternate free-style canonic and unison singing, while a solitary baritone serves as support. It appears in handwritten form in two richly illuminated French manuscripts: the Dijon Chansonnier (c.1465-1469) and the Mellon Chansonnier (c.1475-1476).

Je ne puis vivre ainsi toujours (I cannot live like this forever)
au mains que j’aye en mes dolours (lest for my pains)
quelque confort (I get some comfort)
Une seule heure ou mains ou fort (Only an hour or less or more)
et tou les jours (and every day)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Johann Walter / Martin Luther: Nu bitten wyr den heyligen geyst a 5 (1524/25)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Johann Walter / Martin Luther: Nu bitten wyr den heyligen geyst a 5 (1524/25)
localized.description:
Nu bitten wyr den heyligen geist fur 5
(Nun bitten wir den heiligen Geist for 5 voices)

   0:06   Verse 1 for 5 voice a cappella choir (SATBB)
   1:42   Verse 2 for voices, lute and harp
   3:18   Verse 3 for voices & 5 viols
   4:54   Verse 4 for voices, cornetto and 4 sackbuts

++++++++++

There were two choral settings of "Nun bitten wir den heiligen Geist" composed by Martin Luther's musical protégé Johann Walter: one for 5 vocal parts (presented here) and another for 6 (presented also on this channel, separately). There were several  incarnations of this early Lutheran hymn that reappeared in much grander scale over the next two centuries including a polychoral piece by Michael Praetorius (Musae Sionae, 1605) and a full cantata by J.S. Bach (BWV 385, c.1735). The words of this hymn were derived from a 13th Century Franciscan monk Berthold von Regensburg, and the first recognizable melody comes from an anonymous 15th century German-Bohemian Catholic priest. Johann Walter published his earliest rendition of "Nu bitten wir" as part of a collaboration with Luther in a collection of new Protestant hymns "Eyn geystlich Gesangk Buchleyn" (1524), but only 2 of the 5 partbooks have survived from that first edition. Due to the discovery of later printed editions, we do have the complete set of 5 parts. Unlike some other Lutheran hymns like "Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott," this work is less homophonic -- that is, it is more imitative and contrapuntal like other contemporary non-Protestant motets by contemporaries Gombert and Morales. Walter's score contained only the first of four verses that Martin Luther had written. In this soundtrack, I have included all 4 verses as Luther probably planned. The hymn is based on the plainchant Veni Sancte Spiritus for Pentecost, but this motet is often sung at Christmas.

--------------------------------------------------------------

German text:

Nu bitten wyr den heyligen geyst, 
umb den rechten Glauben aller meyst, 
das er uns behute an unserm ende, 
wenn wyr heym farn aus disem elende. 
Kyrioleys.

Du wertes liecht, gib uns deynen scheyn,
lern uns Jhesus Christ kennen alleyn,
dass wyr an yhm bleyben, dem trewen heyland,
der uns bracht hat zum rechten vaterland.
Kyrioleys..

Du susse lieb schenk uns deyne gunst
las uns empfinden der liebe brunst
Das wyr uns von hertzen eyn ander lieben
un ym fride auff eynem synn bleyben
Kyrioleys.

Du hochster troster ynn aller not.
hilff das wyr nicht furchten schand noch tod
Das ynn uns die synnen nicht verzagen
wenn der feynd wird das leben verklagen.
Kyrioleys.

English translation:

Now we beseech the Holy Ghost
for the true faith most of all,
that he will protect us at our end
when we return home from this misery.
Lord, have mercy.

You, precious light, give us your glow,
Let us know only Jesus Christ
that we stand by him, the faithful Savior
who brought us to the righteous Kingdom
Lord have mercy.

You sweet love, grant us your favor
may we feel the warmth of your love
that we may love one another from our heart
and stay with peace of mind.
Kyrioleys.

You the highest comforter in all travails
help us to not fear the shadow of death
that our senses may not despair
when the enemy shall attack life itself
Kyrioleys.

---------------------------------------------------------------

Description of photos:

1. "Nu bitten wyr," Johann Walter's earliest printed version, 1524
2. Concert of sacred music (with detail of chorus, cornetto & sackbut), Hans Burgkmair, c1530
3. Interior of the Schlosskirche (Castle Church, aka All Saints' Church) looking toward the alter, the site of many sermons by Martin Luther (and perhaps performances of Johann Walter's motets)
4. Concert of angels, Tilman Riemenschneider, c1500
5. Portrait of Martin Luther at around the time of Johann Walter's first publication of polyphonic arrangements of Luther's melodies, Lucas Cranach, 1525
6. Martin Luther's first edition of the Bible in German, title page, 1524
7. Berthold von Regensburg, the monk and preacher who wrote the first verse of "Nu bitten wyr" in the 13th Century, printed in 1447
8. Christ risen, Matthias Grünewald, c 1515
9. Town of Wittemberg during Luther's lifetime with All Saint's Church at left, c1536
10. Cover page of an early Lutheran Bible (depicting Martin Luther to the right of the crucified Jesus), 1550
11. Town band, Hans Holbein & Albrecht Dürer, Nuremberg, 1520

videos.title: [New Rendition] Orlando Gibbons: This is the Record of John (c.1618), Original Pronunciation

localized.title: [New Rendition] Orlando Gibbons: This is the Record of John (c.1618), Original Pronunciation
localized.description:
William Laud, during his tenure as President of St. John's College at Oxford University, commissioned the English composer Orlando Gibbons to write a liturgical piece for an Anglican service at the College Chapel.  This short but expansive anthem adapted from the Gospel of John achieved fame in short order throughout England in the first half of the 17th century. Several copies from that era have survived into our time.  It is an English verse anthem which alternates between a solo performer (usually, a male alto or a  tenor) and a chorus, which repeats the refrains.  The text of this anthem is derived from the Geneva Bible, which was the most widely used English translation for Protestant services prior to the King James Edition. 

In this latest rendition, I have rebalanced the voices, created a more legato effect, corrected some Early Modern English pronunciation, added 4 viols and cornetto to double the chorus and enhanced the reverb / echo (using Audacity). The boy soprano was "sung" by the Prima V2 Vocaloid and the other male voice parts were rendered with Cyber Songman. The instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0.

Text:

This is the record of John,
when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him,
Who art thou?
And he confessed and denied not, and said plainly,
I am not the Christ.

And they asked him, What art thou then? Art thou Elias?
And he said, I am not.
Art thou the prophet?
And he answered, No.

Then said they unto him,
What art thou? that we may give an answer unto them that sent us.
What sayest thou of thyself?
And he said, I am the voice of him that crieth in the wilderness,
Make straight the way of the Lord.

++++++++++

videos.title: Anonymous French: Adieu vous dy (c.1460)

localized.title: Anonymous French: Adieu vous dy (c.1460)
localized.description:
Adieu vous dy

 0:01  Verse 1 (ATT)
 1:23  Verse 2 (ATT with lute, metal-string lute, harp)
 2:50  Verse 3 (male alto, meta-string lute, harp)
 4:05  Verse 1 repeated (ATT & instruments)

This charming rondeau from the Chansonnier Cordiforme (Heart-shaped Songbook) is a sentimental chanson by a poet who recalls his youthful dalliances in Dijon, France. It is similar in spirit and content to a later work by Heinrich Isaac who nostalgically remembers his earlier days in Innsbruck, Austria. The tenor in "Adieu" imitates the cantus in a lower range while the contratenor provides support for both parts. I added lyrics to the Contretenor line which, in the facsimile score, was untexted. Contemporary recordings of this work have all interpreted the untexted part as instrumental.

The MIDI file was originally compiled by BojoPigeon, but I changed the text underlay significantly. The text was entered using Maika, a Spanish language Vocaloid. The instrumental sounds were created using Music Studio 2.0, an iPhone app. The reverb and echo were added using Audacity. Some of the pronunciation may seem unfamiliar to speakers of Modern French as certain conventions have changed over time. For example, it was likely that, in most dialects of the time, that final "e" after consonants were heard as a schwa while "r" and "t" at the ends of lines were enunciated.

Text: 

Adieu vous dy l'espoir de ma jonesse
Adieu, adieu le tresor de liesse
Helas! adieu, mon soulas et deduyt
Adieu Dijon, ou je me suis deduit
Esperant grace de ma chere maistresse.

Quant vers vous n'ay plus sentier ne adresse
D'aucung plaisir, et puis que je vous lesse
Pour le present puisque ainsi suis reduit
  Adieu vous dy...

Le departir de vous tant fort me blesse
Pour la grant joye dont j'ay trouve largesse
Jouer, galler tout le jour et la nuyt
Faire grant chere tousjours menant grant bruit
Mais maintenant, puisqu'il faut que je cesse

Translation:

Farewell, I say to the hope of my youth
Farewell, farewell to the treasure that is happiness
Alas! farewell my solace and delight
Farewell Dijon, where I delighted myself
Hoping for grace from my dear lady.

As for you, I no longer look forward
to any pleasure and thus I leave you
and for the present moment I am lessened
  Farewell, I say...

Leaving you hurt me so
For the great joy wherein I have found so much
Playing, dancing all day and all night
... always making great noise
But now, it is necessary that I stop.

Adieu vous dy...

videos.title: [New Rendition] Ludwig Senfl: Es taget vor dem Walde / Fortuna desperata (c.1530)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Ludwig Senfl: Es taget vor dem Walde / Fortuna desperata (c.1530)
localized.description:
This dual language composition combines an Anonymously produced German folk song "Es taget vor dem Walde" (Descant and Tenor I)  with an Italian language chanson tune "Fortuna desperata" by the Franco-Burgundian master Antoine Busnois (Alto, Tenor II and Bass). Both songs imply a forbidden, secretive love, but maintain a mysterious air regarding any details about the lovers themselves. This is one of countless parodies on the "Fortuna" melody which had been adopted by several other titans of the Franco-Flemish early Renaissance: Heinrich Isaac, Alexander Agricola and Josquin des Prez.

In this latest rendition, I appended the third verse (from the 1534 edition), added natural dynamics, rebalanced the voices, created a more legato effect, corrected a few orthographic errors*, and enhanced the reverb / echo. I also changed the instrumental doubling (bass viol only in Verse 1; lutes, harp and bass viol in Verse 2; recorder, 3 viols, trombone in Verse 3). The vocal parts were "performed" by the the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid.

* According to Timothy McGee, the î is a stand-in for "ai." Thus "Kätterlîn" would be pronounced "kɛ:ttərlaɪn."

videos.title: Loyset Compère: Scaramella fa la galla (c.1490)

localized.title: Loyset Compère: Scaramella fa la galla (c.1490)
localized.description:
Scaramella fa la galla

0:06  Original parody based on Josquin's frottola (ATTB)
1:12  Instrumental setting (2 shawms, 2 trombones)

This parody song by Loyset Compère is a slightly more complex, polyphonic reimagining of the original frottola by his more famous compatriot Josquin des Prez. The "combero" and "berombetta" are likely clarion calls by a trumpet or other loud instruments on the battlefield. The mention of both shoe ("scarpa") and boot ("stivala") in the same sentence may imply that the character being described is both a warrior (or a horseman) and a courtly gentleman. Compère hailed from the same region of the Burgundian hinterlands as dez Prez, and they may have met during their respective travels in the north of Italy during the last decades of the 15th Century.

I entered the text using the Spanish language Vocaloid voice bank Maika. The instrumental sounds were produced using MusicStudio2. In this latest rendition, I slowed the tempo a bit, added some natural dynamics, rebalanced the voices, created a more legato effect and enhanced the reverb / echo.

========

Scaramella fa la galla (Scaramella does the gala*)
Con la scarpa e la stivalla (wearing shoe and boot)
La comberon berombetta. (zombero, borombetta**)

* galla likely refers to a dance (cf. gagliarda) but also has a second meaning which is "inseminate."
** Josquin's original onomatopoeia

videos.title: Georg Philipp Telemann: Aria from Kantata "Seele lerne dich erkennen" (c.1725)

localized.title: Georg Philipp Telemann: Aria from Kantata "Seele lerne dich erkennen" (c.1725)
localized.description:
The cantata "Seele lerne dich erkennen" (TWV 1258) is based on a free-form libretto paraphrased from Chapter 13 in First Corinthians. This first movement is a soprano aria (simple enough for a boy chorister) introduced by a virtuosic recorder soloist. The piece was written in the early days of Telemann's residence in the city of Hamburg and is one short work in a large collection of sacred songs for the Christian calendar titled Harmonischer Gottesdienst. This cantata was specifically intended for the last Sunday before the Lenten season.

The simulated singing was achieved using the Maika Spanish language Vocaloid. I use the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 to generate the instrumental sounds of a recorder ("flauto dolce"), harpsichord, bass viol and double bass (an octave below the viol). I used the suggested figured bass from the original score to fill out the triads and chords in the obbligato keyboard part.

Text:

Seele, lerne dich erkennen! (O Soul, learn to know yourself)
lauter Stückwerk ist zu nennen, (much piecemeal work to be done)
was der Menschen Witz vermag. (what is Man's mind able)
Zur Vollkommenheit zu dringen (Toward perfection to strive)
sind der ird’schen Klugheit Schwingen (are the wings of earthly wisdom)
viel zu schwach, viel zu schwach. (much too feeble, much too feeble.)

2. Kieler Knabenchor, a traditional boys' group that bears some similarity to the Gymnasium student choir directed by Telemann in Hamburg during the 1720s.
3. Vintage photo of Old Hamburg in which many of the homes trace back to Telemann's lifetime (and earlier) prior to their being completely destroyed during WW2; photo from 1910s
4. Alto recorder, Jacob Heytz, c1720
5. Pre-War photo of Old Hamburg streets and homes, 1910s
6. Bass viol, Martin Voigt, Hamburg, 1726
7. Model of the Temple in Jerusalem (Hamburger Tempelmodell) commissioned by Hamburg senator Gerhard Schott, c1692; the design is clearly based on architectural designs current in the late Baroque era. It likely started as a plan for a stage set to be used by the Hamburg Opera Company.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Josquin des Prez: Nymphes des bois (c.1500), a lamentation for Ockeghem (after 1497)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Josquin des Prez: Nymphes des bois (c.1500), a lamentation for Ockeghem (after 1497)
localized.description:
This secularized Requiem was Josquin des Prez's heartfelt tribute to the late, great father of the Franco-Flemish School of Renaissance polyphony, Johannes Ockeghem (c.1410-1497). One might hear, in the background, a steady recitation of the ancient Requiem plainchant melody in the tenor part while the other 4 voices sing more lyrical lines above and below it.  Compared to other contemporary works, Josquin's lamentation has more a "modern quality" about it with its through composed (as opposed to strophic) structure, non- repetition of phrases and fewer melismatic passages.

Among the mourners that Josquin Des Prez includes in his poetry are his Franco-Flemish contemporaries: Josquin himself, Brumel, Pirchon (Pierre de la Rue) and Compere -- who all owed a debt of gratitude to the deceased maestro. There is a Part I and II to the chanson wherein Josquin imitates the style Ockeghem in the first half. The concluding segment (Requiescat in pace or R.I.P.) is entirely in Latin and in unison. The original poem was composed by Jean Molinet shortly after Ockeghem's passing in Februrary 1497, but the Susato version of Josquin's chanson-motet (which I used) is slightly altered, perhaps to better match up to the notes.

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, rebalanced the voices, added natural dynamics, corrected the text underlay (as well as pronunciation), slowed the tempo and enhanced the reverb / echo. As has been my custom with rendering French chansons, I used the Maika Spanish language Vocaloid for all five voice parts.  I have used the linguistic recommendations of Timothy McGee for the pronunciation of early Modern French including the enunciation of final consonants (-s and -z) at the end of phrases.

++++++++++

Original text:

Nymphes des bois, deesses des fontaines,
Chantres expers de toutes nations,
Changez voz voix fort cleres et haultaines
En cris tranchantz et lamentations
Car Atropos les molestations,
Votre Ockeghem par sa rigueur attrape,
Le vrai tresoir de musiqu’et chef d’œuvre,
Qui de trepas, desormais plus ne schappe.
Dont grant doumais g'est que la terre le couvre.

Accoutrez vous d’abitz de deuil,
Josquin, Brumel, Pirchon Compère,
Et plorez grosses larmes d’œil.
Perdu avez votre bon pere.
Requiescat in pace.

(TENOR) Requiem aeternam dona eis Domine
et lux perpetua luceat eis.

--------------------

Translation:

Nymphs, goddesses of the fountains,
Expert singers of every nation,
Change your voices, so clear and lofty,
To penetrating cries and lamentation
Because Atropos*, the onslaught,
Has firmly taken away your Ockeghem,
The true treasurer of music and master,
Who died, and no longer runs free
Such great shame it is that the earth covers him.

Put on the robes of mourning,
Josquin, Brumel, Pierre (de la Rue), Compère,
And weep great tears from your eyes,
You have lost your good father.
May he rest in peace. Amen.

* the Fate who makes death permanent

(TENOR) Grant unto them, O Lord, eternal rest
and let perpetual light shine upon them.

++++++++++

Descriptions of the photos in their order of appearance:

1. "La deploration de Johan Okeghem", Josquin des Prez, publ.1545 (T.Susato), Antwerp
2. Requiem mass, Queen's Book of Hours, Anon. Anglo-French, c1415
3. Kyrie, Missa Ecce Ancilla Domini, J. Ockeghem, Chigi Codex VIII 234, c1500. Many of Ockeghem's works were beautifully rendered by the best copyist of his generation.
4. Cathedral of Saint Gatien in Tours, France, the last town in which Ockeghem resided before his death in 1497.
5. Requiem mass, Royal 2 B VIII f. 144, c1420. Note the clerical singers surrounding the casket
6. Funeral procession, Anon.English, Book of Hours, British Museum 27697, c1420. Ockeghem's funeral was probably also well attended given his fame among prominent figures of his generation and his extensive travels across Europe. He is thought to have been buried at the church of St. Martin in Tours.
7. The altar of St. Gatien where Ockeghem may have performed his Mass for the Dead on the occasion of the funeral of his earthly master King Charles VII.
8. Ockeghem (with dark spectacles) as choirmaster, Anon., c1510, Bibliotheque Nationale in Paris.
9. Portrait of a Musician (? Ockeghem), Anonymous Franco-Flemish, second half 15th cent.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Clément Janequin: J'atens le temps (1540)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Clément Janequin: J'atens le temps (1540)
localized.description:
J'atens le temps

  0:06  Original 4 part chanson (ATTB and harp)
  1:59  Instrumental version (violin, 3 viols and harp)

This tender chanson is short on words (27 total including contractions) but expansive on sentiment.  The lilting quality of the song conveys a peaceful feeling as well as a melancholic, yearning nostalgia. This piece is one of many art songs by Janequin compiled by the prolific Parisian printer Pierre Attaingnant in the volume "Huitieme Livre Contenant XIX Chansons Nouvelles" (8th Book containing 19 New Chansons) in 1540.

++++++++++

Lyrics in Early Modern French:

J'atens le temps ayant ferme espérance
En ce vouloir mes jours je fineray
En attendant aultre ne serviray
Tant m'est de vous doulce la souvenance.

English translation

I wait and pass the time having a firm hope.
In doing so, I shall end my days.
In the meantime, no other shall I serve.
So sweet is the memory of you.

++++++++++

In the most recent rendition, I created a more legato effect, rebalanced the voices, added natural dynamics and enhanced the reverb / echo.  The instrumental arrangements were generated using the MusicStudio2 app on the iPhone. The original MIDI file for this chanson absent the words was uploaded to IMSLP.org by Daniel van Gilst.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Filippo Azzaiolo: Vorrei che tu cantassi una canzone (1557)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Filippo Azzaiolo: Vorrei che tu cantassi una canzone (1557)
localized.description:
Vorrei che tu cantassi una canzone

  0:06  Verse 1 (ATTB a cappella)
  0:50  Verse 2 (ATTB + lute)
  1:34  Instrumental (recorder, lute, harp, bass viol)
  2:16  Instrumental (shawm, 3 trombones)
  2:59  Repeat of Verses 1 & 2 (ATTB with recorder, 3 viols, lute, harp)

The entire corpus of Azzaiolo's surviving works were published by Scotto in Venice between 1557 and 1569. They were called villotte, Italian folk songs, that were arranged for small ensemble. They were differentiated according to their regions of origin, e.g. villotte alla paduana (Padua) or villotte alla napoletane (Naples) etc. This particular song mentions the playing of a viola (viola da braccio?) and violone (bass viola da gamba?) - references to street musicians in a city festival. The singers finish each verse with notes from the standard Renaissance scale ("fa mi la mi so la"), which in this instance also has a double meaning ("Do that only to me"). The "instruments" (viola and violone) are therefore likely specific body parts of two lovers.

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, rebalanced the voices, added "natural" dynamics, doubled the voices with lute on verse 2 and enhanced the reverb & echo. The voice simulations were created using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid. The instrumental lines were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2. 

-------------------

Italian text:

Vorrei che tu cantassi una canzone,
quando mi stai sonando la viola.
E che dicessi fa mi la mi so la
  fa mi la mi so la fa mi la mi so la.

Vorrei lo basso far co'l violone,
Tutto di contrapunto alla spagnuola.
E che dicessi fa mi la mi so la
  fa mi la mi so la fa mi la mi so la.

Translation:

I want you to sing a song,
When you are playing the viol
And you should say "fa mi la mi so la." ("do it to me only.")

I want to play the bass part on a bass viol
All the counterpoint in a Spanish style
And you should say "fa mi la mi so la." ("do it to me only.")

--------------------

videos.title: Anonymous Italo-French / René de Trie: Quan ye voy le duç (c.1360)

localized.title: Anonymous Italo-French / René de Trie: Quan ye voy le duç (c.1360)
localized.description:
Quan ye voy le duç tens venir (Originally, Quant je voi le doz temps venir)

0:06  Canonic madrigal for 3 voices (with a reconstructed tenor)
2:09  Instrumental setting (metal strung lute, psaltery, harp)

The caccia (a chase or a hunt) was a popular musical form during the Italian Trecento (c.1350-1380). The two cantus singers perform a virtuosic duet in near-perfect canon while a tenor intones a slow and steady cantus firmus. In the only surviving score of this particular caccia, the tenor part is untexted and has therefore been assumed to be an instrumental part. 

The lyrics for the caccia come from the first verse of a much longer poem by the 13th Century French trouvère, René de Trie. Several courtly love poems of René's have survived, but unfortunately their associated chanson melodies have been lost. For this soundtrack, I have constructed a tenor "cantus firmus" part by combining the untexted tenor melody from the anonymous caccia and René de Trie's original poem in Late Old French. Because the Italian copyist who created the luxurious manuscript had made several spelling errors in the text underlay, I used instead a late 13th Century manuscript from the Modena Estense Library (the so-called Chansonnier 'H') to recover the obscure song lyrics. The ritornello at the end of the song where the rhythm changes from a 4 to a 9 beat presents a separate set of words unrelated to the René's original troubadour song.

How a French troubadour song from Crusader times was incorporated into an Italian polyphonic piece in the Ars Nova period (more than a century later) is a mystery. Perhaps, among the many expatriates from Italy who had spent time at the Papal Court of Avignon (during the Schism of the Catholic church), a few perhaps returned to their homeland remembering songs from the Languedoc region of France.

For the “singing,” I used the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid and for the instrumental simulations, I used the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. For the pronunciation of late Old French, I applied the recommendations of Timothy McGee in "Singing Early Music."

Original text in Old French with translation:

Quant je voi le doz tems venir, (When I see the sweet times returning)
Que reverdit la pree, (when the meadow grows green again)
Et j’oi le rousignol tentir (and I hear the nightingale tempting [me])
Ou bois soz la ramee, (in the woods under the branches)
Adonques ne me puis tenir (And thus, I cannot hold myself)
De chanter, car tuit mi desir (from singing, because you have my desire)
Et tote ma pensee (and all my thoughts)
Sunt en cele amer et servir (are in this love and service)
Cui j’ai m’amor donee, ([she] whom I have given my love)
Senz repentir. (without regret)

Ritornello:

A vos, signior, (To you)
seron nos tote vie (will be our whole life)
Por cele dame (for this lady)
che damor m’envie (that for love I desire)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Claudin de Sermisy: Jouyssance vous donneray (c.1520)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Claudin de Sermisy: Jouyssance vous donneray (c.1520)
localized.description:
Jouyssance vous donneray

  0:06  Verse 1 of the original chanson (published 1528): ATTB
  1:24  Verse 2 (ATTB) accompanied by Attaingnant's lute reduction
  2:43  Instrumental arrangement (flute, 2 lutes, harp, bass viol)

The Franco-Flemish painting of 3 half-figure women performing music (time mark 2:43) may seem rather contrived and stylized. Upon closer examination, one might see that the score sitting on the table displays the first phrase of Sermisy's chanson "Jouyssance vous donneray." This piece, widely popular throughout the 16th century, was published multiple times by Pierre Attaingnant, the most important publisher and music editor in Paris at the time. He printed the chanson in its entirety for the first time in 1528 and a year later as a lute reduction. Also surviving from the French Renaissance repertoire are 1. a parody mass (Missa Jouyssance) and 2. a basse danse printed in full in Thoinot Arbeau's "Orchesographie" (an instruction manual of early 16th Century French courtly dance published in 1589). The theme of this chanson for 4 voices is one of courtly love, but told from the perspective of a lady who, contrary to expectation, accepts her suitor.

In my latest rendition of this chanson, I reworked the text underlay, created a more legato effect, enhanced the reverb & echo, corrected some pronunciation, added in natural dynamics and rebalanced the voices. I also superimposed on the "singing parts" a slightly abbreviated version of Attaingnant's lute reduction. The vocal simulations were created using Vocaloid 4 and the MAIKA Spanish language voice bank. The instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2 licensed by Steinberg.

Text (in Modern French & English translation):

Jouissance vous donnerai (Pleasure will I give you)
Mon ami et vous mènerai (my love and I will lead you)
La où prétend votre espérance. (where your hope desires)
Vivante ne vous laisserai; (While living, I will not leave you)
Encore quand morte serai, (Even when I am dead)
L'esprit en aura souvenance. (the soul shall remember)

Si pour moi avez du souci (If for me, you have concerns)
Pour vous n'en ai pas moins aussi, (for you, I have no less also)
Amour le vous doit faire entendre. (Love must let you hear it)
Mais s'il vous grève d'être ainsi, (But if it grieves you to be so)
Apaisez votre cœur transi; (Appease your cold heart)
Tout vient à point, qui peut attendre. (Everything comes in time, for one who can wait)

videos.title: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina: Sicut cervus desiderat (c.1580)

localized.title: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina: Sicut cervus desiderat (c.1580)
localized.description:
This brief motet is part 1 of a two part work based on Psalm 41 (Latin Vulgate). It is likely a late composition of Palestrina from a time when he was already a well-established maestro in Vatican circles and was perhaps feeling less constrained by the Council of Trent's preference for plainchant and homophonic liturgical music. The earliest printed edition that contains this piece appeared in 1587, but the actual date of its composition is unknown.

The ATTB choir simulation was produced using the Maika Vocaloid. Reverb and echo effects were added using Audacity. The MIDI file was compiled by Lewis Jones and it can found on CPDL.org .

Text and translation:

Sicut cervus desiderat ad fontes aquarum, 
ita desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus.

As the deer desires after the water fountain
so my soul longs for you, God.

videos.title: Arcangelo Corelli: Violin Sonata Op. 5, No. 12, "La Folia" (1700)

localized.title: Arcangelo Corelli: Violin Sonata Op. 5, No. 12, "La Folia" (1700)
localized.description:
The theme of "La Folia" (sp. "La Follia" i.e. folly) has ancient roots traceable to late 15th century Iberian repertoire. It was formalized in its currently recognizable form (consisting of a sequence of 8 notes) by Jean-Baptiste Lully and his contemporaries sometime in the early 1670s; and, 30 years later, it was immortalized by Antonio Vivaldi and Arcangelo Corelli. Nearly every major European composer in Corelli's lifetime and the generation immediately thereafter (including Bach and Handel) challenged himself to composing some new version of the Folia/Follia variations. Corelli's setting is perhaps the most challenging for performers and the most musically diverse of all the different works from that era. It features both a virtuosic violin solo as well as a difficult basso continuo part for either violone (double bass) or cembalo (harpsichord) or perhaps both (in addition to other instruments such as archlute or theorbo).

This MIDI rendition was created from a score created and uploaded to Musescore.com by Felix Keller (usename: Luempli). Thanks to Keller's excellent transcription, I made only one small note correction based on the original 1700 manuscript (facsimile can be found on IMSLP.org; see link below). I used my iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 to simulate the sound of a Baroque violin, cello, violone (or double bass playing one octave below cello), harpsichord and archlute (an often suggested continuo instrument in Corelli's Rome). I added reverb and echo using Audacity in order to simulate performance in a large ballroom. I did not add any dynamic variation since it is never explicitly indicated in the original score. I only created a slight de-crescendo effect on the many trills throughout the sonata.

Link to the facsimile score: 

https://imslp.org/wiki/12_Violin_Sonatas%2C_Op.5_(Corelli%2C_Arcangelo)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Bartolomeo Tromboncino / Francesco Petrarca: Vergine bella (c.1500)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Bartolomeo Tromboncino / Francesco Petrarca: Vergine bella (c.1500)
localized.description:
Vergine bella

  0:06  Verse 1 for voices (ATTB)
  2:34  Verse 4 for alto and instruments (lute, harp, viol)

"Vergine bella," Tromboncino's song dedicated to the Virgin Mary, is based on a semi-religious poem by the greatest of Italian sonnet writers, Francesco Petrarca (or Petrarch). This sonnet is the last in Petrarch’s collection of 366 masterpieces, "Il Canzoniere." Unlike the amorous poems dedicated to the bard's beloved Laura, this long poem contains a poignancy and sorrow regarding his advancing age and the inevitability of his own end. Most of the song is staid and somber in the manner of an Italian laude (religious ceremonial songs in vernacular), but each verse concludes with a very liberating and expansive Amen. And yet, despite its spiritual character, the lyrics in this frottola captures the language of courtly (platonic) appreciation for an aristocratic Lady such as Tromboncino’s powerful and musically inclined patron, Isabella d’Este.

In this latest rendition, I revised the text underlay in all 4 voices, created a more legato effect, rebalanced the voices, added natural dynamics, corrected pronunciation and enhanced the reverb / echo effect. As before, I used the MAIKA (Spanish language) Vocaloid. Instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.

Text:

Vergine bella, che di sol vestita, (Beautiful Virgin, clothed by the Sun)
coronata di stelle, al sommo Sole (crowned with stars, by the supreme Sun)
piacesti sí, che ’n te sua luce ascose, (pleased, concealing His light)
amor mi spinge a dir di te parole: (Love pushes me to utter words about you)
ma non so ’ncominciar senza tu’ aita, (but I know not how to start without your help)
et di colui ch’amando in te si pose. (and He that lovingly lives in you)
Invoco lei che ben sempre rispose, (I invoke you who always responds)
chi la chiamò con fede: (who is called upon in faith)
Vergine, s’a mercede (Virgin, have mercy)
miseria extrema de l’humane cose (to the extreme misery of human things)
già mai ti volse, al mio prego t’inchina, (You never turn away, so hear my prayer)
soccorri a la mia guerra, (soothe me in my struggle)
bench’i’ sia terra, et tu del ciel Regina. (though I am on earth and you in heaven, as Queen)
AMEN.

Vergine santa d'ogni gratia plena (Saintly Virgin, full of all grace)
che per vera et altissima humilitate (that through true and highest humility) 
salisti al ciel onde miei preghi ascolti (leapt up to heaven, where you hear my prayers)
tu partoristi il fonte di pietate, (you birthed the fountain of piety)
et di giustitia il sol, che rasserena (and sun of justice, that shines through)
il secol pien d'errori oscuri et folti (the age full of error, darkness and fault)
tre dolci et cari nomi ài in te raccolti (3 sweet, beloved, names come together in you)
madre, figliuola et sposa (mother, daughter, spouse)
Vergine gloriosa (Glorious Virgin) 
donna del Re che nostri lacci à sciolti (lady to that King who freed us)
et fatto 'l mondo libero et felice (and made the world free and happy)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Christine de Pizan & Gilles de Binchois: Dueil angoisseux (c.1430)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Christine de Pizan & Gilles de Binchois: Dueil angoisseux (c.1430)
localized.description:
Dueil angoisseus (Text: Christine de Pizan, Music: Gilles de Binchois)

  0:06  Verse 1 of the original chanson (ATTB)
  3:46  Verse 2 by a solo singer with lutes and harp

This poem by Christine de Pizan (original Venetian: Cristina da Pizzano) was written around 1390 as a lamentation commemorating the unexpected death from plague of her husband, Etienne du Castel, royal secretary to the King of France Charles V. Christine de Pizan spent the rest of her life in the intellectual circles of the royal court, devoting herself to the production of writings that detailed the lives and thoughts of aristocratic women (as well as women in general) in late Medieval France. Most of her writings were widely praised and copied repeatedly throughout her own lifetime -- a rare achievement in a time when even the most educated and privileged women were sequestered in the confines of cloisters and palaces. Despite de Pizan's Italian origins, she strongly identified as a French woman (having been raised in France from early childhood) and assimilated herself completely to the Parisian lifestyle and culture.

This recording was created using a MIDI file by Patrick Elvin and uploaded to CPDL.org .  In this latest rendition, I added a second set of lyrics, slowed the tempo (for a more mournful affectation), created a more legato effect, re-balanced the voices, corrected the pronunciation, added natural dynamics, enhanced the reverb / echo and The instrumental sounds were created using MusicStudio2, an iPhone app. 

----------

Text:

Dueil angoisseux, rage desmesurée,
Grief desespoir, plein de forsennement,
Langour sansz fin et vie maleürée
Pleine de plour, d'angoisse et de tourment,
Cuer doloreux qui vit obscurement,
Tenebreux corps sus le point de partir
Ay, sanz cesser, continuellement;
Et si ne puis ne garir ne morir.

Fierté, durté de joye separée
Triste penser, parfont gemissement,
Engoisse grant en las cuer enserrée,
Courroux amer porté couvertement,
Morne maintien sanz resjoïssement,
Espoir dolent qui tous biens fait tarir,
Si sont en moy, sanz partir nullement ;
Et si ne puis ne garir ne morir.

Translation:

Anguished pain, immeasurable rage,
Desperate grief, full of madness,
Languor without end and a life of misfortune,
full of tears, anguish and torment,
Pained heart, which lives obscurely,
Somber body at the point of death,
I have continually without ceasing;
and thus I can neither heal nor die.

Pride, harshness, separate from joy,
Sad thought deeply groaning,
Great anguish that the enclosed heart,
Bitter affliction borne secretly,
Mourning kept without rejoicing,
Painful hope that dries up all good, 
They are in me never leaving;
and thus I can neither heal nor die.

----------
