videos.title: [New Rendition] Philippe Verdelot: Beata es virgo Maria / Ave Maria (c.1525)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Philippe Verdelot: Beata es virgo Maria / Ave Maria (c.1525)
localized.description:
The composer Philippe Verdelot, like his contemporary Adrian Willaert and predecessor Josquin des Prez, was an expatriate from the Burgundian hinterlands who arrived in northern Italy in the second decade of the 16th Century. This Marian motet for 7 voices (SAATTBB) contains two sets of lyrics "Beata es virgo Maria" and "Ave Maria" (the more familiar) sung simultaneously in different voice parts. The first phrase of the Alto line "Ave Maria" seems to take its notes from Josquin's famed "Ave Maria, gratia plena" for 4 voices instead of the more often used plainchant melody. The Franco-Flemish influence is quite apparent with its intricate interweaving counterpoint infused with long melismata in stark contrast to the later works of Palestrina and others of the Counter-Reformationist School. The motet consists of a part 1 and part 2 which were copied separately in the surviving manuscripts.

In this latest rendition, I pitched the voices up a half step (A=466Hz), created a more legato effect, corrected some pronunciation, added natural dynamics to all voice parts, rebalanced the voices and enhanced the reverb / echo.  The original MIDI file without the words was created and uploaded to CPDL.org by Jay Lane. 

++++++++++

Latin text:

Beata es, Virgo Maria, 
quae Dominum portasti creatorem mundi: 
genuisti, qui te fecit, 
et in aeternum permanes virgo.
Ave Maria gratia plena, Dominus tecum.
genuisti, qui te fecit, 
et in aeternum permanes virgo.

Translation:

You are blessed, Virgin Mary,
who carried the Lord, Creator of the world
You birthed him who made you
and you remained a virgin forever.
Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord with you.
You gave birth to him who made you
and you remained a virgin forever.

+++++++++

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous French & Gabriel Bataille: Patoureau m'ayme tu bien? (c.1610)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous French & Gabriel Bataille: Patoureau m'ayme tu bien? (c.1610)
localized.description:
Based remotely on a chanson for 7 voices by the Franco-Flemish composer Jean de Castro some decades earlier, this trio by Gabriel Bataille for 2 voices and lute accompaniment is a dialogue between two shepherds: one male, one female. In the brief exchange, there is a playful flirtation between two pastoral characters in a manner similar to the duets from the Italian operas of Claudio Monteverdi and Michelangelo Rossi.

In this latest rendition, I slowed the tempo to suit the fast ornaments, rebalanced the two voices, sharpened the bass voice so that it sounds less muffled, created a more legato effect, enhanced the echo and reverb, switched out the harpsichord for a chitarrone and corrected some pronunciation. videos.title: Jean Mouton or Adrian Willaert: Salva nos Domine (c.1500)

localized.title: Jean Mouton or Adrian Willaert: Salva nos Domine (c.1500)
localized.description:
This short motet for 6 voices (SAATBB) was intended for the contemplative and meditative office of Compline, or Prayer at the End of the Day. Its popularity is attested by the many copies that circulated around Europe throughout the first half of the 16th century -- most of the earliest versions appearing in Italy. The presumed composer (according to the score that I used for this video) is Josquin's pupil and French church composer Jean Mouton. Other sources have attributed the same or similar work to the master himself, Josquin des Prez, or to Mouton's younger Flemish contemporary Adrian Willaert. But given its structural similarity to another often performed Mouton motet "Nesciens mater," I believe that Mouton is the correct attribution. As in the "Nesciens," two middle voices intone a slight variation on the original chant melody in canon. 

Text and translation:

Salva nos, Domine, vigilantes, custodi nos dormientes:
ut vigilemus cum Christo, et requiescamus in pace.

Save us, Lord while we are wake, protect us while we are asleep:
so that we may keep watch with Christ, and rest in peace.

3. The plainchant "Salva nos domine," Bibliothèque Nationale de France, Ms 15181, 14th Century.
4. Candles burning, a common setting for Compline; video by jrydertr (uploaded to Pixabay).

Boesset was a court composer who, along with his father-in-law Pierre Guedron, shaped the musical landscape around France's royalty (beginning with King Louis XIII) in the first half of the 17th Century. He produced an enormous corpus of secular works known the "Airs de cour" which were most often arias for a solo singer and a lutenist. videos.title: [New Rendition] Martin Luther & Johann Walter: Ein feste Burck ist unser Gott (1544)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Martin Luther & Johann Walter: Ein feste Burck ist unser Gott (1544)
localized.description:
Ein feste Burg is unser Gott

  0:06 Verse 1 for 4 voices (SATB)
  1:19 Verse 2 for tenor solo and lute
  2:32 Verse 3 for tenor, lute and 3 viols
  3:44 Verse 4 for 4 voices & sackbuts

++++++++++

"A mighty fortress is our God," Martin Luther's paraphrasing of Psalm 46 has become the most frequently recited lyrics of the Protestant Reformation.  It was a statement of Luther's personal faith and of his steadfast defiance against both the Papal Inquisition and the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. To the former Augustinian monk, Luther’s personal connection to God became his sole anchor; so much so that he no longer felt bound by any of the mother church's rules of conduct.  "Ein feste Burg ist under Gott" became a militant anthem for the burgeoning Protestant movement that swept across Europe between the mid- to late 16th century. Luther's tune was adapted by all the greatest titans of German music for the next two centuries: Michael Praetorius, Heinrich Schütz, Dietrich Buxtehude, Johann Sebastian Bach, Georg Philipp Telemann and countless others.

This recording is an electronic rendition of Johann Walter's setting for 4 voices first published in 1544. In this latest rendition, I corrected some vowel pronunciations, fixed the text underlay, added natural dynamics, created a more legato effect, rebalanced the voices and enhanced the reverb/echo. The MIDI file was created by Markus Lang (CPDL.org). Instrumental sounds  were generated using MusicStudio2 (an iPhone app).  I avoided using a church organ in the background to respect Luther's distaste for its use as a congregational instrument - perhaps because it was so loud and overwhelming to an audience who needed to hear all the words to his hymns.

++++++++++

3. First two pages of the 95 Theses (Luther's complaints against Church issued indulgences from 1517); this is an 1522 reprint
4. Martin Luther delivering a sermon at All Saints', Lucas Cranach the Elder, 1532
5. Luther arguing his thesis before the Diet of Worms (Luther in the center, Emperor Charles V at right), woodcut, Ludwig Rabus, 1556

++++++++++

videos.title: Anonymous English or Italian: Variations on "La Romanesca" (c.1560)

localized.title: Anonymous English or Italian: Variations on "La Romanesca" (c.1560)
localized.description:
"Romanesca" is a musical construct built over a repeated bass note sequence consisting of at least 8 notes. It had its origins in either Spain or Italy, but in the course of a century and a half, it spawned countless instrumental and vocal settings across all of Europe. The earliest use of this series of notes appears to be in two variations on the Spanish folk song "Guardame las vacas,” which can be found in two printed lute / vihuela tablatures from the early 16th Century by Luis de Narváez and Alonso Mudarra, respectively.  Pachelbel's Kanon is a later variant of the Romanesca scaffolding.

The particular set of variations in this video can be found in an English collection from the mid-16th Century called the Dublin Virginal Manuscript (even though the intended instrument was not specified and the nation of origin was not Ireland.) The mood is very ebullient and the venue was likely a casual one such as a courtly ball. The composer was likely an Italian expatriate at the English court or an Englishman inspired by a then trendy moda Italiana. I removed some of the recommended trills in the original score to give the piece a more staid and steady feeling.

Description of the photos:

1. Facsimile of the original handwritten score from the Dublin Virginal MS, c1570
2. Early harpsichord, Alessandro Trasuntino, Venice, built in 1531
3. Concerto, including the illustration of a woman playing a spinet, Giovanni Antonio Fasolo, c1560
4. Detail of Italian spinet (Metropolitan Museum of Art, NY), built c1540
5. Score for a solo vihuela of "Guardame las vacas," Luis de Narváez, Los seys libros del Delphin de música de cifras para tañer vihuela, Valladolid, 1538; this is first printed European instrumental work containing the Romanesca bass.
6. Complete instrument from #4 above.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Josquin des Prez: Ave Maria, gratia plena a 4 (c.1485)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Josquin des Prez: Ave Maria, gratia plena a 4 (c.1485)
localized.description:
Ottaviano Petrucci published his first collection of Latin motets in 1501 and became the first printer of music to recognize the universal appeal and importance of Josquin de Prez's greatest of antiphons "Ave Maria, gratia plena" for 4 voices. From among the countless musical treasures from all over Europe, Petrucci chose Josquin's "Ave Maria" for the first page of his pilot edition. In this masterpiece, one can hear a clear break from the norms of late Medieval French polyphonic writing.  It has fewer open fifths and octaves than other works from the same period.  It uses more syllabic matching between text and note compared to the impossibly long melismatic passages of earlier Franco-Flemish contemporaries like Ockeghem and Agricola. It begins with a strict 4-voice canon in the cantus that is then repeated in the altus, tenore and bassus - an idea that would be repeated time and again until the late Baroque period (e.g. Bach's 6 part ricercar from the Art of Fugue). The "Ave Maria" then winds through a back and forth dialogue between the two upper register voices and the two lower voices (as in the much larger scale polychoral compositions of Giovanni and Andrea Gabrieli more than a century later). The piece touchingly concludes with a series of chords intoning a solemn plea for the intercession of the Virgin Mary at the end of time ("Oh, mother of God, remember me. Amen.") Most likely, this motet was written during Josquin's long stay at the Vatican in Rome.

In this latest rendition, I rebalanced the voices, corrected a few vowel sounds, created a more legato effect, revised the reverb / echo, added natural dynamics and rearranged the sequence of the digital photos. As before, I used only the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid to simulate a Papal choir with boys and men.

++++++++++

++++++++++

videos.title: [New Rendition] Guarda dona el mio tormento (c.1500)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Guarda dona el mio tormento (c.1500)
localized.description:
Guarda dona el mio tormento (Guarda donna il mio tormento)

  0:06  Verse 1: 4 voices (ATTB), 
  1:04  Verse 2: alto with lute and tambourine
  2:01  Verse 3: 4 voices with instruments (recorder, crumhorns, viol, harp, tambourine)
  2:59  Instrumental arrangement (shawms, trombones)

--------------------

The Italian frottola "Guarda dona el mio tormento" bears striking similarity to the rhythms, harmonies, construct and theme of another contemporary song "L'amor dona, chio te porto" by Giacomo Fogliano (see my video at this link: https://youtu.be/ffmClgj6co0 ). Both these pieces can be found in Petrucci's collection of printed Italian songs as well as in the coarsely handwritten Spanish tome El Cancionero Musical de Palacio. The close similarity suggests that "Guarda dona" too may have also been produced by the Italian composer Giacomo Fogliano. There are several misspellings of the Italian lyrics in the Cancionero de Palacio likely due to a Spanish copyists' unfamiliarity with Italian orthography. The melody was devised using hemiolas, vacillating between 6/8 and 3/4 time.  The overall structure is homophonic, which was typical of secular Italian (as well as Iberian) music of that period. It was also common practice to perform secular songs with instruments alone or in combination with vocalists: hence, the 4 different combinations in this video. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, adjusted the text underlay, inserted a 3rd verse, rebalanced the voices, added natural dynamics and augmented the reverb and echo.

--------------------

videos.title: [New Rendition] Mateo Flecha el Viejo: La  Bomba (c.1550)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Mateo Flecha el Viejo: La  Bomba (c.1550)
localized.description:
A collection of 11 so-called ensaladas (or "salads") by the Elder Mateo Flecha (1481–1553) was published in 1581, posthumously, by his nephew Mateo Flecha the Younger. Each ensalada is a short story, full of humor, sarcasm, exaggeration and fantasy. It is a mixture of both secular and religious influences with ecclesiastical Latin texts interspersed in a long and expansive Spanish villancico. It is a blend of traditional elements with its somewhat repetitive and simple homophonic base that alternate with the newer, more complex, Renaissance polyphony prescient of later madrigal writing. One might imagine the grandiosity of early Italian opera combined with the satirical storytelling of Cervantes. In an amusing turn of events, as the danger subsides, Flecha interjects long melodic segments using only the syllables of "Dindirindin" (or "Dendereden) to simulate a lute or vihuela.  He even experiments with chromaticism and dissonance in the rhythmic segments.

The full text of the song can be found at this website:

https://www.musicaantigua.com/las-ensaladas-de-flecha-1-parte/

Briefly, in this tale, the captain of a ship shouts to the crew to get all hands on deck during a powerful and deadly storm.  As the situation becomes increasingly more dire, the sailors turn towards prayer for the various incarnations of the Virgin Mary and the Saints. The images of the perils associated with seafaring were undoubtedly very familiar to many Spaniards during the Age of Exploration when countless galleons were lost at sea due to tempest, piracy or battle. Flecha may have composed this medley during his tenure at the castle of Arévalo as music teacher (1543-1548) to the daughters of his powerful patron, the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.

This words for the soundtrack were inputted using the MAIKA Spanish language voicebank and the Vocaloid 4 program. The original MIDI file was compiled and uploaded by Brian Russell to CPDL.org. I adjusted the tempi for each of the many short segments in this piece according to my own preferences and are different from the original recommendations submitted by Mr. Russell. In the latest rendition, I added natural dynamics, created a more legato effect, corrected some pronunciation, rebalanced the voices, adjusted the reverb / echo and changed some of the tempi. Note that the pronunciation of Spanish is a simulation of 16th Century courtly dialect according to recommendations in "Singing Early Music" by Timothy McGee.

Partial translation of text (the complete text is too massive for this space):

videos.title: Stephan Mahu: Ein feste burg ist unser Gott (c.1540)

localized.title: Stephan Mahu: Ein feste burg ist unser Gott (c.1540)
localized.description:
This motet by the Lutheran composer Stephan Mahu stands in stark contrast to other "Ein feste burg" settings from the same period with its more complex imitative polyphony in the style of contemporary Franco-Flemish maestri. The original hymn tune by Martin Luther is repeated back and forth in slightly modified form between 5 voices, but is most preserved in the tenor.

I used the Spanish language Vocaloid MAIKA to simulate a small German choir of 5 voices. I rendered only the first 2 of the 4 verses in the interest of avoiding repetition. I used the open source Audacity program for PC to add some reverb and echo.

Text:

1. Ein' feste Burg ist unser Gott,
ein' gute Wehr und waffen;
er hilft uns frei aus aller Not,
die uns jetzt hat betroffen.
Der alt' böse Feind,
mit Ernst er's jetzt meint,
groß Macht und viel List
sein' grausam' Rüstung ist,
auf Erd' ist nicht seinsgleichen.

2. Mit unsrer Macht ist nichts getan,
wir sind gar bald verloren;
es streit't für uns der rechte Mann,
den Gott hat selbst erkoren.
Fragst du, wer der ist?
Er heißt Jesus Christ,
der Herr Zebaoth,
und ist kein andrer Gott,
das Feld muß er behalten!

Translation (by Frederic Henry Hedge):

1. A mighty fortress is our God,
A bulwark never failing:
Our helper He, amid the flood
Of mortal ills prevailing.
For still our ancient foe
Doth seek to work his woe;
His craft and power are great,
And armed with cruel hate,
On earth is not his equal.

2. Did we in our own strength confide,
Our striving would be losing;
Were not the right Man on our side,
The Man of God's own choosing.
Dost ask who that may be?
Christ Jesus, it is he;
Lord Sabaoth is his name,
From age to age the same,
And He must win the battle.

Description of the photos:

1. Score of the Discant (soprano) line, Stephan Mahu, Der newen deuschen geistlichen lieder, 1544
2. Portrait of Martin Luther as Junker Joerg, Lucas Cranach, 1522
3. Tower of Schlosskirche (All Saints'), Wittenberg inscribed with "Ein feste Burg"; Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses on its doors in 1517
4. Hymn "Ein feste burg," the original melody by Martin Luther, 2nd edition.
5. Martin Luther's room at Wartburg Castle (Luther's "Fortress") where the condemned preacher sought refuge from the Inquisition and also created the first complete New Testament translation in German.
6. Wartburg Castle ("a mighty fortress"), Eisenach, Germany; CEPhoto, Uwe Aranas from Wikipedia.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Josquin des Prez: Bergerette savoyene (c.1490)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Josquin des Prez: Bergerette savoyene (c.1490)
localized.description:
Bergerette savoyene (savoysienne)

  0:06  Verse 1 of the original chanson (SATB)
  2:11  Verse 2 (SATB)
  4:16  Instrumental arrangement (2 shawms, 2 sackbuts)

This catchy tune by the early Renaissance master Josquin des Prez was a parody of an earlier French chanson and was probably composed towards the end of his tenure in Northern Italy. There are two other songs of the same title by an anonymous author and by Josquin's esteemed contemporary Loyset Compere; moreover, there is also a full parody mass by the great Franco-Flemish maestro, Antoine Brumel. Copies of Josquin's setting have survived in Petrucci's printed edition Harmonice Musices Odhecaton A (1501, Venice, Italy) and in the Cancionero de Segovia (c.1503, Segovia, Spain). The song has a certain bucolic theme and starts off as an invitation by a gallant knight flirting with a presumed shepherdess. The young lady, however, turns out to be a noblewoman in disguise who definitively shuns and humiliates him. Although des Prez likely wrote the piece while immersed in the world of Italian frottole (like most of his other French language works) this chanson also is based on the imitative polyphonic structure of the Franco-Flemish school.

The words of the chanson were entered using Vocaloid 4 with the MAIKA (Spanish language) voice bank.  The sound of the shawm band was produced using the Music Studio 2 app. The MIDI file with text was created by Andrew Fysh (CPDL.org). I transposed the score up a whole step - thus restoring the original notation. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, added natural dynamics, corrected some vowel sounds, rebalanced the voices and revised the reverb / echo effects.

----------

Text:

1  Bergerette savoyene,
Qui gardez moutons aux praz:
Dy moy si vieulx estre myenne:
Je te donray uns soulas,
Et ung petit chapperon;
Dy moy se tu m'aymeras,
Ou par la merande ou non.

2  Je suis la proche voisine
De monsieur le cura,
Et pour chose qu'on me die,
Mon vouloir ne changera,
Pour François ne Bourgoignon.
Par le cor Dé, si fera,
Ou par la merande ou non.

Translation (adapted from CPDL.org):

HE:  Shepherdess of Savoy,
who watches over the sheep in the fields,
tell me if you will be mine:
I will give you some solace,
and a little hat;
Tell me if you will love me,
whether deserving or no.

SHE:  I am a close relative
of the curate,
and, whatever is said to me,
my desire will not change
for Frenchman nor Burgundian.
By the heart of God, it shall be so,
whether deserving or no.

----------

Description of the photos:

1. "Bergerette Savoyene," first line of the Altus part, Josquin des Prez, Harmonice Musices Odhecaton (ed. Ottaviano Petrucci), 1501
2. Concert, Lorenzo Costa, c1495

4. Resting lamb and Head of a Lamb, Hans Holbein the Younger, 1523

6. Pastorale scenery around the Château de Saumur during harvest season, September, Tres Riches Heures de Duc de Berry, c1416
7. Woman with shearing scissors and sheep, MS M 144, Anon. French, c1490
8. A family of sheep, details from the Tempest, Lindee Climo , 2002 (based on the original "Tempest" by the Italian Renaissance painter Giorgione, c1506)
9. Shawm band (2 shawms and trombone), detail from the Coronation of Pope Pius III, Pinturicchio, 1509

videos.title: John Danyel: Like as the lute (1606)

localized.title: John Danyel: Like as the lute (1606)
localized.description:
This song composed by John Danyel (or Daniel) was scored for cantus, lute and bass instrument (likely a viol) and was based on a sonnet of the same title by his eminent brother, the Elizabethan poet, Samuel Danyel. The "muse," referenced in the poem is both metaphorical (the poet's lute) and also literal (the Danyel brothers' patroness, Mary Sydney, Countess of Pembroke).

Text:

Like as the lute delights or else dislikes
As in his art that plays upon the same,
So sounds my Muse according as she strikes
On my heart strings high tun'd unto her fame.
Her touch doth cause the warble of the sound
Which here I yield in lamentable wise,
A wailing descant on the sweetest ground,
Whose due reports give honor to her eyes.
Else harsh my style, untunable my Muse,
Hoarse sounds the voice that praiseth not her name;
If any pleasing relish here I use,
Then judge the world her beauty gives the same.
O happy ground that makes the music such,
And blessed hand that gives so sweet a touch

For a modern interpretation of this sonnet see this link:

https://allpoetry.com/Sonnet-LVII:-Like-As-the-Lute

Description of the photos:

1. Lute Player, Jan Lievensz, c1629
2. "Like as the lute," complete score, John Danyel, Songs for Lute Viol and Voice, 1606
3. Young lutenist, Gover Flinck, c1630
4. Sir Edward Herbert, Isaac Oliver, c1613
5. Musical group on a balcony, Gerrit van Honthorst, 1622
6. Sleeping Girl, Domenico Fetti, c1620
7. Pair of Lovers, Paris Bordone, c1560
8. Mary Sidney, Countess of Pembroke, Anonymous Flemish, c1600; the sonnet "Like as the Lute" was one of many by John Danyel's brother Samuel contained in the collection "Delia" gifted to the Countess in 1592.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Bartolomeo Tromboncino & Franciscus Bossiniensis: Suspir io themo (1511)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Bartolomeo Tromboncino & Franciscus Bossiniensis: Suspir io themo (1511)
localized.description:
Bartolomeo Tromboncino & Franciscus Bossiniensis: Suspir io themo

This frottola survives only in this reduced form for a solo vocalist and lute accompaniment. The original 4 part version by Tromboncino has not yet been found although it is not difficult to re-construct the polyphonic version from the lute intabulation. Like many of Tromboncino's compositions from this period, it was probably dedicated to the intellectual and influential patron Isabella d'Este. The obligatory accompaniment was written by the Venetian lutenist from Bosnia Franciscus Bossiniensis (keeping in mind that the Republic of Venice in the 15th and 16th Centuries encompassed most of the coastal regions of present day Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.)

In this latest rendition, I further enhanced the natural dynamics, adjusted the timbre of the "vocalist," created a more legato effect, corrected some of the vowel sounds and deepened the reverb.

Text:
Suspir io themo ma piu theme il core
Che de doi mali voi cason sereti
Luno de scoprir lo occulto ardore
Laltro che el pecto mio accenderiti
Chel vento un poco ascosto fa magiore
E acceso el vede ognun tal vui fareti
Donque lassate hormai poi che mia sorte
Voi che tacendo o no io corra amorte

Translation:
I am afraid to breath, but my heart is even more afraid
of two bad things you keep secret:
The one to find the hidden passion
The other which lights up my breast
That a little breeze further inflames 
And when everyone sees it, you will do it that way
Therefore leave me now to my fate
Whether you are silent or not, I race toward death

Description of photos:

1. "Suspir io themo" score for voice and lute, Franciscus Bosseniensis, ed. O. Petrucci, 1511
2. Musical seal of Isabella d'Este, Studiolo, Ducal Palace, Mantua
3. Isabella d'Este bust, Gian Cristophoro Romano, c1500
4. Parnassus, Andrea de Mantegna, 1497, originally displayed in Isabella d'Este's Studiolo in Mantua
5. Portraits of Isabella and Beatrice d'Este with lute, Sala del Tesoro, Palazzo Costabilii, Benvenuto Tisi da Garofalo, c1506

videos.title: [New Rendition] Josquin des Prez: Scaramella va alla guerra (c.1490)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Josquin des Prez: Scaramella va alla guerra (c.1490)
localized.description:
Scaramella va alla guerra

0:06  Instrumental arrangement (recorder, lute, harp, viol, tambourine)
0:40  Original frottola (ATTB)
1:15  Instrumental arrangement (2 shawms, recorder, 2 trombones)

This whimsical piece may have had more than one verse at one time, but only this set of lyrics (see below) has survived in the three illuminated manuscripts copied in late 15th and early 16th Century Florence. Josquin des Prez (or Jusquino d’Ascanio as he was known in Italy) was the premiere maestro of Franco-Flemish polyphony. Yet, while in the employment of his Italian masters, first in Ferrara and then in Milan, he adopted the Italian predilection for lighter, homophonic music. (A later parody by Compère has a more complex contrapunctal structure with imitative entrances more typical of the Franco-Flemish school of Josquin's generation. ) In this satirical ditty, a lance bearing warrior is depicted as a kind of bumbling fool. But, if one puts aside the battle references, the song's true meaning is likely an oblique reference to a sexual encounter. The "zombero" and "borombetta" are likely clarion calls by a trumpet, shawm or other loud instruments on the "battlefield."

For this soundtrack, I downloaded James Gibbs' corrected MIDI of "Scaramella" from the website CPDL.org. I entered the text using the Spanish language Vocaloid voice encoder Maika. The instrumental sounds were produced using MusicStudio2. In this latest rendition, I sped up the tempo, created a more legato effect, added in natural dynamics, re-ordered the instrumental sequence and removed the Compere setting (which I also re-rendered).

=========

Text (and translation):

Scaramella va alla guerra (Scaramella goes off to war)
colla lancia et la rotella (With lance and shield)
La zombero boro borombetta, (La zombero boro borombetta)
La boro borombo (La boro borombo)

Scaramella fa la gala (Scaramella does the gala*)
colla scharpa et la stivala (with shoe and boot)
La zombero boro borombetta, (etc)
La zombero boro borombo (etc)

* "do the galiarda" (a dance) or "he inseminates."

=========

Illustrations:

1. Knight attacking a snail, Brunetto Latini, Li Livres dou Tresor, c 1325
2. "Scaramella va alla guerra," cantus and tenor lines, MS Banco Rari 229, Florence, c.1492
3. Landsknecht from the backside, Albrecht Durer, 1503
4. Battle between Heraclius and Chosroes, Piero della Francesca, 1466
5. Detail of a herald blowing a trumpet from #4

videos.title: [New Rendition] Cristóbal de Morales: O sacrum convivium (c.1540)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Cristóbal de Morales: O sacrum convivium (c.1540)
localized.description:
This motet for 5 voices (SAATB) by Cristóbal de Morales was dedicated to the Feast of the Blessed Sacrament. This dramatic, imitative polyphony anticipates the rich, expansive sonority of Palestrina's later masterpieces of the 1560s and 70s.  Morales' work is divided into two parts of which the second half contains the more complex counterpoint. Morales was a Spanish composer who was likely employed by the Vatican when he published this motet. A mostly intact score of the manuscript, significantly water-damaged, is maintained by the Sistine Chapel archives. Because the new St. Peter's basilica was under construction at this time, actual performances of choral music may have been limited to other smaller churches nearby.

The original MIDI file was compiled by Nancho Alvarez and uploaded to the website: https://www.uma.es/victoria/morales.html#motetes . Other modern scores can be found at cpdl.org.

I used the Spanish language voice bank MAIKA and the Vocaloid 4 voice encoder to enter the Latin text. I altered some of the text underlay to allow for a more fluid melody line. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, rebalanced the voices, corrected some vowel sounds, added natural dynamics and enhanced the reverb / echo.

Text:

O sacrum convivium, in quo Christus sumitur;
recolitur memoria passionis ejus;
mens impletur gratia;
et futurae gloriae nobis pignus datur.
Alleluia

Translation:

O blessed banquet, in which Christ is received;
recalled is the memory of his passion
the mind full of grace;
and to us the promise of future glory is given.
Hallelujah

Description of photos:

1. "O sacrum convivium," first line of the damaged (but still legible) score of the cantus line, Cristóbal de Morales, Sistine Chapel MS #13, c.1545
2. Musical angels, detail from Glory of Angels, Santa Maria dei Miracoli (Saronno), Gaudenzio Ferrari, c1540
3. Last supper, Juan de Juanes, 1562
4. Averoldi polyptych, Titian (Tiziano Vecelli), 1522
5. Disputation of the Sacrament, Apostolic Palace (Rome), Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio), 1510
6. Angel Gabriel of the Annunciation bearing the banner "Ave gratia plena," detail from the Averoldi polyptych, 1522
7. Holy Sacrament, detail from the Disputation of the Sacrament
8. The Last Judgement, Michelangelo Buonarotti, Sistine Chapel, painted around 1540. Morales likely witnessed the completed fresco as the paint was still drying.

videos.title: Anonymous French-Burgundian: Jay pris amours (c.1460)

localized.title: Anonymous French-Burgundian: Jay pris amours (c.1460)
localized.description:
"Jay pris amours" (also spelled J'ay prins amours" in several sources) was one of the most widely copied chansons in 15th Century France. They appear in the many richly illuminated manuscripts of the Central Loire Valley compiled between 1460-1480. There is even a full score of "Jay pris" carved into the wooden panels at the Studiolo of the warrior-scholar Federico da Montefeltro at the Palazzo Ducale in Urbino. The version used for this soundtrack, which is only very slightly different from other contemporary settings, appears in the so-called Chansonnier Cordiforme (Heart-shaped Songbook) -- appropriately so since this chanson (like many others in the same collection) is a philosophical musing of a gentleman in love. As was typical of art songs in the mid-15th Century, this piece is chock full of imitative polyphony and long melismata.

I created the vocal simulations for a cantus/altus/tenor choir using MAIKA, a Spanish language Vocaloid. The instrumental sounds of two medieval lutes (one gut string and the other metal) and harp were generated using Music Studio 2.0, an iPhone app. Reverb and echo were later added using Audacity. The MIDI file was compiled by Bojopigeon and can be found on the Musescore website. The text underlay was mostly adapted from the score of Laborde Chansonnier posted on this website: https://chansonniers.pwch.dk

Text (and translation):

J’ay pris amours a ma devise (I have taken love as my method)
pour conquerir joyeuseté; (to conquer joyousness)
heureux seray en cest’ esté, (Happy shall I be this summer)
se puis venir a mon emprise. (if I can go on my quest)

S’il est aulcun qui m’en deprise, (If anyone despises me)
il me doit estre pardonné. (I should be pardoned)

J’ay pris amours a ma devise
pour conquerir joyeuseté.

Il me semble que c’est la guise, (I believe that this is the way)
qui n’a riens, il est debouté,  (he who has nothing, he is rejected)
et n’est de personne honnoré; (and no person honors [him])
n’esse pas donc droit que je vise? (thus is it not right that I seek it?)

Description of the photos:

1. "Iay pris amours," cantus part, Anonymous French, Chansonnier Cordiforme, c1470
2. Cuer (heart) reading the message of love on a dark stone, Livre du cuer d'amours espris de René d'Anjou, Barthélemy d'Eyck, c1460
3. "Iay pris amours," intarsiated on the studio wall of the Palazzo Ducale in Urbino, c1475
4. "Vous cervir," ([I] serve you), a message carved onto a gold ring, English, c1480
5. "Iay prins amours," full score, Anonymous French, Laborde Chansonnier, c1465; perhaps the oldest surviving manuscript copy of the chanson
6. Angel playing lute, detail from a Madonna painting, Gerard David, c1480
7. Musicians in the Garden of Pleasure, from Roman de la Rose, Brit.Lib. Harley 4425, Guillaume de Lorris; Jean de Meun, c1490
8. Mary Magdalene, Quentin Metsis, c1480

videos.title: Henry Purcell: Aria "Ah Belinda" from Act 1 of "Dido and Aeneas" (c.1688)

localized.title: Henry Purcell: Aria "Ah Belinda" from Act 1 of "Dido and Aeneas" (c.1688)
localized.description:
"Ah Belinda" is the introductory aria from Act I sung by Dido to her principal attendant Belinda. Dido is Queen of Carthage and the main character in Purcell's tragic opera "Dido and Aeneas." Foreseeing the potential conflict between her love for the war refugee Aeneas (from the recently defeated city state of Troy) and her sworn duty as ruler of her vast realm, Dido, expresses a sense of despair. 

The vocal simulation was created using the Prima V2 Vocaloid. I adjusted Vocaloid's pronunciation presets to recreate the sounds of late Early Modern English pronunciation in London in the mid- to late 17th Century. The instrumental simulation was generated using Music Studio 2.0 (iPhone app) from Sternberg.

Text:

Ah! Belinda,
I am press'd with torment
not to be confess'd.
Peace and I are strangers grown.
I languish till my grief is known
yet would not have it guessed.

Description of the photos:

1. "Dido and Aeneas," Jan van den Hoecke, 1635
2. "Aeneas and Dido in Carthage," Claude Lorrain, 1675
3. "Dido and Aeneas," Nathaniel Dance-Holland, 1766
4. "Aeneas departs from Dido," Guido Reni, c1630
5. "Death of Dido," Andrea Sacchi, c1650
6. Musicians in a pastoral setting, Donato Creti, c1695

videos.title: John Danyel: Now the earth, the skies, the air (1606) (Original Pronunciation)

localized.title: John Danyel: Now the earth, the skies, the air (1606) (Original Pronunciation)
localized.description:
This late Elizabethan madrigal was scored for 2 sopranos (each accompanied by his or her own lute), tenor and bass. The 1606 edition makes explicit the seating arrangement of each of the performers. The two sopranos face one another while the tenor sits to the left of soprano 1 and the bass to the left of soprano 2. The song was printed in London and dedicated to an Anne Grene, daughter of Sir William Grene of Milton. The lyrics are based on Petrarch's Canzoniere #164 (Or che ’l ciel et la terra e ’l vento tace) and #310 (Zephiro torna, e’l bel tempo rimena). As with many English composers of his generation (and the Italian madrigalists of earlier decades), John Danyel adopted the romantic poetry of the Petrarchan sonnets.

The vocal simulations were created using the Prima V2 (soprano 1), Avanna (soprano 2), Cyber Songman (tenor and bass) Vocaloids. I adjusted Vocaloids' phonemic presets to approximate an Early Modern English pronunciation for an Elizabethan or Shakespearean audience.

Text:

Now, the earth, the skies, the air, all things fair
seems new borne thoughts t'infuse
whilst the returning spring that joys each thing
and blasted hopes renews
when only I alone left to moan
find no times borne for me.
No flow'rs no meadow springs
no bird sings but notes of misery.

Description of the photos:

1. Score of "Now the earth," for two sopranos, two lutes, tenor and bass, "Songs for the lute viol and voices," John Danyel, London, 1606
2. Woman playing lute and singing, Artemisia Gentileschi, 1629
3. "Allegory of Love: Happy Union," Paolo Veronese, c1575
4. Cover page of "Songs for the lute viol and voices," John Danyel, London, 1606
5. Allegory of Spring and Summer, Tintoretto, c1585
6. Rinaldo and Armida, Anthony van Dyck, London, c1629

videos.title: [New Rendition] Claudin de Sermisy & Thomas Crecquillon: Amours partez (c.1525-1540)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Claudin de Sermisy & Thomas Crecquillon: Amours partez (c.1525-1540)
localized.description:
Amour partez

  0:00  Original chanson (ATTB) (publ.1529) by Claudin de Sermisy
  1:08  Parody chanson (SATB) (publ.1545) by Thomas Crecquillon
  2:37  Pavane based on "Amours partez" (cornetto, 3 sackbuts, kettle drum)

These two very different versions of the chanson "Amours partez" come from two of the most prominent composers of the Franco-Flemish High Renaissance. De Sermisy had acquired his homophonic style from the frottole and villancicos of the Spanish-Italian schools while Crecquillon used the somewhat more complex polyphonic textures of the Netherlander school connected to Josquin, Arcadelt and Willaert. I created both a purely vocal and an instrumental "performance" of Sermisy's setting.

The MIDI files were created and uploaded by André Vierendeels to CPDL.org.  I added text using the Yamaha Vocaloid encoder with only the MAIKA (Spanish language) Vocaloid. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, adjusted the balance between the 4 vocal parts, added natural dynamics, corrected a few vowel sounds and slowed the tempo. I also doubled the voices in original chanson with lute. The instrumental parts were added using my iPhone app Music Studio 2.

Text:
Amour(s) partez, ie vous donne la chasse,
non pas pour mal que mon cuer vous procure,
mais faulx semblant qui met toute sa cure
à decepvoir banit de ma grace.

Translation:
Love(s), go away, I give you chase,
not for any bad that my heart grants you,
but a false pretense which puts all its care
to deceptively banish from my grace.

Description of photos:

1. "Amours partez," Claudin de Sermisy, Trente et une chansons musicales a quatre parties, 1529
2. Four musicians singing, detail from Garden of Pleasure from British Library, Harley MS 4425, Roman de la Rose, Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun, c1500
3. Four singers in a garden, detail from an illuminated score of a Kyrie in the Chigi MS VIII.234, Vatican Collection, Anon. Franco-Flemish, c1500
4. A young man kneeling before the goddess Venus, from British Lib, Harley MS 4425, Roman de la Rose, Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun, c1500
5. Four instrumentalists in a garden, detail from an illuminated score of a Kyrie in the Chigi MS VIII.234, Vatican Collection, Anon. Franco-Flemish, c1500
6. Gallery musicians with brass instruments, Giorgio Vasari, 1545
7. Wild flowers in the garden of Château de Fontainebleau, by Orelian, on Pixabay.

videos.title: Anonymous Italian / L. Giustinian: Ben so che la mia mente (c.1460)

localized.title: Anonymous Italian / L. Giustinian: Ben so che la mia mente (c.1460)
localized.description:
This gentle, Petrarca-esque love poetry from the Neapolitan collection El Escorial IV.a.24 was likely written by the Venetian poet and Classical scholar Leonardo Giustinian in the early 15th Century. The musical score, with its complex polyphonic structures and long melismas is a later creation, likely by a Franco-Flemish composer at one of the many wealthy courts of Northern Italy. The copyist's text underlay is a bit challenging to interpret, but I used facsimiles of the original score to create this modern vocal rendition. 

The vocal simulations were generated using Maika, a Spanish language Vocaloid. The instrumental sounds of recorder, medieval lute, harp and viol were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 licensed by Steinberg.

Text (and translation):

Ben so che la mia mente (I know so well my mind)
ognor desiri (desiring all the time) 

Strugom'et, ardo duna piera viva (Longing, I burn with living fire)
che rompre non se puol per lacrimare  (that cannot be put out with tears)

Solo per ben amare (Only to love dearly)
che non me vole aitare (though no one wants to help me)
ni aver pieta del mio languire (nor have pity for my languishing)

Description of the photos:

1. "Ben so che la mia mente," page 1, Cancionero El Escorial IV.a.24
2. Garden of Love, Anon. Italian, c1470
3. Man and Woman at Casement, Filippo Lippi, c1444
4. "Ben so che la mia mente," page 2, Cancionero El Escorial IV.a.24
5. Triumph of Love, Chastity and Death, Girolamo da Cremona, c1460

videos.title: Walter Frye: Ave regina caelorum (c.1460)

localized.title: Walter Frye: Ave regina caelorum (c.1460)
localized.description:
Copies of this brief motet appear in three French chansonniers from the late 15th Century (as well as in one contemporary Italian source). However, only one, the Leuven Chansonnier contains the complete, intact score for all three voice parts (cantus, altus and tenor). Nearly nothing is known about the English composer Walter Frye, and his music survives only in Continental sources. The natural supposition therefore has been that he spent part of his musical career in France or the Netherlands, since at least one work attributed to him, "Tout a par moy" is an original (that is, non-parodied) French chanson. 

I used the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid to simulate medieval Latin with a slight Anglo-French pronunciation scheme as would have been expected in Frye's musical circle. I applied additional reverb and echo with Audacity open-source software for the PC.

Text (and translation):

Ave regina caelorum, (Hail, queen of heaven)
Mater regis angelorum (Mother of the king of angels)
O Maria, flos virginum, (O Maria, flower of virgins)
Velut rosa, velut lilium. (As the rose and the lily)

Funde preces ad Filium (Shower prayers on the son)
Pro salute fidelium, (for the salvation of the faithful)
O Maria, flos virginum, (O Maria, flower of virgins)
Velut rosa, velut lilium. (as the rose and the lily)

Descriptions of the photos:

1. "Ave regina celorum," Walter Frye, Leuven Chansonnier
2. "Coronation of the Virgin", Filippo Lippi, Spoleto Duomo, 1467
3. "Mary, queen of Heaven," Master of St. Lucy Legend, c1485; the musical score held up by the angels is apparently Frye's "Ave regina" tune.
4. Coronation of the Virgin, Fra Angelico, c1432
5. The crowned Virgin and child Jesus, Jan van Eyck, c1435

videos.title: [New Rendition] Arnoldus von Bruck: Gott der Vater wohn uns bei (c.1534)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Arnoldus von Bruck: Gott der Vater wohn uns bei (c.1534)
localized.description:
Von Bruck, a Catholic Netherlander who served at the pleasure of the burgeoning Hapsburg court of Archduke Ferdinand, was a curious figure who successfully straddled a complicated world divided between Protestant and Catholic camps. This German hymn is one of the most widely used melodies in the Lutheran tradition although a similar pre-Reformation tune devoted to the Virgin Mary from the early 15th century has been found. The text and melody of von Bruck's version are adapted from Luther's musical protégé Johann Walter. As a composer who traveled widely throughout the German speaking territories of the Holy Roman Empire, von Bruck probably felt comfortable keeping an open mind about sources of musical inspiration.

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, added natural dynamics in all voices, rebalanced the parts, adjusted the reverb & echo and corrected some of the spelling using facsimiles of the original print. As before, I used MAIKA, a Spanish language Vocaloid for all four voice parts.

Text (and translation):

Gott der Vater wohn uns bei (God, the Father, dwell by us)
und laß uns nicht verterben, (and let us not perish.)
mach uns aller Sünden frei (Make us free of all sins)
und helf uns selig sterben! (and help us to die blessed)
Fuer dem Teufel uns bewahr, (Keep us from the Devil,)
halt uns bei festem Glauben, (hold us in strong faith)
und auf dich laß uns bauen, (and on you we will build)
aus Herzem grund vertrauen, (trust you from the bottom of our hearts)
dir uns lassen ganz und gar, (to you let us completely)
mit allen rechten Christen, (with the all righteous Christians)
entfliehen Teufels Listen, (escape the Devil's deceit)
mit Waffen Gotts uns fristen. (with God's weapons defend us)
Amen, amen, das sei wahr, (Amen, amen that's true)
So singen wir: Hallelujah. (Thus we sing: Hallelujah)

Description of photos:

1. "Gott der Vater wohn uns bei," descant part, Johann Walter; the source for von Bruck's parody, 1524
2. Concert of sacred music, Hans Burgkmair, c1530
3. St. Stephen church interior, Zagreb, Croatia, where von Bruck was employed for a time
4. "Newe deudsche geistliche gesenge," cover page, editor Georg Rhaw, 1544; the second publication which contains von Bruck's "Gott der Vater"
5. Map of Vienna in the 16th century
6. Christ risen, Matthias Grünewald, 1515

videos.title: [New Rendition] Jacobus Arcadelt: Salve regina (c.1540)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Jacobus Arcadelt: Salve regina (c.1540)
localized.description:
Salve regina in 3 parts

  0:06  Prima pars (Part 1): SATTB
  3:44  Secunda pars (Part 2): ATT
  5:15  Tertia pars (Part 3): SATTB

This Marian motet derives its text and melody from one of the oldest non-scriptural plainchants in the Catholic liturgy. Arcadelt likely composed this choral masterpiece for the papal choir in Rome during the construction of the new basilica of St. Peter. Jacques (or Jacobus) Arcadelt was one of many Flemish composers hired by the Church of Rome, and his works (including this piece) were neatly copied into the Vatican Apostolic archives (Cappella Sistina MS #24). This Salve is typical of a pre-Tridentine style with its polyphonic complexity and imitative passages among the five vocalists (SATTB). One can hear structural and thematic similarities between this work and the much older "Salve regina" for 5 voices by Josquin des Prez, Arcadelt's predecessor at the Sistine Chapel.

I created this MIDI file from an old score uploaded to IMSLP.org and added the Latin text using the Maika Spanish language Vocaloid. I changed some of the original text underlay to make it less awkward. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, slowed the tempo, added natural dynamics, rebalanced the voices, enhanced the reverb & echo. I also pitched it up a semitone to approximate the natural range of boy sopranos in the superius / cantus part.

Text:

[Prima pars]
Salve, Regina, Mater misericordiæ,
vita, dulcedo, et spes nostra, salve.
Ad te clamamus exsules filii Hevæ,
Ad te suspiramus, gementes et flentes
in hac lacrimarum valle.

[Secunda pars]
Eya, ergo, advocata nostra, illos tuos
misericordes oculos ad nos converte;

[Tertia pars]
Et Jesum, benedictum fructum ventris tui,
nobis post hoc exsilium ostende.
O clemens, O pia, O dulcis Virgo Maria.

Translation:

[Part 1]
Hail, Queen, Mother of Mercy,
Hail, our life and sweetness and hope.
To you we cry out,
Exiled children of Eve;
To you do we sigh heavily,
Lamenting and weeping in the valley of tears.

[Part 2]
Thus, our advocate,
please turn your merciful eyes toward us.

[Part 3]
And Jesus, the blessed fruit of thy womb
Show (him) to us after this exile
O merciful, O pious,
O sweet Virgin Mary.

Description of the photos:

1. "Salve Regina," prima pars, cantus part, J. Arcadelt, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, MS Cappella Sistina 24, copied c1545
2. Sacra Conversations, Palma Il Vecchio, c1520
3. "Salve Regina" plainchant, St. Gallen MS 390, copied around 980 C.E.
4. Madonna di San Salvatore, Antonio Begarelli, Modena, c1535
5. The new St. Peter's Basilica under construction, Maerten van Heemskerck, c1535
6. Annunciation, Domenico Beccafumi, c1545
7. Angel Gabriel holding up the banner of the Virgin Mary "Ave gratia plena," details from the polyptych of Averoldi (Santi Nazaro e Celso, Brescia), Titian, 1522
8. Madonna and Child surrounded by musical angels, Bernardino Luini, c1545
9. The baldacchino of St. Giovanni Laterano, Rome
10. "Salve regina," tertia pars, cantus part, J. Arcadelt, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, MS Cappella Sistina 24, copied c1545
11. Madonna col Bambino e i Santi Margherita, Girolamo e Petronio, Mazzola Francesco detto il Parmigianino, c1529
12. La Pietà, Michelangelo Buonarroti, c1499, undoubtedly a familiar sight to Arcadelt who frequented the halls of the Vatican.
13. Close-up of the Virgin Mary from La Pietà
14. Concert of angels, detail from fresco by Gaudenzio Ferrari, Santa Maria dei Miracoli Saronno, c1535
15. Day of Judgment, Michelangelo Buonarroti, c1535; The fresco adorning the Sistine Chapel was completed around the time that Arcadelt composed the "Salve Regina," and perhaps conducted its performance; "Salve Regina" is a song imploring the Virgin Mary to intercede in this life as well as in the next and, most of all, at the end of time.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous French et al.: Ces facheux (c.1520-1545)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous French et al.: Ces facheux (c.1520-1545)
localized.description:
Ces facheux sotz

  0:06  Original 4 part chanson (ATTB)
  1:10  Lute reduction by Pierre Phalèse
  2:07  Si placet variant (recorder, lute, harp, viol)

This light and spirited chanson is based on a love poem by an anonymous French poet likely from the late 15th Century. I have chosen three different arrangements (including a lute reduction by Pierre Phalèse).

The MIDI file for the lute reduction was created and uploaded by Serge Gerbode for his website lutemusic.org. The vocal realization was created using the MAIKA Spanish language voice bank for Vocaloid. The instrumental variant was created using Music Studio 2, an iPhone app. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, added some natural dynamics, rebalanced the voices, altered the reverb & echo, corrected some misspellings from the original score and adjusted some Vocaloid phoneme presets.

Text (and translation):

Ces facheux sotz (These regrettable fools)
qui mesdisant d'aymer (who slander love)
et n'en eurent de leur (and had none from their)
vie cognoissance (life knowledge)
je vous jure dieu et ma conscience (I swear to God and my conscience)
quils ont grant tort (that they are greatly mistaken)
dung tel plaisir blasmer (to place blame on such pleasure)

Description of the photos:

1. Discantus part from "Ces facheux," Det Kongelige Bibliotek Samling 1848, c1525
2. Detail of Musicians in the Garden of Pleasure, Roman de la Rose, Harley MS 4425
3. Lute intabulation of "Ces facheux" from Des chansons reduictz en tabulature de lut, Pierre Phalèse, 1546
4. Detail of a female lute player from Prodigal Son, Anonymous Franco-Flemish, c1550
5. Courtly musicians with audience, Niccolò dell'Abbate (School of Fontainbleau), c1550
6. Female musicians, Master of the Half Lengths, c1540

videos.title: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina: Salvatorem expectamus (c.1585)

localized.title: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina: Salvatorem expectamus (c.1585)
localized.description:
This short responsory for the Festival of the Annunciation was produced by the maestro of the Papal Choir, Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, and not by Gregorio Allegri (Palestrina's student) as has been presumed due to a misattribution in the late 18th Century by a French copyist. There is one surviving "original" manuscript which contains this piece in the Vatican Library which was likely compiled towards the end of (or even after) Palestrina's very long career in Rome. The earliest manuscript source of this piece is MS Cappella Sistina 72 which was compiled in the late 16th Century (when Allegri was still a very young child).

Six-part polyphony with a SSATTB ensemble was typical for Palestrina who wrote many of his masses using that specific vocal combination. As is typical of the master, there are many passages in this motet where there is a more or less vertical alignment of the voices with clear enunciation of text as was demanded by the Counter Reformation papacy.

I downloaded the MIDI file compiled by Wim Looyestijn from CPDL.org. I used the Spanish language Vocaloid Maika for the chorus and applied reverb & echo with Audacity. The pitch has been elevated by a whole tone from the original score to capture the range of boy sopranos which were regularly employed in Vatican services.

Text:

Salvatorem expectamus Dominum Jesum Christum,
qui reformabit corpus humilitatis nostrae,
configuratum corpori claritatis suae.

Translation:

We await the savior, our lord Jesus Christ
who changes our humble body,
conforming to the body of his luminescence.

Description of the photos:

1. Sistine Chapel Choir, Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres, 1848; this work is based on an early painting by Agostino Tassi, early 17th Century
2. The Annunciation of the Virgin Mary, Giovanni Lanfranco, c1620
3. Choir gallery in the Sistine Chapel with the grand golden music stand
4. The angel Gabriel, Annibale Carracci, c1600
5. Ecstasy of Santa Cecilia, Bernardo Cavallino, 1645

videos.title: [New Rendition] Juan de Anchieta: Con amores la mi madre (c.1500)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Juan de Anchieta: Con amores la mi madre (c.1500)
localized.description:
Con amores, la mi madre

  0:06  Original villancico (ATTB)
  2:25  Instrumental arrangement (flute, lute, harp, viol)

This villancico by the Basque-Spanish composer Juan de Anchieta has an overall homophonic structure with no imitative lines among the voices. Its steady and rich harmonies anticipate the Italo-Iberian madrigal style of later generations. It is unusual that the work is written in a 5 rhythm. Perhaps it was something Anchieta borrowed from Basque folk music. Unlike other contemporary works, the central figure of the piece seems intentionally ambiguous with regard to gender.

The voice simulations were created using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid. The instrumental sounds were generated using Music Studio 2. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, added natural dynamics, rebalanced the voices, slowed the tempo and corrected some of the phonemes.

Text (and translation)

1. Con amores, la mi madre (With all this love, my mother)
con amores m'adormi (with all this love I went to sleep)
Asi dormida soñava (Thus sleeping, I dreamt)
lo que'l coraçon velava (what the heart observed)
que'l amor me consolava (because love consoled me)
con mas bien que mereçi (with more than I deserved)

2. Con amores, la mi madre (With all this love, my mother)
con amores m'adormi (with all this love I went to sleep)
Adormaciome el favor (Let me sleep)
que amor me dio con amor (that love gave me so lovingly)
dio descanso a mi dolor (It gave rest to my pain)
la fe con que le servi (for the loyalty with which I served love)

Description of the photos:

1. "Con amores mi madre" 1st line of the cantus, Juan de Anchieta, Cancionero de Palacio, c1500
2. Alhambra in Granada, the pleasure palace of the Spanish kings conquered and occupied by Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand in 1492 from the last Nasrid rulers.
3. Concert with singers and lute, Lorenzo Costa, c1490
4. Garden of Alhambra, a probable venue for de Anchieta who provided entertainment to the royal court.
5. "Con amores mi madre" complete score (with the 2nd set of lyrics annotated at the side), Juan de Anchieta, Cancionero de Palacio, c1500
5. Angel playing flute, detail from Madonna and Child, Bernardo Luini, c1520
6. Musicians at the Temple of King David, Queen Isabella's Breviary, illuminated by an anonymous Franco-Flemish artist before 1495

videos.title: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina: Jubilate Deo a 5 (1593), a motet for Epiphany

localized.title: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina: Jubilate Deo a 5 (1593), a motet for Epiphany
localized.description:
This short motet for Epiphany (commemorating the visitation of the Magi to the baby Jesus) was one of a large collection of works compiled near the end of Palestrina's life. Known as the Offertoria, the archive contains 65 unique compositions signifying the festival days of the Catholic liturgical calendar. Palestrina created several settings of "Jubilate Deo" during his lifetime starting with two (one for 5 voices and another for 8) in a 1575 publication (Third Book of Motets).

I used a MIDI file compiled and uploaded to CPDL.org by Pothárn Imre. I applied the MAIKA Spanish language voice bank for the 5 vocal parts and converted the pronunciation of phonemes to mimic a more Italian accent. I added reverb and echo with Audacity.

Text and translation:

Jubilate Deo, omnis terra; (Rejoice in God, all the land)
  servite Domino in lætitia. (serve the Lord happily)
Intrate in conspectu (and come before)
  eius in exsultatione, (him in exultation)
  quia Dominus ipse est Deus. (because the Lord is God)

Description of the photos:

1. Saint Peter's Basilica alter, a place of familiarity to Palestrina who spent most of his carrier directing the Papal Choir or composing music for the Vatican audience.
2. Adoration of the Magi, Giorgio Vasari, 1566
3. Baldacchino, St. Peter's Basilica, Wikimedia on Pixabay
4. Adoration of the Magi, Scarsellino, c1575
5. Central dome of St. Peter's, Glavo on Pixabay

videos.title: Heinrich Isaac: Ach was will doch mein hertz (c.1500)

localized.title: Heinrich Isaac: Ach was will doch mein hertz (c.1500)
localized.description:
Most likely, Isaac composed this German language Lied either during his tenure at the Viennese court of Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I or his many journeys to the Bavarian city-states.  In its entirety, the song is a courtly romance about a woman and spans 3 verses (of which this is the first). However, only the 1st verse is written out in Johannes Ott's collection (1544), the edition that I used for this soundtrack.

The vocals were generated using MAIKA, a Spanish language Vocaloid. The reverb and echo were added using Audacity. I added trills to the "r" in deference to the Southern German dialects.

Text:

Ach was will doch mein hertz damit.
Kleglicher bitt ruff ich und schrei,
dabei mich hart betrübt und übt
mein gmüt durch schwers verlangen.

Allein so ich der zeit gedenk,
mich hart bekrenck nach solcher freud
und meid meins hertzen gir,
in mir ist all kürtzweil vergangen.

Seid ich mein lust an liebes brust
nit büssen mag. Das klag ich.
Wenn was mein hertz
het freud und schertz ein kurtze nacht
hat bracht der tag mir als zu sorgen.

Translation:

Oh, what does my heart want with that?
I call out and cry out a pitiful request,
grieving hard though offering
my kindness for difficult demands.

But when I think of that time,
striving hard for such joy
and put aside my heart,
everything has recently passed by me.

Since I don't want to atone
for the desire of my dear breast. I complain about that.
When my heart has a short night of joy and jokes,
the day brings me more worries.

Description of the photos:

1. Score for the Discantus, Heinrich Isaac, editor Johannes Ott, 1544
2. Wooden sculpture of a young lady, Anonymous Lower Rhine, c1530
3. A choir overseen by Isaac and Senfl at the court of Emperor Maximilian I, Hans Burgkmair, 1526
4. Bust of a young man, Anonymous Flemish, Metropolitan Museum NYC, c1510
5. Garden of Pleasure with Maximilian and Maria of Burgundy at the fore, British Library Harley MS 4425, c1490
6. Isaac portrait, detail from #3 above.

videos.title: Gabriel Mena: No puede el que os ha mirado (c.1497)

localized.title: Gabriel Mena: No puede el que os ha mirado (c.1497)
localized.description:
Gabriel Mena: No puede el que os ha mirado

  0:06  Original villancico for ATTB
  1:35  Instrumental arrangement (4 viols)

This short villancico by the poet and court composer Gabriel Mena is another small treasure scribbled as an afterthought in the margins of the vast collection of Spanish tunes, El Cancionero Musical de Palacio. Mena was likely one of the latest composers to have been represented in this great tome.

The original score and MIDI file for this piece were transcribed into digital format by Bojopigeon and uploaded to musescore.com. I added the text underlay to the other 3 voices and converted the MIDI into simulated male voices using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid. The viol sounds were generated using Music Studio 2.0, and iPhone app.

Text (and Translation)

No puede el que os ha mirado (He who has seen you)
vivir con vos engañado. (Cannot live deceived about you.)

Mirar vuestra hermosura (To see your beauty)
Ha sido tan gran ventura, (has been such great fortune)

que qualquier mal ó tristura (that whatever is bad or sad)
que venga es bien empleado. (which comes [my way] has been well spent)

Description of the photos:

1. "No puede el que os ha mirado," original score for all 4 voices inserted into the corner of a page at a later time, Gabriel Mena (?), Cancionero de Palacio
2. Leda and the Swan, Ghirlandaio, Michele Tosini, c1565
3. Vous ou Mort (You or Death), Anon. Franco-Flemish, Brit. Museum, c1470
4. Nasrid columns, Alhambra Palace.
5. The Triumph of Venus, Palazzo Schifanoia, Francesco del Cossa, c1470

videos.title: [New Rendition] Henry VIII: Thow that men do call it dotage (c.1510)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Henry VIII: Thow that men do call it dotage (c.1510)
localized.description:
Unlike the bombastic rowdiness of "Pastyme with good companye," this rather slow and plaintive song by King Henry VIII is aligned more with the centuries-old tradition of courtly love as it was expressed among literate noblemen of late Medieval Europe. The poetry is more nuanced than the music itself, which is quite simple and basic. Most of King Henry's compositions come to us from his early years as the newly anointed English monarch (c.1510-1514) during a time of celebration and optimism at the royal court. Nearly all of his works are contained in the collection known as British Library Addendum 31922 (a.k.a. Henry VIII's Songbook).

In this latest rendition, I rendered all 3 voice parts using male "singers" impersonated by the English language Vocaloid, Cyber Songman. I created a more legato effect in all the parts, added natural dynamics, corrected some of the Early Modern English pronunciations, made a more expansive sound and added a metal-strung lute (a cittern) pattern to the instrumental group. Also, accompanying the solo alto are viols and sackbuts.

Original text (with the modern English):

Thow that men do call it dotage. (Though that men do call it dotage)
who louyth not wantith corage (Who loves, not wants, courage.)
And who so euer may loue gete. (And whosoever may love get)
Frome venus sure he must it fett. (From Venus surely he must it fetch)
Or elles from her which is her hayre. (Or else from her which is her heir.)
& she to hym most seme most fayre. (& she to him must seem most fair.)
Wyth ee and mynd doth both agre. (With eye and mind do both agree)
There is no bote. ther must it be (There is no but -- there must it be!)
The ee doth loke and represent. (The eye does look and represent,)
But mynd afformyth with full consent. (But mind affirms with full consent.)
Thus I am fyxed with owt gruge, (Thus am I fixed without grudge:)
Myne ey with hart doth me so Iuge. (My eye with heart does judge me so.)
loue maynteynyth all noble courage. (Love maintains all noble courage.)
who loue dysdaynyth ys all of the village (Who love disdains is all the village)
Soch louers though thay take payne. (Such lovers, though they take pain,)
It were pete thay shuld optayne. (It were pity they should obtain.)
For often tymes wher they do sewe. (For often times where they do sue)
Thay hynder louers that wolde be trew. (They hinder lovers that be true.)
For who so louith shuld loue butt oone. (For who loves should love one.)
Chaunge who so wyll I wyll be none. (Change who so will, I will be none.)

Description of the photos:

1. "Thow that men do call it dotage," score for ATB, composed by King Henry, Henry VIII Songbook (Brit. Lib. Add. MS 31922)
2. The royal lion, Hampton Court Palace gateway
3. "HK" initials of "Henry, King" (or perhaps Henry and Katherine) forming a golden band on his armor, c1515
4. Amour overshadowing an uncertain lover, Roman de la Rose, Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun, British Library Harley 4425, c1490
5. A royal feast with musicians, Anon. French tapestry commissioned by Henry VIII, Great Hall, Hampton Court Palace, 
6. A gallant knight presenting himself before the goddess Venus, Roman de la Rose, Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun, British Library Harley 4425, c1490
7. The younger more contemplative King Henry VIII, c1509
8. "Thow that men do call it dotage," the 9 additional couplets of the complete poem by Henry VIII

videos.title: [New Rendition] John Taverner: Benedictus from "Gloria tibi Trinitas" (c. 1520)

localized.title: [New Rendition] John Taverner: Benedictus from "Gloria tibi Trinitas" (c. 1520)
localized.description:
"In Nomine" was the most widely parodied tune in 16th Century England. It evolved from a short segment of the Benedictus from John Taverner's Missa Gloria tibi Trinitas. Although copied during the Elizabethan period, the original composition was likely written by a still Catholic leaning Taverner in the reign of King Henry VIII before the Dissolution of the Monasteries. To date, there are more than 150 surviving parodies of the "In Nomine" ranging from William Byrd all the way through the early 21th Century. One can hear a compositional style reminiscent of late 15th century and early 16th English repertoire with its high sopranos, complex imitative polyphonies and very long, meandering melismas. The original Plainchant "Gloria tibi trinitas aequalis una deitas et ante omnia saecula" appears as a recurrent cantus firmus melody throughout the mass, but most prominently in the altus and tenor of the Benedictus. The piece begins somberly in the lowest 3 voices (Tenor 2, Bass 1 and Bass 2) sustaining a steady and mystery-laden passage on the words "Benedictus qui venit." (Blessed is he who comes). Then suddenly the darkness is shattered by the outer voices (Cantus, Altus, Tenor 1, Bass 2) on the words "IN NOMINE DOMINI" or "In the name of the Lord". Then finally, a dramatic conclusion is gloriously realized by the full choir (CATTBB) singing "Osanna in excelsis." (Hosanna in the highest.)  This gradual buildup to a grand choral finale was fairly commonplace in this period as can be heard in William Mundy's "Vox patris." ( https://youtu.be/K6uuWhhQtOQ )

I compiled the MIDI file myself. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, corrected some of the pronunciation, added natural dynamics and rebalanced the voices. I used the MAIKA Spanish Vocaloid in all 4 voice parts, but I altered some of the phonemes to imitate Anglicized Latin.

Description of the photos:

1. Christ Church Cathedral, Oxford, where Taverner was employed during this period
2. Superius part from the Benedictus movement of the Missa Gloria tibi Trinitas, John Taverner, Baldwin Partbooks, MS 979, copied c1575
3. Latticed ceiling of Christ Church, Oxford
4. Christ Church Cathedral, choir
5. Hampton Court Palace, Henry VIII's pleasure palace, where Taverner may have conducted some of his later church music
6. "Gloria tibi Trinitas," plainchant, MS 30, Abbey St Lambrecht, Steiermark, Austria, 14th Century
7. Hampton Court Palace Chapel choir at sunset.

videos.title: Ivan Garcia-Garcia / Guillaume de Machaut: Chanson d'amour (Ce qui soustient moy) (2021)

localized.title: Ivan Garcia-Garcia / Guillaume de Machaut: Chanson d'amour (Ce qui soustient moy) (2021)
localized.description:
Ivan Garcia-Garcia / Guillaume de Machaut: Chanson d'amour (2021)

"Chanson d'amour" is Garcia-Garcia's modern take on a medieval rondeau of the same title "Ce qui soustient moy" (but with an altogether different tune) by the master of 14th Century French polyphony, Guillaume de Machaut (c.1300-1377). This modern piece by Ivan Garcia-G uses Machaut's lyrics and incorporates several elements of French Ars Nova repertoire: 6/8 meter, long melismas, single syllables broken up by one note rests, pre-1450 cadences, etc. Ivan's music has a more melodic quality that is perhaps more comfortable to our modern sensibilities than Machaut's. He originally scored the music for recorder, voice and lute and generously uploaded his MIDI and pdf score to musescore.com. 

For the full score: 

https://musescore.com/user/31566834/scores/6866952

The lute part is written out with completed chords. Because early 14th Century music did not yet have a system of tablature notation for plucked instruments, chords were likely improvised by medieval lutenists according to now lost rules of performance.

Garcia-G's own MIDI interpretation of this piece can be found here:

https://youtu.be/E1jkSNlXbl8?si=cDODmNzXXEami9TN

I have used the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid to simulate Middle French pronunciation. I applied the pronunciation scheme recommended by Timothy McGee in "Singing Early Music" as well as the polyglot website Wiktionary. I added the sound of a metal-strung medieval lute and recorder using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 from Steinberg.

Text:

Ce qui soustient moy, m'onneur et ma vie
Aveuc Amours, c'estes vous, douce dame.

Long, près, toudis serez, quoy que nuls die,
Ce qui soustient moy m'onneur et ma vie.

Et quant je vif par vous anemie,
Qu'aim miex que moy, bien dire doy, par m'ame:
"Ce qui soustient moy, m'onneur et ma vie
Avec Amours, c'estes vous, douce dame."

Translation:

That which sustains me, my honor and my life,
with Love — it is you, sweet lady.

Far, near, all this will be, no matter what they say,
That which sustains me, my honor and my life,

And when I live, quickened by you
who loves better than I, I should well say, by my soul:
“That which sustains me, my honor...

videos.title: [New Rendition] Loyset Compère: Magnificat sexti toni (c.1480)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Loyset Compère: Magnificat sexti toni (c.1480)
localized.description:
As mentioned in Josquin Desprez's Lamentation on the Death of Johannes Ockeghem, Loyset Compère was one of several leading composers inspired and possibly trained by the great Flemish master. There are two surviving Magnificats by Compère; both likely composed during his tenure in Milan (but published much later). The particular Marian antiphon on this soundtrack has many similarities to the works of his better known contemporary, Josquin des Prez. The frenetic canon between the middle voices is reminiscent of Josquin's 4-part figuration of the chanson "De tous biens plaine" with two tenors in canon with one tenor in close pursuit of the other.  The duet of the cantus and tenor followed by the pairing of the countertenor and bass in the last verse is instead reminiscent of another Marian motet by Josquin, the "Ave Maria gratia plenia" for 4 voices. The skill required to perform a work like this would have required considerable nimbleness and experience. Such virtuosic performances were probably commonplace for the world class choir in service of Compère's patron, Galeazzo Maria Sforza, Duke of Milan (1466-1476).

I used a MIDI file compiled by John Hetland and upoaded to the website cpdl.org . I added the Latin text using the MAIKA Vocaloid, a Spanish language voice bank. In this latest rendition, I corrected the pronunciation (from French to Italian Ecclesiastic Latin), created a more legato effect, adjusted the relative tempi of both the plainchant and the choruses, added natural dynamics to the voices and rebalanced the voices. 

Text:

Magnificat, anima mea, Dominum
et exultavit spiritus meus in Deo, salutari meo.
Quia respexit humilitatem ancillæ suæ:
ecce enim ex hoc beatam me dicent omnes generationes.
Quia fecit mihi magna, qui potens est, et sanctum nomen eius,
et misericordia eius a progenie in progenies timentibus eum.
Fecit potentiam in brachio suo,
dispersit superbos mente cordis sui.
Deposuit potentes de sede et exaltavit humiles;
esurientes implevit bonis et divites dimisit inanes.
Suscepit Israel puerum suum recordatus misericordiæ suæ,
sicut locutus est ad patres nostros, Abraham et semini eius in sæcula.
Gloria Patri, et Filio, et Spiritui Sancto:
Sicut erat in principio, et nunc, et semper, et in sæcula sæculorum. Amen.

Translation:

My soul magnifies the Lord.
And my spirit has rejoiced in God my salvation.
For he has respects the lowliness of his handmaiden:
Behold, from now, all generations shall call me blessed.
For he who is almight has made me great: and holy is his Name.
And his mercy is for them who fear him: to all future progency.
He has shown his strength with his arm:
he has disposed of the proud in the imagination of their hearts.
He has pulled down the mighty from their seat:
and raised the humble.
He has filled the hungry with good things:
and the rich he has sent away with emptiness.
Remembering his mercy has sustains the children of Israel:
As he promised to our forefathers, Abraham and his seed for ever.

Glory be to the Father, and to the Son: and to the Holy Ghost;
As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be: world without end. Amen

videos.title: William Newark: Thus musyng in my mynd (c.1480) (Original Pronunciation)

localized.title: William Newark: Thus musyng in my mynd (c.1480) (Original Pronunciation)
localized.description:
William Newark was one of the earliest composers associated with the Tudor court. He was the master of music for King Henry VII (the first Tudor monarch) and was briefly rehired by King Henry VIII. He was both court musician and director of the Chapel Royal choirboys.

This unusual piece was likely an early work of Newark's with its free-style melodic line and complex imitative polyphony. It includes long melismas that are infused with sudden transitions into triplet rhythm (interestingly on the phrase "so sodenly will chaunge"). Similar passages appear in the English repertoire throughout the second half of the 15th Century.

I used the MIDI file compiled by Bojopigeon. The pdf score can be found on Musescore.com. I used the PRIMA V2 and Cyber Songman Vocaloids to simulate the superius, altus and tenor voices. The instrumental sounds of 2 lutes and harp were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0.

Original text (and Modern English interpretation):

Thus musying in my mynd (Thusly I turn it over in my mind)
gretly marvelying (marveling so much)
hougheuyr such dyversyte (how, such transformation)
in on person may be (can come over one individual)
so goodly, so curtesly, so gentill ([One moment], so good, courteous, gentle)
in behavying (in demeanor)
and so sodenly will chaunge (so suddenly changes)
in euery degre (in every way)
As solen as stately as strange (and becomes sullen, arrogant and bizarre)
toward me (towards me)
as I of aquayntance (as I knew [her])
had nevyr byn a fore (had never been before)
wher fore I hope to fynde (I hope to find)
to fynd a speciall remedy (a special fix)
to itt ouyr pass (so that it passes)
and thynk there on no more (and I no longer contemplate this matter)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous Spanish: Harto de tanta porfia (c.1470)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous Spanish: Harto de tanta porfia (c.1470)
localized.description:
Most likely composed by a Franco-Burgundian or a Flemish influenced Spaniard at the court of Castile, this villancico appears prominently in the first few pages of Cancionero Musical de Palacio. It is likely one of the earlier compositions included in this vast collection of Spanish language repertoire. It is more characteristic of late Medieval music rather than Renaissance with its use of imitative lines instead of homophonic, chordal progressions of later villancicos, its reliance on very long melismata and the frequent appearance of open fifths and octaves at cadences. The lyrics were supposedly written by Íñigo López de Mendoza, 1st Marquis of Santillana and poet, who was active at the court of Juan II de Castilla around 1450.

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, added some natural dynamics, corrected a few phonemes, adjusted the reverb & echo, inserted a few pauses and rebalanced the voices. The vocals were generated using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid and the instrumentals were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. The score was was copied and uploaded to cipoo.net by Marco Gallo.

++++++++++

Text (and translation)

Harto de tanta porfia (Weary of so much obstinacy)
sostengo bevir tan fuerte (to live, I remain so strong)
qu’es triste el ánima mia (how sad is my soul)
fasta que venga la muerte (until death comes)

En tus manos la mi vida (In your hands, my life)
encomiendo, condenado. (I entrust, condemned)
Ten piedad merecida  (give me well-deserved mercy)
por que m’has desamparado. (for you have abandoned me.)

Fin hara la profecia (The prophesy shall be) 
dada por mi mala suerte (about my bad destiny)
qu’es triste el ánima mia (how sad is my soul)
fasta que venga la muerte (until death comes)
