videos.title: Henry VIII: Quam pulchra es et quam decora (c.1530)

localized.title: Henry VIII: Quam pulchra es et quam decora (c.1530)
localized.description:
Before King Henry VIII gained his notoriety as a murderous tyrant and serial womanizer, he had also been described as a polyglot, a musician, a composer and a man of letters.  This motet for 3 male voices, Henry's only surviving religious work, survives in the Baldwin Commonplace Book, a late 16th Century manuscript dedicated almost entirely to the great Elizabethan composers: William Byrd, William Mundy, Thomas Tallis, Christopher Tye and Robert Parsons.

Its primitive counterpoint and meandering melismata harkens back to the English composers of the previous century, John Plummer and John Dunstable (who also created a setting of "Quam pulchra es et quam decora" for 3 voices). The melody is adapted from a plainchant of the same title. There are brief segments when all 3 voices sing in close imitation and other segments in which 2 of the 3 voices pair off in duet. No one has been able to prove its true purpose and origin, but given the tender, intimate theme from the Song of Songs, it may have been Henry's appeal to Anne Boleyn (who seems to have had a fondness for church music) prior to their marriage in 1532/1533.

Text:

Quam pulchra es et quam decora carissima in deliciis (tuis)
Statura tua assimilata est palmæ, et ubera tua botris
Caput tuum ut carmelus.
Collum tuum sicut turris eburnea.
Veni dilecte mi; egrediamur in agrum(/hortum)
Et videamus si flores fructus parturiunt,
si floruerunt mala punica. Ibi dabo tibi ubera mea.

Translation from Myles Coverdale, 1535

O How fair and lovely art thou, my darling, in (your) pleasures?
Thy stature is like a date tree, and thy breasts like the grapes.
The head that standeth upon thee is like Carmel
Thy neck is as it were a tower of ivory
O come on my love, let us go forth in to the field(/garden)
and go see if the grapes be grown
and if the pomegranates be shot out.
There will I give thee my breasts.

videos.title: Gabriel Mena: La bella mal maridada (c.1500)

localized.title: Gabriel Mena: La bella mal maridada (c.1500)
localized.description:
La bella mal maridada

  0:06  Verse 1 (ATTB)
  2:00  Verse 2 (Tenor on cantus firmus, recorder, lute, harp, viol)
  3:55  Verse 3 (Alto, lute, harp, viol)

This villancico from the Cancionero de Palacio is a courtly love song that harkens back to the leitmotif of Petrarch who pined away endlessly yearning for a married woman, Laura. This work comes from Gabriel Mena who was court singer and composer serving King Fernando II de Aragón (although he likely also served Isabel I and Fernando I in his younger days). The score was copied somewhat sloppily by an anonymous copyist and is difficult to read; it was likely an archival copy rather than a performance edition.

The MIDI was generated by Bojopigeon and uploaded to Musescore. I incorporated some of the suggested text underlay for the superius line from Bojopigeon, but I made several minor changes and added all the lyrics to the other 3 vocal parts. I used the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid for the voices and the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 for the instrumental simulations.

Text (and translation):

La bella malmaridada, (O beautiful one so unhappily married)
de las más lindas que yo vi, (among the most lovely I've beheld)
miémbresete quán amada, (remember how loved)
señora, fuiste de mi. (you were by me, Lady)

Mira cómo por quererte (See how much for loving you)
tienes al cabo mi vida, (you possess at last my life.)
y, si tú fueras servida,  (and if I served you)
dichosa fuera mi suerte. (blessed would be my fortune)
Mas pues no te pena nada  (It does not bother you at all)
quanto yo peno por ti, (how much I pity you)
miémbresete ...

Mirarás qu'en tu serviçio (You see how in your service)
es ya pasada mi vida. (my life has passed)
Siendo tú d'ello servida, (If I served you)
fuere ninguno con beneficio. (no one [else] would benefit)
Mas pues no se te dió nada  (But nothing was given to you)
quanto yo pasé por ti, (of what I offered)
miémbresete ...

¡Triste de ti que padeçes (Sorrow to you who suffers)
mil enojos cada ora, (a thousand strikes every moment)
en poder de quien ynora  (in the power of one who ignores)
lo mucho que tu mereçes! (how much that you deserve)
Tú lloras de malcasada, (You cry from your bad marriage)
yo porque te conocí  (and because I knew you)
Si ás de tener amado, (If you have to take a lover)
señora, tomes a mi. (Lady, take me!)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Mateo Flecha el viejo: Riu riu chiu (1556)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Mateo Flecha el viejo: Riu riu chiu (1556)
localized.description:
Unlikely "Verbum caro factum est," another anonymously composed Christmas carol from the famed Cancionero de Uppsala, "Riu riu chiu" is not based on any liturgical text and was likely intended as a popular song for a wider audiences. Each phrase is short in length, simple in meaning and appropriate even for young children. It is joyful and optimistic both in music and narrative. This villancico is comprised of a simple back and forth exchange between a baritone soloist and the full chorus which repeats the same hymn 8 times. 

I used the MIDI file created by James Gibb which can be found on the website CPDL.org . In this latest rendition, I adjusted the pronunciation of Renaissance Spanish, created a more legato effect, rebalanced the voices, changed the superius to a female alto, changed the instrumentation (plucked strings to crumhorns) and added some natural dynamics.  

Text:

Chorus:
Riu riu chiu, la guarda ribera; (Ríu, ríu, chíu, the river guard [intones])
Dios guardo el lobo de nuestra cordera. (God kept the wolf from our Lamb)

1. El lobo rabioso la quiso morder, (The rabid wolf sought to bite her)
Mas Dios poderoso la supo defender; (But almighty God knew to defend [her])
Quisola hazer que no pudiese pecar, (He made so that she could not sin)
Ni aun original esta Virgen no tuviera. (so that original sin does not touch her)

2. Este qu'es nacido es el gran monarca, (This one who is born is the great king)
Christo patriarca, de carne vestido; (Christ, the Patriarch, clothed in flesh)
hanos redimido con se hacer chiquito, (he redeemed us when he himself a tiny child)
a un qu'era infinito, finito se hiziera. (though he was infinite, he would be finite)

3. Muchas profecias lo han profetizado, (Many prophesies have predicted it)
Ya un nuestros dias lo hemos al consado (and in our days, we have arrived there)
A dios humanado vemos en el suelo, (God made man [so that] we see [him] on earth)
Yal hombre nel cielo porquel le quistera. (and the man in heaven because he loved in)

4. Yo vi mil garzones que andaban cantando, (I saw a thousand boys go singing)
por aquí volando, haciendo mil sones, (while flying here, creating a thousand sounds)
diciendo a gascones: "Gloria sea en el cielo (telling shepherds "Glory be in heaven)
y paz en el suelo", pues de sus nasciera. (and peace on earth," for he is born)

5. Este viene a dar a los muertos vida (This one comes to give life to the dead)
y viene a reparar de todos la caída; (and comes to save all who are fallen)
es la luz del día aqueste mozuelo; (He is the light of the day)
este es el cordero que San Juan dixera. (This is the lamb of which Saint John spoke)

6. Mira bien queos quadre que ansina lo oyera, (Behold with care if one [wants] to hear)
Que Dios no pudiera hacer la mas que madre, (that God can make of her no greater mother)
El quera su padre hoy della nascio (She gives birth to the father)
Y el que la drio su hijo so dixera. (and said he is the son)

7. Pues que ya tenemos lo que deseamos, (We have that which we desire)
todos juntos vamos, presentes llevemos;  (Together we go carrying presents)
todos le daremos muestra voluntad, (We will all give our will [to God])
pues a se igualar con el hombre viniera. (who can come and be one with man)

videos.title: Pierre Certon: En esperant (c.1540)

localized.title: Pierre Certon: En esperant (c.1540)
localized.description:
En esperant je viz en grand langueur

  0:06  Original chanson for 4 (SATB)
  2:44  Instrumental version (recorder, lute, harp, bass viol)

This courtly chanson by the prolific maestro of French secular songs, Pierre Certon, comes from a 1541 collection published by Pierre Attaingnant. Most likely, the music was intended for the royal audience of King Francis I and his retinue. It was not uncommon to perform secular songs as instrumental arrangements during this period.

The original MIDI file and score were created by André Vierendeels and uploaded to CPDL.org. I added the words using the MAIKA Vocaloid and added reverb / echo using Audacity. The instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. Note that the familiar pronunciations and spellings are those of early Modern French.

Text:

En espérant je viz en grand langueur,
en languissant, je meurs de desplaisir.
Car en t'aymant, on a de toy rigueur.
Et qui te hayt, de toy reçoit plaisir.
Ainsy convient pour le meilleur choisir:
que je te haye en faisant mon debvoir,
et sans toy aucune amour avoir,
pour estre aymé et vivre à mon désir.

Translation:

In hoping, I live in endless languor,
In languishing, I die of displeasure.
Because in loving you, we have harshness from you,
While he who hates you, receives pleasure from you.
So it is suitable to choose the best
that I hate you doing what I must,
and without having any love for you,
To be loved and live to my desire.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Alessandro Striggio: Arse cosi per voi (1560)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Alessandro Striggio: Arse cosi per voi (1560)
localized.description:
Arse cosi per voi

  0:06  Original madrigal for 5 voices (SSATB)
  1:58  Instrumental arrangement for 2 soprano recorders, lute, harp, bass viol

Alessandro Striggio made his mark in the midst of the Italian High Renaissance, between the earlier Franco-Flemish innovators like Adrian Willaert and the later native composers like Giovanni Gabrieli, Pierluigi da Palestrina and Luca Marenzio. In the frenetically imitative back and forth between the 5 voice parts, one can anticipate Thomas Morley's Italianate madrigals and caccia in faraway England. Striggio is best remembered for his titanic 40 part motet "Ecce beatam lucem" to which Tallis' 40 part motet "Spem in alium" may have been a competitive response.

I used a MIDI file compiled and uploaded to CPDL.org by Renato Calcaterra.  I added text using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid. The instrumental simulations were generated with the Music Studio 2 app on the iPhone. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato line, added a more prominent reverb / echo effect, rebalanced the voices, changed the cantus to a female vocal, corrected some vowel sounds and added some natural dynamics.

Text (and translation):

Arse così per voi donna'l mio core (My heart burns like this for you Lady)
Il primo di' ch'intento vi mirai (whose first intention is to admire you)
Che certo mi pensai (I thought that certainly)
Che non potess'in me crescer più ardore (I could not increase passion even more)
Ma'in voi beltà crescendo d'hor'in hora (but your beauty grows hour by hour)

videos.title: [New Rendition] John Taverner: Kyrie Leroy (c.1520)

localized.title: [New Rendition] John Taverner: Kyrie Leroy (c.1520)
localized.description:
The Leroy Kyrie was copied by hand long after Taverner's death. It is a stand alone Kyrie unattached to any other known mass movements.  Most likely it was used an introit to a pre-Protestant mass in Henry VIII's time or during Mary I's reign. It has the qualities of early Renaissance / late Medieval Anglo-Catholic church music from the period of the Eton Choirbook -- in particular, the extremely long melismata, the boy soprano part and the open intervals of fifths and octaves. The title "Leroy" may refer to either a royal composer who wrote a secular song (on which the Kyrie may be based), or it was a dedication to Henry VIII who was one of Taverner's allies.

In this latest rendition, I shifted the pitch up half a step to conform to early Tudor choirs that regularly employed high boy sopranos. I also created a more legato effect, added "natural" dynamics in all the voices, adjusted the reverb / echo, slowed the tempo and rebalanced the voices.

1. "Kyrie Leroy" Cantus ("Triplex") part, John Taverner, Gyffard MS, copied c1570
2. Christ Church Cathedral interior, Oxford; one of the most likely venues for Taverner's church music during his early tenure as Cardinal Wolsey's chapel musician.
3. Choir and choirmaster situated around a large music stand, Book of Hours, Anon. French, NYPL, c1450; probably this was the basic spatial arrangement for all church choristers in the Tudor period.
4. Christ Church Cathedral ceiling
5. 14th Century stained glass window commemorating the murder of Thomas Beckett by the soldiers of King Henry II, one of the few works of art that ironically survived the purge of Catholic symbols during Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries; this historic event was probably a point of reference for Taverner who witnessed the destruction of this and other churches in southern England. He was likely familiar with this window and its historical significance.
6. Christ Church Cathedral, Oxford, England.

videos.title: Nicola Matteis: 3 movements from Ayrs for the Violin, 1st Part (1676)

localized.title: Nicola Matteis: 3 movements from Ayrs for the Violin, 1st Part (1676)
localized.description:
3 movements from Ayrs for the Violin

  0:06  Alemanda (violin, cello, harpsichord)
  4:02  Aria: Allegro (violin, cello, chitarrone)
  5:20  Aria: Gavotta (violin, cello, chitarrone)

Nicola Matteis was one of the earliest Italian violinists to have made a career in London. On the cover page of one of his published works, he describes himself as the Neapolitan ("Napolitano"). Some scholars regard him as the composer who shifted the English school away from the formal, French style of the Versailles court towards a more casual and free style of Italian chamber music. These short pieces are similar to the later, more developed, trio sonatas of Arcangelo Corelli and Antonio Vivaldi. The four volumes of the Ayrs for Violin are as much a compilation of music as it is a pedagogical tool for informing the public about performance practices of the period. For example, the dynamics, trills and slurs are all precisely notated.

I obtained the original MIDI files from Bojopigeon's uploads at Musescore.com. I adjusted some of the trills and added additional continuo instruments.

videos.title: Henry Purcell: Fairy Queen. Act III: If loves a sweet passion & Symphonia (1692)

localized.title: Henry Purcell: Fairy Queen. Act III: If loves a sweet passion & Symphonia (1692)
localized.description:
Fairy Queen Act III

  0:06 If love's a sweet passion (Prelude, Aria and Chorus)
  2:19 Symphony while the Swans come forward

This short excerpt from Purcell's Fairy Queen is the introduction to Act III, also named "Bottom's masque." The semi-opera, which likely was a celebratory work marking the 15th wedding anniversary of co-regents Mary II and William, was inspired by Shakespeare's Midsummer Night's Dream. However, the plot line (like in the earlier Purcell opera, King Arthur) was completely transformed into a lighter, more farcical production even by the standards of Shakespearian comedy. In this part of the performance, Titania (the Fairy Queen), upon whom a spell was cast by an angry Oberon (the Fairy King) and causes her to fall in love with the first creature she encounters, Bottom (a human transformed into a donkey). The events all take place in an enchanted forest of magic and fantasy.

For the vocals, I used the Prima V2 Vocaloid for the soprano solo. For the chorus, I used Prima V2 and Avanna for the soprano and Cyber Songman for the male parts. As always, I used Music Studio 2.0 (iPhone app) for the instrumental parts. The MIDI was reconstructed from a piano reduction by the Ukrainian transcriptionist Ihor Oliukha and an early 20th Century score by John South Shedlock. I adjusted the English pronunciation to approximate vowel sounds in the late Restoration Era.

Text:

[Soprano aria]
If Love's a sweet passion, why does it torment
If a bitter, oh tell me whence comes my content
Since I suffer with pleasure, why should I complain
When I know, 'tis in vain?
Yet so pleasing the pain is, so soft is the dart,
That at once it wounds me tinkles my heart.

[Chorus]
I press her hand gently, look languishing down,
And by passionate silence, I make my love known.
But oh, how I'm blest, when so kind she does prove,
By some willing mistake, to discover her love.
When in striving to hide, she reveals all her flame,
And our eyes tell each other, what neither dares name.

8. Portrait of Queen Mary II, c1692

videos.title: [New Rendition] Antoine Brumel / J. Ockeghem: Du tout plongiet / For seulement (c.1490)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Antoine Brumel / J. Ockeghem: Du tout plongiet / For seulement (c.1490)
localized.description:
Du tout plongiet / Fors seulement

This beautifully textured masterpiece by Antoine Brumel (or possibly Alexander Agricola based on the eccentric ornamentation) contains some unusual features for that period. It excludes any soprano or alto parts, and the lowest voice dips to an incredible 2 Cs below middle C).  The score would most aptly fit a TTBB quartet. Additionally, it interweaves two different French tunes into one. The "Du tout plongiet" of Antoine Brumel supplies the outer voices (tenor, baritone and low bass) while the superius from "For seulement,  l'actente que je meure" by Johannes Ockeghem is transposed down an octave plus a whole tone into the second tenor range. As in other parody pieces, this complex work consists of a straightforward cantus firmus line in the middle voice and 3 other lines with intricately ornamented lines. It is reminiscent of Agricola's 6 part version of "Fortuna desperata" or Josquin Desprez's reworking of "De tous biens pleine" for voice and instruments. Although printed in the early decades of the 16th century, the song may have originally been composed in the late 15th century - perhaps before or around the time of Ockeghem's death. Some of the cadential formulas in "Du tout plongiet" were rather "retro" by the 1510s when the earliest copies were made. It also has a rhythm that is highly irregular and unpredictable like some older 15th century works and unlike the later Franco-Flemish works such as Josquin's "In te Domine speravi" or "Mille regretz." 
 
"Du tout plongiet" comes to us from two sources: the exquisite Chansonnier of Margaret of Austria (a.k.a. Bibliothèque royale de Belgique ms 228) and the Basevi Firenze ms 2439. As was common for books gifted to aristocratic patrons, the Brussels ms 228 is one of the most elaborately illuminated manuscripts of the Franco-Flemish Renaissance. 

The French text for this piece was entered using the Vocaloid voice encoding program from Yamaha and the MAIKA voice bank. In this latest rendition, I enhanced the intensity of the voices, adjusted the reverb & echo, created a more legato effect, fixed some of the vowel pronunciations, added some natural dynamics and rebalanced the voices so that highlights from each voice part can be better heard.

French text:

Du tout plongiet au lac de desespoir,
Trouve me suis sans attente n'espoir
D'avoir jamais des biens de Fortune;
Mais, se trouver puis scayson oportune,
Je me assairay d'en quelque chose avoir.

Translation (from David Munrow)

Plunged deep in the lake of despair,
I can neither expect nor hope
ever to enjoy Fortune's gifts.
But if I have the opportunity,
I shall endeavour to enjoy some.

Descriptions of the photos:

1. The superius (Tenor 1) line from "Du tout plongiet", Brumel / Ockeghem, Brussels ms 228
2. You or Death, detail from ornamental shield, c1480
3. The cantus firmus line with the words "For seulement", Brumel / Ockeghem, Brussels ms 228
4. Orfeo playing and singing for the beasts of the forest, Luca della Robbia, c1439
5. Amour and the Lover, from Roman de la Rose, British Library Harley 4425,

videos.title: [New Rendition] Nicolas Gombert: Mille regrets for 6 voices (c.1535)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Nicolas Gombert: Mille regrets for 6 voices (c.1535)
localized.description:
Mille regrets was one of the most popular French chansons of the first half of the 16th century. The earliest version, a piece for 4 voices (ATTB) has been attributed to Josquin des Prez, the most highly regarded of early Renaissance composers. Within two decades of Josquin's death, there were multiple lute reductions (including one by the Spaniard Narvaez), a parody mass for 6 voices (by Cristobal Morales), a pavane (Tielman Susato) and three new chanson realizations (one by Gombert and two by Susato) all with the same title and thematic core. According to the Spanish court lutenist Luys de Narvaez, the original composition by Josquin was one of the favorites of the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V, himself a progeny of the Franco-Flemish homeland and one of the great patrons of early Sixteenth Century music.  Gombert was one of the court musicians of the Emperor for an uncertain period of time. Here is a link to my video containing the original Mille regretz tune: 

https://youtu.be/1kBqQUITU9w

This MIDI file compiled by Brian Russell and uploaded to CPDL.org . I added the French text using the Spanish language voice bank (MAIKA) and the Vocaloid 4 encoder. In this latest rendition, I added some natural dynamics, rebalanced the voices, slowed the tempo, corrected a few vowel sounds, adjusted the reverb / echo, created a more legato effect and clarified the lower voices.

Text:

Mille regretz de vous abandonner (A thousand regrets for parting from you)
Et d'eslonger vostre fache amoureuse, (and leaving your loving face)
Jay si grand dueil et paine douloureuse, (I have great sorrow and pain)
Quon me verra brief mes jours definer. (that it seems my days are finished)

2. The courtyard of the palace of Emperor Charles V, Alhambra, Spain: a possible venue for musical performance in Gombert's time
3. "Mille regretz," cantus part, Josquin des Prez, the original chanson on which Gombert's piece is based.
4. Woodcut of Josquin des Prez, 1611; based on an earlier portrait from the early 16th century that is now lost.
5. Emperor Charles V after the Battle of Mühlberg, Titian, 1548

videos.title: [New Rendition] Juan Vásquez: Que sentis (1560)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Juan Vásquez: Que sentis (1560)
localized.description:
Very little is known about the Spanish Renaissance composer Juan Vásquez despite his large output. He was a member of the choir of Badajoz Cathedral in his youth and, later, its music director. In his last decade of life, he wrote secular music for his patron, the wealthy and powerful Don Antonio de Zuñiga of Seville. His secular villancicos form a collection of mature Renaissance polyphony reminiscent of the works of Cristóbal Morales and Francisco Guerrero.

This soundtrack was created using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid.  I slightly adjusted the preset Castilian phoneme to simulate Spanish pronunciation in the mid-16th century. In this latest rendition, I slowed the tempo, clarified the soprano voice, rebalanced the voices, corrected some vowel sounds, created a more legato effect and added some natural dynamics.

Text:

¿Qué sentís, corazón mío, (How do you feel, my heart)
No decís, (You do not say)
Qué mal es el que sentís? (how bad is it that you feel?)
¿Qué sentistes aquel día (What did you feel that day)
Cuando mi señora vistes, (when you saw my lady)
Que perdistes alegría, (that you lost joy)
y descanso despedistes? (and rest departed)
Como a mí nunca volvistes? (How you never returned to me)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Alexander Agricola: Fortuna desperata a 6 (c.1490)

Alexander Agricola's 6 part realization of Antoine Busnois' famed chanson contains the original 3 vocal parts plus 3 highly ornamented lines likely intended for instruments. The presumed instrumental parts are non-imitative (unlike in Josquin's "Fortuna" arrangement) and intricately polyphonic. Perhaps each singer, whose individual line is simple and familiar, sang while accompanying himself (or herself) with an instrument like a lute or harp.

I used the MAIKA Vocaloid for the 3 voice parts and added the instrumental sounds using Music Studio 2.0, an iPhone MIDI editor. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, corrected some vowel pronunciation, rebalanced the voices, added some natural dynamics and reduced the accents on the leading notes.

Text (& translation):

Fortuna desperata (Desperate fortune)
Iniqua e maledecta, maledecta (wrong and cursed)
Che de tal dona electa (that of such a fine lady)
La fama hai denigrata. (has denigrated her reputation)

O morte dispietata (O ruthless Death)
Inimica e crudele, e crudele (hostile and cruel)
Che d'alto più che stelle (That from a place higher than the stars)
L'hai cusì abassata. (it drops down like this)

Meschino e despietata (Wretched and in despair)
Ben piangere posso may, posso may (I can never cry enough)
Et desiro finire, (And I want to end)

videos.title: Henry Purcell: 2 instrumental selections from Act IV and V of "The Fairy Queen" (1692)

localized.title: Henry Purcell: 2 instrumental selections from Act IV and V of "The Fairy Queen" (1692)

0:06  Symphony & Canzon [Act IV] (trumpets, tympani, strings, basso continuo)
2:06  Chaconne [Act V] (oboe, bassoon, strings, basso continuo)

Henry Purcell (1659-1695) is remembered as one of England's finest composers, alongside William Byrd and Thomas Tallis.  And unlike the German expats who came shortly thereafter (George Frideric Handel and Gottfried Finger), Purcell was a native Englishman. He was a versatile musician: a writer of operas, anthems, chamber works, keyboard solos, etc. He remained current with the innovations on the European Continent, incorporating the grandeur of Louis XIV's French court band as well as the operatic coloratura of the northern Italian singers.  Like Mozart a century later, Purcell began as a child prodigy, and matured into a composer of tremendous output who died young at the age of 36.  

The inspiration for the Fairy Queen was an anonymous re-imagining of William Shakespeare's Midsummer Night's Dream. The music is rather simplistic, but confident and assertive during a period of relative calm in the London music scene. It may have been intended for a royal audience, specifically Queen Mary II and her co-regent William III, on the occasion of their 15th wedding anniversary.

John Adson (c.1587-1640) was an English composer born in the Elizabethan era who lived many years in France serving the Duke of Lorraine, Charles III.  He returned to reside in London but died shortly before the England's Civil War broke out between the Royalists and Parliamentarians.  Almost nothing is known about the details of his life other than his career as a wind player in the Royal Band and Theatre under England's King Charles I. He is remembered mainly for this collection of 5 and 6 part dance music, the Courtly Masquing Ayres, which he published in 1621. Each ayre is a pairing of a movement in a 4 beat followed by a movement in 3 - a juxtaposition based on the pavan-galliard model from a century earlier.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Jacobus Clemens non Papa: Ego flos campi (c.1550)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Jacobus Clemens non Papa: Ego flos campi (c.1550)
localized.description:
This choral masterpiece is based on one of the most beloved love poems from the Song of Songs in the Old Testament. Throughout the 16th Century across Catholic Europe, these romantic Hebrew verses were transformed into countless devotional motets for the Virgin Mary. The richness of sound in Clemens' setting stems from the 7 voices spread out over a wide vocal range. One can hear the evolving polychoral form (familiar to fans of Willaert and the Gabrielis) with an echo between the upper three voices (2 cantus and 1 alto) and the lower four voices (2 tenors and 2 basses). 

In this latest rendition, I rebalanced the voices, added some natural dynamics, created a more legato effect, adjusted the Latin pronunciation to a more French sound (as was the likely norm in Flanders of the mid-16th Century), added some more reverb / echo and generated a softer tone for the boy sopranos.

Text and translation:

Ego flos campi et lilium convallium.
Sicut lilium inter spinas sic amica mea inter filias.
Fons hortorum puteus aquarum viventium quae fluunt impetu de Libano

I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.
As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.
Fountain of gardens, well of living waters and briskly flowing from Lebanon.

videos.title: Gilles Binchois (de Binche): A solis ortus cardine (c.1435), 2 settings for 3 and 4 voices

localized.title: Gilles Binchois (de Binche): A solis ortus cardine (c.1435), 2 settings for 3 and 4 voices
localized.description:
A solis ortus cardine

  0:06  A solis ortus cardine for 4 voices (ATTB)
  1:49  A solis ortus cardine for 3 voices (ATB)

These two vastly different settings by Gilles Binchois (a.k.a. de Binche) were both based on the same Plainchant. Although they were likely composed in the same decade, the four part version on this soundtrack shows a more mature, "Renaissance-like" quality with its imitative polyphony and complex counterpoint. The three part variant is, instead, more "primitive" in certain regards with its homophonic structure, polyrhythms, parallel fourths and stereotypical medieval cadences. Binchois wrote these pieces, probably, during his long tenure at the Burgundian court of Philip the Good (le Bon). The dates for the composition of both these works can be surmised from the approximate dates when they were were copied into two manuscript collections (c.1430-1440). The original chant was written by a 5th century cleric Coelius Sedulius and is perhaps the oldest surviving Christian poem. 

The original MIDI files were created and uploaded to CPDL.org by Brian Russell (3 part setting) and Eric Kaashoek (4 part setting). I added the text using Vocaloid 4 and the Spanish language voice bank Maika. I incorporated the recommended pronunciation of late Medieval French Latin from Tim McGee in his textbook "Singing Early Music." In this latest rendition for the 4 voice setting, I have corrected the vowel sounds, rebalanced the voices, created a more legato effect and improved on the reverb / echo.

Text (and translation):

A solis ortus cardine (From the rising sun)
ad usque terrae limitem (to the ends of the earth)
Christum canamus principem, (We sing of Christ the prince)
natum maria virgine. (born of the Virgin Mary)

videos.title: Jacopo da Bologna: Fenice fu' e vissi (c.1350)

localized.title: Jacopo da Bologna: Fenice fu' e vissi (c.1350)
localized.description:
This medieval "madrigale" is typical of the Italian Trecento with its free style alto and tenor voices chasing after one other - sometimes in imitation and sometimes in hocket form. It was written by the Italian Ars Nova composer Jacopo da Bologna perhaps in the period immediately after the Black Death (1347-1351) during which millions around the world perished.

The phoenix and dove are creatures frequently depicted in Medieval bestiaries. They symbolized resurrection (or hope) and faithfulness, respectively. Perhaps these were vital sentiments among the survivors of the worst natural calamity to visit the human race. It was for their generation a miracle that they lived and loved once more after such a terrible "winter."

Text:

Fenice fu' e vissi pura e morbida,
  Et or son transmutata in una tortora
  Che vollo con Amor per le bell' ortora
Tal vissi e tal me vivo e posso scrivere
  ch'a donna non e piu che onesta vivere
Arbero secco n'acqua torbida
 non me diletta. may per questo dubito
 va nel astate l'inverno ven e subito

Translation:

I was a phoenix and I lived pure and soft,
  and now I am transformed into a turtle dove
  that flies through the beautiful orchard
So I lived and I can write
  that to a woman there is nothing more than to live honestly
Dry trees and turbid water
  do not delight me, but for this doubt
  go in the summer, the winter comes suddenly

1. "Fenice fu' e vissi," Jacopo da Bologna, Squarcialupi Ms., c.1400
2. Phoenix, Livre des proprietés des choses, Bibliothèque Nationale de France, fr. 136, c1450
3. Turtledoves, Livre des proprietés des choses, Bibliothèque Nationale de France, fr. 136, c1450
4. Poesies Jugement du roi de Boheme, Guillaume de Machaut, c1355
5. Angel playing harp, Cathédrale Saint Julien du Mans Fresque, 14th century
6. Stylized portrait of Jacopo da Bologna, Squarcialupi Ms., c.1400

videos.title: [New Rendition] Costanzo Festa: Quando ritrovo (c.1535)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Costanzo Festa: Quando ritrovo (c.1535)
localized.description:
Quando ritrovo, la mia pastorella

  0:06  Original madrigal in 4 parts (ATTB a cappella)
  1:34  Pavana "Quando ritrovo" (shawm, 3 trombones, drum)

Costanzo Festa's secular songs were a transitional form between the frottola (which consisted of multiple repeats in an ABBA format for different sets of lyrics) and the newly developing madrigal (which had a through-composed structure). For example, in this song, there are almost no repeats except in the very short final phrase. This piece is representative of a relatively new theme in popular Italian music that included a flirty, somewhat risqué, conversation between lovers in a pastoral setting as is often graphically depicted in the pastoral paintings of Titian (Tiziano Vecellio) and later Tintoretto. Its light, crude humor is a departure from the bitter and melancholic airs of the the courtly love theme so typical in the previous century. 

In this latest rendition, I switched the soprano and alto lines as was originally intended by the composer. I also created a more legato effect with more open vowel sounds and a better balance of male voices. The vocal simulations were created using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid. The instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0.

Text:

Quando ritrovo la mia pastorella (When I find again my peasant girl)
Al prato con le pecor' in pastura, (Grazing the sheep in the pasture)
Io mi gli accost' e presto la saluto. (I accost her and salute her right away)
La mi risponde "Tu sia el benvenuto" (She responds: "Welcome!")
Et poi gli dic' in quella, "O gentil pastorella, (And then I say "O gentle girl)
Non men crudel che bella, (Not any less cruel than beautiful)
Sei del mio ben ribella;  (You reject my goodwill)
Deh non esser ver me cotanto dura". (Don't be so hard on me")
Così rispond' anch'ella, (She replies like this)
"Disposta son a quel tuo cor desia, ("I am disposed to that which your heart desires)
Ma se non hai denari, va alla tu via. (But if you have no money, be on your way!)"

2. The Three Ages of man. Tiziano Vecellio, c1514
3. Shepherd and Nymph, Tiziano, c1570
4. Gallery musicians, detail of shawms and trombone, Hans Holbein the Younger, c1520

6. Angels playing shawms and trombone, detail from Assumption of the Virgin, Carlos Frei, c1530

videos.title: Heinrich Isaac: Kyrie from "Missa Carminum" (c.1500)

localized.title: Heinrich Isaac: Kyrie from "Missa Carminum" (c.1500)
localized.description:
Kyrie from "Missa Carminum"

  0:06  Kyrie eleison I
  0:45  Christe eleison I
  1:47  Christe eleison II [parody on "Innsbruck"]
  2:37  Kyrie eleison II

Missa Carminum [Song Mass] is a unique parody mass in which each movement derives from a different secular song of Germanic origin. For example, the "Christe eleison II" incorporated one of Isaac's two settings of the Austrian folksong "Innsbruck ich muss dich lassen." (See my earlier upload: https://youtu.be/qwptiRWwSII?si=9Rz5kVM80kP0ptZ-). The original "Innsbruck" Lied was likely dedicated to his patron, Emperor Maximilian I, who hailed from the Alpine city of Innsbruck. It is also quite possible that Isaac performed this piece both at the Imperial court of Vienna as well as at the Basilica Santa Maria del Fiore (in Florence) where he was formerly a singer and later its program director.

I used a MIDI file created by Ulrich Alpers (IMSLP.org). The voice simulations were generated using the MAIKA Vocaloid, and the reverb / echo effects were added using Audacity v.3.3 .

Description of the photos:

1. Kyrie from Missa Carminum, Heinrich Isaac, Universitätsbibliothek Ms 36, Jena, Germany, c1500
2. Emperor Maximilian I at Mass, Hans Weiditz, c1515; note the organ at center left.
3. Santa Maria del Fiore, interior
4. Boys singing in a choir, detail from Cantoria (the organ loft where Isaac may have directed the choir), Luca della Robbia, Santa Maria del Fiore, c1435
5. Dome of Santa Maria del Fiore
6. Il Duomo of Santa Maria del Fiore

videos.title: John Bedingham: Myn hertis lust (c.1450)

localized.title: John Bedingham: Myn hertis lust (c.1450)
localized.description:
The surviving secular compositions by John Bedingham (a.k.a. Bedyngham or Boddenham) appear in the French "Mellon Chansonnier" (Yale-Beinecke Collection MS 91) as well as other Continental chansonniers, but the composer is thought to have lived only in England his whole life. The popularity of this song can be attested to by the number of copies distributed across Europe early in the second half of the 15th Century including Florentine (Florenz 127 & Riccardiana II MS 2356), Neapolitan (Escorial B) and French sources (Chansonnier Pixérécourt). In three of these manuscripts, "Myn hertis lust" is presented as a French chanson "Grand temps ai eu desiree." This song for 3 voices is written for alto, tenor and bass, and the Mellon manuscript also includes the complete lyrics in late Middle English text - a rarity in that period. The theme of this "English chanson" is one of Courtly Love in which a gentleman avidly pursues a lady who does not return his affections. 

The MIDI file from which this soundtrack was rendered comes from the meticulously assembled website of the Japanese early music group Aeolian Consort. I used the Cyber Songman Vocaloid for the 3 male voice part to generate the song and I utilized the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 for the instrumental sounds (plectrum lute, citole and harp). The simulation of Late Middle English is based on recommendations by Timothy McGee in "Singing Early Music." I applied a pronunciation scheme likely used leading up to the Great Vowel Shift of the mid-1400s.

Original text (with Modern English)

Myn hertis lust, sterre of my confort (My heart's desire, star of my comfort)
which is the guide unto my parfaite liffe (which is the way to my perfect life)
Cherati, that welle of pleasaunce and disport (Charity that well of pleasure and entertainment)
Whom that y serve with herte attentiffe (whom I serve with attentive heart)
And sithe for you is my care and striffe (and a sigh for you is my sadness and struggle)
Off womanhede so have upon me routhe (From [your] lady's virtue have pity on me)
Sithe y, pray you, mene veray and trouthe (I sigh, I beg you, by way of reality and truth)

Description of the photos:

1. "Myn hertis lust," alto part, John Bedingham, Mellon Chansonnier, Yale Beinecke MS 91
2. Arcita and Palemone admire Emilia in her garden, from Boccaccio's Teseida, Anon. French, c1460
3. Angel playing psaltery, detail from a larger polyptych, now largely lost, Hans Memling, c1480
4. Lover and Lady, Cristine de Pizan, Harley Ms 4431, f376, c1414
5. Lovers in a garden, Anon. French, c1470
6. "Myn hertis lust," verse 2, alto part, same at #1

videos.title: Josquin des Prez & Johannes Ghiselin: la Spagna (c.1495) (Part 3 of 3)

localized.title: Josquin des Prez & Johannes Ghiselin: la Spagna (c.1495) (Part 3 of 3)
localized.description:
La Spagna. Part 3 of 3.

  0:06  La Spagna by Josquin des Prez (2 cornetti, shawm, 2 trombones, drum)
  3:30  La Spagna by Johannes Ghiselin (2 shawms, 2 trombones, drum)

The la Spagna settings by des Prez and Ghiselin based on the "Re di Spagna" bassadanza tenor, represent a high point in early Italian Renaissance music with their elaborate Franco-Flemish polyphony and grandiosity. The two composers were known to have met in northern Italy, specifically in Ferrara, where Ghiselin was employed by the intellectually gifted and politically astute Lady Isabella d'Este (later the Marchioness of Mantua). Both composers were much celebrated in Italian aristocratic circles (as well as in Rome in the case of Josquin) throughout the last decade of the 15th Century.

MIDI for La Spagne (Josquin des Prez) uploaded by Christian Mondrup to IMSLP.com.
MIDI La Spagna (Johannes Ghiselin) uploaded by Albert den Teuling to IMSLP.com.

Description of the photos:

1. "La Spagna Tantz," bassus I part, Josquin des Prez, MS Gamle kongelige Samling 1872 (Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Denmark), copied around 1540
2. Mounted trombones and shawms, from Triumphs of Maximilian, Hans Burgkmair, 1526
3. Sforzesco Castle (Milan) which Josquin likely frequented in the 1490s, photo from Igor Saveliev (Pixabay)
4. "The Horse," a modern recreation of the original Leonardo da Vinci "Cavallo" in Milan, a familiar sight for Josquin during his tenure with Cardinal Ascanio Sforza.
5. The "Old" Saint Peter's Basilica prior to its reconstruction in the 1500s; a place well known to Josquin who was employed there in the second half of the 1490s and perhaps the early part of the 1500s.
6. Graffiti of Josquin (Josquinus) on the walls of the Sistine Chapel.
7. Shawm band, detail from "Garden of Love," Cristoforo de Predis, c1470
8. Ceiling of the Ducal Palace of Mantua, commissioned by Isabella d'Este, patron of music and employer of Johannes Ghiselin.
9. Beatrice e Isabella d'Este looking down from a balcony. Isabella, herself a lutenist, hired many a great composer and performer for concerts in her chambers at the Ducal Palace of Mantua.

11. Isabella d'Este portrait after Leonardo da Vinci's sketch, date unknown
12. Dancing Muses beneath Mars and Venus, from "La Parnasse," Andrea Mantegna, painter in the employ of Isabella d'Este, 1497

videos.title: Anonymous Franco-Flemish (?): Bassadanza la Spagna (Part 2 of 3) (c.1490)

localized.title: Anonymous Franco-Flemish (?): Bassadanza la Spagna (Part 2 of 3) (c.1490)
localized.description:
La Spagna. Part 2 of 3.

  0:06  La Spagna #1 (cornetto, shawm, 2 trombones, drum)
  1:50  La Spagna #2 (2 cornetti, 2 trombones, drum)

These two anonymously composed bassadanze were hand copied (perhaps by the Bolognese music director Giovanni Spataro) into a large volume of sacred and secular music by composers of different nationalities (French, Italian, Spanish and Flemish). A quick review of the authors named in the codex reveals that most were residing in Northern Italy at the end of the 15th Century. The intricate polyphonic interchange between the upper two voices in both bassadanze suggests a Franco-Flemish origin, but until other copies of the works can be found that can establish a definitive attribution, we will likely never know. In both pieces, the "Re di Spagna" cantus firmus can be found in the tenor voice.

Both MIDI files were compiled and uploaded to IMSLP.org by Ulrich Alpers. I used the MIDI editor Music Studio 2.0 on the iPhone to simulate instruments of the early Italian Renaissance.  I also utilized the open source program for the PC Audacity to enhance the reverb and echo effects.

2. Aristocrats dancing the basse dance beneath the gallery musicians, from "Roman de Renaud Montauban – The marriage of Renaud and Clarisse" Loyset Liédet, BnF. Bibliothèque de l’Arsenal Ms-5073, c.1470

videos.title: Antonio Cornazano & Guglielmo Ebreo: Bassadanza la Spagna (Part 1 of 3) (c.1455)

localized.title: Antonio Cornazano & Guglielmo Ebreo: Bassadanza la Spagna (Part 1 of 3) (c.1455)
localized.description:
La Spagna. Part 1 of 3.

  0:06  Tenore Il Re di Spagna (hurdy-gurdy, tambourine, drum)
  1:42  La bassa castiglya / Falla con misura (shawm, trombone, drum)

The basse danse (bassadanza) likely originated in the Netherlands in the first half of the 15th century but appeared in various incarnations across all of Western Europe throughout the 16th century.  There are more than 100 surviving setting of the La Spagna theme including instrumental, vocal, secular and sacred parodies. This simple, slow cantus firmus melody which does not seem particularly stirring or catchy, became the most widely parodied tune for the multitude of leading Renaissance composers including Josquin des Prez and Heinrich Isaac.  

The first of the two pieces in this video is the original tenor of the tune titled "Il Re di Spagna." it comes to us from a dance treatise by Antonio Cornazzano (or Cornazano) "Libro dell'Arte del Danzare," first issued in 1455 (reissued in 1465) and dedicated to the Lady Ippolita Maria Sforza, offspring of the rulers of Milan and later spouse to the King of Naples. Ippolita (Hyppolita) was a highly educated and capable woman skilled in international diplomacy but also a patron of the arts, music and dance.

The second of the two pieces, "la Bassa [danza] castiglya" (a.k.a. "Falla con misura) by the dance master Guglielmo Ebreo da Pesaro is the earliest surviving "La Spagna" setting that adds a florid superius overlay superimposed the popular cantus firmus. There is uncertainty whether the original melody was in 2/4 or 6/8 time, but the meter of Guglielmo's setting is the first that was clearly 6/8 time and was representative of most early Renaissance bassadanze.

The original MIDI file for the "Falla con Misuras" (Guglielmo Ebreo) was uploaded by Dillon Upton to IMSLP.com. The tenor to "Il Re di Spagna" is my own arrangement from Cornazano's 1465 manuscript.

Description of the photos:

1. "Tenore del re di Spagna," the original bassadanza tune from which all subsequent variations developed, Libro dell'Arte del Danzare, second edition Antonio Cornazano, 1455
2. Ippolita Maria Sforza portrayed as Salome dancing at the court of King Herod, Benozzo Gozzoli, c1462
3. A noble lady from Naples (likely Ippolita Maria Sforza), Francesco Laurana, c1473

7. Three dancers and a harpist from "De Pratica Seu Arte Tripudii," Guglielmo Ebreo, 1463

videos.title: [New Rendition] Bartolomeo Tromboncino: Chi in pregion (c.1500)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Bartolomeo Tromboncino: Chi in pregion (c.1500)
localized.description:
Chi in pregion

  0:06  Verse 1 for 4 voices (ATTB a cappella)
  1:59  Verse 2 for alto + accompaniment (lute, harp, bass viol)
  3:50  Instrumental setting (recorder, lute, 2 crumhorns, bass viol)

There are two remaining copies of Tromboncino's "Chi in pregion" both published by the famed Venetian publisher Ottaviano Petrucci: one written out for 4 voices (1507) and one for solo vocalist with lute accompaniment (1508). The reference to a "prison" of love may somehow be connected to Tromboncino's period of incarceration in Mantua in 1499 for the alleged murder of his wife whom the composer had found with her lover. After his release from prison, he was almost immediately employed as court musician by the illustrious and intellectually gifted Marchesa Isabella d'Este, one of the great patrons of the arts and music in Renaissance Italy. The structure of this particular work resembles Josquin's "In te Domine speravi" with its smoothly flowing melody line in the superius, a somewhat more intricate accompaniment in the middle voices and a very long final note in the top voice accompanied by faster moving notes in the middle voices. 

I created the MIDI file for this song based on the modern edition of Petrucci's 8th Book (Libro Octavo) of Frottole edited by Lucia Boscolo. I added text using the MAIKA Spanish language module in Vocaloid 4. The instrumental sounds were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. In this latest rendition, I rebalanced the voices, corrected minor errors in pronunciation, created a more legato effect in all the voices, created a more textured instrumental setting, adjusted the tempi and augmented the reverb / echo effects.

Text:

Chi in pregion crede tornarmi
ha sue rheti indarno tese
[per]ché la fiamma che me accese
piu non ha forza abrusciarmi

se fu grande la beltade
dove fui nei llacci avolto
maggior fu la crudeltade
che hora mi fa rimanir sciolto
ho di mano il foco tolto
a chi piace di stentarmi

Imprisoned, he believes in coming back
In vain, tightened his own net
Because the flame which burned me
no longer has the strength to curb me

If the beauty was great
where I was ensnared in captivity
Greater was the cruelty
that now makes me stay unbound
I have removed from my hand the fire
of him who (in the past?) likes to struggle

1. Score of the superius line from "Chi in pregion" by Tromboncino, Frottole Libro Octavo, edited by O.Petrucci, Venice, 1507
2. View of the city of Mantua in Tromboncino's time. Domenico Morone, 1494
3. Palazzo del Capitano in Mantua, located in the center of the Piazza, no doubt a daily sight for the composer and perhaps a frequent venue for his performances.
4. Minerva expelling Vice from the Garden of Virtue, Andrea Mantegna, 1502, a work probably commissioned by Isabella d'Este, Tromboncino's patron and advocate in Mantua.
5. Palazzo Ducale Mantua, the main residence of Isabella d'Este.
6. The glorious ceiling of Isabella d'Este's apartment and studio (Ducal Palace in Mantua) where many musical concerts were organized.
7. Intarsia illustrating musical instruments of Isabella d'Este (including recorders, cornetto, viola da braccia and Renaissance guitar), Antonio & Paolo Mola, 1505

11. A wall panel engraved with the Marchesa's name in Latin.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Henry VIII: Instrumental Consort music (c.1515)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Henry VIII: Instrumental Consort music (c.1515)
localized.description:
Henry's Consort Music

  0:06  Consort II (cornetto, 2 trombones)
  1:00  Consort IV (recorder, cittern, bass viol)
  1:46  Consort V (recorder, cittern, bass viol) 
  2:59  Taunder naken (cornetto, 2 trombones, drum)

These four works attributed to King Henry VIII were copied by hand and combined with 30 others works by the royal composer in a grand archive of Tudor court music known as Henry VIII's Songbook (British Library Additional Manuscript #31922).  The collection is a rare English chansonnier likely copied around 1518 for the court musicians in service of the king. Along with his signature piece "Pastyme with Good Companye," these works expressed a lighthearted, although sometimes melancholic, spirit from the earliest period of Henry's long, troubled and turbulent career.  At the time of these compositions, the brutal misogyny and murderous rage of his later years were still more than a decade away.

"Taunder naken" is Henry's most complex work both melodically and rhythmically. It contains a floridly embellished upper instrumental part attached to a basse dance tune rooted in the popular Dutch-Flemish folk melody " 't Andernaken al op den Rijn." For the other 3 consort pieces, I followed John Stevens' (Musica Britannica, Vol. 18, 1962) ficta recommendations at the cadences (specifically, F to F# and C to C# substitutions).

The so-called "Consort" pieces are short untitled, un-numbered instrumental pieces by various composers including the King himself. My instrumental simulations were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. In this latest rendition, I used only the works of Henry VIII; also, I adjusted the tempi and tweaked the reverb / echo and balance of instruments.

8. Trombonist among gallery musicians, Anonymous German, Nuremburg, c1520

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous English: And I war a maydyn (c.1510) (Original Pronunciation)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous English: And I war a maydyn (c.1510) (Original Pronunciation)
localized.description:
This anonymously composed song for five voices is contained in the Henry VIII Songbook (a.k.a. British Library MS Add. 31922). The collection includes 20 songs and 13 instrumental works by King Henry VIII as well as a variety of compositions by his contemporaries, both English and Continental. Unlike the other pieces in this tome, "And I war a maydyn" is almost entirely homophonic and resembles more the Anglican hymns written more than a century later and even some of the early church music in Colonial America. The song narrates the imagined exploits of a young girl mingling in courtly circles on her path towards Ladyship. It is also intermingled with the unsubtle touch of  a rising English nationalism.

The original MIDI file without the words was downloaded from the Japanese recorder website of the Aeolian Consort and it was transposed down one octave to fit the range of human voices. In this latest rendition, I used only the Cyber Songman Vocaloid for all 5 parts.  The instrumental sounds (lute, flute, dulcian, harp, 2 viols) were created using Music Studio 2. 

Text (and Modern English):

And I war a maydyn (And I was a maiden)
as many one ys (as any one might be)
For all the golde in Englond (For all the gold in England)
I wold not do amysse (I would not go astray)
When I was a wanton wench (When I was still a conceited girl)
of twelve yere of age (twelve years old)
These cowrtyers with ther amorus (these courtiers with their flirtations)
they kyndyld my corage. (they kindled my courage)
When I was come [un]to (When I was)
the age of fifteen yere, (fifteen years old)
In all this lond, nowther fre nor bond, (in all this land, neither free nor bound)
Methought I had no pere (I thought I had no equal)

Description of photos:

1. Cantus line of "And I war a maydyn," Anonymous English, Henry VIII's Songbook, c1518
2. Courtly lovers, Hans Holbein the Younger, c1530
3. Portrait of Anne Boleyn from Hever Castle, probably representing her image as a young woman at the French court (note the French head dress), dated 1533
4. Hampton Court Palace, Henry VIII's pleasure palace where much of England's courtly music was presented.

videos.title: Claude Gervaise / Pierre Attaingnant: Les Pavanes et Gaillardes (c.1550)

localized.title: Claude Gervaise / Pierre Attaingnant: Les Pavanes et Gaillardes (c.1550)
localized.description:
Pavanes et Gaillardes

  0:06  Pavanne passemaize (Livre 6) (flute, lute, harp, viol)
  1:11  Gaillarde passemaize (Livre 6) (recorder, viols, tambourine)
  1:44  Pavane venissienne (Livre 4) (cornetto, 3 viols, drum)
  3:56  Pavane #6 (Livre 4) (cornetto, 3 trombones, drum)
  5:07  Gaillarde #6 (Livre 4) (cornetto, 3 trombones, drum)
  6:09  Pavane #12 (Livre 4) (cornetto, 3 trombones, no percussion)

Gervaise and Attaingnant were each well established publishers of music granted exclusive privileges to print musical score by the King of France, Francis I (François 1er). The two men collaborated to preserve for posterity some of the greatest masterpieces of French Renaissance music - both vocal and instrumental. The two printers were also accomplished arrangers of music in their own right and created memorable harmonizations for otherwise simple tunes.

The middle of the 16th century was the hayday of courtly dance music, particularly, the pairing of a pavan (pavane or pavanne in French) and a galliard (gaillarde in French). The pavane was a slow, stately dance suggestive of a military procession in 2 or 4 rhythm while the galliard was the more lively variation on the pavane melody in a 3 or 6 rhythm.

The original MIDI files for the pieces were created by bojopigeon and uploaded to musescore.com. All MIDI edits were performed on the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 and the reverb / echo effects were added using Audacity.

videos.title: Juan Cornago: Morte merce (c.1450)

localized.title: Juan Cornago: Morte merce (c.1450)
localized.description:
This late Medieval song of courtly love for 3 voices appears in multiple sources associated with the Aragonese-Neapolitan court of the late 15th century (Montecassino 871 & Escorial IV.a.24). Cornago, a Spanish composer, likely wrote this piece during his tenure in Naples. There is also a significant altered variant in a Franco-Savoian collection Chansonnier Cordiforme. One can hear the structural similarities with later villancicos and frottole of the early Renaissance in Spain and Italy, respectively: particularly, the simple melodies and the homophonic alignment of the voices. The sequence of the 4 verses are ABAB with the A sections in a 3 rhythm and the B sections in a 2 rhythm. 

I used MAIKA, a Spanish language Vocaloid for the 3 male vocals (alto, tenor, bass) and added reverb with echo using Audacity. The instrumental simulations of medieval lutes and harp were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. 

Text (and translation):

Morte, merce, gentile aquil' altera (Mercy, Death, that other gentle eagle)
Qu'il tempo passa e crudelta me sfida (as times passes, cruelty provokes me)
E senza guida solo me trovo in guerra (and without guidance, I find myself at war)

Amor cum larco teso al co m'aferra (Love, with tense bow against my heart)
Que romper non se po' l'aspra cadena (that hard chain cannot be broken)
Dal primo jorno strecta (from the very first day)
que me conduce a sy crudel martiri (that I am lead to such cruel suffering)

Amor m'asale, credendo a luy fugire (Love assails me, believing I can flee)
Cerchando escampo, e mi ritrovo in focho (seeking escape, I find myself on fire)
A pocho a pocho moro e vivo pocho (Little by little I die and live only a little)

Sperando ardendo ormai de jorno in jorno (Hoping, fervently day by day)
Lieto vederme solo con dolze riso (to see me happy with only a sweet smile)
Da poi che m'a conquiso (because she has conquered me)
Mostra mi crudo e non me val defesa (proved me raw and without defense)

1. Complete score of "Morte merce" from Cancionero de Montecassino
2. "Vous ou Mort (You or Death)," a ceremonial shield capturing the spirit of courtly love; a young knight declares his love for an elegant lady, without whom he is as good as dead; Anonymous Franco-Flemish, c1470
3. Orfeo singing with lute for the beast of the forest, Luca della Robbia, c1439
4. Angel playing lute, Gerard David, c1480
5. The knight Cuer ("Heart") reads a warning on a black stone in the midst of his quest for unrequited love (while in the background Desire sleeps), René d'Anjou with illustrations by Barthélemy d'Eyck, Livre du cuer d'amours espris, c1457

videos.title: Francis Pilkington: Rest sweet nymphs (1605)

localized.title: Francis Pilkington: Rest sweet nymphs (1605)
localized.description:
This Elizabethan madrigal is a pastoral lullaby by a young man with amorous intent for a young woman (or perhaps several young women). It infuses the gentle air of a child's lullaby (cf. Byrd's lullabies) with the lustier elements of pastoral songs from the same period.

I used the Prima v2 Vocaloid for the cantus part and the Cyber Songman Vocaloid for the alto / tenor / bass parts. The three verses are each matched up with three possible settings: SATB + lute  (as suggested in the original score), soprano solo with lute and bass viol, and SATB doubled by viol quartet &accompanied by lute. I applied (as much as the Vocaloid phoneme adjustment capabilities allow) Professor David Crystal’s recommendations for the pronunciation of Early Modern London English.

Text with Modern English spelling:

1  Rest, sweet nymphs, let golden sleep
Charm your star brighter eyes,
While my lute the watch doth keep
With pleasing sympathies.
Lulla, lullaby. Lulla, lullaby.
Sleep sweetly, sleep sweetly,
Let nothing affright ye,
In calm contentment lie.

2  Dream, fair virgins, of delight
And blest Elysian groves,
While the wand'ring shades of night
Resemble your true loves.
Lulla, lullaby. Lulla, lullaby.
Your kisses, your blisses,
Send them by your wishes,
Although they be not nigh.

3  Thus, dear damsels, I do give
‘Good night’, and so am gone:
With your hearts’ desires long live,
Still joy, and never moan.
Lulla, lullaby. Lulla, lullaby.
Hath pleased you and eased you,
And sweet slumber seized you,
And now to bed I hie.

videos.title: Dietrich Buxtehude: Herr wenn ich nur dich hab, BuxWV 38 (c.1680)

localized.title: Dietrich Buxtehude: Herr wenn ich nur dich hab, BuxWV 38 (c.1680)
localized.description:
Buxtehude wrote two very different settings of Psalm 74, which have been catalogued as BuxWV 38 and 39, respectively. #38 is an aria with tenderness both in the instrumentation (solo violins in the middle pitch range) as well as in the lyrics. It was probably written in the early period of Buxtehude's long tenure at Marienkirche (St. Mary's Cathedral) in Lübeck. It has a melodic simplicity that harkens back to the monody of the Venetians at the turn of the 17th Century.

I used the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid for the boy soprano sound and I used the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 for the instrumentals (2 violins, cello, violone, organ and chitarrone).

Text:

Herr, Herr, wenn ich nur Dich hab',
so frag' ich nichts nach Himmel und Erden.
Wenn mir gleich Leib und Seel' verschmacht', 
so bist Du doch, Gott, allezeit
meines Herzens Trost,
so bist Du doch, Gott, allezeit
meines Herzens Trost und mein Teil.
Alleluia.

Translation:

Lord, Lord, if I have You alone,
I do not ask for heaven and earth.
If my body and soul shall pass away,
You will still be, God, forever,
my heart's comfort,
You will still be, God, forever
my hearts comfort and my part.
Hallelujah

1. Soprano vocal line from "Herr, wenn ich nur Dich hab," Dietrich Buxtehude, copied by Gustaf Düben, c1680
2. Entrance way to Marienkirche in Lübeck where Buxtehude spent most of his musical career as music director and organist, Pixabay

videos.title: Arcangelo Corelli: Concerto Grosso No. 4 in D major, Op. 6 (c.1690)

localized.title: Arcangelo Corelli: Concerto Grosso No. 4 in D major, Op. 6 (c.1690)

  4:42  Vivace

Although the earliest published edition of the complete Opus 6 concerti by Corelli appeared in 1714, it is thought that most of the works were composed between 1680-1690. This set of 12 multi-movement concerti became a model for George Frideric Handel's famed Opus 3 and Opus 6 collections also containing 12 concerti grossi each. In Corelli's Opus 6 collection, each concerto is presented as a double duet. There are two dueling concertini violins (accompanied by a concertino cello) juxtaposed against two dueling ripieni violins (accompanied by viola and basso continuo).

The original MIDI file, which I rendered using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0, can be found on Musescore. The original MIDI was generated by Quasi Cantando and can be found at musescore.com.

videos.title: Ludovico Balbi: Hierusalem surge (1578)

localized.title: Ludovico Balbi: Hierusalem surge (1578)
localized.description:
This short motet was composed by Ludovico Balbi, one of the many musicians in residence at the Basilica San Marco in Venice during the early tenure of Andrea and Giovanni Gabrieli. This "Jerusalem arise" motet setting is one of several from the 16th Century. The text comes from the Old Testament chapter Baruch 5:5 and 4:36.

The original MIDI file was compiled by William Chimiak and uploaded to cpdl.org. I added the Latin text using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid and simulated a church ensemble (cornetto, 3 viols, organ, chitarrone) using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. 

Text (and translation):

Jerusalem surge, (Arise, Jersusalem)
et sta in excelso, et vide (and stand on high, and witness)
jucunditatem quae veniet tibi (the joyousness that comes to you)
a Deo tuo. (from you God)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Filippo de Lurano: Salve sacrata (c.1500)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Filippo de Lurano: Salve sacrata (c.1500)
localized.description:
Salve sacrata

  0:06  Instrumental intro (cornetto, 3 trombones)
  0:47  Verse 1 for voices alone (ATTB)
  1:28  Verse 2 for ATTB + ensemble (recorder, lute, harp, viol)
  2:09  Verse 3 for ATTB + lute
  2:50  Verse 4 for ATTB + church organ

The Lauda was an Italian genre of spiritual music coming from a centuries-old folk tradition rather than the refined and complex polyphony from the Franco-Flemish masters of the late 15th and early 16th centuries. Filippo da Lurano is mostly remembered for his simple, straightforward secular frottole.  And similar to the frottole, his laude consisted of short, catchy melodies in the superius, a non-liturgical text in the vernacular Italian, a predictable rhythm and a basic homophonic accompaniment. I have created three possible arrangements -- all of which were likely to have have been utilized in the early 16th Century. I included an a cappella setting, a "secular" setting with chamber ensemble, a version doubled by lute and a final version doubled by church organ.

This MIDI file I created using a facsimile from the pages of Petrucci's Laude Book 2. I changed only one note near the end of the bass part in order to correct a probable misprint and avoid a crashing dissonance. I also adjusted the final cadence with a ficta. I added the words using Vocaloid 4 and MAIKA (Spanish language module). The instrumental sounds were generated on my iPhone using MusicStudio2. In the latest version, I generated a more legato effect, fixed some vowel sounds, rearranged the instruments, added some natural dynamics and changed the reverb / echo effects. I also corrected a ficta at the cadence.

Text (and translation):

Salve sacrata e gloriosa insegna (Greet the holy and glorious sign)
Dove fu morto qual che tutto move (where he died, which moves everyone)
E'cio che rede el sol guberna e regna (and also governs and reigns alone)
Ne senza lui dal ciel mai gratia piove (without him, grace does not rain down from heaven)
Se esser nostra salute sosti degna (if you are to be our well-being, stay worthy)
Ogni comesso error da nui rimove (remove every error we make)
E vengate pieta di nostra sorte (and take pity on our life)
Dandone pace in vita e poi la morte (give us peace in life and also in death)

Qui aymant bien est bien aymay, (He who loves well is well loved)

videos.title: Thoinot Arbeau: Quatre Branles (c.1560)

localized.title: Thoinot Arbeau: Quatre Branles (c.1560)
localized.description:
0:06  Branle Cassandre (recorder, 3 viols, tambourine)
0:42  Branle Pinagay (recorder, 3 viols, tambourine)
1:12  Branle de l'Official (violin, 3 viols, tambourine)
1:53  Branle d'Ecosse (recorder, 3 viols, drum)

The cleric Thoinot Arbeau published his "Orchesographie," an encyclopedic book of dances in 1589. Nearly all the sample tunes the he included were, however, much older, and some can be traced back to the first quarter of the 16th Century. As the pages of the tome demonstrate, the individual steps of the dance are meticulously printed beside their matching notes from the melody line of each tune. The branle was a popular set of dances used for courtly balls in which couples held hands as they processed in a line of dancers and swayed from side to side. It was common practice to present sets of 4 branles as a single work. The listener will likely notice the Christmas carol "Ding dong merrily on high" embedded in the top line of "Branle de l'Official."

The MIDI files for these arrangements were generated from pdf scores uploaded by Steve Hendricks to the website:  https://sca.uwaterloo.ca/sca/Hendricks/
Since Arbeau published only the melody lines for all 4 branles, it is likely that the other 3 voices in these MIDI files are the work of Steve Hendricks and his associates based on French dance music from the mid 16th Century. My instrument simulations were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0.

videos.title: Anonymous German: Ein feste burg is unser gott (c.1540)

localized.title: Anonymous German: Ein feste burg is unser gott (c.1540)
localized.description:
0:06 Verse 1 (SATB a cappella)
1:29 Verse 2 (soprano & 3 viols)
2:52 Verse 3 (bass transposed up an octave & lute)
4:15 Verse 4 (SATB & church organ)

This 4 voice setting of "Ein feste Burg" appears in one of the largest collections of German Protestant hymns and motets compiled during the lifetime of Martin Luther. The original cantus firmus by Luther can be found in the bass. The harmonization is reflective of Franco-Flemish polyphony in the early 16th Century with steady outer voices and moving inner voices. The lyrics are Luther's translation of Psalm 46 from the Latin "Deus noster refugium."

Text in modern German (& translation)

1. Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott, (A mighty fortress is our God)
Ein gute Wehr und Waffen. (a firm shield and weapon)
Er hilft uns frei aus aller Not, (he helps free us from all need)
Die uns jetzt hat betroffen. (that has now overtaken us)
Der alt böse Feind, (the ancient evil fiend)
Mit Ernst er’s jetzt meint. (in ernest he now means ill)
Groß Macht und viel List (great power and much skill)
Sein grausam Rüstung ist. (his armor is cruel)
Auf Erd ist nicht seinsgleichen. (on earth he has no equal)

2. Mit unsrer Macht ist nichts getan, (With our power nothing is done)
Wir sind gar bald verloren. (we are immediately conquered)
Es streit’t für uns der rechte Mann, (He fights for us, the righteous man)
Den Gott hat selbst erkoren. (whom God himself chose)
Fragst du, wer der ist? (Ask you, who is this?)
Er heißt Jesus Christ, (Jesus Christ is his name)
Der Herr Zebaoth, (the Sabbath lord)
Und ist kein ander Gott. (there is no other god)
Das Feld muß er behalten. (he must hold the field)

3. Und wenn die Welt voll Teufel wär (and though devils fill the world)
Und wollt uns gar verschlingen, (all willing to devour us)
So fürchten wir uns nicht so sehr, (so fear we not much)
Es soll uns doch gelingen. (it shall not overpower us)
Der Fürst dieser Welt, (the prince of this world)
Wie saur er sich stellt, (though grim he seems)
Tut er uns doch nicht. (does us not [harm])
Das macht, er ist gericht’t. (the deed, he has judged)
Ein Wörtlein kann ihn fällen. (a little word can slay him)

4. Das Wort sie sollen lassen stahn (That word they shall allow to stay)
Und kein’ Dank dazu haben. (and have no thanks for it) 
Er ist bei uns wohl auf dem Plan (He stands by us on the plain)
Mit seinem Geist und Gaben. (with his spirit and gifts)
Nehmen sie den Leib, (though they take our life)
Gut, Ehr, Kind und Weib, (our goodness, honor, child and wife)
Laß fahren dahin. (let these go away)
Sie haben’s kein Gewinn. (they have no victory)
Das Reich muß uns doch bleiben. ([for] the Kingdom [of God] will still remain)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Petronio Franceschini: Trumpet Sonata in D major (c.1680)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Petronio Franceschini: Trumpet Sonata in D major (c.1680)
localized.description:
Sonata in D major for 2 trumpets (Petronio Franceschini)

  0:06  Grave
  1:11  Allegro
  2:41  Adagio
  4:23  Allegro

Petronio Franceschini was a cellist by trade and one of the early masters of the musical "School of Bologna."  He devoted his energies to composing mostly for the church but also created opera as was expected of all respectable composers of that period. The city-state of Bologna enjoyed a period of relative political calm and artistic "renaissance" that lasted nearly a 100 years between 1650 and 1750.  During the span from around 1680-1700, the trumpet superseded the wooden cornetto in Italy as the lead "brass" instrument and came into its own as a solo instrument for virtuosi performers.  One can hear the echo effect between the two trumpet soloists that harkens back to the early Italian church sonatas from the period of Giovanni Gabrieli and Dario Castello.

The artworks (paintings and sketches ) are contemporary with the music and includes the masterpieces of Guercino and others who were associated with the Bologna School and other regional guilds.  Like the music of that epoch, the paintings are filled with a fantastical grandeur.  The facial expressions of their subjects capture the ethereal qualities of angels and saints ecstatically contemplating an otherworldly realm. Yet there is also an intimacy and sensuality that makes even the sacred art appear much more fluid and secular then in earlier centuries.

The original MIDI file was created and uploaded by Michel Rondeau to IMSLP.com.  I extensively edited the files to reflect the balance of a small Baroque orchestra consisting of 1-2 trumpet soloists, 4-5 violins, 1-2 violas, 2 celli, small harpsichord and double bass. In this latest rendition, I softened the violins and trumpets, created a more staccato effect in the strings for clarity and re-imagined the trills in both the trumpets and violins.

videos.title: [New Rendition] John Taverner: Quemadmodum (c.1540)

localized.title: [New Rendition] John Taverner: Quemadmodum (c.1540)
localized.description:
Although this work bears the first word of the 41st Psalm (Clementine Vulgate Bible), the motet may never have been intended for anything other than an instrumental ensemble of 6 viols or recorders. The full score, which is contained in the Baldwin Partbooks, has no text attached to it and no specific instruction about performance recommendation. It was likely a very late composition by John Taverner and is more similar to Tallis' middle period compositions than to Taverner's earlier masterpieces. It was scored for lower voices (not the high boy sopranos of previous decades), and it contained short phrases with one note per syllable (i.e. absent the impossibly long melismata utilized by pre-Reformation composers in Catholic England). If it had ever been performed by a church choir, it would have likely been presented at the Gothic cathedral of St. Botolph, the last place where Taverner was employed.

In this latest rendition, I have rebalanced the voices, created a more legato effect, added natural dynamics, corrected some vowel sounds and raised the pitch by a whole step. The MIDI file and the text underlay were created by Humphrey Thompson and they both can be found on CPDL.org. The pronunciation of the Latin is Anglicized. The vocal simulations were generated using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid.

Text (and translation):

Quemadmodum desiderat cervus (Just as the deer desires)
ad fontes aquarum, (the streams of water)
ita desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus. (My soul desires after you God)
Sitivit anima mea (My soul thirsts)
ad Deum fortem, vivum; (for the strong, living God)
quando veniam et apparebo ante faciem Dei (when I shall come and appear before the face of God)

videos.title: Anonymous English: My woefull hert (c.1470)

localized.title: Anonymous English: My woefull hert (c.1470)
localized.description:
This English chanson bears striking structural similarities to some French chansons from previous generations at the Burgundian courts. One might hear the very long melismata and complex imitative passages reminiscent of Binchois and other mid-century Franco-Flemish composers. The language is a mix of late Middle English and early Modern English with the spelling tending more towards the former.

In order to create this MIDI, I used a modern transcription by John Stevens (Early Tudor Songs and Carols, Musica Britannica). I made a few corrections in the text underlay using a facsimile edition of the complete Ritson Manuscript (British Library, Add. 5665). The voice simulations were create using the Prima v2 Vocaloid for the alto part and the Cyber Songman Vocaloid in the lower voices. The instrumental sounds were generated using an iPhone MIDI editing app Music Studio 2.0. I reconstructed a late 15th century English pronunciation using Tim McGee's "Singing Early Music." The middle of the 15th century was a period of rapid change in the so-called "Great Vowel Shift," and there is no uniformity in an "accepted" pronunciation scheme.

Middle English text (with translation):

My woefull hert of all gladnesse baryeyne
    (My woeful heart deprived of all happiness)
enforsed me this complaynte for to make
    (forced me to make this complaint)
Wheche y have songe wit weepyng eyen twayne
    (which I have sung with both eyes weeping)
Full ofte er this, y shall undertake
    (Full often before this, I shall undertake)
Till gode tydyngs com my sorwoe to slake
    (Until good news comes to relieve my sorrow)
Y most obey fortune's ordinaunce
    (I must follow fortune's decree)
For yet y am all drowned in the lake
    (For still I am completely drowned in the lake)
Of sorfull joie and paynefull plesaunce
    (Of sad joy and painful pleasure)

Ffor sche weche ys of all godely the best
    (for she is the best among good women)
To myn entent, and so sayeth mo' than y
    (for all intents, and speaks more than I)
Is full but late out of her kindly rest
    (but lately instead of her kind way)
Into great sekenesse weche holdith her grevosly
    (a deep sickness has taken her hostage)
Now I pray god, and that right hertely
    (Now I pray to God and heartily so)
That she be voided out of the grete grevaunce
    (that she come out of great grievance)
Ffor till she amende y shall have nought truly
    (Because until she changes, I truly have nothing)
But sorfull joy and paineful plesaunce
    (except sad joy and painful pleasure)
