videos.title: Johann David Heinichen: Concerto for Oboe & Violin (Vivace), S240 (c.1725)

localized.title: Johann David Heinichen: Concerto for Oboe & Violin (Vivace), S240 (c.1725)
localized.description:
Johann Heinichen (1683-1729), master of music at the height of the Baroque era in Dresden was all but forgotten until the late 20th Century. A handful of his concerti were resurrected in 1993 through the fine recordings of Reinhard Goebel and Musica Antiqua Köln in a well-regarded digital recording of the "Dresden Concerti." These works recall the spirited affect of the Venetians from an earlier generation: namely, the exuberant energy of Vivaldi's fast movements and the poignancy of the wind solos in Albinoni's oboe concerti.  This Concerto movement (Vivace) survived thanks to the manuscript of Heinichen's pupil, Johann Georg Pisendel.

This electronic simulation of a Baroque chamber band was generated using a MIDI editor on Music Studio 2.0 (an iPhone app from Steinberg). I used Pisendel’s manuscript to insert the original dynamic markings. I tried to simulate a group consisting of solo oboe, solo violin, 3 violin 1, 3 violin 2,  2 violas, 2 celli, harpsichord and double bass.

Description of the photos:

1. Pages 1 & 2 of Johann G. Pisendel's conductor's score for Heinichen's Oboe Concerto, S240.
2. Baroque oboe, Jakob Denner, c1730
3. Morning haze over the Dresden city skyline, photo by Porzhidaeva (Pixabay)
4. Baroque violin, Antonio Stradivarius, c1680
5. Street level view of Dresden's Baroque architecture, photo by Porzhidaeva (Pixabay)
6. Augustus II of Saxony ("The Strong"), portrait by Louis de Silvestre, c1725; Heinichen's main sponsor during his many years in Dresden.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous Spanish: Desposastes os señora (1556)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous Spanish: Desposastes os señora (1556)
localized.description:
Desposastes os señora 

  0:06  Original villancico for 3 (TTB) doubled by viols
  2:38  Instrumental arrangement for vihuela, lute and harp
  
This anonymous villancico bears structural and thematic similarities to other 3 part polyphonic treasures in the collection El Cancionero de Uppsala (a.k.a. Cancionero del Duque de Calabria). Other examples of this are two that I previously released on this channel:

     Si la noche haze escura: https://youtu.be/QC71p0sEsWg
     Si nos huviera: https://youtu.be/FVxg75FmLhw

Despite its rather bare bones part writing with frequent octaves, fifths and fourths, the canonic counterpoint is quite refined and warm compared to the simpler writing of the early 16th Century. Despite its gently lilting tune, the text expresses bitter, vengeful and uncharitable sentiments.

The original MIDI file was created and uploaded to CPDL.org by André Vierendeels. I entered the vocal simulations using the MAIKA Spanish language voice bank and the VOCALOID 4 voice encoder.  I adjusted the Vocaloid presets to approximate 16th Century pronunciations. Instrumental sounds were generated using Music Studio 2. In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, rebalanced the voices, adjusted the reverb / echo and doubled the voices with viols.

Text (and translation):

Desposastes os señora, (You married, Lady)
solo por de mi os quitar, (only so you can rid of me)
casareys y habreis pesar. (You shall marry and be burdened)

Pues que tan mal gualardon, (Well, what a really bad reward)
a los mis servicios distes. (you gave me for my services)

Vuestro bravo coraçon, (Your brave heart)
ya esta en tiempo de amansar, (it's time to tame)
casareys y habreis pesar, (You shall marry and be burdened)
 
Que pagueis lo que hezistes, (You will pay for what you did)
lo que no lleva Razon. (What Razon does not carry...)

videos.title: Mikołaj Zieleński: Tu es Petrus (c.1610)

localized.title: Mikołaj Zieleński: Tu es Petrus (c.1610)
localized.description:
Mikołaj Zieleński's musical training may have taken place in Rome, but he spent most of his life travelling far and wide within the boundaries of modern day Poland. His polychoral music is reminiscent of the compositional trends developed in late 16th century Venice and adopted in early 17th century Germany (by the likes of Hassler and Praetorius). This Latin motet for 8 voices is divided into two choirs likely positioned at opposite ends of a cathedral in a manner similar to Giovanni Gabrieli's grand masterpieces: one upper range (SATT) and the other lower (ATTB). The two choirs pass the same phrases back and forth as if in echo and then join together in a grand cadence. This motet can be found in a large collection of Offertories published in Venice in 1611; the book's publication was sponsored by the Archbishop of Gniezno, Wojciech Baranowski.

In this soundtrack, I doubled Choir I with 2 violins, 2 tenor gambas, organ 1 and chitarrone. I doubled Choir II with tenor cornetto, 3 trombones and organ 2. The original MIDI file was created by Anna Maria Sitkiewicz and can be found on CPDL.org. The vocal simulations were generated using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid and the instrumental sounds were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0.

Text:

Tu es Petrus
et super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam
et portae inferi non praevalebunt adversus eam.
Et tibi dabo claves regni caelorum.

Translation:

You are Peter
and upon this rock I will build my church
and the gates of Hell shall not prevail against it.
and I will give you the keys to Heaven.

Description of the photos:

1. The modern day nave and alter of Gniezno Cathedral, a probable venue for Zieleński's choir. Although the cathedral has retained much of the original structure, its interior was destroyed multiple times since the 17th Century due to repeated fires and wars.
2. Cover page of the organ partbook for the motet "Tu es Petrus," Venice, 1611
3. Modern day organ and ceiling of the Gniezno Cathedral; Most likely the original setup in Zieleński's time had two such organs placed at either end of the nave.
4. Musical angels, Guido Reni, Cappella di S Andra Chiesa di S Gregorio (Rome); details of trombone, violin, cornetto -- an instrumental complement that was common in Zieleński's time.
5. The original 12th century doors of Gniezno Cathedral
6. The penitent St. Peter, El Greco, c1595
7. Christ delivering the keys of the church to St. Peter, Perugino, Sistine Chapel (Vatican) c1482

videos.title: Diomedes Cato: 3 pieces for lute (c.1605)

localized.title: Diomedes Cato: 3 pieces for lute (c.1605)
localized.description:
Three lute pieces by Diomedes Cato:

  0:02  Prelude des preludes
  1:40  Favorito
  4:23  Fantasy

Although born in Treviso, Italy, Diomedes Cato made his career composing music and performing concerts at the courts of Poland and Lithuania. Nevertheless, his fine reputation as a composer spread far and wide across northern Europe. His works can be found in multiple sources from several nations. For example, the "Prelude" and "Fantasy" presented here were copied by hand into an English collection "The Lutebooke of Herbert, Lord of Cherbury (1610)." These pieces have a lilting, meditative quality about them similar to the "Airs de Cour" popularized in 17th Century France. The "Favorito" comes to us from a Flemish collection printed by Joachim van den Hove in 1612. Other works have survived in Swedish, Italian and German collections.

The original MIDI file was compiled by Serge Gerbode and uploaded to his website lutemusic.org. I tweaked the sound using the iPhone MIDI editor Music Studio 2.0 and the open source software Audacity.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous Spanish: Verbum caro factum est (c.1550)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous Spanish: Verbum caro factum est (c.1550)
localized.description:
Verbum caro factus est

  0:06  Plainchant "Verbum caro"
  0:21  Four-part villancico for voices (ATTB)
  1:47  Instrumental arr. (shawm, 2 crumhorns, trombone, tamborine, recorder)

This mostly homophonic 16th century Spanish villancico was intended for the Christmas season and derives its melody line from a Plainchant with the same title. The author of the 16th Century version (perhaps Mateo Flecha) adopted the first nine notes of the original Latin chant (F-F-F-E-G-G-A) for his cantus line. In the polyphonic version, one can hear the festive spirit and the driving 6/8 rhythm that might make it more appropriate for dance music - perhaps a galliard for a secular occasion. Songs of this type, like Josquin's "In te Domine, speravi," are sometimes described as "macaronic" because they vacillate between two or more languages (usually Latin and one other).  The book from which this song comes to us, El Cancionero de Upsala, has a convoluted history. It's editor was Venetian, the patron was an Calabrian duke, the pieces are mostly in northern Spanish dialects and the collection is housed in Uppsala, Sweden. 

The words were entered using the MAIKA voice bank in VOCALOID 4. The instrumental sounds were created using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.  The original MIDI file was uploaded to CPDL.org by Paco Marmol and Manolo Casaus, but I added an additional repeat to include the second verse. In this latest rendition, I changed the instrumentation, adjusted the reverb / echo, created a more legato effect in the voices, rebalanced the voices, switched the top line to a "female" alto and corrected the pronunciation to reflect a more northern Spanish dialect from the early 16th Century.

Text:

Verbum caro factum est (The word was made flesh)
Porque todos os salvéis, (so that all of you are salvation)

Y la Virgen le dezía: (And the Virgin said to Him)
Vida de la vida mia, (Life of my life)
Hijo mio, ¿qué os haría, (My son, what shall I do for you?)
Que no tengo en qué os echéis? (for I have nothing with which to cover you)
O riquezas (temporales/terrenales), (O wealthy ones of the world)
¿No daréis unos pañales (Do you not give a sheet of cloth)
A Jesus que entre animales (to Jesus who among the animals)
Es nasçido según véis? (is born that you may see)

Description of photos:
1. "Verbum caro" plainchant, Cistercian Antiphon collection MS#1799, Austrian, 13th Century. There are even older manuscripts with the same notes (F-F-F-E-G-G-A) going back to the 12th Century.
2. "Verbum caro factum est" for 4 voices, Cancionero de Uppsala, 16th Century Spanish MS, published in Venice, 1556
3. The infant Jesus holding a lamb, Bernardino Luini, c1520
4. Adoration of the Magi, Paolo Veronese, 1582
5. Three musicians playing crumhorns, Heinrich Aldegrever, 1551
6. Spanish musicians playing shawms and trombone, details on a medallion, Juan Marin y Bautista Vazquez, Sevilla, 1564
7. Angel playing recorder, detail from Virgin and Child, Giovanni Bellini, 1488

videos.title: Anonymous Italian: Bella gerit (c.1476)

localized.title: Anonymous Italian: Bella gerit (c.1476)
localized.description:
Bella gerit

  0:06  Original song (male alto, lute, psaltery, harp)
  1:12  Original song (ATTB + plucked strings)
  2:18  Instrumental arrangement (2 shawms, 2 sackbuts, drum, plucked strings)

This very short, 4-part polyphonic song in simple Latin, was carved note for note into the elaborately inlaid wood panels lining the duke's palace in Urbino, Italy. Although the woodcarver was likely using a contemporary chansonnier as his source, no print or manuscript copies of this composition have survived. The song was dedicated to Federico III da Montefeltro, one of the greatest patrons of the arts in the Renaissance era. Federico had begun his career as a victorious warrior on the battlefield and subsequently became lord of Urbino. Despite his military prowess, he had always viewed himself as an intellectual powerhouse and invested tremendous resources patronizing some of the greatest artists, scientists, philosophers and architects of his generation. 

I transcribed the entirety of the 4 part motet using a black-and-white photo of the mensural notation etched onto the walls of the Palazzo Ducale in Urbino. I made minimal corrections to the original score since the artist had done an admirable job of copying the music accurately. The rhythm of the music is suggestive of a basse dance  (switching between 3/4 and 6/8 time) except for the brief intrusion of four modal chords based on the four syllables of FE-DE-RI-CUS (Federico in Latin) in the middle of the piece.

I used the MAIKA Vocaloid to simulate four male singers and the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0 to generate the instrumental sounds. I used a more archaic sounding metal strung lute to double the top line. I also added a drum beat to emphasize the sometimes obscure 3 rhythm and to capture the martial spirit of the piece.

Text:

Bella gerit musasque colit (He conducts war and worships the Muses)
Federicus ! (Federico)
Omnium maximus italorum dux (Greatest leader of the Italians)
fortis atque domi (and powerful at home)

videos.title: Pierre Certon: Si iay eu tousiours (c.1540)

localized.title: Pierre Certon: Si iay eu tousiours (c.1540)
localized.description:
Si iay eu tousiours (Si j'ay eu tousjours)

Although Pierre Certon was a member of the clergy and a prominent choirmaster, his most enduring works have been his chansons of which many have survived thanks to the diligence of his Parisian publishers such Pierre Attaingnant. Unlike his mentor Claudin de Sermisy, Certon’s chansons were more freely composed with less reliance on chordal harmonies.

mesprisant e a que chascun prise (disdainful to everyones praise)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Dieterich Buxtehude: Allegro from Sonata in a minor (BuxWV 272) (c.1670)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Dieterich Buxtehude: Allegro from Sonata in a minor (BuxWV 272) (c.1670)
localized.description:
Allegro from Sonata for violin and viola da gamba in a minor

The violin sonatas of Buxtehude derive in part from the Venetian church repertoire of the early 17th century (sonata da chiesa) as well as the Viennese school of Heinrich Biber. They evoke the whimsical improvisations and the dramatic flare in the works of Dario Castello, Claudio Monteverdi and Girolamo Frescobaldi with their alternating solos by violin and viola da gamba. This intermediate sonata form would eventually evolve into the more structured and stylized late Baroque apex form of Corelli, Bach and Handel. In this Allegro, one can hear the basso continuo melody repeated more than 25 times throughout the movement -- in the ostinato style of a Baroque chaconne. There is certain opera-like back-and-forth dialogue between the violin and the bass instrument (in this case, a viola da gamba) throughout the piece.

In this latest rendition, I adjusted the attack and decay of the violin patch, created a more legato effect, tweaked the reverb effect and rebalanced the instruments. As before, I used the Music Studio 2.0 app for the iPhone from Steinberg.

----------

videos.title: [New Rendition] Johann Pachelbel: Canon and Gigue in D (c.1690)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Johann Pachelbel: Canon and Gigue in D (c.1690)
localized.description:
Johann Pachelbel: Canon and Gigue 

  0:06  Canon (Kanon)
  4:48  Gigue

The most enduring musical canon of all time is perhaps that of Johann Pachelbel (1653-1706). No one knows the exact date nor the occasion on which the piece was performed, but some have speculated that it may have been a musical gift for the wedding of J.S. Bach's eldest brother, Johann Christoph (1694). If so, it was written at the end of the composer life perhaps in his final decade when he resided in the town of Nuremberg. Others have viewed the work as a purely academic exercise from a much earlier period (perhaps as far back as 1680).  The tune begins in the bass line with 8 simple notes of melody and then repeats the same 8 notes in ostinato style for the full duration of the canonic movement. The score has only 4 instrumental voices: 3 violins and basso continuo.

This electronic version of the Canon and Gigue was adapted from a MIDI file that I edited extensively.  The original raw digital file was compiled and uploaded by an anonymous author on the website kunstderfuge.com.  In this latest rendition, I tweaked the violin sound to produce a more "archaic" quality, adjusted the attack / decay, rebalanced the instruments and added a double bass to the mix (one octave below the bass gamba).

The photos in this video are described below. 

1. Full score of Pachelbel's Canon, 19th cent. manuscript; this is the oldest extant copy of the Canon since the original is now lost.
2. "Sunshine" violin, Antonio Stradivarius, 1677
3. Court musicians, Antonio D. Gabbiani, c.1685
4. "Cipriani Potter" violin, A. Stradivarius, 1683
5. David Leeuw and Family, Abraham van den Tempel, 1671

videos.title: Niccolò Broco: O tientalora (tiente alora) (c.1500)

localized.title: Niccolò Broco: O tientalora (tiente alora) (c.1500)
localized.description:
O tiente alora (a.k.a. tentalora, tientalora, tente alora)

  0:06  Verse 1 (ATTB + lute)
  1:10  Verse 2 (alto, medieval lute, psaltery, bass viol)
  1:58  Verse 3 (tenor, lute)
  2:46  Verse 4 (alto, recorder, medieval lute, psaltery, bass viol)
  3:34  Verse 5 (ATTB + lute)

This lesser known composer of the late 15th and early 16th centuries was prominently represented in Ottaviano Petrucci's 8th Book of Frottole. Other than the approximate dates of his career, almost nothing else is known about this writer of Italian secular music. This polyphonic realization is wrapped around a familiar Italian folk song which can be heard in the tenor line (see Verse 3). Its theme is one of courtly love -- specifically a yearning for a lady who is ever distant. The song was very popular at the time and had numerous contemporary variations - both vocal and instrumental. In this latest rendition, I entered all 5 verses. The translation was a bit challenging because not all the words in the text can be found in Modern Italian, and spellings of words had not been standardized in that era. For example "tiente" in the title probably meant tempt (tenta/tentare). One translator from in an old 1970s LP surmised that it meant "stop" (which does not go well with the context). Other ambiguities should also be mentioned. "Fora" is likely "fuori" (outside) and "mora" probably meant "delay" (as in Latin) instead of "mulberry" (as in Modern Italian). They were either derived from an extinct dialect or borrowed from another language.

The MIDI file for this piece is my own that I transcribed it from a modern Italian score. I added the text using the Vocaloid voice encoder and the Spanish language module MAIKA.  In this latest rendition, I corrected some of the vowel sounds, adjusted the balance of the voices, tweaked the reverb & echo, created a more legato effect and added all 5 verses instead of just the first 2. I generated the instrumental sounds using my iPhone synthesizer program Music Studio 2. Reverb was added using Audacity. Verses 1 and 5 are presented by the full chorus, verses 2 and 4 highlight the cantus part and Verse 3 reminds the listener of the original folksong melody.

Text and translation:

O tiente alora, (O tempt [me] now)
non voler che per ti mora ([I] wish that you not delay.)
El tuo vago e dolce aspecto (Your lovely and sweet appearance)
mi consuma e struge ogn' hora. (consumes and destroys me always.)

El mio cor che tanto t'ame (My heart that loves you so much)
e che sempre si te honora (and that always honors you).
Arde in mezzo de una fiamma (It burns in the center [of me] like a flame)
che mia vampa dentro e fora (that is my passion inside and out)

Ti me dai troppo tormento (You give me so much torment)
dolce e cara mia signora (my sweet and dear Lady)
dame almen qualche contento (Give me at least some joy)
che alquanto mi ristora.  (that somewhat restores me)

Per ti, donna, i' vo disperso (Because of you, I am lost)
per lo mondo in la malora (the damned world)
che sconfito e fia sumerso (is defeated and submerged)
chi di donna se inamora.  (for him who is in love with a woman)

Ora adonque, donna, aiuta  (Now thus, Lady, help)
el tuo servo che non mora (your servant without delay)
Se la vita fia perduta ([for] though my life be lost)
non fia persa l'alma ancora (the soul is not yet lost)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Dario Castello: Sonata prima (1629)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Dario Castello: Sonata prima (1629)
localized.description:
Very little is known about the composer Dario Castello (c.1590-c.1658) other than that he was one of the many well regarded maestros at the Basilica San Marco in Venice.  He worked in the shadows of the grand titans of Venice of the likes of Claudio Monteverdi and Giovanni Gabrieli. This sonata from the collection "Sonate concertate in stil moderno, Libro II" was written for sundry instruments.

In this most recent rendition, I used the sound of a cornetto (a wooden trumpet) in the soprano line. Basso continuo parts include a church organ, trombone and chitarrone. The original MIDI file was uploaded by Andrea Friggi to the website IMSLP.com.  The .xms file that lead to this soundtrack was generated using the MIDI editing app on the iPhone Music Studio 2.0. I made the following changes to the earlier .xms file. I slowed the tempo, tweaked the attack / decay and adjusted the reverb. Although the combination of cornetto, trombone and organ was probably quite common in the early 17th century, the attack and decay properties of the individual instruments are so vastly different that it must have been a challenge to play together accurately, especially in a large, live space as San Marco.

localized.description:
Girolamo Frescobaldi was the principal organist at St. Peter's Basilica in Rome for most of his career.  Today, he is remembered alongside Monteverdi as one of the most influential composers of both secular and ecclesiastical music in the transition period between the late Renaissance and early Baroque.  The "Capriccio sopra un sogetto" anticipates later compositions of the Baroque with its well organized thematic development and flowing fugal counterpoint. This soundtrack was created using a MIDI files compiled by the Japanese recorder ensemble Aeolian Consort. In general, capricci were free style compositions, often loosely organized fugues, that allowed authors to explore various contrasting themes within a certain limited set of musical parameters.

videos.title: George Frideric Handel: "As steals the morn" from HWV 55 (1740)

localized.title: George Frideric Handel: "As steals the morn" from HWV 55 (1740)
localized.description:
This duet for soprano and tenor (accompanied by oboe, bassoon and strings) is the final aria and penultimate movement of an allegorical opera fancifully titled "L'Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato (the happy one, the pensive one and the moderate one)" (HWV 55). Based in part on two poetic works by John Milton a century earlier, Handel's text was arranged by the librettist Charles Jennens (of "Messiah" fame). "As steals the morn" is a reworking of Prospero's philosophical musings in Shakespeare's Tempest, Act V, Scene 1. Although the majority of the original opera has gone largely neglected for most of the last three centuries, this aria has been a favorite hit since Handel's own lifetime and was included as a high point in several of his outdoor performances at Vauxhall Gardens. The words "truth does fancy's charm dissolve" seems to extoll the Enlightenment belief that clarity of thought triumphs over all things fantastical. 

The original MIDI file was created by HTimetey and can be found on the musescore.com website. I used the Primo V2 and Cyber Songman Vocaloid to synthesize the "vocal" parts, and I used the Music Studio 2.0 app for the iPhone to simulate the orchestral sounds.

Text:

As steals the morn upon the night,
And melts the shades away:
So truth does fancy's charm dissolve,
The fumes that did the mind involve,
Restoring intellectual day.

videos.title: Pierre Phalese the Elder: 2 Passomezzi (1568)

localized.title: Pierre Phalese the Elder: 2 Passomezzi (1568)
localized.description:
2 passomezzi

  0:06  Passomezzo
  2:55  Passomezzo d'Italye

The elder Pierre Phalèse, like his Flemish contemporary Tielman Susato, was one of the most recognized music publishers of the 16th Century culling masterworks from nearly every genre across Continental Europe. During his long career, he produced more than 130 unique volumes of popular chansons, dance pieces, motets, masses and magnificats. Unlike Susato, however, Phalèse also published a large body of virtuosic lute solos in very precise tabulature form.  His passamezzi, which were variations on Italian folk melodies, were constructed over a repeating bass line. His use of increasingly more complex divisions gives us an idea of how ornamentation was imagined and applied throughout the High Renaissance. The MIDI file from which this rendition was generated was originally compiled and uploaded to the website lutemusic.org by Serge Gerbode.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Antony Holborne: The Fairie Round (a galliard) (1599)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Antony Holborne: The Fairie Round (a galliard) (1599)
localized.description:
Galliard Fairie Round

  0:06  Version 1 (3 violins, tenor viol, bass viol, harpsichord, theorbo)
  1:40  Version 2 (3 recorders, crumhorn, bass viol, harpsichord, theorbo) + lute

This short piece (a galliard alternating between 3/4 and 6/8) was included in a collection of secular music (mostly dance tune) for 5 instruments each - principally violins, viols and woodwinds. It is the only work from the Renaissance era to have been included on the Golden Record place aboard the Voyager I spacecraft which launched in 1977 and departed the Solar System in 2012.

The theme of fairies was trending in the late Elizabethan period with the likes of Edmund Spenser in his series of epic poems "The Fairie Queen" (1590-96) and William Shakespeare in his comic play "Midsummer Night's Dream" (c.1596). The pdf score from which I created the MIDI the whole was uploaded to IMSLP.org by Christian Mondrup. In this latest rendition, I changed the instrumentation, adjusted the timbre of the stringed instruments and tweaked the reverb. On the second round, I superimposed Holborne's lute arrangement for the "Fairie Round" from a lute tabulature printed in the same period.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Johann Sebastian Bach: Brandenburg Concerto #2, BWV 1047 (c.1718)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Johann Sebastian Bach: Brandenburg Concerto #2, BWV 1047 (c.1718)
localized.description:
Brandenburg Concerto #2 in F major, BWV 1047

  0:06  Allegro
  5:35  Andante
  8:52  Allegro assai

The Second "Brandenburg" Concerto is likely the most frequently performed work by Johann Sebastian Bach in the modern era. Yet in his lifetime, it was hardly noticed as a work of any importance.  The man to whom Bach dedicated this autographed copy of six concerti, Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, was probably not a connoisseur of fine music and failed to appreciate the monumental gift he had been bestowed. Also, he may not have had an instrumental complement that could execute such a complicated work of music. Bach's collection disappeared for more than a century but amazingly reappeared unblemished in the early 18th Century. It is a purely secular work from his early traveling years that appeared long before his massive output of church cantatas and his offering of grand oratorios for the congregation of St. Thomas in Leipzig.

Despite its obscure beginnings, a recording of the first Allegro movement from this Concerto (along with many other recordings) was etched onto a gold plated disk and mounted onto the side of NASA's Voyager I spacecraft; and thus, a piece of music thoroughly neglected at its inception has come to symbolize humanity’s accomplishments in the vastness and eternity of space.

Similar to some of Vivaldi's concerti, this Bach masterpiece contains more than one solo instrumentalist.  The 4 solo instruments are trumpet, recorder (or flute), violin and oboe - each taking turns performing its own virtuosic lines. For this recording, I downloaded MIDI files from IMSLP.com (compiled and uploaded by Michel Rondeau) and tweaked the sounds of each instrument using the Music Studio 2 app on the iPhone. In this latest rendition, I altered the individual instrumental patches to achieve a more archaic sonority, adjusted the reverb, slowed the tempo, reshaped the trills, added in the dynamic markings that Bach recommended and rebalanced the instruments to highlight the solo passages. For the video, I cropped the entirely of Bach's original score from a facsimile. My arrangement is as follows: 4 solo parts (alto recorder, clarino trumpet, oboe d'amore, solo violin), harpsichord, 2 violins I, 2 violins 2, 1 violas, 1 cellos and 1 double bass.

videos.title: Edmund Turges: Enforce yorselfe as goddes knyght (c.1485) (Original Pronunciation)

localized.title: Edmund Turges: Enforce yorselfe as goddes knyght (c.1485) (Original Pronunciation)
localized.description:
Enforce yorselfe as goddes knyght (Enforce yourself as God's knight)

This secular song for 3 voices was preserved in a neatly handwritten collection of English language works known as the Fayrfax Manuscript. It was written by the composer Edmund Turges, mostly remembered for his ethereal church motets in the Eton Choirbook.  Its long-winded melismatic cadences are typical of an older style of Anglo-Burgundian music from the early to middle 15th century. The theme of the piece is a patriotic one (perhaps dedicated to one of the many English campaigns against the French): a kind of prayer and battle cry for a soldier preparing for war. It calls to mind the English battle hymn "Agincourt carol" and the Franco-Flemish "L'homme armé." "Sovereign lord" probably refers to King Henry VII, the first Tudor monarch and father to Henry VIII.

Unlike my earlier rendition, I used an English language Vocaloid (Cyber Songman) for this soundtrack. Although there is debate around late Middle English pronunciation because the 15th Century was period of dramatic shifts in vowel sounds. Here are some recommended sound adjustments. The initial "k" in knyght was probably enunciated although not in every dialect. The "y" in words like "knyght" "ryght" and "myght" were pronounced as "əi" instead of "ai." Some words may be recognizable to modern readers but retained their archaic form such as "strenketh" (strengthen) and "goddes" (God's). 

Text:
Enforce yorselfe as goddes knyght (Enforce yourself as God's knight)
to strenketh yowr comyns in ther ryght. (to strengthen your commands in there right)
Soverayn lord in erth most excellent (Sovereign Lord in earth most excellent)
Whom god hath chose oure gyde (whom God has chosen as our guide)
to be with gyffts great & evident (to be with gifts great and evident)
of marshall power & also hye dignite (of martial power and also high dignity)
Sith it is so now, let yowr labor be (Since it is so now, may your efforts be)

videos.title: Anonymous Italian: In focho, in focho (c.1490)

localized.title: Anonymous Italian: In focho, in focho (c.1490)
localized.description:
This frottola by an anonymous Italian composer is one of many similar works bound in a beautifully illuminated, late 15th century manuscript (Chansonnier I-MOe alfa f9.9). Although its theme is one of courtly love in the Medieval tradition, the words are expressed in a gentle, philosophical manner suggestive of the sonnet writer Francesco Petrarca.

I added the words using a facsimile of the original manuscript which can be found at IMSLP.org. I used the Maika Spanish language Vocaloid to generate the vocal simulations and added instrumental sounds (lutes, harp, flute) using Music Studio 2 (an iPhone app). The translation is a bit approximate and may need some minor correcting.

In focho, in focho la mia vita passa (in fire, in fire my life goes on)
et come espente l'uno (and as the one is spent,)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Tomaso Albinoni: Oboe Concerto, Opus 9, No. 2 (1722)
localized.description:
To skip to a different movement, click on the time stamp below:

  0:00   Allegro
  4:24   Adagio
  7:50   Allegro

Tomaso Giovanni Albinoni (1671-1751) composed a great number of concerti for violin and assorted other instruments.  His best known among these has been the D minor Oboe Concerto (No. 2) from Opus 9.  It was dedicated to Duke Maximilian of Bavaria by way of a 1722 printed edition from the Netherlands.  Most striking is the middle Adagio movement in which the solo oboist sustains long, plaintive notes over the string section's arpeggios. The slow segment is sandwiched between two jaunty Allegro movements that recall the lively spirit of Vivaldi and other Venetian compatriots of the High Baroque in Northern Italy. The original MIDI file was compiled by kmaster300 and uploaded to the website musescore.com . I used the sound patches for solo oboe, violins 1, violins 2, violas, celli, double bass and harpsichord. In this latest rendition, I spatially separated the violins, added more heft to the continuo line, adjusted the reverb / echo, created a more delicate sounding set of trills, adjusted the attack / decay of the oboe sound and added a bit of dynamics to the strings. I kept most of kmaster300's exquisite ornaments in the solo oboe part, but I did switch some of B♮s for B♭s (or vice versa) in the 3rd movement to eliminate certain dissonances.

videos.title: Giovanni Gabrieli: Jubilate Deo a 15 (1597)

localized.title: Giovanni Gabrieli: Jubilate Deo a 15 (1597)
localized.description:
This grandiose polychoral motet for 15 voices by Giovanni Gabrieli was created expressly for the uniquely powerful acoustics beneath the dome of la Basilica San Marco. In this soundtrack, I have divided the "singers" into three 5 part choruses (SSATBar, SSATBar and TTTBB). Chorus 1 is doubled by 2 cornetti, 3 trombones and organ. Chorus 2 by 2 violins, 3 viols, chitarrone and violone. Chorus 3 by 5 trombones and organ. In the same 1597 publication that contains this 15 part motet, one can also find several instrumental canzon, some of which are specifically designated as solos for cornetti. The text is combination of different Psalm texts.

Text:

Iubilate Deo omnis terra: exultate iusti in Domino,
et gloriamini omnes recti corde.

Quoniam exaudivit Dominus deprecationem meam:
Dominus orationem meam suscepit.

O laeta dies, O fausta dies, haec dies quam fecit Dominus.
Exultemus et laetemur in ea.

Translation:

Rejoice in the Lord all the earth: rejoice, you righteous in the Lord,
and glorify, all who have a good heart.

Because the Lord hath heard my pleas:
The Lord has received my prayer.

O happy day, O joyful day, this day which the Lord made.
Let us rejoice and be happy in him.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Georg Philipp Telemann: Overture in A minor for flute (c.1730)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Georg Philipp Telemann: Overture in A minor for flute (c.1730)
localized.description:
The A minor Overture (a.k.a. TWV 55:a2) is the 1st movement of a 7 movement Suite that Telemann modeled after the Suites of his French contemporaries Hotteterre, Rameau and François Couperin.  Telemann's selection of the flute as his solo instrument was a particularly Parisian choice.  The so-called "galant" style of the court at Versailles called for a lighter, non-dogmatic yet elegant form.

This video includes a reproduction of the complete manuscript of Telemann's A minor Suite Overture (Darmstadt University and Library), likely copied by the composer (or at least with the composer's permission).  The MIDI file was generated using the pdf scores for the 5 individual parts by Mario Bolognani (IMSLP.org).  I arranged the parts to feature solo transverse flute, violins 1, violins 2, violas, cellos and basso continuo (harpsichord and double bass).  In this latest rendition, I lightened the trills, added dynamics as marked in the original score, slowed the tempo a bit, rebalanced the instrumental sounds and adjusted the reverb.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Thomas Tallis: Loquebantur, variis linguis (c.1555)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Thomas Tallis: Loquebantur, variis linguis (c.1555)
localized.description:
Although transcribed in neat handwriting around the year 1570 (a decade and a half into the Queen Elizabeth's reign), "Loquebantur" retains many of the elements of pre-Reformation church music and has been dated to the late period of Queen Mary's reign (c.1555-1558). Like most other works contained in the Baldwin Manuscript (Oxford 979-83), the text is Latin instead of English. The structure of the piece is also more traditional with its prominent soprano duet, an imitative polyphony, the antiphonal arrangement and interjections of plainchant. Also the sequence of repeating progressively shorter segments of the main chorus is reminiscent of other Tallis antiphons as well as the works of John Sheppard and William Mundy. This motet celebrates the Feast of Pentecost and recalls Jesus' apostles who suddenly spoke in different languages to spread the word of the Gospels.

I used the pdf score uploaded to CPDL.org by Ross Jallo and transposed it down a minor third to attain the approximate, original range of the piece.  I entered the Latin text using MAIKA, a Spanish language voice module for the Vocaloid 4 program.  In this latest rendition, I adjusted the reverb, corrected a few vowel sounds, added some natural dynamics and created an more legato effect. 

Text:

(chant) Loquebantur...

(chorus) ...variis linguis apostoli. Alleluia. 
Magnalia Dei. Alleluia.

(chant) Repleti sunt omnes Spiritu Sancto, et coeperunt loqui.
(chant) Gloria Patri, et Filio, et Spiritui Sancto.

The Apostles spoke in different languages. Hallelujah.
of the greatness of God. Alleluia.

They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak.
Glory to the Father, Son and Holy Ghost.

5. Ceiling of the Chapel Royal, Hampton Court

videos.title: [New Rendition] Georg Philipp Telemann: Wassermusik (TWV 55:C3). Ouverture (1723)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Georg Philipp Telemann: Wassermusik (TWV 55:C3). Ouverture (1723)
localized.description:
Although Telemann travelled throughout Europe, he likely identified himself as a resident of the city of Hamburg in Northern Germany.  At one time or another, he was music director for the Hamburg Opera House, the Boys' Music School and all five of the main Protestant churches whose tall steeples marked the city skyline.  His Water music (Wassermusik), also known as the Hamburg Ebb und Fluth (Ebb and Flow), was a secular work for small chamber ensemble celebrating his City's standing in Europe as a hub of maritime activity and naval military prowess. The sole surviving manuscript edition of this opus, copied by Christoph Graupner, is scored for 2 oboes, bassoon, violins 1, violins 2, viola and bass continuo. One can hear the "galant" style of the French schools of Rameau and Couperin with dance-like inégal rhythms and simple melodies. The music is light and casual unlike the weightier German and Austrian themes of Buxtehude, J.S. Bach and Biber. During Telemann's lifetime, this particular collection of stylized dance movements became one of his most enduring achievements.

----------

In this electronic rendition created with an iPhone app MusicStudio2, I also added the sounds of double bass (one octave below cello) and harpsichord. Because I could not locate a MIDI file that was scored for all 7 independent parts in the original score (including 3 double reeds AND 4 strings), I compiled my own MIDI by extrapolating the notes from a pdf file of the complete score by Mario Bolognani at IMSLP.org. In this latest rendition, I refined the sonority of the violins, re-balanced the wind and string sections and adjusted the reverb / echo settings.

----------

7. The altar of St. Michael's Church
8. St. Mary's, the main Catholic church, not directly linked to Telemann but an unmistakable Hamburg landmark. 
9. View of Hamburg, Elias Galli, c1680

videos.title: Si par souffrir: the original chanson and its variants (c.1540)

localized.title: Si par souffrir: the original chanson and its variants (c.1540)
localized.description:
Si par souffrir

  0:06  Jean Courtois' original 4 part chanson (ATTB) accompanied by Narváez's lute setting
  1:53  Tielman Susato's Pavane "Si par souffrir" (cornetto, 3 trombones, tympani)
  3:57  Jean Lecocq's 5 part parody chanson with canon (AATTB)

Although Jean Courtois had a limited output during his lifetime (or perhaps, more likely, his other creations have been lost over the centuries), this little treasure of a chanson was preserved thrice over thanks to the diligence of the Flemish publisher and composer Tielman Susato. In the 1544 publication "Le Quatrieme Livre des Chansons," Susato printed the original 4 part chanson in 4 separate partbooks. In 1551, Susato realized his own parody -- a solemn pavane in his most famous of Renaissance collections "Het derde musyck boexken" (a.k.a. "Le Danserye"). Before that, in 1545, Susato had also published Jean Lecocq's 5 part "Si par souffrir" which contains a canon in the two cantus parts. The chanson was unquestionably popular throughout central Europe in the 1540s; there were also two additional lute intabulations from the same period -- one by a Southern German Hans Newsiedler and the other by a Spaniard Luys de Narváez. The theme of the song is a veiled reference to courtly love. An earlier Anonymous chanson with the same title, but different melody, was published more than a decade earlier by the Parisian Pierre Attaingnant.

In this latest rendition, I have added a hint of natural dynamics, created a more legato effect, adjusted the reverb (and echo), slowed the tempo and added lute accompaniment to the original chanson using Narvaez's setting. I also added Jean Lecocq's canonic parody. The original MIDI files for both vocal settings were compiled and uploaded to CPDL.org by André Vierendeels. The MIDI for the Narvaez lute setting was created by Serge Gerbode and can be found on his website lutemusic.org. In the lute accompaniment, I changed all of Gerbode's F# to F to be compatible with the original mode used by Courtois.

Text and translation:

Si par souffrir l'on peult vaincre fortune, (If by suffering, Fortune can be vanquished)
je croy en fin le pris me demeurer (I believe in the end, the prize will be mine.)
car nuict et jour je ne fais que penser (Because night and day, I am made to think)
a ma douleur et soubdain' infortune. (about my pain and my sudden misfortune.)

2. "Taste," from the Lady and Unicorn series, details from a French tapestry, c1500
3. A tapestry of courtly love depicting a lowly musician charming an aristocratic Lady, probable a often repeated event across Europe throughout the 15th and 16th centuries, Anon. French, c1490
4. A gallant delivering his message of love to the goddess Venus, Roman de la Rose, Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun, MS Harley 4425, Bruges, c1500
5. Cornetti and sackbut players, Giorgio Vasari, 1545

videos.title: Bartolomeo Tromboncino: Ostinato vo' seguire (1509)

localized.title: Bartolomeo Tromboncino: Ostinato vo' seguire (1509)
localized.description:
Ostinato vo' seguire

  0:06  Verse 1 (SATB, lute, harp, bass viol)
  1:56  Verse 2 (soprano, bass lute)
  3:16  Verse 3 (soprano, lute, harp, bass viol)
  4:36  Verse 1 repeated (SATB, recorder, lute, harp, bass viol)

This frottola by the Italian master Tromboncino is unusual with its freely moving cantus part since most works of this genre conformed to a more rigidly vertical homophony. It probably required a more skilled soprano to perform the part successfully especially with an alto line whose notes are staggered by a whole or a half beat.

Modern performances that include all four vocal parts are rare since the publisher Ottaviano Petrucci wrote out lyrics only for the soprano line. The theme is one of courtly love but the target of the affection is somewhat abstract and platonic. In this latest rendition, I added the second and third verses which were published only in the another Petrucci edition containing lute song settings by Franciscus Bosseniensis. I also slowed the tempo and created a more legato effect.

Text (Translation):

Ostinato vo' seguire (Stubbornly I will follow)
La magnanima mia impresa (my magnanimous venture)
Fame Amor, qual voi offesa (Starved Cupid, what offends you)
S'io dovesse ben morire (if I were to die well.)
Ostinato...

Fa me, Ciel, fa me, Fortuna (Do me, Heaven and Fate)
Bene o male como a te piace (good or bad as it pleases you)
Ne piacer ne ingiuria alcuna (No pleasure nor injustice)
per avilirmi o far piu audace (conquers me nor makes me more bold)
Che de l'un non son capace (That the one I am not able [to catch])
L'altro piu non po' fuggire (The other I cannot flea)
Ostinato...

Vica or perda, io non l'attendo (Win or lose, I don't anticipate)
De mia impresa altro che onore:  (from my venture anything other than honor)
Sopra il ciel beato ascendo (Onto blessed heaven I rise)
S'io ne resto vincitore; (If I am stay victorious)
S'io la perdo, alfin gran core (If I lose her, in the end, my heart)
Mostrara l'altro desire. (Will show the greatest desire)
Ostinato...

videos.title: Antonio Scandello: 3 Neapolitan canzone in Saxony (1566)

localized.title: Antonio Scandello: 3 Neapolitan canzone in Saxony (1566)
localized.description:
Three Neapolitan songs arranged by Antonio Scandello

  0:06  Voria che tu cantass'una canzone (CtTTB)
  1:17  Voria che tu cantass' (recorder, lute, harp, viol, spinet)
  2:25  Core mio bello (ATTB)
  3:17  Core mio bello (recorder, lute, harp, viol)
  4:07  In tutto voi chio moro (recorders, crumhorn, viol)

These Italian canzone from the High Renaissance has quite the mix of international elements. Antonio Scandello, a Northern Italian composer from Bergamo, arranged these and other folksongs from Naples, published them in Nuremberg and dedicated them to his patron Augustus, the Elector of Saxony. Scandello, like many other Italian expatriates in the second half of the 16th Century were hired for music making at royal courts throughout Northern Europe.

Scandello's "Voria che tu" is a variation based on the same tune as Azzaiolo's "Vorrei che tu," but with a slightly more playful and antiphonal effect on the "fa-mi" refrain. "Fa mi la mi sol la" is the solmization of the modal notes F-E-A-E-G-A, but it also literally translates to "do it only to me." Despite the songs' Southern origins, Scandello may be recalling his northern roots by using the Venetian spelling on words like "voria" ("vorrei" in Modern Standard Italian). Or it may be an alternate spelling of the Neapolitan "vurria."

The second song "Core mio bello" is more strictly homophonic like earlier Italian frottole and Spanish villancicos. There are also some syncopations and hemiolas in the rhythm that make for some odd emphases on otherwise non-stressed syllables in the Italian language. For example the word "sempre" which in spoken Italian should be "SEM-pre" is sung as "sem-PRE" and "fantasia" which is ordinarily "FAN-ta-SI-a" is pronounced "fan-TA-si-A." 

The vocal simulations were created using the MAIKA voice bank and the VOCALOID 4 software. The instrumental sounds were generated using Music Studio 2. In this latest rendition, I adjusted the reverb, created a more legato effect, corrected some vowel sounds, altered the instrumentation and added an extra instrumental piece at the end. All MIDI files were compiled by Andreas Stenberg absent the Vocaloid "singing."

Text

Canzona #14:
Voria che tu cantass' una canzone (I wish you will sing a song)
Quando mi stai sonando la viola (while you play the viola for me)
E che dicessi fa mi la mi sol la. (and chant fa mi la mi sol la)

Canzon #15:
Core mio bello, cor' in zucherato (My beautiful heart of sweetness)
core che mi stai sempre in fantasia (that keeps me always in dreams)
pigliati quanto voi la vita mia. (take all you want of my life)

4. Concert at a Venetian palace, Giovanni Antonio Fasoli, c1560

6. Woman with mirror, Titian, c1515
7. Pastoral concert, Anon. Italian, c1560
8. Concert, Callisto Piazza, c1555; note the two recorders, lute and viol.
9. Discantus from "In tutto voi chio moro" Scandello, 1566
10. Moritz Castle, a frequent venue for Scandello who spent most of his musical career in Dresden in service of the Electors of Saxony, Moritz and later Augustus.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Thomas Stoltzer: Herr wie lang (c.1525)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Thomas Stoltzer: Herr wie lang (c.1525)
localized.description:
This German spiritual Lied for 5 voices (STTBB) composed by Thomas Stolzer was published as one of many Lutheran hymns and motets by the publisher Georg Rhau in the city of Wittenberg -- the center of the Reformist movement. Although based on the 13th Psalm of Hebrew scripture, the song may have had some historical connection to the long persecution of early Protestants during the Church's inquest against its founder, or perhaps it addresses (in the abstract) the general suffering that late medieval communities experienced in daily life due to plagues, famines and other natural as well as man-made calamities. A sense of deep yearning for a better future is communicated through the many repetitions of key phrases.

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, corrected some pronunciation, shifted the pitch up a half step, rebalanced the voices, slowed the tempo, added pauses between the 3 verses, adjusted the reverb / echo and eliminated some electronic glitches. The voice simulations were generated using the Maika (Spanish language) Vocaloid. The MIDI file used in this video was compiled and uploaded to CPDL.org by Sabine Cassola.

Text in modern German:

Herr, wie lang willst du mein so gar vergessen?
Wie lang verbirgest du dein Antlitz vor mir?
Wie lang soll ich Rat suchen in meiner Seele
und Leid tragen in meinem Herzen?
Herr, wie lang soll sich der Feind
über mich erheben?

Schau doch und erhör mich, Herr mein Gott,
erleucht meine Augen,
daß ich nicht im Tod entschlafe,
daß nicht mein Feind sich rühme,
er sei mein mächtig worden,
und meine Widersacher sich nicht freuen,
daß umgestossen sei.

Ich hoff aber auf deine Güte,
mein Herz freuet sich deins Heils.
Ich will dem Herrn singen
daß er mir wieder aufgeholfen hat.

Translation:

Lord, how long will you forget about me?
How long are you hiding your face from me?
How long should I seek counsel in my soul
and bear suffering in my heart?
Lord, how long should the enemy
rise above me?

Look and listen to me, Lord God,
enlighten my eyes
that I do not rest in death,
that my enemy does not boast, that
he rules over me,
and that my adversaries are not happy
that he has been knocked down.

I hope for your goodness,
my heart looks forward to your salvation.
I want to sing to the Lord
that he has helped me again.

Description of the photos:

1. Cover page of George Rhau's Newe Dudsche Geistliche Gesenge (New German Spiritual Songs), 1544; this collection contains Stoltzer's "Herr wie lang"
2. King David with psaltery singing the Psalms, Anonymous South German, Ms Harley 2953, c1530
3. First page from Genesis (the title in Hebrew is pronounced be-re-sheet), personal copy of a Jewish bible from which Luther derived his psalm translations, Anon. Italian, Brescia, 1494
4. Castle Church (Schlosskirche) of Wittenberg, the site of Luther's 95 Theses posting.
5. The table of contents page from Rhau's Newe Dudsche Geistliche Gesenge, 1544
6. Psalm 13 in Latin, from the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry, whose original illustrators died of plague.
7. Martin Luther's translation of Psalm 13, reprinted in 1573
8. Concert of angels, Tilman Riemenschneider, c1500
9. King David praying to God, Anon. French, c1420
10. View of the city of Wittenberg
10. King David playing his harp and singing, Gerrit van Honthorst, 1622, created about 8 decades after the song, but seems to capture the feeling of the original song.

videos.title: Adrian Willaert: Qui veult aymer (c.1540)

localized.title: Adrian Willaert: Qui veult aymer (c.1540)
localized.description:
Qui veult aymer (Qui veut aimer)

  0:06  Original chanson for 6 voices (SSTTBB)
  2:20  Instrumental setting for 2 cornetti and 4 trombones

This short 6 part chanson is a madrigal written for 3 pairs of singers: 2 cantus, 2 tenor and 2 bassus. Each pair is performing a partial canon. Such a style of polyphony was likely adapted from Willaert's mentor Jean Mouton whose motet "Nesciens mater" for 8 singers (4 pairs of canonic parts) bears a striking resemblance. Although this work was composed in the midst of Willaert's tenure at St. Mark's in Venice, it is very different from his Italian language compositions which tended more towards homophony and away from imitative passages. One might imagine the eventual transformation of Willaert's canonic imitations into the more ambitious antiphonal echo of later polychoral works by his students Andrea and Giovanni Gabrieli.

Text:

Qui veult aymer, il fault estre joyeulx
et aller veoir sa dame souveraine.
deux ou trois fois ou quatre la semaine
pour en avoir ung baiser gratieulx.

He who want to love must be happy
and go to see his sovereign lady
two or three times or four (times) a week.
to have a graceful kiss.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous Spanish (or Portuguese): Ollademe, gentil dona (c.1490)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Anonymous Spanish (or Portuguese): Ollademe, gentil dona (c.1490)
localized.description:
Ollademe, gentil dona

Although very simple in both melody and harmony, this villancico of unknown origin is unusual in its design.  The score explicitly suggests a him (El) and a her (Ella) to sing the lyrics alternatingly -- somewhat like an operatic performance (still more than a century away). The song's theme is a common one for the late Middle Ages: a man of uncertain background presents himself before a lady of noble upbringing, but he is quickly shunned and turned away even before he has had the chance to prove himself worthy. The rhythm is a 6/8 beat and has a certain basse dance-like feel. The single reference to a town, Santaren, is likely the central Portuguese city of Santarém. Hence the gallant young man may be a traveler from neighboring Portugal who does not speak the noble lady's "refined" Catalan dialect. In fact, several Portuguese words are interspersed throughout the song ("do" instead of "de" as well as "muito" instead of "mucho.") Because there were many Portuguese composers at the Catalan court, this kind of scenario may have played out frequently. Margaret Philpot's excellent recording attributes this piece to the composer Juan del Encina, but the original manuscript does not cite any author, and thus I have designated the creator as "Anonymous."

I used an old Spanish score from the 1960s to create the MIDI file and then entered the lyrics using Vocaloid 4 and the MAIKA voice bank.  I did not use modern Spanish or Catalan pronunciation but followed the suggestion of Timothy McGee in his textbook Singing Early Music for Early Modern Spanish and Portuguese. I generated the sound of the Renaissance ensemble (recorder, lutes, citole, harp, spinet and viols) using Music Studio 2, an iPhone app.  In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, corrected some pronunciation, removed the brief rests between the 6 verses, switched the top voice to a female alto and added an ensemble of plucked instruments and viols to double the voices. I also alternated solo and chorus "performances" instead of keeping the same chorus on every verse as in the previous rendition.

Text:
Ollademe, gentil dona (Hear me, gentle Lady)
y valey por vosa fey (and I wish for your faith)
que so da casa do Rey (that I am of the house of the King) 
De menigo so criado (I am raised from youth)
No paço mas que ninguen (and eat no more than anyone)
So fidalgo aprovado (a well regarded nobleman)
da villa de Santaren (from the village of Santaren)
Ollademe sin desden (Hear me without disdain)
y valey por vosa fey (and I want your faith)
que so de casa do Rey (that I am of the house of the King)
etc.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Cristóbal de Morales: Circumdederunt me (c.1545)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Cristóbal de Morales: Circumdederunt me (c.1545)
localized.description:
Circumdederunt me

  0:06  Original motet for 5 voices
  1:55  Organ setting

This brief motet was likely intended for the funeral of an important Spanish dignitary although no specific occasion was named in the 1549 Toledo manuscript which contains the sole remaining copy of "Circumdederunt me." It may have been originally used in 1545 for the funeral of the wife of King Philip II of Spain, Maria of Portugal, but that evidence is very circumstantial.  It was definitely re-purposed and used for a memorial service in Mexico for the former Holy Roman Emperor Charles V of the Hapsburg dynasty who died a year earlier in 1558. For that grand occasion, the motet may have served as an Introit for a more formal ritual like a Requiem Mass (Missa pro defuntorum) or perhaps even used as a processional piece in a royal entourage.

In this latest rendition, I created a more legato effect, switched the upper voice from male alto to boy alto, adjusted the reverb / echo, added an organ setting (instead of a brass processional), added natural dynamics, slowed the tempo and rebalanced the voices.

Text:

Circumdederunt me gemitus mortis:
dolores inferni circumdederunt me.

Translation:

The sighs of death have surrounded me:
the pains of Hell have wrapped around me.

Description of photos:

1. Funeral procession for Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (Carlos I of Spain)
2. Cristóbal de Morales presenting a Mass to the Pope, Liber secundus Missarum
3. Sketch of an old man in thought with studies of water, Leonardo da Vinci, c1513
4. Office for the Dead (Requiem mass), Willem Vrelant, c1470
5. Choir music stand in the Cathedral of Segovia, 16th Century
6. Memorial epitaph for the Emperor Charles V, Real Sitio de San Lorenzo, El Escorial.

videos.title: [New Rendition] Johannes Ockeghem: Ma bouche rit (c.1470)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Johannes Ockeghem: Ma bouche rit (c.1470)
localized.description:
This chanson for 3 voices by Ockeghem was, in its day, one of the most popular musical compositions -- included in more than 30 illuminated manuscripts as well as in Ottaviano Petrucci's first printed volume of music (Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, 1501). Its theme is one of courtly love -- of an unattainable lady and the ceaseless yearning of a lonely man.  

In this latest rendition, I corrected some pronunciation, created a more legato effect, rebalanced the voices and inserted pauses between the verses. I also doubled the voices with plucked instruments (medieval lute, psaltery and harp). I created the MIDI file from a score and then added the text using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid.  

Text

A. Ma bouche rit et ma pensee pleure 
mon oeil s'es joie et mon cueur maudit l'eure
qu'il eust le bien qui sa sante dechasse
et le plaisir qui la mort me pourchasse
sans reconfort qui m'aide ne sequeure

B. Ha! cueur parvers, faulsaire et meisongier
dictes comment avez ousé songier
que de faulcer ce que m'avez promis.

b. Puisqu'en ce point vous vous volez vengier
Pensez bien tost de ma vie abregier
Vivre ne puis au point ou m'avez mis.

a. Vostre pitié veult donques que je meure
mais rigueur veult que vivant je demeure
ainsy meurs vif, et en vivant trespasse,
mais pour celer le mal qui ne se passe
et pour couvrir le deul ou je labeure

A. Ma bouche rit... etc.

Translation:

My mouth smiles while my mind weeps
My eye rejoices and my heart curses the day
that took the prize which captured its health
and the pleasure that becomes the death of me
without consolation to help nor comfort me.

Ha! Heart that is perverse, fake and deceiving
tell me how you have dared to imagine
to falsify that which you have promised.
Since on this point you, you want to avenge
Think quickly to shorten my life
I can't live like this.

I your compassion wills that I die
But [my] rigor wills that I stay living
so I die living, and living die
but to hide the pain that does not go away
and to cover up the sorrow I endure.

My mouth smiles ... etc.

1. Illuminated copy of "Ma bouche rit" from the Laborde Chansonnier, c1470
2. A gallant lad being lead by a lady into a secret garden of pleasure, Harley MS 4425, c1490
3. Illuminated copy of "Ma bouche rit" from the Wolfenbuettel Chansonnier, c1470
4. Lady and the Unicorn, from a series of allegorical tapestries, this one is titled Taste, c1500
5. Detail of the Lady from #4
6. Illuminated copy of "Ma bouche rit" from the Dijon Chansonnier, c1470
7. A ceremonial shield titled "You or Death"
8. Detail of the Lady from #7

10. Detail of the chevalier from #7
11. The Seven Liberal Arts, detail from The Consolation of Philosophy, illuminated by Maître de Coëtivy, c1465. Lady Philosophy (with her entourage of Muses) consoles the master Boethius who has been condemned to die and is awaiting the end. Somehow, Boethius, whose imprisonment and execution were political events in late Roman times, were incorporated into the imagination of the Medieval mind. The concepts of loss of hope for a happy life and the platonic love that dedicated an abstract noble lady were elements first described in Boethius' writings and may have been the underpinnings of courtly romance.

videos.title: Christ ist erstanden: 3 Reformation settings (c.1525)

localized.title: Christ ist erstanden: 3 Reformation settings (c.1525)
localized.description:
Christ der ist erstanden (a.k.a. Christ ist erstanden)

  0:06  Motet for 6, Ludwig Senfl (SAATTB)
  2:03  Motet for 4, Arnoldus von Bruck (4 sackbuts)
  3:52  Motet for 4, Thomas Stoltzer (STTB)

All 3 settings of this ancient German hymn were printed in one large tome by the Protestant Reformist Georg Rhau (Rhaw) in 1544.  The 6 part motet was composed by the Swiss Lutheran Ludwig Senfl who began his career as a music director at the Catholic Viennese court of Emperor Maximillian I.  The textless 4 part arrangement is by the Flemish Catholic composer von Bruck who wrote many songs in the Early High German language during the height of the Lutheran Movement. The original modal tune is quintessentially Teutonic and is neither Protestant nor Catholic in spirit.  It is a hymn hailing the resurrected Christ and was usual sung in the leadup to Holy Week. Both the melody and the lyrics can be traced as far back as the 12th Century and was translated from the Latin chant "Victimae pascali." The version by Bruck sounds similar to the Lutheran hymns of later times with its more or less homophonic structure and 6/8 rhythm (as can be heard in "Joseph lieber, Joseph mein" and "Puer natus in Bethlehem.") The more austere 4 voice motet by Stoltzer has a more "retro" quality with long melismata and imitative canons in the Franco-Flemish tradition.

All "vocal" parts were entered using the Vocaloid 4 (Yamaha's voice encoding) software and the MAIKA Spanish language voice bank. The instrumental sounds were simulated using MusicStudio2 on the iPhone.  The original MIDI file without the lyrics was compiled and uploaded by Helmut Kickton. The link can be found at CPDL.org . The MIDI for the Stoltzer setting was created by André Vierendeels (also on CPDL.org), but I adjusted the text underlay in several places for all 4 voices.

Text of the Senfl version:

Christ der ist erstanden (Christ He is risen)
Alleluia (Hallelujah)
von der Marter alle. (from all his martyrdom)
Des sollen wir alle froh sein, (We will all be glad)
Christ will unser Trost sein. (that Christ will be our comfort)
Kyrieleis. (Kyrie eleison)

Text of the Stoltzer version:

Christ ist erstanden (Christ is risen)
von der Marter alle. (from all his martyrdom)
Des sollen wir alle froh sein, (We will all be glad)
Christ will unser Trost sein. (that Christ will be our comfort)
Kyrie eleison. (Kyrie eleison)

videos.title: [New Rendition] Adrian Willaert: Cantai hor piango (1559)

localized.title: [New Rendition] Adrian Willaert: Cantai hor piango (1559)
localized.description:
Cantai hor piango for 6 voices

   0:06  Part 1. Cantai hor piango (AATTTB)
   3:11  Part 2. Tengan dunque (AATTTB)

This madrigal with its restrained emotions is somewhat suggestive of the gentle yearnings eloquently expressed in Francesco Petrarca's 14th Century sonnet of the same title. The metrical lines of Petrarch's medieval poetry were respectfully reshaped into a song of quiet passion with its steadily repeated notes, consonant harmonies, narrow pitch range and understated polyphony by the Flemish Renaissance master Adriano (Adrian) Willaert. Just as the original poem was divided into two distinct parts expressing contrasting sentiments, so too was Willaert's canzona segmented into two movements conveying differing feelings. Beneath the anguish of an unrequited, courtly love is also Petrarch's unceasing sorrow over losing his life-long Muse, Laura de Noves, to the Black Plague in 1348. In this work (as in others), Petrarch admits that the experience of unfulfilled love, albeit painful, is far better than never having known love’s pleasure at all.

In this latest rendition, I made a few corrections in pronunciation, added some dynamic variability, swapped the top alto line with a female instead of a male voice, created a more legato effect and adjusted the reverb slightly. I used the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid to simulate medieval Italian phonemes.

Text:

Cantai, or piango, et non men di dolcezza
del pianger prendo che del canto presi,
ch’a la cagion, non a l’effetto, intesi
son i miei sensi vaghi pur d’altezza.
Indi e mansuetudine et durezza
et atti feri, et humili et cortesi,
porto egualmente, né me gravan pesi,
né l’arme mie punta di sdegni spezza.

Tengan dunque ver’ me l’usato stile
Amor, madonna, il mondo et mia fortuna,
ch’ i’ non penso esser mai se non felice.
Viva o mora o languisca, un piú gentile
stato del mio non è sotto la luna,
sí dolce è del mio amaro la radice.

Translation:

I sang, now I weep, and there is no lesser
sweetness in weeping than in singing,
because the cause and not the effect,
is in my senses, eager for my Lady.
Thus there is gentleness and harshness,
cruel or humble or courteous acts,
equally, I carry without being weighed down.
The sharp indignities of Love’s weapon does not break me.

Take me then in the usual manner.
Love, my lady, the world and my fortune.
I will never think that I am not happy.
Alive, or dead, or languishing, there’s no better
state than this under the moon.
So sweet is the root of my bitterness.

videos.title: Tielman Susato: Pavane "la Bataille" (1551)

localized.title: Tielman Susato: Pavane "la Bataille" (1551)
localized.description:
Tielman Susato (c.1510-c.1570) was a publisher, composer and instrumentalist of German origin who established his musical career in Flemish Antwerp.  He printed musical masterpieces by some of the most immortalized French and Franco-Flemish composers of his generation.

Many of the 57 pieces in the "Danserye" collection are homophonic arrangements of Flemish folk songs or French chansons from 1530 and earlier. They range in mood from the plaintive melancholy of the "Pass et medio" to the rough-and-ready grandiosity of the "Pavane La Bataille."  The "la Bataille" (sometimes referred to as "la Guerre") theme was adapted countless times throughout the first half of the 16th Century. There are at least 4 instrumental arrangements for band (Attaingnant, Susato, Moderne, Phal​è​se and Gervaise) as well as a playful chanson by Janequin (which may have been the progenitor for all the other variants) and a theatrical ensalada by Mateo Flecha. One can imagine a royal entourage preceded by brass and percussion instruments.

The MIDI files that were used to create this video can be found on the website abcnotation.com. The original files were uploaded by Frank Nordberg to the website musicaviva.com (which no longer exists). The instrumental sounds of cornettino (playing one octave above the original notation), shawm, 3 sackbuts and tympani were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.

5. Sackbut player from "Gallery musicians," Anon. German, Nuremburg, c1530

videos.title: [New Rendition] Heinrich Isaac: Ne piu bella di queste (c.1490), anthem for the city of Florence

localized.title: [New Rendition] Heinrich Isaac: Ne piu bella di queste (c.1490), anthem for the city of Florence
localized.description:
Ne piu bella di queste

This anthem with its four verses was likely written for an outdoors performance at one of the annual Florentine carnevali during the later years of Lorenzo il Magnifico, patron of the arts.  It was composed by the great master from the Netherlands, Heinrich Isaac, who had adopted Florence as his primary residence in his final years and may have been a choir director at the central cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore (Il Duomo di Firenze). This patriotic song invokes the Roman goddesses, Juno, Minerva and Venus as inspirations for the sophistication, influence, intellect, beauty and artistry of the city of Florence, arguably the birthplace of the Italian Renaissance. One can hear the alternating 2/2 and 3/2 rhythms as if invoking a march and then a basse dance.

The Italian text was entered using the Maika Spanish language Vocaloid; the instrumental sounds of shawms, sackbuts and Renaissance percussion were generated using the iPhone app Music Studio 2.  The original MIDI file was created by Alpert Ulrich and can be found on CPDL.org. In this latest rendition, I corrected some vowel sounds, created a more legato effect, added some natural dynamics, added percussion in the background, adjusted the reverb / echo effects and fixed some of the text underlay.

Text (Translation)

1 Ne più bella di queste, ne più degnia, (No greater beauty than these, no greater respect)
Si truova alcuna idea, 
Iunon vedete che nel ciel su regnia. (See Juno who in heaven reigns)
Vedete Citherea, (See Citherea)
Madre dolze d'Amore, (Sweet mother of Love)
Vedete qui Minerva, (See here Minerva)
Che gli ingegni conserva, (who cherishes intelligence)
El Martial furore, (And warlike fury)
Domma coll' Arete et colla Sapienza,  (tames with virtue and wisdom)
Venuti insieme ad abitar Fiorenza. (Come together to live in Florence)

2  Fiorenza, tu sarai la più famosa (Florence, you shall be the most famous)
Cipta che vegha el sole, (city under the sun)
Di lor presenza sarai gloriosa. (in their presence you shall be glorious)
Iunon tuo stato vuole (Juno your state wants)
Crescere et in concordia (to grow and in harmony)
Tener donne et mariti (to keep the ladies and the gentlemen)
E ciptadini uniti (as citizens united)
Terra sanza discordia, (land without discord)
Fara el popol fruire fuor d'ogni usanza (you make the people prosper with all your traditions)
Sano et gagliardo et sempre in abbondanza. (healthy and vigorous and always in abundance)

3  Minerva saggia ci dara vittoria (Wise Minerva shall give it victory)
Contro animici in guerra, (against her enemies in war)
Fara ti trionphar con somma gloria (to triumph in full glory)
Et per mare et per terra (by sea and by land)
In tutte le buone arte (in all the good arts)
O di mano o d'ingegnio. (or by hand or ingenuity)
Sola passera el segnio (alone shall pass the mark)
Felice in ogni parte, (happy in all parts)
Tochando el cielo colla superba chioma, (touching the sky with its superb mane)
Fiorenza, bella figluola di Roma. (Florence beautiful daughter of Rome)

4  Ma Vener bella sempre in canti e'n feste, (But Venus dances always in song and feast)
In balli e'n noze et mostre, (in dances and weddings and shows)
In varie foggie et nuove sopraveste, (in various shapes and new uniform)
In torniamenti et giostre (in tournaments and jousts)
Fara galante et belle (and shall be gallant and comely)
Tutte donne et donzelle. (all the ladies and girls)
Con amorosa vista, (with amorous looks)
(Con amorosa vista)
Terra sempre Fiorenza in canto et riso (The land of Florence is always in song and laughter)
Et dirassi Fiorenza el paradiso. (and I shall say that Florence is paradise)

videos.title: Pierre Attaingnant: 5 Basses Dances (c.1530)

localized.title: Pierre Attaingnant: 5 Basses Dances (c.1530)
localized.description:
Five Basses Dances:

 0:06   Basse dance #9 "la Brosse" (published in 1530)
            (recorder, 2 shawms, tenor viol, bass sackbut, drum, tambourine)
 2:14   Basse dance #8 (1530)
            (4 viols, lute, harp)
 3:17   Basse dance #6 "la Magdalena" & Tourdion (1530)
            (recorder, dulcimer, harp, bass viol, drum, tambourine)
 5:42   Basse dance #3 (1530)
            (4 viols, drum)
 7:03   Basse dance #1 (1547)
            (cornetto, 3 sackbuts, drum)

Pierre Attaingnant, was the most prolific archivist, arranger and editor of secular and sacred music in the first half of the Sixteenth Century.  He is remembered by musicologists and early music enthusiasts around the world as the "imprimateur par excellence" (the most excellent printer") of French music of the High Renaissance.  Around 1528, the French King François I granted him a license to print music on a grander scale than ever before anywhere in Europe. And to this end, Attaingnant employed a new system of movable type that improved on technologies that the Venetian printer Ottaviano Petrucci had devised a generation earlier.   

The basse dance (la bassadanza in Italian) was a popular European courtly pastime in the late 15th century and early 16th centuries. It roughly translates to a "low dance" and implies less jumping and fewer elaborate flourishes. Mostly written in 6/4 or 3/2 rhythm, it often stood alone as a dance form (as can be attested in Margaret of Austria's exclusive collection of basse dance tunes with their respective moves). At other times, the basse dance was followed by a tourdion. Many of the basse dance melodies were based on popular French and Italian songs.

++++++++++ 

Thomas Morley's First Booke of Consort Lessons featured instrumental arrangements of songs and dances by the pre-eminent masters of English Renaissance music in the age of Elizabeth I: William Byrd, John Dowland, Richard Allison and others. The so-called broken consort consisted of 6 instrumental members: treble viol (or violin), transverse tenor flute (or recorder), lute, bandora, cittern and bass viol. Arrangements could also be made for cornetts and sackbuts or for viol consort. The melody line of "Captain Pipers Galliard" is recognizable as a well known Dowland lute song "Can she excuse."

In this electronic rendition, I used MusicStudio2 to emulate the sounds of Renaissance chamber instruments.  I used pdfs created by Steve Hendricks on the website sca.uwaterloo.ca and converted those files to MIDI. I also took the liberty to create a version of M.'s Almaine for Renaissance brass instruments and Oxenford's Maske for recorder solo based on the embellished lute part. In this latest rendition, I chose a different set of pieces and combination of instruments. I also used a different reverb setting and articulation scheme.

videos.title: Josef Mons: Fuga from Canzon Quarta (c.2009)

localized.title: Josef Mons: Fuga from Canzon Quarta (c.2009)
localized.description:
This short piece is another work by the contemporary composer Josef Mons whose style is often suggestive of the Italian Mannerist School of the early 17th Century. This third and final movement, a fugue, from Mons' Canzon 4 is unusual for its 5/4 rhythm which, at times, sounds like a different rhythm depending on which notes the performers start their playing. The free-style imitative passages are reminiscent of the melismatic phrases and independent part-writing of the Franco-Flemish masters from the late 15th and early 16th centuries (e.g. La Spagna variations). Unlike some of the other more chromatic works by Josef Mons, this piece has a mostly modal quality (with only a couple of ficta at the cadences).

The MIDI file was compiled by the composer himself, and I used the iPhone app Music Studio 2 to simulate the sounds of a cornetto, tenor viol, tenor sackbut and a chamber harp (doubling the sackbut). I added a bit of reverb and echo using Audacity. In real life, the piece (along with the other 2 movements) was premiered in Dortmund in 2010 by Mons’ trio ensemble in a church using two recorders and a viola.

5. Tenor sackbut, Grinnell College collection, 17th century

videos.title: Heinrich Isaac: Sanctus from "Missa Wohlauff Gsell von hinnen" a 6 (c.1496)

localized.title: Heinrich Isaac: Sanctus from "Missa Wohlauff Gsell von hinnen" a 6 (c.1496)
localized.description:
Sanctus a 6 from "Missa Wohlauff Gesell von hinnen"

  0:06  Sanctus (SAATTB)
  1:40  Pleni sunt (SATB)
  3:01  Osanna in excelsis (SAATTB)
  4:24  Benedictus (SAT)
  6:20  Qui venit (SAT)
  7:42  Osanna in excelsis (SAATTB)

Heinrich Isaac was employed simultaneously by two of the most prominent European patrons of music and the arts in the late 15th and early 16th centuries: Lorenzo de' Medici in Florence and Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I in Vienna. Although Isaac likely parodied Josquin's French language chanson "Comment peult avoir," the mass is remembered as the "Missa Wohlauff Gesell" because Isaac dedicated the mass cycle to Emperor Maximilian and a Viennese audience which likely knew the tune by its original German title. Isaac's Benedictus section is structurally and stylistically most similar to Josquin's chanson. The only remaining copy of the complete mass is preserved in a Bavarian chansonnier. Isaac had earlier composed a similar, albeit less well developed, parody mass based on the same melody but for 4 voices instead of 6. This complex masterpiece, although written for 6 distinct voice sections, alternates between 3, 4 and 6 voices within each mass movement. I doubled the voices with a pipe organ in this soundtrack based on the iconography of Maximilian's court artist who depicted an organist accompanying the church chorus (see time mark 1:40).

The vocal simulation was created using the MAIKA Spanish language Vocaloid and the pipe organ sound doubling the voices was added with the iPhone app Music Studio 2.0. I shifted the pitch up a half step in all 6 voice parts to approximate an A=466Hz. The original MIDI file was compiled and uploaded to CPDL.org by John Hetland, but I made extensive changes to the text underlay. I also restored the original pitch range by shifting down a minor 4th.

2. Interior of the Duomo, Santa Maria del Fiore, where Isaac was likely employed as music director and composer at the time of the writing of the mass.
3. Singing choristers, Cantoria, Santa Maria del Fiore, Luca della Robbia, c1438; it situated near the organ loft where Isaac likely directed his choir.
4. Emperor Maximilian I at Mass, Hans Weiditz, c1515; note the chorus on the right side with a full complement of singers and a bellows organ at the left side of the panel.
5. Innsbruck, Austria, Maximilian's home base.
6. The crowned Emperor Maximilian I, Bernhard Strigel, c1507
